title: UniLatent: Cross-Embodiment Transfer via Latent Observation Alignment
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026
summary: Robot datasets are costly to collect and are usually tied to a specific embodiment, making it difficult to reuse demonstrations across robots with different geometry, appearance, and kinematics. We introduce UniLatent, a cross-embodiment transfer framework that reduces the embodiment-induced observation gap in a shared latent space. UniLatent renders paired source-target robot observations in simulation and aligns a source visual encoder to a frozen target encoder. A policy trained on encoded source demonstrations can then run directly on target observations, with no pixel-level image translation. Across three simulation tasks and two target robot arms, UniLatent reaches up to 93% zero-shot success, exceeding the strongest pixel-translation baseline by over 30 points on average. In real-world xArm-to-Franka transfer, fine-tuning with only 10 target demonstrations per task yields 27/30 successful rollouts. Code, videos and data are available at https://selina2023.github.io/unilatent/.
full_text: Robot datasets are costly to collect and are usually tied to a specific embodiment, making it difficult to reuse demonstrations across robots with different geometry, appearance, and kinematics. We introduce , a cross-embodiment transfer framework that reduces the embodiment-induced observation gap in a shared latent space. renders paired source--target robot observations in simulation and aligns a source visual encoder to a frozen target encoder. A policy trained on encoded source demonstrations can then run directly on target observations, with no pixel-level image translation. Across three simulation tasks and two target robot arms, UniLatent reaches up to 93 zero-shot success, exceeding the strongest pixel-translation baseline by over 30 points on average. In real-world xArm-to-Franka transfer, fine-tuning with only 10 target demonstrations per task yields 27/30 successful rollouts. Code, videos and data are available at . Introduction Large-scale and diverse data is a key driver of recent progress in robot learning~ FMs_robotics_2023_survey_1,FMs_robotics_2023_survey_2,zhong2025surveyVLA , and recent efforts have produced sizable manipulation datasets~ open_x_embodiment_rt_x_2023,khazatsky2024droid,bu2025agibot_iros . However, existing robot data is highly imbalanced across embodiments, which concentrates on a small set of popular arms and grippers, while many other platforms remain underrepresented. Meanwhile, collecting real-world data is often costly and embodiment-specific, since demonstrations largely depend on the robots' morphology, end-effector geometry, reachable workspace, appearance, and kinematics. As robot hardware continues to diversify and advance, recollecting the same task for every new embodiment does not scale. This motivates methods that reuse source-robot demonstrations and allow policies to transfer to unseen robots with little or no target data. A key challenge in cross-embodiment transfer is the embodiment-induced visual gap. In many existing datasets with third-person camera views, the robot often occupies a large portion of the image, and changing the arm or gripper alters not only appearance but also self-occlusion, contact geometry, and the visibility of task-relevant objects, which causes noticeable performance degradation when deploying a vision-based policy on a new robot~ chen2024mirage,chen2024roviaug . Prior work addresses this gap by editing source demonstration frames through masking~ lepert2024shadow , inpainting~ chen2024mirage , or diffusion-based generation~ chen2024roviaug to match the target visual domain. While intuitive, pixel-space translation can introduce errors in segmentation, robot geometry, and contact regions, creating systematic discrepancies from true target observations. Moreover, translated frames can create a synthetic visual domain that differs from real target observations, causing policies to overfit to translation artifacts and limiting their ability to generalize across tasks and viewpoints. We introduce UniLatent, which reduces the embodiment-induced observation gap in latent space rather than pixel space (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). In simulation, we render large-scale paired observations in which source and target robots reach matched end-effector poses under the same camera and randomized scenes. These pairs train a source encoder to map each source image into the latent space of a frozen, pretrained target encoder, so that matched poses on the two robots receive the same representation. A policy trained on encoded source demonstrations is then deployed on the target robot by encoding its observations with the same frozen target encoder, with no image synthesis at test time. Our contributions are two-fold. (i) Paired rendering and observation alignment. We introduce a simulation-based pipeline that generates large-scale paired observations of different robots at matched end-effector poses and uses them to align visual encoders across embodiments. (ii) Latent-space policy learning. We train flow-matching policies on source demonstrations encoded in the aligned latent space, enabling zero-shot transfer to unseen target embodiments in simulation and data-efficient few-shot transfer in the real world. In simulation, raises mean target success from 44.5 with the strongest pixel-translation baseline to 76.0 ; in the real world, it completes 27/30 rollouts versus 23/30 for RoVi-Aug pretraining and 11/30 for target-only training. Related Work Visual adaptation in robotics. Vision-based policies are brittle under visual shifts caused by lighting, texture, backgrounds, and viewpoints. Domain randomization broadens the training distribution by varying rendering factors in simulation~ tobin2017domainrandomization , while sim-to-real methods learn mappings between visual domains~ james2019sim,ho2021retinagan,rao2020rl . Recent data augmentation methods further use photometric, semantic, or generative edits on real robot data to improve robustness~ bharadhwaj2024roboagent,yu2023scaling,tian2024vista,chen2024semanticallycontrollable,yuan2025roboengineplugandplayrobotdata . These approaches are effective for appearance and viewpoint changes, but most assume that the robot embodiment is fixed. In our setting, the robot itself changes, so the visual shift is tied to kinematics, gripper shape, self-occlusion, and contact cues. Policy learning across embodiments. Robot-generalist policies train across many robots or condition on embodiment descriptors~ black2025pi0,octomodelteam2024,intelligence2025pi05,chen2018hardwareconditioned . Other work studies shared action abstractions, universal actions, or large multi-embodiment datasets~ yang2024pushinglimits,doshi2024scalingcrossembodied,salhotra2023actionmismatch,zheng2025universalactions . These methods are promising when broad real-robot coverage is available, but such coverage is expensive and uneven across platforms. targets a complementary regime: given demonstrations from a source robot and a desired target robot, we learn a target-consistent observation space from simulation-rendered pairs and reuse the source data without requiring a large multi-robot dataset. Cross-embodiment transfer. A related line studies cross-embodiment imitation from third-person or human video prompts, including skill discovery from human and robot videos~ xu2023xskillcrossembodimentskill , imitation under mismatched execution~ kedia2025oneshotimitationmismatchedexecution , and video-conditioned policy learning~ jain2024vid2robotendtoendvideoconditionedpolicy . Human-to-robot and human-to-humanoid transfer bridges an even larger embodiment gap, using egocentric human video~ kareer2025egomimic,kareer2025emergencehumanrobottransfer , human-video editing~ lepert2025phantom , whole-body shadowing~ fu2024humanplus , or sim-to-real RL from a human demonstration~ lum2025crossinghumanrobotembodimentgap . These works are complementary to our setting: they interpret human or video demonstrations as task specifications or retarget human motion, whereas we study robot-to-robot reuse of source demonstrations for a specified target embodiment. More recent methods reduce embodiment shift by modifying images. Mirage cross-paints robot pixels~ chen2024mirage ; RoVi-Aug synthesizes robot and viewpoint augmentations~ chen2024roviaug ; and Shadow masks robot regions to avoid robot-specific appearance~ lepert2024shadow . While these methods can improve over direct transfer, pixel editing can discard gripper or contact information or introduce geometry that is inconsistent with the real target observation. instead aligns encoders and acts in latent space. This removes the need for test-time image translation and lets the target observation encoder define the representation used by the deployed policy. Cross-embodiment and domain-invariant representation learning has also explored alignment objectives in different settings, , inverse RL~ zakka2021xirl , time-contrastive video representations~ sermanet2018tcn , and adversarial sim-to-real alignment~ tanwani2020dirl . Closest to ours, Wang et al.~ wang2024crossembodiment align an adapted-domain latent space to a frozen anchor domain without pixel translation, using unpaired adversarial and cycle-consistency objectives. instead constructs explicit correspondence by rendering both robots at matched TCP poses, which reduces alignment to supervised feature regression onto a frozen pretrained target encoder. Problem Statement sec:prob_stmt We study robot-to-robot cross-embodiment imitation, where demonstrations collected on a source robot are used to learn a policy for a different target robot with minimal or no target-robot demonstrations. Each robot observes the task through RGB images and executes actions through a shared Cartesian end-effector interface. In our setting, the robots are single-arm manipulators with parallel-jaw grippers, but they may differ in geometry, kinematics, gripper appearance, self-occlusion, and robot-object contact cues. We assume access to source demonstrations , where each trajectory is collected on under a fixed third-person camera. The goal is to learn a target policy that solves the same task on . We further assume access to kinematic and visual models of both robots ( , URDF or USD assets) in a simulator with inverse kinematics. These models provide paired observations for visual alignment, without requiring target demonstrations or task-success supervision on the target robot. Source demonstrations need not be collected for alignment; alignment consumes only robot models, inverse kinematics, and rendering. Method: sec:method Given source demonstrations collected on , learns a latent-space policy that transfers to with few or no target demonstrations. The pipeline has four stages (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). We first (i) render paired source--target observations in simulation (Sec.~ rendering ) and (ii) align a source encoder to a frozen target encoder (Sec.~ alignment ). We then (iii) train a latent policy on encoded source demonstrations and (iv) deploy it on through the target encoder (Sec.~ policy ). Paired Image Generation rendering We sample manipulation-relevant end-effector poses within the robots' reachable workspace, solve inverse kinematics for both embodiments, and render both robots from the same camera under the same randomized scene. The source and target images in each pair share the same task-relevant pose but differ in robot geometry and appearance. This produces paired RGB images in IsaacLab/RoboVerse~ mittal2025isaaclab,geng2025roboverse (Fig.~ fig:paired_img_gen ). The pose generator combines broad workspace sampling with a manipulation prior so that rendered pairs emphasize poses that can occur in demonstrations and avoid unreachable or visually uninformative configurations. We match poses at the tool-center point (TCP), defined as the midpoint between the parallel-jaw fingertips, apply robot-specific TCP offsets, and retain only samples for which inverse kinematics succeeds for both embodiments. Domain randomization varies backgrounds, lighting, object assets, distractors, and small camera perturbations while preserving pairwise action correspondence. These choices make the supervision robust to appearance changes without requiring the renderer to synthesize photorealistic target demonstrations. Our generic pairs (about 100k) use this broad randomized sampling, with roughly 20 of poses drawn from ManiSkill, LIBERO, RLBench, and RoboSuite trajectories that share no tasks with our evaluation suite. Optional task-specific pairs (about 10k) additionally use the evaluation task's object assets and poses. Observation Alignment alignment We instantiate a source encoder and target encoder from DINOv2-base~ oquab2024dinov2learningrobustvisual . title: BATCH: Behavior Alignment for Cross-Embodiment Learning from Humans
comment: Project website: https://batch-embodiment.github.io/
summary: Human demonstrations provide a scalable source of diverse manipulation data, but leveraging them for robot learning remains challenging due to differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action spaces, and temporal structure. We introduce BATCH, a cross-embodiment learning framework that explicitly aligns human and robot behaviors. BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to establish cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. We further introduce two complementary training objectives that leverage these correspondences within an autoregressive videoaction diffusion model: behavior-aligned co-training and human-to-robot style transfer. On real-world manipulation tasks, BATCH improves generalization to unseen task configurations compared with training on unaligned data and prior cross-embodiment baselines, with additional gains from the style-transfer objective. Our results demonstrate that explicit behavior alignment enables more effective transfer from human demonstrations to robot policies.
full_text: Human demonstrations provide a scalable source of diverse manipulation data, but leveraging them for robot learning remains challenging due to differences in embodiment, viewpoint, action spaces, and temporal structure. We introduce BATCH, a cross-embodiment learning framework that explicitly aligns human and robot behaviors. BATCH learns self-supervised temporal representations with a cycle-consistency objective to establish cross-embodiment correspondences without manual annotation. We further introduce two complementary training objectives that leverage these correspondences within an autoregressive video-action diffusion model: behavior-aligned co-training and human-to-robot style transfer. On real-world manipulation tasks, BATCH improves generalization to unseen task configurations compared with training on unaligned data and prior cross-embodiment baselines, with additional gains from the style-transfer objective. Our results demonstrate that explicit behavior alignment enables more effective transfer from human demonstrations to robot policies. 4pt Introduction colback=gray!8, colframe=gray!45, boxrule=0.5pt, arc=2pt, left=6pt, right=6pt, top=5pt, bottom=5pt, title=Questions, coltitle=black, fonttitle= , Human demonstrations offer a scalable way to expand the scene and behavior diversity of robot datasets. In particular, wearable egocentric sensing devices, such as smart glasses~ engel2023project , provide a lightweight and portable solution for capturing natural human manipulation across diverse environments, while on-device SLAM cameras enable accurate hand-pose tracking. Despite this promise, directly leveraging human demonstrations for robot learning remains challenging due to the substantial embodiment gap between humans and robots, including both visual appearances and physical motions. Prior studies have shown that directly co-training on cross-embodiment data can improve visual robustness and policy generalization to unseen backgrounds and objects~ kareer2025egomimic, yang2026data . Yet cross-embodiment data is not simply additional data from a different visual domain: even when performing the same task, humans and robots can differ substantially in execution speed, temporal structure, action spaces, and visual observations due to differences in embodiment. Human demonstrations may also contain irrelevant segments that have no corresponding robot behavior. As a result, naively scaling human demonstrations does not necessarily provide useful supervision for robot behavior. Instead, models can separate the two embodiments and rely on embodiment-specific cues, limiting the extent to which human experience transfers to robot control. Empirically, this can lead to diminishing gains or even negative transfer as more poorly matched human data is incorporated~ wei2025empirical, punamiya2026egoverse . We therefore hypothesize that effective cross-embodiment transfer requires explicitly establishing behavioral correspondences between human and robot trajectories, providing a learning signal for identifying task-relevant structure that should transfer while discounting embodiment-specific variation. We define behavior alignment as establishing temporal frame-level correspondences between equivalent phases of task execution across embodiments, based on task-relevant states and interactions rather than embodiment-specific appearance, viewpoint, or action representation. The key challenge is to discover these correspondences automatically, without requiring manually annotated phase labels or frame-level matches between human and robot trajectories. Achieving this requires features that capture behavioral progression over time while suppressing embodiment-specific variation. Prior non-learning approaches commonly apply dynamic time warping (DTW) over actions or static visual features, which can be unreliable under large embodiment gaps or when visual states are ambiguous. Instead, we learn self-supervised features with a temporal cycle-consistency objective~ dwibedi2019temporal, donahue2024gtcc , where each frame representation incorporates information from multiple neighboring frames to capture behavioral progression rather than relying on a single observation. We then apply subsequence DTW in this learned feature space to retrieve temporally corresponding human and robot segments, accommodating differences in execution speed and unmatched segments. -1 Another key contribution of our approach is how we leverage the aligned trajectories for cross-embodiment learning. We instantiate our method within an autoregressive video-action diffusion model~ ye2026world pretrained on in domain robot demonstrations, and finetune with two complementary objectives over aligned human and robot trajectories. A behavior-aligned co-training objective learns visual dynamics and motions from both embodiments, while a cross-embodiment style-transfer objective translates human observations into temporally corresponding robot-domain videos. Together, these objectives learn from both embodiments while explicitly coupling them under matched behavior, enabling more effective transfer from diverse human demonstrations to robot policies. We evaluate our approach on two manipulation tasks from EgoVerse~ punamiya2026egoverse : single-arm Object in Container, which requires continuous execution, and bimanual Cup on Saucer, which requires precise grasping and bimanual coordination. We consider out-of-domain test scenarios presented in the human demonstrations but absent from the robot training data. Across the two tasks, our approach improves out-of-domain policy performance by an average of 45 over co-training alone and 138 over the robot-only pretrained model. Removing behavior alignment substantially degrades performance, highlighting the importance of reliable human-robot correspondences, while the style-transfer objective provides further gains with aligned pairs. These results demonstrate that both establishing behavioral correspondences and effectively leveraging them are critical for cross-embodiment transfer. Related Work related_work Video Temporal Alignment. Video temporal alignment establishes frame-level correspondences across videos of similar behaviors despite variations in embodiment, viewpoint, and appearance. One foundational class of approaches is Temporal Cycle-Consistency (TCC)~ dwibedi2019temporal,hadji2021representation , which learns a shared embedding space from unaligned videos without manual labels by enforcing cycle-consistent nearest-neighbor matches. GTCC~ donahue2024gtcc further improves the robustness of TCC through multi-neighbor, multi-cycle matching modeled with Gaussian mixtures. In robotics, TCC-style representations have been used to derive dense task-progress rewards for cross-embodiment learning~ zakka2022xirl . Separately, Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) is a common technique used to align cross-embodiment demonstrations with different execution speeds~ punamiya2025egobridge,liu2025immimic,yang2026data . Our approach combines GTCC and DTW: GTCC learns cross-video correspondences in a shared embedding space, while DTW produces globally consistent temporal alignments across human and robot demonstrations while accounting for different execution speeds. Cross-Embodiment Learning from Human Data. Human demonstrations provide scalable manipulation data with greater scene and behavior diversity than costly robot demonstrations, but effective transfer remains challenging due to embodiment gap. Prior attempts include learning shared skill representations~ xu2023xskill,pmlr-v305-kim25d , using transferable intermediate representations such as object flow~ pmlr-v270-xu25a , or editing human videos into robotized demonstrations~ lepert2025masquerade, lepert2025phantom, wang2026ego2robot . However, these approaches can be limited in scalability with additional processing and tuning. More recent approaches directly co-train on human and robot data~ kareer2025egomimic,qiu2025humanoid,yuan2025motiontrans,tao2025dexwild,zhu2026emma,punamiya2026egoverse , with follow-up works seeking to improve cross-embodiment transfer through observation alignment~ punamiya2025egobridge , embodiment-agnostic visual prediction~ li2026egowam , or image- and action-space alignment~ li2026matters . Our work studies whether temporal behavior alignment between human and robot trajectories can further support cross-embodiment transfer while integrating naturally into existing co-training formulation. Video Action Models jointly model future visual observations and robot actions, providing richer supervision by learning scene dynamics alongside robot control. Early methods such as GR-1 and GR-2 combine visual generation with action prediction~ wu2024unleashing,cheang2024gr . More recent approaches, including UVA~ li2025uva , UWM~ zhu2025uwm , and VideoVLA~ shen2025videovla , more tightly couple video and action modeling, while Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmospolicy , DreamZero~ ye2026world , LingBot-VA~ li2026lingbot , and LingBot-VA 2.0~ zhang2026lingbotva2 scale this paradigm with large video backbones and video-action pretraining. Our work builds on this paradigm to study cross-embodiment policy learning from behaviorally aligned human and robot trajectories. Method sec:method Cross-Embodiment Behavior Alignment subsec:behavior-alignment -1 We consider human and robot demonstrations of the same manipulation task. Following EgoVerse~ punamiya2026egoverse , human demonstrations are collected using Aria glasses, while robot demonstrations are collected through teleoperation (see Appendix~ for data collection details). Despite sharing the same task objective, the two datasets can differ substantially in embodiment, background, viewpoint, and execution speed, making direct frame-level matching unreliable. We therefore seek a representation that is robust to these cross-embodiment differences while preserving temporal task progress. Starting from pre-extracted image features, we learn a shared temporal embedding space using the self-supervised cycle-consistency objective of donahue2024gtcc , encouraging human and robot frames at corresponding stages of task execution to be close in the learned space. These correspondences are characterized by similar object states and interactions rather than visual appearance alone. To further account for differences in execution speed, we recover explicit frame-level correspondences using subsequence dynamic time warping (DTW), which finds the minimum-cost alignment in the learned embedding space while allowing non-uniform temporal warping. For a robot query segment \(X^ \) of length \(N\) and a human target segment \(X^ \) of length \(M\), we denote the corresponding embeddings as \( _ 1:N =f_ (X^ )\) and \( _ 1:M =f_ (X^ )\), respectively. Feature extraction. We extract per-frame feature maps of shape \(1024 14 14\) using a frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 encoder he2016deep . For each frame \(t\), features from the causal temporal window \([t-k+1,t]\) of length \(k\) are stacked and processed by two sequential 3D convolutional layers. The resulting representation is max-pooled over space and time and projected by a three-layer MLP to a 128-dimensional embedding. Multimodal soft nearest neighbors. title: A four-view smartphone video dataset of a robot-held flexible strip, with camera poses and a 3D LaGSplat baseline
comment: 2 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Dataset and checkpoints: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23601189. Training code: https://github.com/LouenPottier/lagsplat-mpov. Interactive demo: https://louenpottier.github.io/xrdays.html
summary: This note describes a multi-view video dataset of a deformable object driven by a measured input, with the measured pose of every camera, and a first 3D result obtained on it with LaGSplat. LaGSplat learns from video a low-dimensional latent state that is both the generalized coordinate of a learned dissipative Lagrangian and the conditioning variable of a Gaussian Splatting decoder; fitting the decoder in 3D calls for synchronized multi-view footage, which the original paper only had from synthetic renderings. Here a robot arm moves a flexible strip by oscillating along a one-dimensional path, and four iPhones, three fixed and one handheld, film it for ten minutes. The videos are synchronized, the cameras are posed from the scene, and the position of the gripper is given per frame as the input of the system. LaGSplat fitted on this data with the gripper acceleration as a forcing term renders held-out views at 26 to 33 dB PSNR and runs as a real-time interactive demo in a web browser. Dataset, checkpoints and training code are public.
full_text: This note describes a multi-view video dataset of a deformable object driven by a measured input, with the measured pose of every camera, and a first 3D result obtained on it with LaGSplat~ pottier2026lagsplat . Please cite this note when using the dataset. LaGSplat learns, from video, a low-dimensional latent state that plays two roles at once: it is the generalized coordinate of a learned dissipative Lagrangian, and the conditioning variable of a Gaussian Splatting decoder whose primitives are explicit points that move with the object. A force applied on the reconstructed object then enters the equations of motion as the generalized force , with . Fitting the decoder in 3D calls for synchronized multi-view footage. In~ pottier2026lagsplat , the 3D experiments use synthetic views rendered by SHARP; this dataset and the results below are not part of it. Setup. A robot arm holds a flexible strip, about 23\,cm long, in a gripper. The end effector moves by jerks along a nearly one-dimensional horizontal path; after each jerk the strip oscillates freely and its motion decays. Four iPhones film the scene at and \,fps. Three of them (iphone0, iphone1, iphone2) are fixed and mounted rigidly to one another; iphone0 is a different model from the other three. The fourth, iphone3, is handheld and moves around the scene for the first seven minutes, then is held nearly still. In a separate session, with every object in the room still, robot included, iphone3 filmed the same room in two clips, which give a static reconstruction of the room (Fig.~ fig:views ). Synchronization. The coarse offsets come from a clap and from the motion of the arm, whose jerks form an irregular, hence unambiguous, sequence of instants. The clock rates, read on the container timestamps, are not equal: over the recording, iphone0 drifts by frames with respect to the three others. All four videos are therefore resampled on the clock of iphone1: frame of every video shows the same instant, taken as the nearest source frame, with a residual of at most half a frame (8\,ms). Each video has frames ( \,s). Camera geometry. No calibration target was filmed; all poses come from the scene. The world frame is the camera frame of iphone0 (OpenCV convention), and the unit of length is the distance between iphone0 and iphone1 (about \,m). 0pt Fixed cameras: focal lengths, radial distortion and poses are solved by a joint bundle adjustment on manually clicked correspondences. To check the result, points are triangulated from iphone0 and iphone1 only, then projected into iphone2: they fall to \,px from where they appear in its image. Handheld camera: one pose per frame, by PnP against a SIFT map built from iphone3's own frames. Poses with too few inliers or with non-physical jumps are removed: of the frames have a pose. Static clips: structure from motion with COLMAP on key frames, aligned to the world frame by a similarity. A block of poses had been placed on the wrong side of a nearly symmetric cabinet; these are corrected and flagged. State and zones. The motion of the arm has a single parameter. The file state.csv gives it per frame as , the arc length of the gripper along its path, tracked in iphone1; it is the measured input of the system. The same file gives the latent state of the strip, as encoded by the baseline below, for reference. The file zones.json gives two oriented boxes in the world frame (Fig.~ fig:views ): the zone contains the strip, the zone the moving part of the arm. Baseline. We fit LaGSplat in 3D on this dataset, with three changes to~ pottier2026lagsplat . (i) The arm is an input: the decoder is conditioned on and the dynamics is , with constant mass and dissipation and an invex potential , which has a single minimum. The acceleration of the gripper enters as a forcing term, in the same way as the pressure forcing of~ pottier2026lagsplat . (ii) The affine decoder is replaced by a shared deformation network that outputs the displacement, scale, rotation and colour of each Gaussian. is no longer constant and is computed at the current state; the force transport is unchanged, since it needs explicit moving primitives, not a linear decoder. (iii) The background is a static reconstruction of the room from the static clips; only the Gaussians in the zone depend on , those in the zone on alone. The model has about Gaussians, and the camera poses are refined during training. On the last \,s, held out, the rendered images (960\,px) reach a PSNR of to \,dB for the fixed cameras and \,dB for the handheld one; restricted to the projection of the zone , which contains the strip, to \,dB and \,dB. Held-out images of the static scene reach \,dB, after a gain and bias per colour channel. For the dynamics, rollouts are started from the measured state on the held-out part; their RMS error, divided by the standard deviation of , is over \,s and over \,s. The model runs as a real-time 3D demo in a web browser, in which the strip responds to forces applied with the mouse: . Limitations. The calibration error is a few pixels, not sub-pixel, and some poses of iphone3 are wrong during the handheld part. is read in one view, in pixels. title: How Many Demonstrations Does a VLA Need? On the Sample Efficiency of VLA Finetuning
comment: 16 pages, 10 figures, CoRL Workshop
summary: Pretrained vision language action (VLA) models show strong zero-shot performance, but are rarely deployed directly and are often first post-trained on demonstrations from the target setting. Yet VLAs are typically compared by zero-shot or full-data fine-tuned success, revealing little about the data and compute required for adaptation. We study adaptation efficiency for six VLAs ($π_{0}$, $π_{0.5}$, and GR00T N1-N1.7) on four LIBERO suites, varying both demonstrations and training steps. This reveals differences hidden by full-data fine-tuning: models within two points on the full LIBERO-Spatial dataset differ by up to $3\times$ in success with 50 demonstrations. $π_{0.5}$ needs $2$--$5\times$ fewer demonstrations than $π_{0}$ and is the most sample-efficient model at every budget, with the largest gap on the long-horizon suite. Within GR00T, N1.5 adapts more efficiently than N1.6 and N1.7 on three of four suites, despite their stronger zero-shot performance. We study one pretraining factor behind these differences by freezing the VLM during finetuning: this severely degrades the $π$ models, whose VLM is jointly trained with the action expert during pretraining, but barely affects GR00T models. Finally, validation loss on held-out demonstrations tracks closed-loop success within a suite, but understates how much more sample-efficient $π_{0.5}$ is than $π_{0}$.

Introduction sec:intro State-of-the-art robot manipulation policies are typically obtained in two stages. A generalist policy is first pretrained on large and diverse robot and web data, and is then fine-tuned on demonstrations collected in the target deployment setting. What ultimately determines the usefulness of a pretrained policy is therefore not only how well it performs out of the box, but how efficiently, in demonstrations and in compute, it can be adapted to a new setting. Despite this, VLAs are usually compared through zero-shot evaluations or through success after fine-tuning on a full benchmark dataset~ black2025pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05,nvidia2025grootn1,bjorck2025grootn15 . Neither number measures the cost of adaptation. Yet many practical deployments have only a limited number of demonstrations, which makes adaptability under a demonstration budget an important measure of a pretrained policy. This gap matters in practice. Fine-tuning on the full LIBERO-Spatial dataset compresses five of the six models we study into a 97-99 band but with 50 demonstrations, the same five models span 31-94 . Models with stronger reported zero-shot performance, trained on more data with more parameters, can match their predecessors at full data and still require up to twice the data or compute to get there. We present a systematic study of VLA adaptation efficiency under behavior cloning, which is usually the standard way pretrained VLAs are fine-tuned on new tasks. We compare two families. ~ black2025pi0 and ~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 share the same PaliGemma VLM backbone and a flow-matching action expert, and differ primarily in their pretraining recipe. The GR00T N1, N1.5, N1.6, and N1.7 models~ nvidia2025grootn1,bjorck2025grootn15,nvidia2025grootn16,nvidia2026grootn17 are successive iterations, consisting of a VLM paired with a diffusion-transformer action head. Each reports to improve on its predecessor's generalist performance. Within each family, the pretrained models act as a natural experiment over pretraining recipes, which would otherwise require prohibitively expensive pretraining ablations. Our contributions are: A large-scale study of VLA sample efficiency. We fine-tune six VLAs on four LIBERO suites of increasing difficulty and measure adaptation along two axes: the number of demonstrations needed to reach a given success rate, and the number of optimization steps needed with the full dataset. The study comprises 120 fine-tuning runs and nearly 1400 checkpoint evaluations, more than 550k simulated episodes in total (Sections~ sec:setup - sec:results-efficiency ). Evidence that zero-shot and full-data comparisons do not capture adaptation efficiency. is 2--5 more demonstration-efficient than and outperforms every GR00T model at every budget, with the gap growing on the long-horizon suite. Within GR00T, N1.5 outperforms the stronger zero-shot models N1.6 and N1.7 at every tested budget on Spatial, Object, and Goal. An analysis of where adaptability resides. We study one pretraining axis, whether the VLM is trained jointly with the action head by freezing the VLM during fine-tuning. This is catastrophic for the family but nearly free for GR00T models. (Section~ sec:results-freeze ). An evaluation of an offline proxy for adaptability. Closed-loop budget sweeps are expensive. We test whether validation loss, which is available during training, can stand in for closed-loop success when measuring sample efficiency (Section~ sec:results-proxy ). Related Work sec:related Pretrained VLAs. Generalist VLAs couple a pretrained VLM with an action decoder trained on large robot datasets. ~ black2025pi0 attaches a flow-matching action expert to PaliGemma. ~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 keeps this architecture and changes the pretraining recipe, co-training on heterogeneous robot, web, and high-level subtask data. GR00T N1~ nvidia2025grootn1 pairs a VLM with a diffusion-transformer action head, and its successors~ bjorck2025grootn15,nvidia2025grootn16,nvidia2026grootn17 revise the backbone, the action head, and the training data. Other pretraining choices include action tokenization~ pertsch2025fast and implicit world modeling~ zheng2025flare . Adapting VLAs. A growing body of work improves how VLAs are adapted, through better fine-tuning recipes~ kim2025oft , parameter-efficient tuning~ ferchau2026lora , object-centric or future-conditioned adaptation for few-shot settings~ li2025controlvla,nguyen2026foca , one-shot skill adaptation~ zhao2025mosvla , and regularizers that preserve pretrained representations during fine-tuning~ huang2026maps,kachaev2025dontblind . These methods typically take the pretrained model as given. We study a complementary question: under behavior cloning which is usually the default adaptation procedure how strongly does the choice of pretrained model determine the data and compute needed to learn on new tasks? Data efficiency and pretraining for adaptation. Data quantity and quality are known to dominate imitation learning outcomes~ mandlekar2022robomimic,lin2025datascaling , and the choice of VLM backbone affects VLA performance~ zhang2026vlm4vla . title: CPNav: Calibrated Vision-Language Navigation for Object-Goal Search in Unseen Environments
summary: Directing a robot to locate a target object in unseen environments remains a central challenge in embodied AI. Vision-Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions. We introduce CPNav, a navigation framework that combines collision-aware planning with statistically calibrated VLM action scoring for map-free object-goal navigation. From RGB-D input, CPNav constructs a navigability map, generates collision-free motion primitives, and queries two VLMs for goal detection and action scoring. The resulting scores are calibrated offline via conformal prediction (CP) using oracle actions obtained through a tree-structured exploration procedure with backtracking, providing finite-sample guarantees at a user-specified risk level. The CP layer is model-agnostic and can wrap any VLM policy. Online, calibrated VLM scores guide action selection, while a tree-structured exploration history records alternative actions and allows backtracking. We evaluate CPNav in both simulation and real-world hardware settings. In AI Habitat simulation, compared with the uncalibrated baseline method, CPNav achieves relative SR and SPL improvements of 6.2% and 11.4% on HM3D v0.2, and 12.4% and 8.8% on MP3D, respectively. In real-world deployment on a modified Hiwonder MentorPi robot, the corresponding improvements in SR and SPL are 24.9% and 15.2%, respectively. Code is available at https://github.com/practice-lab-ucla/CPnav.

Vision--Language Model (VLM)-based methods provide rich semantic reasoning but often produce uncalibrated and overconfident action decisions. In real-world deployment on a modified Hiwonder MentorPi robot, the corresponding improvements in SR and SPL are 24.9 and 15.2 , respectively. Code is available at github.com/practice-lab-ucla/CPnav . Introduction Robotic navigation in complex unseen indoor environments remains challenging because effective decision-making must tightly couple low-level path planning with high-level semantic understanding, while generalizing to novel layouts without prior maps or goal location information SemanticNavSurvey . Traditional rule-based planners can handle geometric obstacle avoidance but rely on hand-tuned rules and expert knowledge, making them brittle in unforeseen situations cadena2016past . In contrast, learning-based navigation planners, particularly those based on reinforcement learning (RL), often require painstaking reward shaping and large-scale training data dulac2019challenges . Such RL-based planning approaches still struggle to generalize across diverse and unseen environments generalization_gap . A key limitation of both rule-based and purely learning-based navigation methods is the absence of semantic understanding, which is essential for efficient goal-directed behavior in realistic environments. Object-goal navigation benefits from reasoning about object-object and object-scene relationships and from leveraging commonsense priors about given environment layouts. By integrating these semantic priors, the robotic agent can effectively constrain the search process, significantly reducing the branching factor of the search tree and prioritizing paths that align with contextual expectations. Semantic information and common sense reasoning allow the agent to infer the probable locations of goal objects even when they are not present within the agent's current field of view Chaplot2020ObjectGoal . Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) such as Gemini gemini2023 , LLaVA liu2023llava , and GPT openai2023gpt4 enable injection of commonsense and scene priors into navigation, bridging geometric perception and high-level planning ha2023semantic . Through large-scale multimodal pretraining, these models acquire semantic priors that support generalization to previously unseen environments, reducing reliance on environment-specific training gadre2023cow, hendrycks2021natural . Although pretrained VLMs supply strong semantic cues, their internal heuristics, which are the learned rules that guide their behavior, are not calibrated for sequential decision making robot_ask_help . VLM outputs are optimized for token prediction or image-text alignment rather than long-horizon action selection under physical constraints. As a result, they often assign non-trivial confidence to unsafe, redundant, or goal-irrelevant actions ahn2022as, kadavath2022language . In this work, we tackle the problem of unreliable high-level action scoring in unseen environments. Without an explicit mechanism to quantify and control confidence, VLM-driven navigation can assign non-trivial scores to semantically plausible but suboptimal or unsafe actions. Over long horizons, such miscalibration can manifest as inefficient exploration, excessive backtracking, and action loops. Conformal Prediction (CP) provides a principled statistical mechanism to address this issue by converting uncalibrated model scores into prediction sets vovk2005algorithmic, angelopoulos2023conformal . Rather than trusting raw VLM confidences, CP uses a held-out calibration set to compute thresholds that control the error rate at a user-specified risk level. Under the assumption of exchangeability, this ensures that the probability of excluding the correct action is bounded by the calibration threshold, independent of the VLM architecture or training process. Building on this principle, we introduce , illustrated in ~ , a conformal prediction-augmented navigation framework that integrates semantic reasoning with statistically calibrated decision-making. The main contributions of this work are as follows: (1) We introduce a conformal calibration layer that converts uncalibrated VLM action scores into statistically valid prediction sets, guaranteeing under exchangeability that an oracle-consistent trajectory is retained with probability at least , where is the user-specified risk level. (2) An offline oracle-path search is formulated to identify oracle-aligned trajectories by maximizing the minimum VLM action score along a successful path, enabling trajectory-level conformal calibration for long-horizon embodied navigation. (3) Calibrated prediction sets are integrated into a tree-structured exploration policy, where calibrated VLM scores guide action selection and the stored tree supports backtracking. Related Work Recent work leverages the zero-shot reasoning of VLMs for embodied navigation SemanticNavSurvey, gadre2023cow, ha2023semantic, chu2026abot , covering end-to-end navigational question answering and spatial reasoning goetting2024vlmnav, shah2023lm-nav, zhou2024navgpt, zhou2024navgpt2 , hierarchical world-model and long-horizon planning wang2025tpmddn, zhang2025mem2ego, cai2025clcotnav , task-preferenced grounding wang2025tpmddn , and zero-shot semantic localization with frontier-based exploration gadre2023cow, Chaplot2020ObjectGoal, VLFM . However, these methods treat VLM outputs as absolute truths, so agents are misled by hallucinated relevance or overconfident scores for inaccessible paths robot_ask_help, ahn2022as , underscoring the need to calibrate VLM uncertainty. Uncertainty in learned perception and planning modules is commonly quantified with Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) and their approximations such as Monte Carlo dropout gal2016dropout , deep ensembles lakshminarayanan2017simple , or post-hoc calibration of softmax confidences gawlikowski2023survey . However, BNNs and ensembles require access to model weights and multiple forward passes or multiple trained models, incurring substantial training and inference cost lakshminarayanan2017simple, gawlikowski2023survey , and their confidences remain heuristic without finite-sample guarantees. These methods are also tied to a specific architecture and training procedure, so uncertainty estimation for large language and vision-language models typically falls back on sampled or verbalized outputs kadavath2022language, shorinwa2025survey . Formal guarantees instead come from probably approximately correct (PAC) techniques such as PAC-Bayes policy bounds majumdar2021pac and PAC confidence sets calibrated on held-out data park2020pac , or from robust control bounding a learned perception map's error dean2020robust , which respectively require a good prior or known linear dynamics. Conformal prediction avoids these limitations. It is model-agnostic and applies to any pretrained model without retraining, weight access, or multiple forward passes, needing only a held-out calibration set to produce prediction sets with distribution-free coverage angelopoulos2023conformal, mei2024perceive and, with a finite-sample correction, the same PAC-style guarantee vovk2013conditional . Conformal prediction (CP) provides a distribution-free framework for uncertainty quantification with finite-sample coverage guarantees vovk2005algorithmic, angelopoulos2023conformal , and several recent works have integrated it into robotics pipelines. CP has been utilized in perception and object detection to transform standard classification outputs into class prediction sets, preventing autonomous systems from making overconfident but incorrect categorical decisions mei2024perceive . Beyond perception, CP has been applied to motion prediction and trajectory forecasting, where it constructs uncertainty-aware prediction tubes around learned dynamics models, enabling downstream planners to account for bounded future-state uncertainty lindemann2023safe, dixit2023adaptive, sheng2024safe, srinivasan2026safety . Existing work on high-level navigation focuses on uncertainty-aware stopping or downstream confidence estimation rather than sequential action calibration explore_until_confident, robot_ask_help, liang2024introspective . These methods decide when to stop exploration but give no statistical guarantees for navigation actions. We apply CP directly to VLM-based action scoring, constructing calibrated prediction sets that govern the navigation policy. Method We consider object-goal navigation in previously unseen indoor environments. An embodied agent is initialized at an unknown pose, , where denotes the planar position and denotes the robot orientation. Given a target object category , such as chair, bed, or toilet, the goal is to navigate to any visible instance of that category without prior knowledge of the map or goal location. At each time step , the agent receives an RGB-D observation and its pose . Based on the current observation history, the agent selects a motion command , where denotes the commanded heading direction relative to the robot's current pose and denotes the commanded travel distance. proposes collision-free candidate actions from RGB-D input and queries two VLMs: a stopping VLM that decides goal-reaching and computes a global semantic value, and an action VLM that scores each candidate. title: Detecting and Explaining Robot Policy Failures from Sparse Internal Features
summary: Visuomotor policies can handle many robot manipulation tasks, but understanding their failures remains difficult. Unfamiliar conditions and small action errors can lead to failure, yet watching the robot alone tells us little about what went wrong inside the policy. We introduce MIND (Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Diagnosis), a method that looks inside a trained policy to detect failures during execution and identify the internal concepts involved. MIND uses a sparse autoencoder to break down the policy's internal activations into features that can be studied individually. We give meaning to these features by linking their activity to the robot's position, movement, and surroundings, and by steering their activations to examine how they affect the robot's actions. From successful and failed executions, we learn how the features behave on the way to a failure. During execution, MIND flags deviations from these patterns and uses the meaningful features contributing most to the change to describe the problem. Experiments in simulation and on a physical robot show that changes in these internal features help detect and explain failures. By using the same features for detection and diagnosis, MIND connects failure signals to understandable changes inside the policy.
full_text: Visuomotor policies can handle many robot manipulation tasks, but understanding their failures remains difficult. Unfamiliar conditions and small action errors can lead to failure, yet watching the robot alone tells us little about what went wrong inside the policy. We introduce MIND (Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Diagnosis), a method that looks inside a trained policy to detect failures during execution and identify the internal concepts involved. MIND uses a sparse autoencoder to break down the policy's internal activations into features that can be studied individually. We give meaning to these features by linking their activity to the robot's position, movement, and surroundings, and by steering their activations to examine how they affect the robot's actions. From successful and failed executions, we learn how the features behave on the way to a failure. During execution, MIND flags deviations from these patterns and uses the meaningful features contributing most to the change to describe the problem. Experiments in simulation and on a physical robot show that changes in these internal features help detect and explain failures. By using the same features for detection and diagnosis, MIND connects failure signals to understandable changes inside the policy. Introduction sec:intro Mechanistic interpretability (MI) -- the study of a trained network to understand its decision-making process through the features it represents instead of its individual neurons elhage2022superposition, bricken2023monosemanticity, templeton2024scaling -- has recently gained popularity in robot learning to understand the internal operations of vision-language-action (VLA) policies brohan2023rt2, kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, pi05_2025 . Some of these works use MI to `read' a policy's internal representation lu2025probing, molinari2025emergent, drvla2025, jin2026event, grant2026features , while others use it to steer the policy in a closed-loop manner haon2025mechanistic, buurmeijer2026observing . The former train linear probes alain2016probes on the hidden layers of a VLA lu2025probing, molinari2025emergent , or decompose them into sparse-autoencoder features whose meaning is then checked by clamping a feature while the robot runs drvla2025, jin2026event, grant2026features , whereas the latter use feed-forward directions or linear observers to control what the robot does. This paper belongs to the first group of work -- MIND clamps a feature in closed loop only to verify that the policy acts through it templeton2024scaling , never to control the robot. The primary motivation to `read' a VLA policy's internal representation is to understand how and why VLA policies -- which show remarkable performance on standard manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO liu2023libero -- fail sharply under rather simple perturbations, such as a change in the camera viewpoint or in the robot's initial state fei2025liberoplus , and even within their training distribution, where small action errors compound over a long horizon ross2011dagger, ahmed2026tail . When such a policy fails, watching the robot shows what went wrong -- e.g., the gripper closing short of the bowl -- but not why, because the process by which the policy turns an observation into an action, hereafter referred to as the Thought Process of the Policy or TPP, stays hidden inside the network. The major enabler of contemporary MI research is the sparse autoencoder (SAE) bricken2023monosemanticity, cunningham2023sparse . An SAE reconstructs each activation vector as a sparse sum of learned vectors elhage2022superposition . In language models many of these respond to a single concept far more selectively than individual neurons bricken2023monosemanticity, cunningham2023sparse, gao2024scaling , and amplifying or ablating one of them changes the model's output in a targeted manner templeton2024scaling, marks2024sparse -- much like adding a steering vector to the activations turner2023steering . drvla2025 report a similar finding for VLAs, showing that SAEs decompose the internal representations of and OpenVLA into largely interpretable and steerable . This opens up an exciting new research direction where MI can be leveraged to look inside VLAs and identify the changes in the TPP that accompany a task failure. However, drvla2025 also conclude that most of these are memorized -- they fire on a narrow set of episodes or scenes instead of across many -- with at most one in ten classed as general, and fewer than one in two hundred on OpenVLA. Their SAE is fitted on the activations of all tokens of a frame averaged into one vector, and each is named by a person who inspects the episodes on which it fires, so a name is never tested on episodes outside that inspection. In this paper, we argue that this conclusion depends on how the MI pipeline is constructed -- an SAE fitted on every token separately, with each name selected by a fixed rule and kept only if it still holds on held-out episodes, extracts many general from VLA policies. On the other hand, failure itself has been studied widely, and run-time detectors flag a failing execution from the actions, the uncertainty or the internal features of a policy sentinel, fiper, xu2025faildetect, gu2025safe, seligmann2026vlafail -- SAFE, for instance, shows that the activations of a VLA carry the information that a task is failing gu2025safe . Most of these detectors, however, compress that information into a single score, so their alarm informs that a failure has occurred without identifying what in the TPP went wrong. We propose MIND -- Mechanistic Interpretability for Neural Diagnosis -- a framework to track and interpret the TPP in order to detect and explain VLA policy failures. MIND 1) trains an SAE on the activations of the policy at every token during task execution, 2) gives each a name from a set of predefined concepts related to manipulation tasks, keeps the name only if it still holds on held-out episodes, and, for a decision concept, checks by clamping the in closed loop that the policy acts through it, and 3) monitors these during task execution, raises an alarm when their activity departs from that of successful executions, and reports the named that contributed most to the alarm. MIND therefore can explain a failure from the policy's own perspective -- for example, when the gripper closes short of the bowl, an observer cannot tell whether the policy misjudged where the bowl is or decided to close too early, but if the for the upcoming gripper-closing decision is active while the for the gripper-near-bowl state remains inactive, MIND reports the failure as an `early closure decision' instead of a `poor estimation of the bowl position'. Extensive evaluation of MIND in simulation with OpenVLA kim2024openvla , pi05_2025 and LingBot-VLA wu2026lingbot , and on a physical robot running demonstrates its performance in detecting and explaining VLA policy failures. In OpenVLA, clamping a single named raises the share of steps that move the named way from -- to -- for twelve of fourteen motion concepts, and in all three policies the named detect failures as well as the dense activation -- an AUROC of against on , with half the false alarms. Our contributions are: We extract sparse basis features of a VLA whose names are selected on one set of runs and remain precise on unseen initial states and on an unseen task, where the neurons, residual coordinates and random directions of the same policy provide none (Sections~ sec:method and~ sec:results ). We verify in closed loop that the policy acts through these basis features, since clamping one basis feature steers the arm while random ones of equal magnitude do not (Section~ sec:results ). We build a run-time monitor that raises an alarm from the same basis features and identifies the internal quantities responsible for it, evaluated on three policies in simulation and on a physical robot (Sections~ sec:setup and~ sec:results ). Unlike a number of recent works on policy safety zhang2026probeact, sinha2024realtime, liu2023reflect, ahmed2026tail , MIND does not offer a way to recover from failure. Rather, the goal of MIND is to understand what the policy represented when it failed -- as opposed to just informing that a failure has occurred -- which will in turn facilitate designing a recovery mechanism. Method sec:method sec:method:system MIND decomposes the TPP of a VLA policy into basis features with human-readable names, and it detects and explains a failing attempt through those same basis features. The basis features come from the activation , the vectors that one layer of the policy returns at step . The method rests on two conditionals: (i) if each activation decomposes into numbers of which only a few are non-zero, each number follows one quantity of the TPP; (ii) if each number also has a human-readable name that holds on unseen attempts at run time, the TPP at every step reads as the list of named basis features that are on. Failure detection is a product of the two: a score computed from the same numbers separates a failing attempt from a successful one, and tracing that score back to the numbers and their names reports the failure from the policy's own perspective. Figure~ fig:system draws the pipeline on the running task, in which the robot picks up a black bowl and places it on a plate. After the preliminaries of Section~ sec:method:prelim , we construct the autoencoder and the naming rule of MIND that satisfy (i) and (ii) in Sections~ sec:method:sae and~ sec:method:name , and build the failure detector and its explanation on them in Sections~ sec:method:monitor and~ sec:method:cause . Preliminaries sec:method:prelim In a VLA policy , an episode is one attempt at a task, from the initial state of the scene to the goal or the step limit. At each step the policy receives frame , the current camera image, and a fixed instruction in words. Each layer of the policy writes one vector of width per position, where a position, or token, is one patch of the image, one word of the instruction or one part of the coming action. The activation that layer returns is dense, with almost every coordinate non-zero at almost every step. No single coordinate of has a meaning that a human can name, such as the gripper grasping the black bowl. The reason is superposition elhage2022superposition . title: Spatial Representation Distillation and Knowledge Routing for Vision-Language-Action Models
comment: NeurIPS 2026 Camera-ready
summary: Understanding three-dimensional physical structure has become essential for vision-language-action models (VLAs). However, existing approaches either rely on explicit geometric inputs at inference time or adopt a single visual pathway, potentially compromising the visual-semantic knowledge inherited from pre-trained models. We present SPARK-VLA, Spatial Representation distillation and Knowledge routing for VLAs, a preserve-specialize-route framework for spatially adapting VLAs without requiring external 3D inputs or experts at inference. SPARK-VLA consists of two key components: (1) spatial representation distillation, which transfers 3D understanding from a frozen 3D expert to a LoRA-adapted visual branch by aligning attention responses while preserving the original visual pathway, and (2) a lightweight knowledge router, which selectively forwards action-relevant visual tokens to the language model using routing supervision derived from action-loss gradients. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, and real-world manipulation, SPARK-VLA achieves strong performance with only a 0.5B language backbone and approximately 53M trainable parameters, providing an effective and parameter-efficient approach to 3D-aware VLA learning. Code is available at https://github.com/park-jungin/spark-vla.
full_text: Method Motivation and overview r 0.55 Overview of . Trainable modules are represented in the red boxes. fig:overall Existing efforts to enhance vision-language-action models (VLAs) with spatial intelligence generally follow two directions: introducing explicit 3D inputs, such as depth maps or point clouds, or implicitly injecting spatial knowledge into the visual representation. While the former often depends on additional sensing or reconstructed 3D signals, the latter can weaken the generic visual-semantic capability inherited from strong pre-trained vision-language backbones by forcing a single visual pathway to absorb both general perception and spatial reasoning. To address this issue, we propose , which preserves the original visual pathway while introducing a lightweight spatially adapted pathway. During training, we use a pre-trained 3D expert ( , VGGT~ vggt ) to distill spatial knowledge into the adapted branch. To effectively use the two branches, we further introduce a lightweight knowledge router that takes visual tokens, conditions on the language instruction, and predicts token-wise gate probabilities indicating which tokens are useful for action generation. The selected tokens are then forwarded to the language model for action prediction, allowing to exploit complementary generic and spatial cues while suppressing redundant or noisy representations. Note that the 3D expert is used only during training and is discarded at inference time. The overall architecture of our is shown in . Spatial representation distillation To incorporate spatial understanding into the VLA's visual encoder without disrupting its original visual-semantic capability, we introduce a spatially adapted branch built on the pre-trained visual encoder. Let denote the visual encoder of a pre-trained vision-language model ( , Qwen2.5-VL~ qwen25 ) and denote its LoRA-adapted counterpart, where only the low-rank parameters are trainable. Given an RGB observation , extracts two complementary representations: where preserves generic visual-semantic knowledge and is adapted to capture spatial reasoning. During training, we further employ a pre-trained 3D encoder as a frozen teacher that provides spatial supervision to the adapted branch. In this way, the original branch preserves the pre-trained visual representation, while the adapted branch learns to encode additional spatial knowledge. Instead of directly forcing the adapted branch to mimic the output representation of the 3D teacher, we distill attention responses~ v-lynx . Our key idea is to preserve compatibility with the original transformer structure by teaching the adapted branch how to attend in a spatially informed manner. At the -th layer of , we obtain the query, key, and value embeddings, denoted by , , and . From the frozen 3D teacher, we extract the corresponding key and value embeddings, denoted by and . We then compute two attention responses using the same query embedding : where denotes the scaled dot-product attention. Using the same query while replacing the key-value pairs allows the teacher response to specify how the adapted visual branch should interact with the attention mechanism to remain compatible with spatial knowledge. The attention response distillation objective for spatial representations is defined as: where denotes the loss. By aligning attention responses across layers, the adapted branch acquires geometry-aware behavior from the 3D teacher while retaining the original visual pathway for generic scene understanding. Knowledge routing While and provide complementary generic and spatial cues, not all tokens are equally useful for a given instruction and action prediction. Directly feeding all tokens from both branches into the LLM may introduce redundant or noisy information, especially when spatially adapted tokens are irrelevant to the current instruction. We therefore introduce a lightweight knowledge router that feeds instruction- and action-relevant visual tokens into the LLM. We first collect the visual tokens from the generic and spatial branches and denote the merged token set by where is the total number of visual tokens. As shown in , the knowledge router consists of (1) a linear layer to project into the same dimensional space with the text embeddings ; (2) a cross-attention layer to compute the correlations between the visual and text representations; and (3) a lightweight MLP (Linear-GeLU-Linear). The output of the last linear layer followed by a Sigmoid activation serves as the gate probabilities : where is a sigmoid function and is a temperature parameter to control the sensitivity. Once the gate probabilities are obtained, we select the top- tokens among all tokens: where returns the indices of the largest gate probabilities, indicates the routing ratio, and prevents overly sparse routing. We then project the selected tokens to the LLM's input space by fusing them according to their spatial positions. At each spatial position, the routed representation is constructed from the selected tokens among its generic and spatial pair. When both tokens are selected, their embeddings are concatenated and projected into the LLM input space. If only one token is selected, it is concatenated with a zero embedding of the same dimension and passed through the same projection. Positions for which neither token is selected are discarded. This position-aware fusion preserves the alignment between generic and spatial knowledge, while producing a compact set of visual tokens with a unified input format for the LLM. The main challenge in training the knowledge router is that there is no supervision signal indicating which visual tokens should be preserved. Instead of relying on heuristic salience measures~ spec-prune-vla, vla-pruner or learning token selection only through downstream action optimization~ cog-vla, semantic-vla , we derive routing targets from the gradient of the action loss with respect to the router gate probabilities. Given the action loss , the gradient of w.r.t. the gate probability , , , measures the influences of the -th gate on action prediction. A negative gradient indicates that increasing the gate probability would reduce the action loss, suggesting that the corresponding token is useful. Therefore, we define the importance score as Since only routed tokens are forwarded to the LLM, the instantaneous gradients provide supervision only for the currently selected subset. We therefore maintain a momentum-based moving average of token importance scores, allowing tokens that are not selected in the current step to still contribute to router training through their accumulated utility. The detailed update rule is provided in . From , we construct a gating target : where denotes the momentum-updated importance score. This gating target enables the router to learn action-aware token selection without explicit token-level annotations. We train the knowledge router with the classification problem. To handle the imbalance between selected and discarded tokens, we adopt the focal binary cross-entropy loss~ focal : where . To further stabilize routing behavior, we additionally impose a budget regularization term that encourages the average routing ratio to match the target ratio and an entropy regularization term that controls the uncertainty of the gate probabilities: The final router objective is defined as where and control the impact of budget constraint and entropy regularization, respectively. By combining the knowledge routing with gradient-based pseudo supervision, the proposed knowledge router learns to preserve action-relevant visual tokens from both the generic and spatial branches while suppressing redundant or noisy representations. Training objective is trained with three objectives: the action loss, the spatial representation distillation loss, and the knowledge router loss: where balances the contribution of the spatial distillation term. We use regression for the action loss. Please see for training details.

title: EmbodiedIntentBench: Benchmarking Intent-Driven Runtime Adaptation for Mobile Robotic Missions
comment: Paper is currently under review. Authors' version posted for personal use and not for redistribution
summary: Mobile robotic sensing systems must adapt to operator requirements, limited resources, changing connectivity, and observation opportunities shaped by physical motion. Evaluating runtime strategies therefore requires assessing whether their decisions fulfill mission objectives, beyond isolated perception accuracy or execution efficiency. We present EmbodiedIntentBench, a benchmark for intent-driven runtime adaptation in mobile robotic missions. It represents mission intent through structured contracts for coverage, temporal evidence, reporting, urgency, and resources, and couples simulated unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) workloads with causal, resource-accounted execution. Computation decisions affect mission time, resource use, and which observations can contribute evidence. We evaluate fixed and adaptive perception strategies in multi-phase missions and under changing urgency, connectivity, and battery conditions. In the multi-phase Depot study, a configuration with 87.5% full-bank target recall across visible target observations completes only 1 of 16 missions, whereas a lower-recall configuration completes 14. In an ablation, ignoring execution-induced observation loss increases aggregate mission success and reverses the ordering of two runtime strategies. Replays using Jetson AGX Orin CPU and GPU profiles change the relative success of local and remote strategies. In selected Jetson GPU-profile replays, intent-driven adaptation reduces modeled task energy by up to 28% with unchanged mission success. EmbodiedIntentBench provides an extensible framework for evaluating runtime decisions against mission fulfillment under physical and resource constraints.
