Introduction sec:intro Mobile robotic systems, particularly unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), are increasingly employed in mission-critical applications such as search and rescue, disaster response, and infrastructure inspection~ bhattacharjya2025avery,cladera2025air,farahani2026evlm . Advances in language-guided robotics and intent-driven embodied intelligence are enabling operators to specify what a mission must accomplish, rather than prescribing how individual sensing and computation tasks should be executed~ cladera2025air,bhattacharjya2025avery,farahani2026evlm, 10.1145/3715014.3722081 . However, translating such high-level natural-language intent into effective runtime behavior remains challenging under constrained onboard computation, limited energy, and variable network connectivity~ bhattacharjya2025avery . Consider a UAV deployed to locate stranded individuals following a flood, where an operator requests verified locations to support rescue operations (Fig.~ fig:motivation (a)). An initial search may prioritize broad target coverage, while subsequent rescue operations may require corroborated findings or more timely updates. Although these requests concern the same environment, they impose different evidence, timing, and resource requirements~ bhattacharjya2026floodreasonbench . Mission intent describes an operator's desired outcome and is represented through a structured contract, which can be supplied directly or constructed from a supported natural-language request. Fulfilling such requirements cannot be assessed through perception accuracy or execution efficiency alone. A correct prediction may arrive too late, while a timely detection may lack sufficient evidence for confirmation. Even with sufficient evidence, reporting errors or resource violations can prevent mission completion. Consequently, successful individual computations do not necessarily translate into successful mission execution~ weng2026multi, chen2026controller . These distinctions become particularly important for mobile robotic systems, where physical motion creates time-sensitive observation opportunities. As a UAV traverses its environment, useful views emerge and disappear with changing viewpoints, occlusions, and target visibility. A computationally demanding perception configuration may improve an individual prediction while preventing subsequent observations from being processed (Fig.~ fig:motivation (c))~ soyyigit2025mural, 10.1145/3774906.3800471 . Such tradeoffs also depend on whether computation executes onboard or remotely (Fig.~ fig:motivation (b)), with different implications for latency, communication, and energy consumption~ kim2026approxbit, azimi2026cloud, candal2023drone . Runtime decisions must therefore be evaluated through their contribution to mission fulfillment, rather than isolated measures of prediction quality or execution efficiency. Prior work has established the importance of evaluating robotic computation in the context of physical execution and downstream task performance~ bala2024ooda . MAVBench~ boroujerdian2018mavbench characterizes interactions among computation, physical dynamics, and resource consumption, while RobotPerf~ mayoral2024robotperf and A2Perf~ uchendu2025a2perf provide robotic computing benchmarks. Streaming perception~ li2020towards, yang2022streaming and control-aware prediction~ mcallister2022control highlight the importance of prediction timing and downstream consequences. More recently, DEEP~ cong2026decision and LIBERO-Dynamic~ ren2026libero examine decision-level computation value and inference latency. However, these approaches do not jointly evaluate runtime computation against explicit mission requirements involving accumulated evidence, temporal verification, reporting, and resource constraints. This motivates a fundamental question: Addressing this requires explicit mission requirements, causal accounting of computation and observation opportunities, and evaluation of whether accumulated evidence and reports satisfy the intended mission. To this end, we present , a benchmark for evaluating intent-driven runtime adaptation in mobile robotic missions (Fig.~ fig:motivation (d)). operationalizes mission intent through structured mission contracts specifying target coverage, temporal evidence, verification, reporting, urgency, and resource constraints. It combines Gazebo-based UAV workloads~ koenig2004design with causal, resource-accounted execution; using shared recorded trajectories, it measures how runtime computation changes observation availability, resource use, and mission fulfillment. The current evaluation isolates computation decisions over fixed recorded UAV trajectories; navigation and physical control are outside its scope. We demonstrate through two complementary case studies. The first examines perception choices in multi-phase Lake and Depot missions (lake and warehouse) involving coverage, repeated confirmation, timely reporting, and fresh revisits. The second investigates runtime adaptation under changing urgency, connectivity, and battery conditions using whole-model local and remote execution. We also examine how mission requirements can guide when perception stops, using Jetson-derived profiles and measuring energy for selected schedules on the device. Our evaluation reveals that a configuration achieving 87.5 full-bank target recall (across visible target observations) completes only 1 of 16 missions, whereas another with lower recall completes 14. Further validation shows that ignoring execution-induced observation loss can overestimate mission success and reverse the relative ranking of runtime strategies. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: Intent-driven mission specification. We introduce structured mission contracts expressing operator objectives through explicit requirements for target coverage, temporal evidence, verification, reporting, urgency, and resource constraints. Causal, resource-accounted execution. We develop an evaluation methodology coupling runtime computation with physically situated observation opportunities, accounting for how processing delays, communication, and onboard resource consumption affect mission evidence. Mission-level evaluation and diagnostics. We connect runtime decisions to evidence acquisition, confirmation, reporting, and mission fulfillment, enabling analysis of the requirements and execution conditions underlying mission outcomes. Extensible benchmark and empirical characterization. We provide configurable workloads, reference strategies, and extension interfaces, demonstrating discrepancies between perception performance and mission success, the effects of causal execution, and the consequences of changing resource conditions. A public artifact provides code, inputs, and reference results for the dynamic study and the Jetson and intent-driven analyses; Appendix A describes its scope. The complete benchmark artifact, including the multi-phase workloads and prediction banks, will be released upon acceptance. A structured mission contract defines successful execution, while a runtime policy selects computation configurations based on mission requirements and current system state. Causal, resource-accounted execution determines result availability, resource consumption, and subsequent observation opportunities. Admitted outputs contribute to mission evidence and reporting, which are evaluated against the contract. This separation enables controlled comparisons of runtime strategies without prescribing a particular perception model or adaptation algorithm. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:architecture (a), an operator-facing request is represented through a structured mission contract that makes the intended sensing objectives and execution requirements explicit. For example, a request to locate stranded individuals and report verified positions can specify the required target coverage, corroborating observations, and reporting constraints. The contract provides a common interface between operator intent, runtime policies, and mission evaluation. Requirements are expressed through a validated JSON-based specification, which can be supplied directly or constructed from supported operator-facing descriptions. The benchmark operates on the structured requirements rather than assuming unrestricted natural-language interpretation during execution. title: ReSkill: Selective Self-Improvement for Robot Manipulation
comment: Submitted to intelligent computing for embodied AI and robotics
summary: Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. We present ReSkill, a selective self-improvement framework that concentrates revision on capability gaps. A coding agent constructs an object-centric task graph from an instruction and a skill library, then uses node-level execution records to locate failures. At the task level, it revises stage organization, hand-off conditions, and recovery routes; at the skill level, it strengthens perception, motion, manipulation, and verification capabilities that repeatedly fail. Candidate revisions undergo full-task evaluation and paired comparisons before adoption, allowing local changes to accumulate into validated skills and an independently executable policy. The agent participates only during development; the deployed policy calls the retained skills without invoking the agent at run time. On the same development set, average success across ten RoboDojo tasks rises from 30.0% for the initial versions to 86.2% for the final adopted programs; retained programs achieve 83.6% in recorded robustness and model-selection evaluations. Across eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 rebuilt-simulation trials and 62 of 80 real-robot trials (77.5%). The median revision changes only three functions, approximately 0.5% of a program, while 39% of task-specific functions in later-added tasks directly reuse existing implementations. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks.
full_text: What should a robot improve for a new manipulation task? The tool-storage example isolates a missing tilt-aware seating skill. End-to-end adaptation retrains a task policy, while an Agent-as-Policy handles the current episode through repeated model calls. ReSkill revises the task graph and local skills during development, validates the changes, and retains reusable skills and an executable policy requiring no run-time Agent calls. fig:teaser Self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks requires deciding what to reuse, where to improve, and which changes to retain. These results show how locating local deficiencies, validating candidate changes, and accumulating reusable skills can improve execution of compositional manipulation tasks. Introduction sec:intro When a robot encounters a new manipulation task, the capability it lacks often covers only part of the task. A compositional task may involve observation, approach, grasping, transport, placement, and return; existing controllers or skills can already handle many of these stages, while a few fail on new objects, layouts, occlusions, or execution conditions. Robot foundation models have expanded robots' ability to act on visual and language inputs brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0 , while language-model agents have enabled flexible task decomposition and skill coordination ahn2022saycan,liang2023cap . Nevertheless, new multi-stage tasks are often treated as unified learning or adaptation problems. This can require relearning capabilities the robot already has and increase the costs of data, computation, and real-world interaction. This raises a more fundamental question: when a robot encounters a new compositional manipulation task, what exactly should it improve? Existing research addresses this problem through end-to-end policy learning, skill composition, and agent self-improvement, but still lacks explicit modeling of where capability gaps occur. End-to-end policies map observations and task instructions directly to actions brohan2023rt2,black2024pi0 , making it difficult to distinguish stages that already work reliably from those that need improvement. Agentic manipulation systems based on task decomposition, programmatic control, and skill calls ahn2022saycan,liang2023cap,singh2023progprompt,huang2022innermonologue flexibly compose existing capabilities, but mainly improve how those capabilities are organized and used: when a skill repeatedly fails under new conditions, replanning or calling the same skill again does not change the skill itself. Voyager accumulates executable skills, Reflexion stores reflections from task feedback, and Self-Refine iteratively critiques and revises model outputs wang2023voyager,shinn2023reflexion,madaan2023selfrefine . For robot manipulation, candidate revisions must also be assessed across layouts: an improvement on a few development scenes may not persist under different initial conditions. The unresolved question is therefore: how can a robot first locate the capability gaps in a task, improve only those parts, and reliably judge whether the improvement is real and worth retaining and reusing? We introduce ReSkill, a framework for selective self-improvement on compositional manipulation tasks (Figure~ fig:teaser ). The robot first identifies the task structure and assesses its existing capabilities, then concentrates improvement on the gaps that remain. A coding agent serves as the learning orchestrator, constructing an object-centric task graph from a task description and, optionally, one demonstration. Each node specifies a skill call, its object roles, entry and completion conditions, and budget; edges specify success, failure, and recovery routes. Within this graph, explicit geometric routines handle stages that can be programmed directly, and library skills cover interactions the robot already knows how to perform. Repeated execution failures reveal the unresolved stages or skills and direct the agent's revisions, allowing development to preserve and build on capabilities that already work. Improvement proceeds at two scales, using the same node-level execution records and visual traces. At the task level, the agent locates the earliest stage that deviates and revises stage decomposition, hand-off conditions, skill bindings, or recovery procedures. For example, in cup nesting it changes the release-stage completion condition to require both release and the intended nesting relation, while keeping the grasping and insertion skills unchanged. At the skill level, improvement is organized around four types of reusable capability: perception skills estimate object geometry, motion skills generate feasible trajectories, manipulation skills perform interactions such as grasping and placement, and verification skills check outcomes and guide correction. Failure evidence accumulated across tasks identifies which skill needs strengthening; validated improvements are shared through the skill library or transferred into other task programs. New tasks therefore start from the existing task with the closest skill requirements. Every revision at either scale must pass multi-stage evaluation before adoption. Candidates are screened on a few development layouts, evaluated on the full development set and robustness layouts, and compared with the incumbent on paired test layouts available only to the orchestrator. When results are close, paired evaluations are repeated on layouts where outcomes disagree. This links local revision to evidence that determines whether an improvement should be retained and reused. We evaluate ReSkill on ten RoboDojo simulation tasks chen2026robodojo and eight real-world tasks on the Xtrainer platform. For each real-world task, a single teleoperated demonstration is used to rebuild the corresponding scene in MuJoCo (real-to-sim); development takes place in the rebuilt environment, and the resulting program is deployed on the real robot (sim-to-real). This process supplies a development environment for real-world tasks and is not itself part of the method. The coding agent participates only during development, revising task graphs and skills, submitting evaluations, and deciding which revisions to adopt; the deployed program is frozen and makes no external large-model calls at run time. Model selection uses test layouts accessed by the orchestrator. On RoboDojo, retained programs make zero run-time API calls and achieve an average success rate of 83.6 across the ten tasks in 337 recorded evaluation episodes. During development, average task success rises from 30.0 for the initial task graphs to 86.2 . On the eight real-world tasks, ReSkill succeeds in 72 of 80 trials in rebuilt simulation and 62 of 80 trials on the real robot. We further analyze revision locality, the evolution of failure types, cross-task skill reuse and how quickly new tasks get started, the role of a single demonstration, and development-agent model usage. Our main contributions are as follows. Selective Self-Improvement via Task Graphs We introduce a selective self-improvement framework that organizes stages, skills, and recovery routes in an object-centric task graph and focuses improvement on the stages and skills that actually fail during execution, rather than relearning the entire task. Two-Scale Improvement: Task-Graph Revision and Skill Reuse We unify failure-driven task-graph revision with skill organization, improvement, and reuse in a single development loop, and provide a multi-stage evaluation and adoption protocol centered on paired comparisons on model-selection test layouts to assess which revisions improve task execution. Empirical Study of How Skills Improve, Transfer and Pay Off We evaluate the framework on ten RoboDojo simulation tasks and eight real-world tasks on the Xtrainer platform, and use more than ten thousand verified simulation episodes and code snapshots from 774 revisions to quantify revision locality, the evolution of failure types, function-level skill reuse, the role of demonstrations, and development cost. Related work sec:related Agentic and self-improving robot systems Recent robot systems increasingly use high-level agents to decompose complex tasks into combinations of programmatic operations and learned skills. SayCan and Code as Policies demonstrate language models' ability to decompose tasks and invoke skills ahn2022saycan,liang2023cap ; the more recent Harness VLA zhang2026harnessvla combines a frozen vision--language--action model with analytic primitives and extends the policy's effective range through re-grounding, staging, and skill orchestration. ASPIRE, Zetta, and RISE explore robot self-improvement through programmatic skill accumulation, failure recovery, and policy-level optimization, respectively lu2026aspire,ding2026zetta,yang2026rise . ReSkill couples task-graph revision with local skill improvement: execution records identify whether a failure calls for a change in task organization or skill implementation, and paired evaluation determines which updates are retained for later tasks. Our central questions are where improvement is actually needed and how improvements can be reliably retained and reused. Skill libraries and code as policies Earlier work on long-horizon bimanual manipulation also used staged learning: Mixline learns subtasks with online reinforcement learning and combines them through offline learning from the resulting trajectories sun2022mixline . Programs provide a natural representation for organizing robot skills: Code as Policies and ProgPrompt use language models to write programs that call perception and control primitives liang2023cap,singh2023progprompt ; Inner Monologue returns execution feedback to the planner as text huang2022innermonologue ; Voyager stores generated skill code in a retrievable library for later tasks wang2023voyager ; and Eureka uses a coding agent to iteratively rewrite reward functions ma2024eureka . ReSkill likewise represents skills and task graphs as programs, but does not generate them on the fly at deployment: programs are repeatedly executed during development, failures are attributed to stages, and programs are frozen after multi-stage evaluation and remain unchanged during deployment. We also measure at the code level how extensively skills are reused verbatim or with rewriting across tasks (Section~ sec:exp-reuse ), a quantity rarely reported systematically in prior work. title: Online Geometric Consistency Assessment of LiDAR Measurements via Recursive Bayesian Comparison
summary: LiDAR-based localization and mapping systems produce registered point clouds that serve as geometric measurements for downstream estimation and navigation. Registration errors introduce duplicated surfaces and structural deformation into these measurements. In the absence of an independent reference, online assessment relies on geometry accumulated from earlier measurements. Such assessment requires tolerance to sampling variation and an accumulation process in which observations enter the history only after evaluation. We therefore formulate a recursive Bayesian comparison that couples geometric assessment with history maintenance. A Normal-Inverse-Wishart model represents historical voxel geometry and its uncertainty, while a weak isotropic reference adapts to current sampling. Comparing the marginal predictive support of the same current points under both models yields Normalized Drift Evidence (NDE). Assessment precedes assimilation: positive NDE triggers an alarm and preserves the preceding historical state; otherwise, the current observations update the history. Across 14 real-world sequences totaling approximately 73 min from four platform types, alarms identified all nine corrupted sequences and were absent from all five consistent sequences. In four representative scenarios with event references, first alarms occurred within 0.9 s of the reference times, with no preceding alarms. Cross-backend evaluation demonstrates consistent responses to reconstructed geometry. Ablation and controlled perturbation results establish the roles of uncertainty modeling, recursive history, displacement, and geometric support. Mean processing time is 4.2--6.1 ms per update at 1 Hz. In ten UAV trials, alarms initiated odometry isolation, landing, relocalization, and mission continuation.
full_text: Online Geometric Consistency Assessment of LiDAR Measurements via Recursive Bayesian Comparison Mingqiao~Han, Qigeng~Duan, Xuchen~Liu, Jinqiang~Cui, Xi~Chen, and Ben~M.~Chen,~ Han et al.: Online Geometric Consistency Monitoring LiDAR-based localization and mapping systems produce registered point clouds that serve as geometric measurements for downstream estimation and navigation. Registration errors introduce duplicated surfaces and structural deformation into these measurements. In the absence of an independent reference, online assessment relies on geometry accumulated from earlier measurements. Such assessment requires tolerance to sampling variation and an accumulation process in which observations enter the history only after evaluation. We therefore formulate a recursive Bayesian comparison that couples geometric assessment with history maintenance. A Normal-Inverse-Wishart model represents historical voxel geometry and its uncertainty, while a weak isotropic reference adapts to current sampling. Comparing the marginal predictive support of the same current points under both models yields Normalized Drift Evidence (NDE). Assessment precedes assimilation: positive NDE triggers an alarm and preserves the preceding historical state; otherwise, the current observations update the history. Across 14 real-world sequences totaling approximately 73 min from four platform types, alarms identified all nine corrupted sequences and were absent from all five consistent sequences. In four representative scenarios with event references, first alarms occurred within 0.9 s of the reference times, with no preceding alarms. Cross-backend evaluation demonstrates consistent responses to reconstructed geometry. Ablation and controlled perturbation results establish the roles of uncertainty modeling, recursive history, displacement, and geometric support. Mean processing time is 4.2--6.1 ms per update at 1 Hz. In ten UAV trials, alarms initiated odometry isolation, landing, relocalization, and mission continuation. Introduction sec:introduction Geometric consistency determines whether repeated LiDAR measurements provide a coherent spatial representation for localization and mapping. Registration errors displace or deform observed surfaces, compromising the geometric information supplied to subsequent estimation and navigation. Weak geometric constraints, sensing degradation, and accumulated drift challenge this consistency during operation~ slam_problem1,tim_dong2023_pve . The estimation system may continue to publish pose and map outputs despite these discrepancies. Online assessment of the reconstructed geometry therefore provides a means of detecting corrupted spatial data and informing the subsequent use of localization outputs~ tim_wu2022_multimodal,related_redundant1 . Existing monitoring methods derive evidence from estimator statistics, prior maps, or the constraints available for registration. Integrity methods relate state uncertainty to fault hypotheses~ osa1,osa2,osa3 , map-based methods evaluate alignment against an established spatial reference~ related_prior2,prior , and degeneracy-aware estimation and multisensor monitoring use internal geometric constraints or modality-specific indicators to guide measurement selection and information fusion~ tim_wu2022_multimodal,related_match1,tim_bai2021_degeneration . Each approach therefore depends on access to a particular estimation model or a prior reference map. Registered point clouds expose geometric discrepancies directly at the output of localization and mapping, independently of the estimator that produced them. In the absence of an independent reference, online assessment of this output relies on earlier measurements of the same scene as the only basis for comparison. Using earlier measurements as the reference raises two difficulties. First, misregistration changes the centroids, orientations, and shapes of repeatedly observed structures (Fig.~ introduction ), while viewpoint, visibility, and point density alter the same quantities during nominal operation; a direct comparison consequently confounds sampling variation with geometric disagreement. Second, gradual drift produces small discrepancies between adjacent observations that accumulate only relative to earlier structure; a comparison limited to the preceding observation remains insensitive to such drift. Detecting both abrupt and gradual corruption thus requires a comparison that accounts for current sampling and a reference that retains geometric information, together with its uncertainty, across successive updates. Such a reference evolves with the incoming measurements, which couples its maintenance to the assessment it supports. Incorporating each observation before assessment allows the observation to modify the historical state against which its own consistency is evaluated, whereas keeping the reference fixed preserves earlier structure but excludes subsequent compatible observations. The central problem is therefore to evaluate current geometry against the preceding history while allowing that history to evolve according to the resulting evidence, which requires an update rule that preserves the temporal order of assessment and assimilation. We formulate this problem through two models of the same current observation. A recursive Normal-Inverse-Wishart model retains historical voxel geometry and its uncertainty, and a weak isotropic reference represents a baseline adapted to the current centroid and total variance. Their marginal predictive contrast expresses the support for historical compatibility relative to the current baseline. Aggregation over sufficiently supported historical voxels yields Normalized Drift Evidence (NDE), which governs both the consistency decision and subsequent history maintenance. The current observation is scored against the preceding state; a positive NDE preserves that state, while a nonpositive or undefined NDE permits the specified recursive updates. The main contributions are: An online consistency indicator for registered LiDAR measurements. We contrast predictive support for identical current observations under persistent historical geometry and a weak reference adapted to current sampling, incorporating geometric uncertainty. A recursive reference governed by consistency evidence. Assessment precedes assimilation, and the aggregate contrast governs historical updates. An alarm retains the preceding state as the reference for subsequent assessments. Geometric corruption detection and closed-loop recovery. Scene, ablation, perturbation, and cross-backend experiments establish detection behavior and the roles of latent modeling, recursive history, and support; UAV experiments demonstrate odometry isolation and recovery. Section~ sec:related_work reviews related work, Section~ sec:methodology develops the consistency monitor, Section~ sec:evaluation presents the experimental evaluation, and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes. Related Work sec:related_work Estimator Integrity and Prior Map Methods Integrity monitoring quantifies localization reliability by combining uncertainty propagation with fault hypotheses. Formulations for particle filter localization~ osa1 , extended Kalman filter (EKF) SLAM~ osa2 , and Kalman filter localization~ osa3 evaluate faults through estimator states, residuals, and uncertainty models. Sequential integrity monitoring incorporates state-domain consistency and multiple-fault bias estimation into protection levels~ tim_shao2025_integrity . Liu et al.~ tim_liu2026_mhss estimate LiDAR-SLAM positioning uncertainty through multifault hypothesis solution separation and Lie-group theory. Linearization and observability affect covariance consistency in EKF SLAM~ slam_ekf , while uncertainty evaluation examines noise and system model mismatch~ tim_yan2026_credible . Prior map methods assess agreement between current measurements and an established environmental representation. Misalignment recognition detects localization failures from observation--map agreement~ related_prior1,related_prior2 , while planar-feature localization quantifies safety relative to a prior map~ prior . Adaptive map updates also sustain long-term localization by responding to matching conditions~ tim_liu2025_adaptive_map . These methods interpret reliability within their localization model and reference representation. The proposed monitor constructs its geometric reference from registered observations collected during operation and retains earlier geometry for subsequent assessments. Registration Constraints and Geometric Consistency Registration monitors assess whether geometry sufficiently constrains pose estimation. X-ICP evaluates LiDAR localizability~ related_match1 ; related methods address degeneracy in navigation, factor graph optimization, SLAM, and multisensor fusion~ related_match2,related_match3,related_hessian1,related_hessian2,related_hessian3 . Bai et al.~ tim_bai2021_degeneration combine outlier rejection, degeneration assessment, and adaptive feature usage in visual-inertial navigation. Recent methods use segment-based visual assistance~ tim_wu2025_segments , intermittent visual--inertial support~ tim_xu2025_intermittent , and texture--geometry coupling~ tim_zheng2025_texture to mitigate degeneracy. PVE-LIOM uses reflectivity-derived pseudo-images for failure and loop detection~ tim_dong2023_pve . Dynamic-object filtering suppresses contamination through visibility and spatial clustering within LiDAR-inertial estimation~ tim_li2026_doflio . Probabilistic geometric models incorporate uncertainty into estimation constraints. UA-LIO uses covariance-aware distribution-to-distribution constraints~ tim_wu2025_ualio , while point, line, and plane uncertainty informs LiDAR-inertial updates~ tim_zhang2026_geometric_uncertainty . Repeated observations of static structures also reveal inconsistency in registered geometry (Fig.~ fig:problem_statement ). The proposed monitor compares marginal support for identical current points under a persistent historical model and a weak observation-adaptive reference. Scoring precedes assimilation; alarms preserve the preceding state for subsequent comparisons, coupling consistency assessment to reference maintenance. Fault Monitoring and Robot Recovery Fault monitoring links measurement reliability to the information sources and control capabilities available during recovery. Wu et al.~ tim_wu2022_multimodal assess the health of localization subsystems using degeneration metrics and select the information sources entering a multimodal state estimator. Related multisensor systems employ diagnosis, reconfiguration, and failure-resistant fusion to maintain localization under faulty or degraded inputs~ us1,related_redundant1,related_redundant3 . The proposed monitor evaluates outputs from different SLAM backends through a common registered-cloud interface. In the UAV implementation, the resulting alarm triggers odometry isolation and landing; relocalization against a retained map then restores odometry for mission continuation. title: From Video to Digital Twin: An Exploratory Study of World Models and Gaussian Splatting on In-the-Wild Video
comment: 35 pages, 14 figures. Supplementary movies and code: https://github.com/pikulsomesh/foodbank-spatial-twin
summary: Generative world models and 3D Gaussian Splatting promise to turn ordinary video into explorable 3D scenes, but little is reported on how they behave on uncurated, in-the-wild footage. We study what these models recover when the only input is a publicly available news walkthrough of a food bank warehouse, with presenters walking through every shot and no drawings, scans or site visit, and we use the result as the geometry of a digital twin. A commercial world model given 20 frames recovered camera poses and metric depth for three areas, which we fused into about 747,000 Gaussian splats for 200 credits (20 US cents). Splat models optimized locally on a CPU, at no credit cost, were photorealistic near the filmed path but degraded quickly away from it. On held-out frames, scored in pixels not covered by people, they reached 21.2 and 23.1 dB PSNR from 64 and 43 training frames, and lost 3.8 and 5.4 dB when given only the 8 frames a world model accepts. Removing the trainer's background fill and person-hull carving raised held-out PSNR, showing that cleaning the space behind moving people costs fidelity in observed pixels while its gain lies where no ground truth exists. Asking the world model to generate views of areas the video never showed failed on the provider's side twice, so extrapolation could not be evaluated and unseen space was filled by a scripted model instead. We also describe the corrections needed to turn world-model output into a valid, metric Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD) asset with its native splat schema, which serves as the only interface to a data layer, a browser viewer, Blender and NVIDIA Omniverse. The findings suggest that today's models recover the observed parts of a real scene cheaply and at metric scale, while few-view fidelity and extrapolating unobserved space remain open. The work is an exploration of these methods, not a deployed product.

Introduction A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical asset that stays synchronized with it through data grieves2017digital,kritzinger2018digital . In industry, twins are used to plan layouts, monitor equipment and rehearse changes before they are made on the floor tao2019digital,fuller2020digital . The geometry of a facility twin is usually the expensive part. It comes from terrestrial laser scanning, photogrammetry campaigns or hand-built computer-aided design (CAD) models, and specialists then import it into a simulation tool. That cost is tolerable for an automotive plant. It is prohibitive for a regional food bank, which runs warehouse-scale cold-chain logistics on a non-profit budget. Two developments change that cost structure. Neural scene representations, and 3D Gaussian Splatting in particular kerbl20233d , produce photorealistic scenes that render in real time from ordinary images. Classical reconstruction recovers camera poses with structure-from-motion schoenberger2016sfm ; neural radiance fields mildenhall2020nerf improved view synthesis but render slowly; learned multi-view geometry such as DUSt3R wang2024dust3r reduces the number of views needed. All of these reconstruct only what was observed. Generative world models ha2018world,brooks2024video go further: from a few views they produce a coherent, explorable 3D world and fill in regions the input never covered. World Labs' Marble worldlabs_marble exposes this capability through an API that returns Gaussian-splat worlds. For a twin, generation has a double edge. It makes a sparse walkthrough usable, but it also invents geometry. Three lines of recent work bear directly on footage like ours. First, feed-forward geometry models predict poses and dense geometry from a handful of unposed images: DUSt3R wang2024dust3r , MASt3R leroy2024mast3r and VGGT wang2025vggt . Sparse-view splatting methods such as FSGS zhu2023fsgs and InstantSplat fan2024instantsplat build on such priors to train Gaussian splats from a few views. Second, in-the-wild reconstruction handles transient content, from appearance embeddings and transient masks for radiance fields (NeRF in the Wild martinbrualla2020nerfw ) to distractor-robust splatting (WildGaussians kulhanek2024wildgaussians , SpotLessSplats sabour2024spotless ); the presenters who walk with the camera in our video are exactly such transients. Third, generative models synthesize unobserved views: multi-view diffusion (CAT3D gao2024cat3d ), video diffusion conditioned on a point cloud (ViewCrafter yu2024viewcrafter ) and interactive world models trained on video (Genie bruce2024genie ). Faster and anti-aliased radiance fields muller2022instantngp,barron2022mipnerf360 set the evaluation conventions we follow: novel-view metrics on held-out frames. We do not benchmark these methods; we use a commercial world model and a standard 3DGS objective as representatives and measure what they recover from one uncurated video. In parallel, Universal Scene Description (OpenUSD), originally from Pixar and now developed under the Alliance for OpenUSD, has become an open, vendor-neutral scene description with layered composition and typed schemas openusd,aousd . Its 26.03 release added the schema family aousd2603,usd_gsplat_schema , so a splat reconstruction is no longer a viewer-specific file. It can sit in the same stage as sensors, equipment and annotations. NVIDIA Omniverse omniverse is a set of libraries that bring OpenUSD data interoperability, RTX rendering and physics simulation into applications. Its licensing is mixed: some components are open source, while the Kit SDK is distributed under NVIDIA's own license terms: the Kit App Template states that its software and materials are governed by the NVIDIA Software License Agreement and the Product-Specific Terms for NVIDIA Omniverse kit_app_template , not an open-source license. Surveys of digital twins identify geometry acquisition, data integration and interoperability as the recurring barriers tao2019digital,fuller2020digital . This work addresses the first and third barriers directly and keeps the second deliberately thin. This paper is an exploratory study of the learning methods behind the first barrier. We ask three questions: what a world model and locally optimized Gaussian splats recover from uncurated, publicly available video with no CAD drawings, laser scans or site visit; whether the generative step can fill in space the camera never saw; and what it takes to carry the result into an open scene format that other tools can use. To answer them we compose existing models into a three-step pipeline (Figure~ fig:overview ) and apply it to one realistic input, a news walkthrough of a food bank. The steps are: Video to digital twin with world models. Blur-aware frame extraction feeds a world model that returns a Gaussian-splat world, which is converted to an OpenUSD stage in metric, Y-up coordinates. Where the camera saw too little, a facility model scripted in Blender fills in the building, published in the same format. Connecting existing data systems on Amazon Web Services (AWS). A serverless API exposes operational data in the twin's coordinate frame through a small, versioned JSON contract. The reference implementation simulates cold-chain telemetry; the contract is designed so that a real sensor feed or warehouse management system can replace the simulator without changing any renderer. NVIDIA Omniverse as the visualization layer. Omniverse renders the USD twin with RTX on a rented GPU; binding live data to scene objects is the planned next step. A browser viewer and Blender read the same USD and the same JSON, so the renderer is a deployment choice rather than an architectural one. We do not propose a new model; the contribution is an empirical account of how current models behave on in-the-wild input. It has three parts: held-out novel-view scores for Gaussian splats trained on the footage, with the number of input frames and the handling of people who walk with the camera varied (Table~ tab:heldout ); a qualitative comparison with a world-model capture from eight frames, including where each fails; and a report that the world model's generative step could not be evaluated because it failed on the provider's side. The engineering needed to use the result (coordinate and packaging fixes that make world-model output a valid metric OpenUSD asset, a data backend, viewers and an operational technology security design) is summarized in Results and detailed in Appendix~ app:system . Food banks are logistics operations: when the Central Texas Food Bank moved into its 135,000-square-foot Austin facility in 2016, the new building held seven times the refrigeration and freezer capacity of the old one ctfb2016facility , and its newer Waco hub combines a warehouse and distribution hub, a kitchen, a food market and a training center in 64,000 square feet kxxv2026waco . Cold storage at that scale is exactly what a twin with live temperatures is meant to watch. The case study is a representative Texas food bank, not a model of any one facility. It is inspired by the Central Texas Food Bank: three of its areas are captured from a public walkthrough of one of that food bank's buildings, and its operating volumes are anchored to published figures for another. The rest of the building is designed for this paper, and all live data is simulated. Table~ tab:provenance states where every part of the twin comes from, and the figures show captured, designed and simulated content so that they can be told apart. The aim is to show what a food bank's twin looks like and what it takes to build one, not to describe a particular site. Results Three steps joined by one open contract The steps share data, not code. Two artifacts cross step boundaries (Table~ tab:contracts ). The reconstruction step publishes a USD package, the SPZ splat file it was converted from (for lightweight viewers) and a metadata file recording scale, ground offset and provenance. The data step publishes a JSON document whose positions are in meters in the same frame as the USD stage. A renderer needs nothing else, which is what lets Omniverse, a browser and Blender coexist (Figure~ fig:overview ). A walkthrough news video yields usable input for three zones The input was a public news walkthrough of a new Central Texas Food Bank facility, which by its broadcaster and on-screen campaign appears to be the Waco hub kxxv2026waco (18\,min\,32\,s, 1920\, \,1080 at 59.94 frames per second) kxxv2026ctfb . Two people appear in almost every shot and a lower-third graphic is burned into each frame, which makes it a realistic rather than a curated input. A multi-image world needs overlapping views of one space, so we targeted a single zone. Surveying the video at one frame every 10\,s gave the candidate zones in Table~ tab:zones . The pallet-racking aisle was captured first, because the camera circles one bay and then looks down the aisle, and because it is the zone that matters most for inventory locations, forklift paths and telemetry. The volunteer sorting room and the client market were captured in a second run, from narrower windows in which the camera moves enough to give overlapping views. The other operating areas of the representative food bank (receiving, freezer, cooler and order staging) were not captured: they are designed footprints in the operations layer, drawn by a modeled facility, not generated or reconstructed geometry (Table~ tab:provenance ). The community kitchen was captured later by local training only. Automatic frame selection failed on this footage. Ranking frames by variance of the Laplacian, a standard sharpness score, rewards in-focus faces, and on this video it selected six near-identical shots of the presenters. title: DreamVLA: From Generated Human Motions to Humanoid Vision-Language-Action Policies
comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026 workshops G2A: From Generative Models to Robot Actions and Open Problems in Contact-Rich Loco-Manipulation
summary: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically depends on substantial robot demonstration data, making human teleoperation a costly and cumbersome bottleneck, particularly for whole-body humanoid interaction. Reinforcement learning in simulation offers an alternative for scaling this data, but designing task-specific rewards remains challenging. To address this, we propose DreamVLA, which uses generated motion trajectories to guide reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, converting them into reliable task execution trajectories. These trajectories train VLA models in simulation without new task-specific teleoperation data. Our central contribution is a reference-conditioned DAgger distillation procedure: after a failed learner rollout, we restart the RL expert from a sampled learner state with the same reference suffix and aggregate successful corrective trajectories, addressing the distribution shift left by offline imitation. We evaluate picking from a platform, opening a drawer, pressing a button, and walking and picking from a platform, with ablations of DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated dataset scale. Project website: ember-center-berkeley.github.io/DreamVLA.
full_text: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies typically depends on substantial robot demonstration data, making human teleoperation a costly and cumbersome bottleneck, particularly for whole-body humanoid interaction. Reinforcement learning in simulation offers an alternative for scaling this data, but designing task-specific rewards remains challenging. To address this, we propose DreamVLA, which uses generated motion trajectories to guide reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, converting them into reliable task execution trajectories. These trajectories train VLA models in simulation without new task-specific teleoperation data. Our central contribution is a reference-conditioned DAgger distillation procedure: after a failed learner rollout, we restart the RL expert from a sampled learner state with the same reference suffix and aggregate successful corrective trajectories, addressing the distribution shift left by offline imitation. We evaluate picking from a platform, opening a drawer, pressing a button, and walking and picking from a platform, with ablations of DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated dataset scale. \\ Project website: . Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer a common interface for mapping visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot behavior. Models such as OpenVLA and GR00T learn from robot demonstrations and can be adapted to downstream tasks through additional training~ openvla,groot . For a humanoid, these demonstrations must coordinate reaching, hand interaction, torso motion, foot placement, and balance. A hierarchical interface can use a low-level (system-1) controller such as SONIC~ sonic to execute robot motion tokens supplied by a higher-level policy or a human teleoperation interface. Using this interface, an operator collects interactive demonstrations for VLA training. Collecting this behavior repeatedly across scene configurations demands operator time, a suitable teleoperation interface, and careful supervision. Increasing the number of tasks and environmental variations therefore increases the human effort required to build useful training data. Simulation offers a way to scale this data, but replacing a teleoperator with an autonomous data generator introduces a control problem. Reinforcement learning in simulation with sparse task success gives a high-dimensional humanoid little guidance for approaching a target while maintaining balance dreamcontrol . Dense rewards can support exploration, yet often require task-specific choices about reaching, posture, contact, timing, and object progress viral,doorman . A policy can also satisfy parts of a reward while producing behavior that is poorly suited to imitation. Consequently, the usefulness of simulated demonstrations depends on both physical task completion and the quality of the behavior used to achieve it. Generative human motion models provide a complementary source of structure. Text and spatial constraints can specify the intended behavior and the location of an interaction, yielding whole-body motion references with a human motion prior. DreamControl combines such references with RL for humanoid scene interaction~ dreamcontrol . This motivates using generated motion as a scalable source of supervision for downstream VLA training. The remaining challenge is to turn kinematic intent into repeatable interactions with movable objects, and then transfer that competence to a policy that receives images and language. Reward design remains part of this process, but references provide a unified framework for task-reward specification. We propose , a framework for producing task demonstrations in simulation from generated human motions and distilling them into a VLA. We first generate task-conditioned references with DreamControl, using OmniControl to constrain relevant human joints at target locations and times~ omnicontrol . After retargeting these motions to the Unitree G1, we train an expert to co-track the humanoid and the interacting object. We use SONIC as the whole-body control backbone~ sonic , and learn residual corrections in its motion-token interface to adapt the reference behavior to contact and randomized physics. The resulting expert acts as an automated demonstration generator: motion synthesis supplies the intended human-like behavior, and RL supplies the physically executed interaction. Successful rollouts are recorded as a LeRobot dataset and used to fine-tune GR00T. This construction is analogous to collecting teleoperation data with a generative model supplying the motion commands. It removes the need to have a human operate the robot for every downstream demonstration while retaining an interface suited to whole-body control. The human motion prior and the pretrained control and VLA backbones remain valuable upstream resources. Our claim concerns eliminating new task-specific teleoperation collection for the simulated tasks, rather than eliminating human data from the pretraining of those resources. We formulate each interactive task using motion references, object behavior, and a success specification; the present study evaluates four tasks. The central research question is how to distill this expert into a VLA that remains competent under its own closed-loop execution. Successful expert trajectories are a useful starting point, but they emphasize states reached by the expert. A student that grasps slightly late, approaches a handle at a different angle, or misaligns its fingertip can visit states absent from that dataset. Its next action changes the next observation, allowing small errors to compound. Collecting more clean demonstrations may improve coverage of nominal behavior without providing the corrective behavior needed after these deviations. Offline imitation alone therefore leaves a gap between supervised action prediction and reliable interaction. We address this gap through a reference-conditioned DAgger distillation procedure that collects corrective trajectories after learner failures. Standard DAgger aggregates expert labels on states encountered by the learner~ dagger , and prior humanoid teacher--student systems such as VIRAL already use online DAgger~ viral . Our task-specific adaptation queries a generated-motion, residual-SONIC expert at a randomly sampled state of a failed learner rollout. The expert resumes with the suffix of the same generated reference, and only successful recovery trajectories are added to the aggregate. This supplies temporally consistent corrective demonstrations for the language-conditioned VLA while retaining the reference context required by the expert. The evaluation is organized around picking from a platform, opening a drawer, pressing a button, and walking and picking from a platform in simulation. These tasks expose distinct interaction requirements: establishing and maintaining a grasp, driving an articulated object, reaching a precise contact target, and combining locomotion with grasping. We present results from controlled studies of the number of DAgger iterations, the residual control formulation, and the amount of generated training data. Together, task completion, motion fidelity, and the student--expert performance gap characterize demonstration quality and the competence retained through distillation. Our three contributions are: A generative demonstration framework. We propose a pipeline that uses generated human motions and residual RL on a SONIC backbone to collect natural, human-like interaction demonstrations for VLA training in simulation, without task-specific human teleoperation collection. A DAgger-based VLA distillation method. We propose using the RL expert to supervise the VLA on learner-visited states, with reference-conditioned expert recovery and success-filtered trajectory aggregation as the methodological contribution. A four-task simulation study with controlled ablations. We evaluate platform picking, drawer opening, button pressing, and walking and picking with controlled ablations of DAgger iterations, residual RL, and generated data scale. Related Work sec:relatedwork Humanoid Motion Tracking and Teleoperation Human-motion priors support humanoid tracking and whole-body control~ deepmimic,amp,phc,exbody2,beyondmimic,asap,pgmt , while camera, VR, and portable interfaces support teleoperation and demonstration collection~ h2o,omnih2o,humanplus,twist,humanoidumi,wb_umi . We use SONIC's motion-token interface~ sonic to turn generated references into autonomous interaction demonstrations. Generated motions supply the nominal commands in our pipeline, and task-specific residual RL adjusts their execution at contact without collecting new teleoperated demonstrations. Vision-Language-Action Learning for Humanoids Humanoid VLAs connect visual-language representations to executable behavior through multimodal pretraining and reusable motor controllers~ groot,groot16,groot17,helix,helix02,helix25 . Synthetic kinematic and optimal-control demonstrations also provide supervision for whole-body visual policies~ vlk,wolfvla . DreamVLA uses a generated-motion, residual-SONIC expert to produce physically executed interactions and reference-conditioned corrective trajectories for GR00T. We fine-tune an existing VLA backbone and study demonstration generation and corrective supervision, without introducing a new model architecture. Visual Sim-to-Real Across Embodiments Across manipulation, legged, and aerial embodiments, visual sim-to-real combines simulated experience with perception randomization, privileged supervision, or reconstructed scenes~ domainrandomization,dexhand,dextreme,viserdex,rialto,transic,dextera,molmobot,flare,perceptivelocomotion,parkour,umi_on_legs,navila,flight . Humanoid pipelines use teacher--student distillation~ viral,doorman . We study VLA distillation in simulation. Our pipeline shares privileged-to-visual supervision with these humanoid systems, while isolating motion-guided expert training and corrective VLA distillation without visual domain randomization. Motion Generation, Retargeting, and Synthetic Demonstrations Language-conditioned motion models provide interaction references~ mdm,t2mgpt,motiongpt,omnicontrol,omomo,chois , while retargeting and demonstration augmentation adapt motions to robot morphology and new scenes~ gmr,omniretarget,mimicgen,skillgen,humanoidmimicgen . Generative video and simulated experts offer complementary routes to synthetic policy data~ gen2act,dreamgen,mimicdreamer,dreamzero,video2policy . We build on DreamControl~ dreamcontrol to produce physically executed SONIC demonstrations from guided human motion. Residual RL resolves the contact dynamics left by kinematic synthesis, and successful-rollout filtering converts the resulting interactions into executable action labels for VLA training. Expert Distillation and Corrective Data Aggregation DAgger-style distillation addresses learner-induced distribution shift~ dagger,hgdagger,rewarddagger,viral . title: Zero-Shot VLA Adaptation with Retrieved Guidance
summary: Pre-training large parametric "Vision-Language-Action" (VLA) models on large demonstration datasets has recently yielded promising results for general-purpose manipulation. However, these models still struggle under even small domain shifts relative to the training data, such as changes in camera viewpoint, background, object identity, or robot morphology. Motivated by the success of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in language models, we pursue retrieval to boost VLA performance. Specifically, we seek to leverage retrieval from domain-mismatched, "in-the-wild" demonstration datasets like DROID to guide a VLA's behavior in a new target domain. To achieve this, we introduce RAGu, which overcomes robotics-specific challenges for RAG: (1) It incorporates simple geometric calibration to transform source demonstrations into the target setup and reduce cross-domain differences. (2) It uses a coarse-to-fine retrieval strategy that selects, from a large pool of pre-warped candidates, the trajectory most compatible with the base VLA. (3) It guides the VLA's flow-matching inference procedure rather than seeking to retrain the base model or expand its limited context window. We evaluate RAGu across real-world, simulation, sim-to-real transfer, and cross-embodiment humanoid manipulation. We find it improves real-world VLA success rates from 20% to 80% and outperforms the closest-related baselines in sim. Project website: raguvla.github.io

Project website: raguvla.github.io INTRODUCTION sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged in recent years as a key step toward generalist robots. However, their ability to generalize still falls short of foundation models in language, vision, and coding. One reason is that, in robotics, both pretraining datasets and the models trained on them remain relatively small, with the latter constrained by the need for near-real-time execution. As a result, VLAs still struggle to generalize across variations in camera viewpoint, scene background, object identity, and robot embodiment. For language models, ``retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)"~ lewis2020retrieval is a well-established technique to boost performance, especially of small models. Given a new query, RAG fetches relevant documents from a large database, typically through nearest neighbor search in an appropriate feature space, and places them into the model's context to guide its performance on the target task. This augments the limited ``parametric knowledge'' of the small language model with ``non-parametric knowledge'' in the form of the retrieved examples. In this paper, we seek to develop a RAG-style mechanism to improve generalization in vision-language-action (VLA) models. We target three key problems in implementing RAG for robotics: (1) Cross-Domain Generalization. Robotic data suffers from severe distribution shifts in camera viewpoints, layouts, and embodiments, unlike the universal token space of LLMs. For a given target scenario, even the best-matched trajectories in large-scale robotics datasets are still likely to exhibit such domain-shifts. Prior robotic retrieval and RAG-style methods therefore restrict retrieval pools to narrow, identical-embodiment datasets or rely on task-specific fine-tuning of policy networks~ memmel2025strap, regent2025, sridhar2025ricl , fundamentally limiting their overall utility. (2) Policy-Aware Retrieval. Good retrievals must be policy-aware. Proximity based on simple measures like geometry do not suffice for a robot policy to follow a retrieved trajectory smoothly and stably. (3) Context-Efficient Adaptation. VLAs have limited context windows that do not permit directly concatenating retrieved demonstration trajectories to current observations. We propose ( ), a zero-shot, training-free VLA adaptation framework depicted in Figure~ fig:metaworld_droid , that handles all three challenges: Cross-Domain Generalization. It handles domain shifts through explicit injection of geometric and semantic priors based on Cartesian spatial traces in source data. Policy-Aware Retrieval. It selects source trajectories for guidance based on compatibility with the VLA rather than only geometric proximity, and this selection is scaled efficiently through offline pre-warping and lightweight online scoring. Context-Efficient Adaptation. Finally, rather than concatenating retrieved examples to the VLA's input, it constructs a test-time guidance field to steer the VLA's outputs. Related Work Retrieval and In-Context Learning for VLAs. Recent methods adapt VLA models using retrieval and in-context examples. REGENT~ regent2025 , RICL~ sridhar2025ricl and RA-VLA~ jang2026ra retrieve demonstrations to improve adaptation to new tasks or environments, while STRAP~ memmel2025strap retrieves relevant sub-trajectories to support test-time policy learning. Unlike our training-free framework, these methods all require in-domain trajectories as source demonstrations to support parametric adaptation. Inference-Time Steering of Generative Policies. Works such as VLS~ liu2026vls , Omniguide~ omniguide2026 , and DemoDiffusion~ du2023demodiffusion frame adaptation as inference-time control by using external energy fields to steer generative policies, similar to our . However, these methods typically assume human demonstrations or depend on sparse, VLM-induced waypoints, and they lack a mechanism to handle large kinematic and spatial mismatches when the guidance comes from structurally different sources. specifically targets this domain mismatch. Cross-Domain Generalization with Trace Spaces. Prior works abstract manipulation into 3D representations~ molmoact2025, liang2026tether, zhang2025peek or train unified models for cross-domain transfer~ shi2025zeromimic, li2025novaflow , yet both rely on parametric training. In contrast, requires no retraining, enabling frozen VLAs to leverage cross-domain trajectories beyond their original distribution. Background sec:background Inference-Time Steering for VLA Policies. At time-step \(t\), we model the VLA as a flow-matching policy that maps a noisy action representation \( A_0 \) to a clean action chunk \( A_1 = [a_t, a_ t+1 , , a_ t+H-1 ] \) over denoising time \( \) ~ omniguide2026, intelligence2025pi05 . During inference time, the model approximately integrates a conditional vector field \( v(A_ , o) \): \[ dA_ d = v(A_ , o), A_0 (0,I), A_ ^ H d , [0,1] (1) \] where \(o\) is the current observation, \(H\) is the horizon length of each action chunk, and \(d\) is robot joint space dimension. This steers action generation at inference time while leaving the policy parameters unchanged. We let \( y = [y_t, y_ t+1 , , y_ t+H-1 ] ^ H d \) denote the desired trajectory over the horizon, and \( _y(A_ ) = 2 \|A_ - y\|_2^2 \). Prior works have assumed \( y \) to be provided from human operator~ omniguide2026 or an external planner~ liu2026vls . In-Domain Trajectory Warping. Recent work such as Tether~ liang2026tether extract critical 3D waypoints \( W = \ w_1, , w_T\ \) from source demonstrations and map them to target waypoints \( W' = \ w'_1, , w'_T\ \) via visual correspondences, to handle novel but within-domain scene configurations. Intermediate actions \( a_t \) between \( w_i \) and \( w_ i+1 \) are then warped to \( a'_t = a_t + ( (1 - )\, d_i + \, d_ i+1 ) \), based on displacements \( d_i = w'_i - w_i \) and interpolation \( [0,1] \) to execute inverse kinematics. As shown in Figure~ fig:metaworld_droid , first filters semantically relevant demonstrations and warps them into the target scene via semantic correspondences, turning cross-domain demonstrations into usable spatial priors. It then retrieves the guiding trajectory via coarse offline dynamic time-warping (DTW)-based pruning followed by policy-compatible selection at inference time, avoiding control-loop overhead. We achieve this by filtering unstructured real-world datasets~ khazatsky2024droid using semantic keywords for broad task categories that share similar kinematic profiles. For example, we query demonstrations with keyword "pick" and "place" included for the task, "putting towel on the plate". See Fig~ fig:metaworld_droid (a). Once these semantic correspondences are established, the remainder of the trajectory warping process proceeds identically to the formulation described in Section sec:background . title: BAT-WAM: Bridging Action and Touch in World-Action Models for Dexterous Hands
summary: Dexterous manipulation with world action models (WAMs) relies on hand configuration and contact information, yet joint-state and whole-hand tactile observations may be partially or entirely missing. RGB images provide scene context and hand-object geometry but are insufficient to reliably recover these missing modalities. We further observe a correlation between hand state and tactile information. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BAT-WAM, a framework that bridges visual, joint-state, and tactile representations for WAMs. BAT-WAM learns separate codebooks and decoders for the tactile and action streams. An RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge connects the two streams for bidirectional learning, while visual information serves as continuous context. Under the HTBench evaluation protocol, BAT-WAM reduces the root mean squared error (RMSE) of tactile reconstruction by 34.73% under fully masked conditions and 38.84% under partially masked conditions, relative to an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint. For future tactile prediction conditioned on target-time RGB and historical actions, it reduces mean RMSE by 85.56% relative to OpenWAM with HandTouch. Real-robot experiments further show that BAT-WAM consistently outperforms related WAM baselines in dexterous manipulation. Generalization experiments on unseen objects and scenes also demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline models. These findings support joint modeling of visual context, hand state, and touch as a representation approach for multimodal WAMs.

Dexterous manipulation with world action models (WAMs) relies on hand configuration and contact information, yet joint-state and whole-hand tactile observations may be partially or entirely missing. RGB images provide scene context and hand–object geometry but are insufficient to reliably recover these missing modalities. We further observe a correlation between hand state and tactile information. Motivated by this observation, we introduce BAT-WAM, a framework that bridges visual, joint-state, and tactile representations for WAMs. BAT-WAM learns separate codebooks and decoders for the tactile and action streams. An RGB-conditioned continuous latent bridge connects the two streams for bidirectional learning, while visual information serves as continuous context. Under the HTBench evaluation protocol, BAT-WAM reduces the root mean squared error (RMSE) of tactile reconstruction by 34.73 under fully masked conditions and 38.84 under partially masked conditions, relative to an image-conditioned HandTouch checkpoint. For future tactile prediction conditioned on target-time RGB and historical actions, it reduces mean RMSE by 85.56 relative to OpenWAM with HangTouch. Real-robot experiments further show that BAT-WAM consistently outperforms related WAM baselines in dexterous manipulation. Generalization experiments on unseen objects and scenes also demonstrate substantial improvements over baseline models. These findings support joint modeling of visual context, hand state, and touch as a representation approach for multimodal WAMs. Introduction sec:introduction Contact-rich dexterous manipulation depends on the interplay between scene geometry, hand configuration, and physical contact. RGB images provide object appearance and visible hand--object geometry; tactile observations (Touch) capture contact locations and pressure distributions; and joint states (States) describe hand configuration and kinematic coordination. These modalities provide complementary information, but similar visual observations can conceal different interaction states. For example, two images of a hand grasping a cup may appear nearly identical, even when one grasp maintains stable contact and the other is beginning to slip. Such ambiguity motivates representations that capture fine differences in hand configuration and contact, consistent with the importance of tactile feedback in reactive manipulation niu2026trex . Recent work has developed several interfaces for incorporating proprioception and dexterous hand states into world action model (WAM) systems. For example, OpenWAM- ~ wang2026openwam linearly projects the robot's 80-dimensional proprioceptive state into a single context token. This token is appended to the language context and conditions both the video and action streams through cross-attention. For dexterous hands, UniDexTok learns discrete state representations through a standardized hand interface, while UniHM couples cross-embodiment hand-motion tokenization with language-guided manipulation fang2026unidextok,zhang2026unihm . These approaches address the challenge of making structured, high-dimensional hand information accessible to token-based models. In parallel, tactile VLA and world action model (WAM) research has expanded the role of touch in policy learning. Tactile-VLA and VLA-Touch incorporate tactile information into action generation, feedback, and control huang2025tactilevla,bi2025vlatouch . VT-WAM, Tactile-WAM, and DreamTacVLA model future tactile observations alongside visual or action information tian2026vtwam,wu2026tactilewam,ye2025dreamtacvla , while -VTLA uses predictive latent tactile tokens to condition action generation neoteai2026n0vtla . Building on these interfaces, we investigate a specific representation problem: how can Touch and Joint supervise one another within an RGB-conditioned interface while retaining their distinct physical meanings and data structures? This question is motivated by the physical coupling between hand configuration and contact. Joint states constrain where fingers can engage an object, while tactile measurements provide evidence about the contacts realized by that configuration. RGB supplies the scene context needed to interpret these relationships. HT-Bench, which pairs egocentric vision with full-hand tactile observations, provides a basis for studying visually conditioned contact representations huang2026htbench . We hypothesize that explicitly learning conditional dependencies between Touch and Joint can help resolve ambiguities that remain in visual observations and support inference when part of either modality is unavailable. We introduce BAT-WAM, a multimodal representation interface designed for use by WAM backbones. BAT-WAM bridges state and contact information, while retaining RGB as the context. A continuous bridging module balances modality-specific token budgets and models interactions among hand configuration, contact state, and scene context. This design preserves distinct quantization and reconstruction pathways for Touch and Joint while allowing their representations to interact. Through conditional reconstruction, each modality can provide information for recovering the other: a modality serves as observed context in one masking configuration and as a supervision target in another, with RGB conditioning the inference. The interface supports both static masked completion and conditional future tactile prediction. Each task explicitly specifies which observations are visible to the model and which signals are used only as supervision. Static completion examines reconstruction of missing information from the available context, while future prediction examines how observed joint-state history informs subsequent tactile states. Our contributions are threefold: We uncover a previously overlooked cross-modal relationship: a strong correlation between dexterous hand states and tactile observations. Building on this finding, we introduce BAT-WAM, a novel cross-modal representation framework that integrates discrete tactile and state representations with continuous RGB context through a multimodal bridging mechanism. BAT-WAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks for masked tactile completion and future tactile prediction, and outperforms the corresponding baselines in real-world experiments and zero-shot generalization evaluations. Related Work sec:related_work Proprioceptive State Representations Proprioceptive state representation learning focuses on encoding internal robot states, such as joint configurations, and integrating them with visual observations. Existing methods adopt different interfaces for incorporating these states: linearly projects continuous proprioceptive states into the Transformer embedding space~ black2024pi0 ; HPT uses embodiment-specific input encoders to map proprioceptive states and visual observations from heterogeneous robots into token sequences processed by a shared backbone~ wang2024hpt ; and discretizes proprioceptive states and encodes them as text tokens through the language tokenizer~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 . These approaches explore continuous embeddings, heterogeneous input alignment, and discrete text encoding, providing different representation interfaces through which policy models can access proprioceptive information. Proprioceptive states can also serve as reconstruction targets for representation learning. For high-dimensional dexterous hands, UniDexTok addresses state heterogeneity across hand embodiments by organizing human and robot joint states through a unified 22-DoF semantic interface and learning embodiment-conditioned discrete state representations~ fang2026unidextok . These studies provide foundations for state integration, cross-modal reconstruction, and unified state representations across embodiments. Building on this direction, BAT-WAM incorporates standardized Joint states and Touch into a common representation interface while retaining separate codebooks and decoders for the two modalities. Conditioned on continuous RGB context, it learns bidirectional dependencies between hand configuration and contact state through conditional reconstruction. Full-hand tactile representation Tactile representation learning includes continuous features, cross-sensor pretraining, and discrete tokenization. Sparsh learned visual-tactile representations with self-supervision, AnyTouch sought a common representation for static and dynamic information across visuotactile sensors, and VITaL supported tactile and non-tactile manipulation policies~ higuera2024sparsh,feng2025anytouch,george2024vital . VQ-VAE provided a standard route from continuous observations to a finite latent vocabulary~ oord2017vqvae , but pressure maps must also retain contact regions, spatial topology, and local intensity. HTBench/HandTouch was the closest full-hand tactile representation setting to ours. It used bimanual pressure maps and egocentric vision to learn discrete tactile representations and reconstruct pressure maps under visual conditioning~ huang2026htbench . BAT-WAM retains this spatial pressure interface but gives Joint state its own codebook and decoder, so configuration information enters the bridge in a reconstructable form. Tactile-enhanced VLA and world-action models Tactile information entered policies through continuous fusion, feedback control, prediction branches, and latent tokens. 3D-ViTac, Reactive Diffusion Policy, and T-Rex used vision and touch for fine-grained or reactive manipulation~ huang2025_3dvitac,xue2025rdp,niu2026trex , while TouchWorld developed a predictive model for tactile forecasting and reactive manipulation~ zhou2026touchworld . In VLA and WAM systems, Tactile-VLA and VLA-Touch used visual-language physical knowledge or layered feedback, while VT-WAM, Tactile-WAM, DreamTacVLA, and -VTLA studied visuotactile action prediction, asymmetric attention, tactile world models, and latent tactile tokens~ huang2025tactilevla,bi2025vlatouch,tian2026vtwam,wu2026tactilewam,ye2025dreamtacvla,neoteai2026n0vtla . These systems demonstrated the value of touch for contact control, but their inputs typically entered as continuous features, external feedback, prediction branches, or latent tokens. BAT-WAM specifies a narrower interface: Touch and states have separately decodable physical vocabularies, cross-modal relations are learned in a continuous bridge, RGB remains continuous context, and the resulting prefix is used for backbone observation optimization. Method sec:method BAT-WAM encodes tactile observations and hand joint states under RGB conditioning, producing a set of additional input tokens for the \( _ 0.5 \) backbone. Figure~ fig:backbone_optimization gives the complete interface. Modality-Specific Tokenizers sec:tokenizers Touch is a dense spatial pressure field, whereas Joint is a low-dimensional vector describing the hand configuration. Given their different data structures, we use a separate encoder , projection layer , codebook , and physical decoder for each modality . The encoder first extracts features, which the projection layer then maps into the quantization space. Let denote the -th projected feature. Quantization is defined as where is the -th codebook vector and denotes the stop-gradient operation. Touch and Joint use separate codebooks. RGB follows an independent continuous encoding path: a frozen SigLIP encoder extracts image patch features zhai2023siglip , and learned queries produce context tokens from these features.
