title: RigidGS: Geometry-Aware Object Decoupling for Rigid-Body Interaction in 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at WACV 2027 (Applications Track). Project page: https://gyreyirisansah.github.io/rigidgs
summary: Interactive VR/MR applications demand photorealistic 3D representations that support real-time rendering and object-level manipulation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, it represents scenes as unstructured, monolithic primitives. Existing object-aware 3DGS methods jointly optimize geometry and semantic states but suffer from two key failure modes: noisy foundation-model masks on complex geometry, and label-geometry coupling, in which co-optimized identity gradients mislabel boundary Gaussians. We introduce RigidGS, an end-to-end pipeline that decouples geometric learning from object identity. We propose a depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement module that addresses two complementary SAM2 failures: over-inclusion on thin structures and under-inclusion on multimodal-depth objects. We then determine object identities entirely upstream via COLMAP projection voting and freeze them during training, directing mask supervision solely toward geometric optimization. Refined masks alone substantially improve competing methods, yet a residual gap in label-geometry coupling persists that our fixed-identity design eliminates. RigidGS outperforms prior object-aware 3DGS methods on LLFF/NVOS, Mip-NeRF~360, and iNeRF360, improving segmentation and boundary IoU by 7.7 and 14.5 points on LLFF/NVOS. Finally, RigidGS enables real-time rigid-body manipulation on Meta Quest~2 without mesh extraction. Our code and project page are available at https://gyreyirisansah.github.io/rigidgs.

Introduction sec:intro Virtual and Mixed Reality (VR/MR) applications require photorealistic 3D scene representations that support real-time rendering and object-level interaction~ vr-gs, vr-splat, gs-verse, xin2025a3fr . While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ 3dgs achieves high-fidelity novel-view synthesis with efficient rasterization, it models scenes as a monolithic set of primitives lacking persistent object membership, preventing the object-level manipulation, removal, and physics-based interaction that immersive environments require~ vr-gs, wang2025decoupledgaussian . Recent approaches add object structure by learning semantic state over the Gaussian field, via identity embeddings~ gaussian-grouping , linear programming~ flashsplat , graph cuts~ gaussiancut , lifted foundation features~ cen2025segment , boundary-adaptive attributes~ Zhang_2025_CVPR , or anchor collections~ zhu2025objectgs . These methods rest on two assumptions that often lead to poor segmentation: that 2D foundation models provide accurate mask supervision, and that semantic identity can be safely co-optimized with geometry. SAM2 frequently errs on complex geometry, showing over-inclusion on thin, elongated structures and under-inclusion on multimodal-depth objects~ Zhang_quantifying . Moreover, co-optimizing identity with geometry induces a label--geometry coupling: semantic gradients depend on the geometry of non-converged neighbors, pulling boundary primitives toward erroneous object ownership. We present RigidGS, an end-to-end framework that decouples geometric learning from semantic identity. RigidGS first corrects the two SAM2 failure modes with a depth- and temporally-aware refinement pipeline: neighboring refined masks are flow-warped into each view and, on disagreement with raw SAM2, trigger re-prompting from depth-consistent donor candidates, after which a strict-grid KNN depth threshold (via Depth-Anything-V2) and a ridge-fill step recover thin structures and remove depth-inconsistent regions. Each Gaussian is then labeled once by COLMAP-projection voting on the refined masks~ colmap with a spatial KNN cleanup, and these labels are frozen before geometric optimization: a 2D mask BCE loss supervises only geometry and appearance while identities propagate unchanged through densification and pruning. Determining identity entirely upstream eliminates the label--geometry coupling that affects methods with learnable per-Gaussian semantic state. Running COB-GS~ Zhang_2025_CVPR with our refined masks substantially closes its background-bleeding gap on multimodal-depth scenes ( IoU on trex; ), yet a residual gap remains because identity is co-optimized: learnable-identity methods avoid collapse only through reactive mechanisms such as COB-GS's boundary-adaptive splitting, at the cost of extra primitives and residual bleed, whereas our fixed-identity design removes the coupling by construction. On LLFF/NVOS~ ren2022neural RigidGS improves IoU by and boundary IoU by points over COB-GS, and also leads on Mip-NeRF~360~ mip-nerf-360 and iNeRF360. RigidGS runs at interactive rates on a Quest~2 deployment. We complement the trained representation with LaMa-based background inpainting and refinement~ lama, spin-nerf, wang2026inpaint360gs, lee2026gpgs , and demonstrate rigid-body interaction via affine transforms on Gaussian subsets, using game-engine physics rather than baking expensive physics-based models~ vr-gs, physgaussian . . [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] A depth- and temporally-aware mask refinement preprocessor that resolves SAM2 over- and under-inclusion, as a drop-in module for 2D-supervised 3DGS methods. A decoupled 3DGS formulation in which object identity is fixed upstream and frozen, restricting the mask loss to geometric optimization and eliminating label--geometry coupling by construction. An end-to-end 3DGS VR system supporting real-time rigid-body manipulation and inpainting, deployed on a Meta Quest~2. Related Work 3D Gaussian Splatting for immersive rendering. NeRF~ nerf introduced coordinate-based volumetric scene representations, but its ray-marching formulation makes real-time interaction difficult. title: Decentralised Drone Swarm Formation under Silent Failures with ACO Pheromone Claims and PSO Tuning
comment: 19 pages, 7 figures, 22 tables. Code, browser demo and raw results are included as ancillary files
summary: We study decentralised drone formation, without a central planner, under the conditions that make it hard: nobody knows how many drones are alive, failures are silent, radio is short-ranged and lossy, and actuation is noisy. In our controller, ant colony optimisation (ACO) allocates drones to picture positions through claims that behave as reinforced, evaporating pheromone and are gossiped between neighbours, so evaporation doubles as failure detection. A particle swarm optimisation (PSO) law flies the drones, a noise-buffered Voronoi filter keeps them apart, and PSO also tunes the controller offline. We prove that claims of destroyed drones vanish within bounded time, that conflicts between drones that exchange tables are resolved consistently, that survivors cover the picture to within a factor of two, and that drones cannot collide while their safety cells are feasible. On held-out seeds and with two tuned configurations, the controller formed the picture in 95-99% of runs in the hardest regime, restored it after a silent loss of half the swarm in 96-100% of runs at normal difficulty, transferred unchanged to eight unseen shapes and to 300 drones, and overlapped in 5 of 21,088 runs. A CBBA-style baseline that shares the evaporating claims but uses argmax without swaps was at least as reliable as ours once tuned with the same budget, and repaired faster, whereas ours generalised better to unseen shapes. The benefit thus comes from the pheromone dynamics and from tuning, not from ACO's stochastic construction or PSO's social terms. A centralised oracle is faster.
full_text: Decentralised Drone Swarm Formation under Silent Failures with ACO Pheromone Claims and PSO Tuning We study decentralised drone formation, without a central planner, under the conditions that make it hard: nobody knows how many drones are alive, failures are silent, radio is short-ranged and lossy, and actuation is noisy. In our controller, ant colony optimisation (ACO) allocates drones to picture positions through claims that behave as reinforced, evaporating pheromone and are gossiped between neighbours, so evaporation doubles as failure detection. A particle swarm optimisation (PSO) law flies the drones, a noise-buffered Voronoi filter keeps them apart, and PSO also tunes the controller offline. We prove that claims of destroyed drones vanish within bounded time, that conflicts between drones that exchange tables are resolved consistently, that survivors cover the picture to within a factor of two, and that drones cannot collide while their safety cells are feasible. On held-out seeds and with two tuned configurations, the controller formed the picture in 95--99 of runs in the hardest regime, restored it after a silent loss of half the swarm in 96--100 of runs at normal difficulty, transferred unchanged to eight unseen shapes and to 300 drones, and overlapped in 5 of 21\,088 runs. A CBBA-style baseline that shares the evaporating claims but uses argmax without swaps was at least as reliable as ours once tuned with the same budget, and repaired faster, whereas ours generalised better to unseen shapes. The benefit thus comes from the pheromone dynamics and from tuning, not from ACO's stochastic construction or PSO's social terms. A centralised oracle is faster. swarm robotics, ant colony optimisation, particle swarm optimisation, decentralised task allocation, collision avoidance, fault tolerance, hyper-parameter optimisation Introduction Drone light shows, search-and-rescue teams and sensor deployments need many inexpensive aircraft to take up a prescribed arrangement while individual aircraft fail, join or lose contact. Formation methods that come with guarantees typically plan every assignment and trajectory centrally, from the positions of all drones~ turpin2014capt . The planner is then a single point of failure and a bandwidth bottleneck. A decentralised swarm, in which every drone decides from local information, removes both. It must, however, answer three questions without a coordinator: who goes where, how to fly there, and how to keep drones from colliding on the way. No single question here is hard on its own. The difficulty is that five conditions hold together in the field: nobody knows how many drones are alive, so any plan that counts the swarm first is outdated after the next loss; failures are silent, because a drone that crashes sends no farewell; radio is short-ranged and lossy, so two drones can believe they own the same position and must settle this without an arbiter; actuation noise moves drones in ways nobody commanded, which eats into every safety margin; every swarm algorithm has parameters, and values that work for one picture or radio condition may fail for another. Swarm intelligence offers a mechanism for most of these conditions. In ant colony optimisation (ACO)~ dorigo1996antsystem,dorigo1997acs,dorigo2004aco , ants coordinate through pheromone that is reinforced while it is useful and evaporates when it is not. Evaporating pheromone is a memory that fades unless it is refreshed, which is exactly what is needed to notice that a silent drone is gone. Reinforcement lets a well-founded claim prevail over a weaker one without a referee. In particle swarm optimisation (PSO)~ kennedy1995pso,shi1998inertia,clerc2002constriction , particles move under inertia and are drawn towards good positions found by themselves and their neighbours. This suggests a motion law that smooths noisy steps, and, used offline, a black-box optimiser for the controller's own parameters. Collision avoidance is the one requirement that we deliberately do not entrust to swarm intelligence. It must hold even while allocation is wrong, so it sits in an independent geometric filter that comes with a proof. ACO and PSO are well established for planning problems. Their use as the online control law of a physical, failure-prone swarm is much less settled, and the evidence offered for such uses is often thin: one scenario, a few seeds, hand-chosen parameters and weak baselines. We therefore pose four research questions and answer each with controlled experiments on held-out seeds. Can strictly local, pheromone-based allocation form a prescribed picture as reliably and quickly as established decentralised allocators, and how far is it from a centralised optimum? Does the swarm repair the picture after silent losses, joins and continuous churn, and what limits the speed of repair? Can collisions be excluded while the population changes, and at what cost? Which ingredients of ACO and PSO actually contribute, and does PSO-based tuning generalise beyond its training conditions? Our contributions are as follows. A controller with three local layers. The controller combines an ACO allocation layer, in which claims act as reinforced, evaporating pheromone gossiped between neighbours, with a PSO motion layer and a noise-buffered Voronoi safety filter. A priority ordering of the picture lets any number of drones form a recognisable image without counting themselves. Analysis. We prove that ghost claims of destroyed drones vanish from every table within bounded time, whatever the topology or packet loss; that a pairwise conflict is resolved consistently whenever the two drones exchange tables; that every prefix of the priority order covers the sampled picture to within a factor of two of the best possible; that the motion law is stable; and that drones cannot collide under arbitrary losses and joins as long as their safety cells are feasible, a condition that can fail in dense jams. We state where each guarantee ends. Evidence. We compare against a centralised optimal oracle and four decentralised allocators that share our motion and safety layers. The strongest of them, a CBBA-style allocator with reset, is also tuned five times with the same budget as our controller. The experiments cover: twelve shapes, eight of which were never used in design or tuning; four difficulty levels; losses, joins, churn and spare drones; swarms of up to 300 drones; ablations of every component; PSO tuning against random search, five runs per tuned controller under a train/validation/test split; two disjoint sets of test seeds, and two tuned configurations of each tuned controller in the main comparisons between them. The main finding is a negative one about the textbook ingredients: once the baseline is tuned as well, ACO's stochastic construction gives no advantage over deterministic construction, and PSO's social terms none over a damped controller. Run with identical parameters, argmax construction without swaps was at least as reliable in the hardest regime; in benign conditions, whichever rule the parameters had been tuned for was faster. What matters are the evaporating pheromone claims and the offline tuning. Artefacts. The simulator, all experiment code, the raw results and an interactive browser demonstration are released with the paper. Related Work Swarm intelligence in robotics. Bonabeau et al.~ bonabeau1999swarm and the survey of Brambilla et al.~ brambilla2013swarm describe stigmergy and self-organisation as the basis of robust, scalable swarms. Rubenstein et al.~ rubenstein2014kilobot showed that a thousand simple robots can assemble prescribed shapes from local rules and gradient information, with a fixed team of identical robots. Ant robots that lay evaporating, repelling traces cover terrain robustly even when robots fail~ wagner1999evaporating,svennebring2004antrobots ; our claim pheromone uses evaporation in the same coordinating role, but for allocation rather than coverage. We address aerial robots that must also avoid each other and that may be removed or added during the mission. Task allocation. Gerkey and Matari\'c~ gerkey2004taxonomy classify multi-robot task allocation. Our setting is single-task robots and single-robot tasks with instantaneous assignment. Dias et al.~ dias2006market survey market-based methods. The consensus-based bundle algorithm (CBBA)~ choi2009cbba resolves conflicts by max-consensus on bids and is the standard decentralised baseline; we reproduce its single-assignment core with and without its reset mechanism. Turpin et al.~ turpin2014capt solve assignment and trajectory planning for formations centrally and with guarantees, and our oracle plays the same role. Pujol-Gonzalez et al.~ pujol2018lorp and Albani et al.~ albani2021hierarchical study allocation under limited communication. Pheromone- and market-inspired UAV coordination has recently appeared in search and rescue~ zhu2026mountain,giacomossi2026market . These works target coverage or task streams rather than a prescribed spatial picture, and none combines claim-pheromone evaporation with a separation filter that comes with a proof. We do not claim primacy; we could not find a head-to-head comparison and therefore built one. Formation control. Planar shapes have been assigned with Fourier descriptors~ petitprez2023planar . Flocking drones with optimised local rules have flown outdoors~ vasarhelyi2018flocking , and learning-based controllers handle dynamic topology~ chen2026madrl . Reynolds' boids~ reynolds1987boids introduced separation, alignment and cohesion. These approaches either form shapes with a fixed team, flock without a prescribed picture, or learn a policy that must be trained. Our controller handles a changing team without training, but it does need a template. Collision avoidance. Reactive separation forces, as in boids, give no guarantee. Reciprocal velocity obstacles (ORCA)~ vandenberg2011orca and buffered Voronoi cells (BVC)~ zhou2017bvc give decentralised guarantees under their assumptions. We adopt BVC because its constraint set is a simple intersection of half-planes whose pairwise disjointness yields a short proof, and we extend it with an explicit noise buffer. Parameter tuning. Hand-set metaheuristic parameters are a known source of unreported degrees of freedom. Eiben and Smit~ eiben2011tuning and the irace package~ lopezibanez2016irace argue for explicit, budgeted tuning, and Bergstra and Bengio~ bergstra2012random show that random search is a strong baseline. We follow this view and tune with PSO against random search under a train/validation/test split. Problem Formulation sec:problem World and agents. drones with unique identifiers move in the square . Every drone senses the relative positions of all drones within a short safety range (defined in Sec.~ sec:bvc ); the safety filter uses only this information. In addition, every drone broadcasts one message per tick over a unit-disk radio graph of range . The message contains its position and its claim table. Every directed message is lost independently with probability , so a drone knows the positions of more distant drones only through the messages that reach it. title: ObjectWorld: Scaling Object-Centric World Models with A Large-Scale 3D Full-Object Flow Dataset
summary: Generative world modeling from large-scale visual data offers a promising path toward scalable robot manipulation. This calls for an intermediate representation that can be supervised at scale and remains actionable for downstream control. We propose 3D full-object flow, an object-centric motion representation that assigns dense 3D trajectories to points across the complete surface of a target object, including its occluded regions. By extending visible-surface object flow to the full object geometry, this representation makes complete object motion explicit and applies uniformly to both rigid and deformable objects. To realize the potential of this representation at scale, we introduce a 1210-hour full-object flow dataset that addresses the scarcity of large-scale supervision for complete 3D object motion. The dataset integrates diverse real-world videos and physical simulations, with a scalable annotation pipeline for recovering full-object motion from real-world observations and quality metrics for systematically assessing annotation quality. We then train a world model that takes an image and a task description as input and predicts dense full-object flow over the reconstructed object geometry. Experiments show reliable annotation quality, data-scalable flow prediction, and effective downstream manipulation across novel scenes and robot embodiments. Project website with additional results and videos: https://nus-lins-lab.github.io/ObjectWorld/.

title: Control-Aware Command Generation for Asynchronous Control and Action Inference with Vision-Based Policies towards Fast Execution
comment: 8th Robot Learning Workshop: Is Physical AI Going Zero-Shot? at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Vision-based control policies, including vision-language-action models, have enabled robots to perform increasingly complex tasks. However, their execution speed is often limited by the high computational cost of action inference. In this work, we investigate what can be achieved at the control level without modifying the underlying policy learning process. We introduce an asynchronous inference and control framework that enables fast task execution while maintaining smooth and stable robot motions. By formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous model predictions as a tracking control problem, our method makes asynchronous inference practical for real robots. We further accelerate execution through adaptive action skipping based on the variance of predicted positions. Experiments with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot demonstrate substantial speedups while preserving high task success rates.
full_text: Vision-based control policies, including vision–language–action models, have enabled robots to perform increasingly complex tasks. However, their execution speed is often limited by the high computational cost of action inference. In this work, we investigate what can be achieved at the control level without modifying the underlying policy learning process. We introduce an asynchronous inference and control framework that enables fast task execution while maintaining smooth and stable robot motions. By formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous model predictions as a tracking control problem, our method makes asynchronous inference practical for real robots. We further accelerate execution through adaptive action skipping based on the variance of predicted positions. Experiments with Action Chunking Transformer and OpenVLA-OFT on a bimanual robot demonstrate substantial speedups while preserving high task success rates. INTRODUCTION Vision-based control policies, including large-scale vision-language-action (VLA) models, have recently been applied to a wide range of robotic tasks~ OXE . Compared with approaches that explicitly estimate object poses, they simplify system design and can be trained from human demonstrations through imitation learning~ Argall09,Osa18 . By leveraging visual and language inputs, such policies have the potential to make robot control more accessible and expand the range of robotic applications. r 9cm Illustration of the proposed framework with asynchronous robot control and action inference. A key challenge lies in generating commands to ensure physically plausible motions. fig:intro In this work, we investigate how task execution can be accelerated without modifying the underlying policy learning process. As shown in Fig.~ fig:intro , we propose a framework that enables asynchronous action inference by formulating the generation of continuous target positions from discontinuous policy outputs as a tracking control problem. The proposed command generator produces smooth motions even when the policy outputs irregular action sequences. Furthermore, we accelerate execution through adaptive skipping of predicted actions based on the variance of predicted position sequences. We evaluate the method on a bimanual robot using both an 84M-parameter transformer policy and the 7B-parameter OpenVLA model, which are not diffusion or flow-matching-based. Experimental results demonstrate substantially faster task execution while preserving task performance. Related Work Vision-based control policies, including large-scale VLA models such as RT-X~ OXE , Octo~ Octo23 , OpenVLA~ Kim25 , ~ Black25 , and ~ pi25 , have recently achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation. Related approaches that predict actions from image observations and robot states have also been widely studied~ Zhao23,Fu2024,Lee25,Zhao25b , with ACT~ Zhao23 being a representative example. A common limitation of these methods is the high computational cost of inference, which slows down task execution. Several recent studies have explored accelerating execution in imitation learning~ Arachchige25,Guo25 . The method of~ Arachchige25 exploits a high-fidelity robot controller to guide action generation, but its applicability to arbitrary robotic platforms remains unclear. Guo et al.~ Guo25 accelerate execution by down-sampling demonstrations before training, yet do not explicitly address motion smoothness during execution. In contrast, our approach focuses on command generation at deployment time. Therefore, our contribution is orthogonal to that of Guo et al.~ Guo25 , and the two methods can be readily combined. A closely related effort is~ Black25_chunk , which tackles discontinuities caused by asynchronous inference through an inpainting formulation inspired by image generation~ Lugmayr22 and diffusion guidance methods~ Song23 . However, the approach is restricted to diffusion or flow-matching policies and is not directly applicable to architectures such as ACT~ Zhao23 or OpenVLA~ Kim25 . Moreover, because it relies on learned action generation, it does not provide explicit guarantees on constraints such as acceleration limits. Preliminary Imitation learning The goal of imitation learning~ Osa18 is to obtain a policy that reproduces the behavior of the expert policy . This problem can be formulated as where is a function that quantifies the difference between the behaviors of and . Given a dataset of the expert behaviors , the popular choice of is the expected KL divergence given by where is the empirical distribution of the expert demonstrations. Minimizing the expected KL divergence in is equivalent to maximizing the expected log likelihood , which is often referred to as behavioral cloning (BC). Action Chunking Transformer One of the widely used imitation learning frameworks for vision-based policies is ACT~ Zhao23 . In ACT, the policy is trained as a part of a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) ~ Kingma14 . The policy with parameters outputs a sequence of actions as where is the observation, is the latent variable, and is the number of actions. The latent variable is sampled from the posterior distribution modeled by an encoder during the training phase, and the latent variable is set as when the policy is deployed. As the policy model generates a sequence of actions, an action at a given time step may be estimated multiple times. In ACT, actions correspond to desired joint positions, . The final action is obtained by aggregating multiple predictions through a weighted average~ Zhao23 , where , and controls the exponential weighting. While ACT and related methods achieve strong empirical performance~ Zhao23,Fu2024,Lee25 , they provide no explicit guarantees on physical constraints such as velocity and acceleration limits. Proposed Framework Control-Aware Command Generation sec:cac In our framework, the actions inferred by the model are interpreted as the desired positions of the robot. Given a sequence of desired positions inferred by the model, we formulate the problem of generating a new sequence of target positions that reliably tracks the inferred actions while satisfying high-speed constraints such as acceleration limits. title: HARP-Bench: Benchmarking Robot Manipulation Around Active Humans
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026
summary: Recent robot manipulation benchmarks have enabled systematic evaluation of general-purpose robot policies across diverse objects, scenes, instructions, and embodiments. However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on HARP-Bench. Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with HARP-Bench demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/UMass-Embodied-AGI/harp.

However, most existing benchmarks still assume that the robot is the only active agent and that task semantics are determined primarily by the instruction and object state. This assumption overlooks a common source of real-world variation: humans actively sharing the workspace. In such settings, humans may reveal an implicit goal, complete part of the task, temporarily change object availability, or constrain safe robot motion while working nearby. We introduce HARP-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in workspaces shared with active humans. HARP-Bench treats human activity as part of the manipulation problem, rather than as background scene variation. It organizes human-present manipulation into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions are instantiated through everyday manipulation tasks, including paired human-present variants for controlled comparison with standard manipulation. HARP-Bench also provides a demonstration-generation pipeline for dynamic human-present settings. We evaluate VLA models, imitation-learning methods, and heuristic policies on . Human-present variations challenge current policies, and higher task success does not consistently improve safety. Quantitative failure analysis identifies manipulation and recovery as the dominant remaining challenges. Training with demonstrations improves human-present performance in simulation. A real-world study on one task family shows improved performance under human contribution, but not interruption, providing initial evidence of the data's utility and identifying limits of transfer. Introduction Recent robot manipulation benchmarks~ rlbench,robosuite,calvin,libero,maniskill3,robocasa,vlabench, robowits have become increasingly scalable and systematic, evaluating policies across diverse tasks, objects, scenes, instructions, embodiments, and temporal horizons. Despite this progress, most benchmarks vary the passive conditions under which a robot acts~ robotwin2, roboeval . Objects, layouts, and instructions may change, but the robot is typically the only agent that changes the workspace. Consequently, the meaning of a task is largely fixed by the language instruction and the current object state. This assumption breaks down in workspaces shared with people, where human actions can alter what the robot should do, which objects are available, and where the robot can move safely. In human-present workspaces, the robot's next action may depend on human activity rather than on object state alone. For example, a person reaching toward a task-relevant object may require the robot to pause, while a person completing part of the task may require the robot to update its plan. More broadly, human activity can change the robot's goal, task progress, object availability, and motion constraints. Evaluating such behaviors requires benchmarks that go beyond standard object-centric manipulation. Several recent benchmarks have begun to consider humans in embodied evaluation. However, most of these settings either operate at a high level of abstraction~ partnr, humanthor , where interaction is represented through planning or skill-level actions, or remain limited in scale and visual richness for evaluating modern vision-language-action manipulation policies~ humanrobotgym . This leaves a gap for scalable, visually grounded benchmarks that test autonomous manipulation policies in human-present workspaces. We introduce , a simulation benchmark for evaluating autonomous robot manipulation policies in human-present workspaces. organizes human activity into four evaluation conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. These conditions capture whether human behavior indicates the robot's objective, completes part of the task, changes object availability or execution timing, or adds motion constraints while working nearby. implements these settings with animated human avatars and closed-loop avatar events during policy rollouts, together with RGB-D observations, natural-language instructions, safety-aware metrics, and data interfaces for VLA and imitation-learning policies. Beyond task design, provides an evaluation and data-generation pipeline for human-present manipulation. Avatar behaviors are triggered during closed-loop policy rollouts, so policies are evaluated against human activity at execution time. also supports scripted demonstration collection, VLA-oriented trajectory recording, and a LeRobot-compatible data interface, with additional conversion paths for other VLA and imitation-learning pipelines. We use to evaluate two expert references and representative imitation-learning and VLA policies under the same human-present evaluation protocol. We report task success across the four conditions, together with aggregate safety metrics and a quantitative failure breakdown. Higher success does not consistently improve safety, and manipulation/recovery dominates the failures of both imitation-learning and VLA policies. Training on demonstrations improves performance on matching human-present variants, suggesting that the benchmark can support both evaluation and data generation for robot policies around active humans. Our contributions are as follows: Benchmark. We introduce , a simulation benchmark with 37 tasks for evaluating robot manipulation in human-present workspaces, organized into four conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. Evaluation. provides closed-loop avatar-driven evaluation, where human activity occurs during policy rollouts. Policies are evaluated by both task success and safety metrics. Data generation. supports scripted demonstration collection, VLA-oriented trajectory recording, and a LeRobot-compatible data interface, with additional conversion paths for other VLA and imitation-learning pipelines. Related Works Robot Manipulation Foundation Models, Data, and Benchmarks Recent robot learning has moved toward general-purpose manipulation policies that map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions. This includes imitation-learning methods, diffusion-based policies, and vision-language-action models trained across diverse tasks and embodiments~ act,diffusionpolicy,dp3,rt2,octo,openvla,pi0,pi05,rdt, lee2025molmoact, bjorck2025gr00t . Their progress has been closely tied to the growth of large-scale robot datasets and open training infrastructure, which provide diverse experience across environments, objects, tasks, and robot embodiments~ bridgedatav2,droid,openxembodiment,lerobot . As these policies become more general, benchmarks are increasingly needed to evaluate not only whether a robot can solve individual tasks, but also how policies generalize across task structure, language, visual scenes, embodiments, and temporal horizons. Existing manipulation benchmarks have expanded along these axes, from reusable simulated environments for language-conditioned manipulation to large-scale benchmarks with diverse tasks, objects, scenes, visual realism, long-horizon structure, and data generation~ rlbench,robosuite,calvin,libero,liberox,maniskill3,robocasa,robocasa365,robotwin2,vlabench,vlaarena, atreya2025roboarena . However, most of these benchmarks still define variation over passive task factors: objects, layouts, instructions, and embodiments may change, while the robot remains the only active agent that changes the workspace. builds on this line of benchmark and data infrastructure, but introduces human-present workspaces as an additional evaluation setting, where human activity can affect the robot's objective, object availability, task progress, timing, and safe motion. Human-Centered Embodied Benchmarks and Avatar Simulation Recent work has introduced humans into embodied and robotic benchmarks through household goals, collaborative planning, human-in-the-loop interaction, high-level assistance, and responsible decision making~ behavior1k,partnr,humanthor,m4bench,niabench,responsiblerobotbench, zhang2024building, zhang2025combo, carroll2019utility . However, these settings often abstract away low-level manipulation execution, focusing instead on planning, user interaction, assistance policies, or risk-aware reasoning and detection. As a result, they do not directly evaluate autonomous manipulation policies acting around active humans from visual observations and language instructions. Low-level HRC work is more directly related, but existing simulation benchmarks are limited in task scale and visual richness~ humanrobotgym , while real-world studies are typically task-specific and difficult to scale~ mosaic, pace,decaf . This leaves a gap for scalable, visually grounded simulation benchmarks for human-present manipulation. Avatar simulation and motion resources make it possible to generate repeatable human activity in simulation~ virtualcommunity,amass,mixamo . builds on these tools to construct controlled human-present manipulation conditions with closed-loop avatar events, safety-aware metrics, and data-generation interfaces for imitation-learning and VLA pipelines. HARP-Bench: Robot Manipulation around Active Humans is a simulation benchmark for evaluating robot manipulation policies in human-present workspaces. It extends standard object-centric manipulation tasks with avatar-driven human activity that can change the robot's objective, object availability, action timing, and motion constraints. The benchmark consists of 37 benchmark tasks organized around four human-present conditions, and provides closed-loop evaluation, safety-aware metrics, and data-generation interfaces for imitation-learning and VLA pipelines. Table~ tab:scope_comparison summarizes the scope of relative to related benchmarks. Task Design is designed around the ways human activity changes a manipulation task. In standard object-centric benchmarks, the robot's objective is usually specified by the language instruction and the object configuration. In human-present workspaces, the same object-level skill may require different behavior depending on what the human is doing. We organize these differences into four evaluation conditions: Cueing, Contribution, Interruption, and Co-presence. Figure~ fig:task_taxonomy illustrates these conditions with representative task instances. Cueing tasks evaluate whether the robot can infer the appropriate objective from human activity. For example, the human may carry an object, offer an object, or perform an ongoing activity that indicates what the robot should do next. Contribution tasks evaluate whether the robot can account for human-completed subtasks, such as a human placing one item while the robot completes the remaining items. Interruption tasks evaluate whether the robot can adapt when the human temporarily changes execution conditions, such as inspecting, holding, or occupying a task-relevant object. Co-presence tasks evaluate whether the robot can complete its original manipulation goal while a human performs unrelated work nearby. These conditions connect to established HRI problems: human-intent inference and human-action prediction for Cueing~ hoffman2024inferring ; human-progress estimation and timely proactive assistance for Contribution~ pace ; reactive task replanning and recovery under asynchronous human actions for Interruption~ decaf ; and human-aware motion planning and shared-workspace safety for Co-presence~ lasota2015analyzing . They respectively capture changes to the goal, remaining subtasks, action availability or timing, and motion constraints. This organization isolates effects on manipulation rather than constituting an exhaustive taxonomy of human behavior. title: DexForesight: Grounding Dexterous Policies with Implicit Spatial Foresight
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures
summary: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4% to 60.5%. On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3% success, compared with 50.0% for the strongest baseline.Project page https://dexforesight.github.io/
full_text: Dexterous manipulation requires rich spatial foresight over both the surrounding scene and the robot hand. Existing world-action models often acquire such predictive knowledge through explicit future prediction. We introduce DexForesight, a framework that learns spatial foresight implicitly by injecting dynamics-aware world representations into the latent space of a dexterous policy. During training, DexForesight learns an action-conditioned spatial world model from offline scene depth, kinematic hand geometry, and demonstration trajectories. The world model predicts 3D hand-point motion and visual feature changes, capturing both articulated hand dynamics and scene changes under demonstrated actions, including the motion of fingers occluded from the cameras. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its predictive world queries, transferring the learned spatial dynamics into policy latents and using them to condition action generation. At deployment, only the policy is retained, operating on RGB observations, language, and robot state without depth input or explicit future prediction. On 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks, DexForesight improves the overall success rate of the base policy from 49.4 to 60.5 . On three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks, DexForesight achieves 58.3 success, compared with 50.0 for the strongest baseline. Project page: https://dexforesight.github.io/ Introduction sec:introduction Controlling a dexterous hand requires anticipating how multiple fingers move relative to an object and the surrounding scene. During a grasp, fingers must move around object surfaces, often while part of the hand is hidden from the cameras. Recognizing the current scene alone is therefore insufficient: the policy also needs information about how actions change the hand--scene configuration. We refer to this predictive understanding as spatial foresight, encompassing both articulated hand motion and changes in the surrounding scene. World action models (WAMs) couple future prediction with action generation, offering a natural route to learning such foresight~ yuan2026fast,yang2026wla . Applying them to dexterous manipulation, however, raises two challenges. First, the spatial information used for prediction must capture more than visible scene surfaces. Even accurate scene depth leaves occluded fingers unobserved, whereas the robot's kinematic model and joint states provide hand-link positions independently of camera visibility. These complementary sources can ground predictions in both scene and hand geometry. Yet requiring estimated depth at deployment~ spatialvla,geovla introduces dependence on an online reconstruction pipeline: depth estimation adds computation, and reliable depth videos require temporal consistency as the hand and objects move~ li2023temporally . The challenge is to exploit this spatial information for learning without making reconstruction a prerequisite for control. Second, predictive knowledge need not be used through explicit future generation. In WAM designs that imagine the future during inference, the model generates future images, motion, or spatial states alongside, or before, its actions~ videovla . These predictions then guide action selection or planning~ pointworld , making future generation an explicit part of the deployed decision process and adding computation at every control step. For dexterous control, however, the key information is how actions change the hand--scene configuration; reconstructing full future observations may additionally require appearance details, such as texture or background, with limited relevance to action selection~ flare . Can a policy instead acquire the predictive features needed for spatial foresight during training, without decoding any future outputs at deployment? These challenges motivate transferring spatial foresight into the policy's latent representations. We introduce DexForesight: Grounding Dexterous Policies with Implicit Spatial Foresight (Figure~ fig:teaser ), which decouples an action-conditioned spatial world model from the policy. The action-conditioned world model learns hand and scene dynamics from training-time signals: scene depth estimated offline from stereo demonstrations with StereoAnyVideo~ jing2025stereo , kinematic hand geometry, and recorded future states. Given demonstrated controls, it jointly predicts displacements of fixed points on the hand, which cover occluded fingers through forward kinematics, and changes in visual features of the observed scene. Both objectives train a shared set of world queries, while depth conditions the backbone on current scene geometry through cross-layer fusion, so no future depth targets are required. We then freeze the world model and transfer its predictive features into the policy through query alignment (Figure~ fig:dexforesight ): policy queries read hidden layers of the VLM backbone, match the frozen world queries, and condition the action expert, linking predictive supervision to action learning within the same policy. At deployment, the policy operates only on current RGB observations, language, and robot state, with no world-model execution, online depth reconstruction, or explicit future generation. DexForesight thus acquires spatial foresight of hand and scene dynamics through action-conditioned prediction during training and carries it into dexterous action generation through the policy's own latent features. Our contributions are: 4pt 0pt We introduce DexForesight, which aligns dexterous policy latents with predictive representations from a frozen action-conditioned spatial world model and uses the aligned features to condition action generation, enabling implicit spatial foresight without world-model execution, online depth reconstruction, or explicit future generation at deployment. We develop an action-conditioned spatial world model using approximately 370 hours of demonstrations across 60 tasks and five categories. Combining offline scene depth with kinematic hand geometry, it jointly predicts 3D hand motion and visual dynamics, providing supervision beyond visible RGB observations. We evaluate DexForesight on 11 DexJoCo simulation tasks~ dexjoco and three real-robot tasks: Close Box, Insert Battery, and Screw On Lid, testing hand--object geometry, alignment under object occlusion, and articulated motion under finger occlusion, respectively. DexForesight achieves 60.5 and 58.3 success in simulation and real-robot evaluations, surpassing the strongest respective baselines by 9.6 and 8.3 percentage points. Related Work Future Modeling for Robot Policies World-action models couple future prediction with policy learning, either by jointly modeling future observations and actions~ uwm,videovla,lingbotva or by incorporating predictive supervision during training without requiring future generation at deployment~ mmact, yuan2026fast,beingh07,flare . Beyond image prediction, EgoWAM~ egowam explores 3D motion flow as a predictive target for human--robot co-training. These approaches motivate learning structured predictive representations, while dexterous manipulation calls for supervision that captures the coordinated motion of articulated fingers, including those hidden from the cameras. DexForesight addresses this requirement by combining scene geometry with kinematic hand representations and jointly predicting action-conditioned 3D hand motion and visual changes. Persistent hand-point targets preserve correspondence across articulated motion and supervise occluded fingers through forward kinematics. The resulting predictive representations are transferred into policy latents, without requiring world-model execution or future decoding at deployment. Spatially Grounded Policies Spatially grounded robot policies introduce geometric structure either directly into the policy~ spatialvla,depthvla,geovla or through representation-level supervision. ReconVLA~ reconvla uses auxiliary reconstruction to improve spatial perception, while Spatial Forcing~ spatialforcing aligns intermediate VLA features with representations from pretrained 3D foundation models, enabling implicit spatial grounding without explicit 3D inputs at deployment. These approaches primarily improve representations of scene geometry, rather than explicitly modeling how an articulated dexterous hand evolves under control. DexForesight instead targets action-conditioned spatial dynamics: it combines offline scene depth with robot kinematics and predicts future 3D displacements of persistent hand points together with visual changes. This embodiment-aware supervision captures hand--scene evolution beyond visible image geometry, including occluded finger motion, while the deployed policy still requires only RGB, language, and robot state. Method sec:method DexForesight uses offline scene depth and hand geometry computed from recorded robot states to train a spatial world model. Given demonstrated actions, the model predicts how points on the hand move and how image features change. We then freeze the world model and align policy queries with its query features. The policy uses these queries to generate actions from current RGB, language, and robot state (Figure~ fig:dexforesight ), without online depth reconstruction or future decoding. Overview. At time , the policy receives multi-view RGB images, a language instruction, and robot state, denoted by , and outputs an action chunk . The world model additionally receives depth and a short history of hand geometry and robot state; we denote its observation inputs by . During training, it also receives a demonstrated control sequence aligned with the future timestamps selected for prediction. The two models produce query features as follows: Here includes the world-model backbone, query reader, and action-conditioned query adapter. The policy query reader attends to selected VLM hidden layers, collected in . Both outputs contain query tokens. is a training-only dynamics-conditioning variable that resolves which control-dependent future is modeled; it is never an input to the policy. Only the policy runs at deployment. Learning Spatial Foresight sec:spatial The spatial world model in Figure~ fig:dexforesight encodes scene observations and hand geometry in a backbone initialized from RynnBrain~ rynnbrain . Depth enters through intermediate fusion blocks. World queries read the resulting hidden states and receive demonstrated controls through an action-conditioned adapter; these queries condition the Hand Flow Expert and the Visual Dynamics Expert. Hand geometry. We sample fixed points on the hand's URDF links and transform them into the robot base frame through forward kinematics using recorded robot states. Each point retains its link assignment and local coordinates across frames, preserving correspondence as the hand articulates. The resulting point clouds specify the positions of hand surfaces, including those occluded in the camera views. A Point-BERT~ pointbert encoder encodes the current point cloud and a short history of hand motion. These hand features enter the backbone alongside RGB, language, and robot-state history. Current and historical hand geometry provide encoder inputs, while future hand-point displacements provide the hand-flow prediction targets. Depth fusion. title: When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary
comment: Technical report, work in progress
summary: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.

Introduction Recent general purpose large models have made substantial progress in spatial understanding openai2026gpt6astra,sun2026smartsight,sun2024chattracker,zhang2026chattracker . As a consequence, coding agents can now control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end. The agent perceives the scene through a camera, calls the robot's pose and manipulation APIs, and directly emits executable control code~ shi2026maestro . Unlike vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAM), which require new data collection and fine-tuning whenever the task or the platform changes, this route needs neither task-specific demonstrations nor retraining, lowering the barrier to deployment and broadening the range of tasks that can be attempted. The most capable models today approach saturation on real-world pick-and-place benchmarks despite never having been trained for robotic manipulation sensenova2026embodiedintelligence,astra-robo-1, roboharm , and this capability is improving with the underlying models. General capability connects the digital and physical worlds, and so does risk. The access to code execution, the web, and local files that makes coding agents useful also exposes them to attack~ sun2026lieddoctorbuypoison . Once the agent controls an actuator, the damage from a successful attack is no longer confined to the computer. Even a benign request can lead to unsafe behavior, such as wiping a power strip with a visibly wet cloth (Fig.~ fig:safety-scenarios a). A malicious user can also exploit the agent's world knowledge and generalization to carry out harmful tasks that a VLA policy could not perform, such as painting prohibited content onto a canvas (Fig.~ fig:safety-scenarios b). A third party can plant instructions in an email that the agent reads during a legitimate task. For example, an injected email may falsely claim that joint 1's maximum rotation is 40 degrees. The agent may then change the configured limit from 320 to 40 degrees, restricting the arm's motion range and reducing its availability (Fig.~ fig:safety-scenarios c). Existing embodied safety evaluations fit this setting poorly. First, most benchmarks study harmful requests issued directly by the user~ robopair,badrobot,safeagentbench,roboharm . They overlook indirect prompt injection~ debenedetti2024agentdojo , a threat built into how coding agents work, because these agents routinely read untrusted content from web pages, documents, and tool outputs. Second, the harmful behaviors they cover are built around the primitive skills of VLA/VLM pipelines, mainly the hazards of pick-and-place~ roboharm . They provide limited coverage of additional harmful tasks enabled by the capabilities of frontier models, such as drawing harmful images. Third, they mostly consider risks that can be spotted from the instruction alone~ safeagentbench,ying2026agentsafe . In the real world, whether an action is dangerous often depends on the state of the environment. For example, turning on an induction cooker is routine, unless the pot on it is empty (Fig.~ fig:benchmark-overview ). In this work, we take a pioneering step toward systematically evaluating the safety of coding agents that control real robots. We introduce , a benchmark of tasks across scenarios, such as office and laboratory. The tasks are evaluated on a physical robot arm, and we also release a simulator that mirrors the real setup to support reproducible follow-up work. groups risks by source into three categories. Robustness, where a benign instruction leads to unsafe behavior. Malicious use, where the user deliberately requests harm, and indirect prompt injection, where adversarial instructions reach the agent through content it encounters during the task. To our knowledge, this is the first evaluation of indirect prompt injection against coding agents in embodied settings. Furthermore, instead of relying on instructions that are obviously harmful, includes cases where the risk only becomes apparent once the instruction is grounded in the observed environment. We evaluate three models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks (Codex), and find substantial safety risks. Our contributions are as follows. We present , the first systematic safety benchmark for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect prompt injection across tasks in scenarios, with both a real-robot setup and a matching simulator. We are the first to evaluate indirect prompt injection against embodied coding agents. We also introduce harmful tasks that exploit capabilities beyond VLA/VLM policies, along with environment-grounded cases that require reasoning over the observed scene to recognize. Evaluating 3 models, including GPT-6-Astra under Codex, revealing substantial safety risks in current systems. Related Work LLMs and Coding Agents for Robot Control VLA models such as RT-2 and OpenVLA learn to map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions using robot demonstrations and pretrained vision-language representations~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2025openvla . WAMs couple action generation with predictions of future observations. DreamZero jointly predicts future video and robot actions and reports zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks, while Motus supports joint video--action prediction within a unified architecture~ ye2026dreamzero,bi2026motus . An earlier line of work used LLMs to generate robot control code~ code-as-policies,huang2023voxposer , but it was limited by the weak spatial perception of models at the time. Today's coding agents differ in two ways. First, frontier models provide strong spatial reasoning~ openai2026gpt6astra,astra-robo-1 . For instance, recent reports show that such agents can discover novel strategies, e.g., using another arm's camera to extend their field of view~ cortex2026roboticsevals . Second, coding agent has access to the same web, file system, and desktop that it uses for daily work. This shared access is what creates the cross-boundary risks we study. Safety of Embodied AI A growing body of work studies the safety of robots driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAM). RoboPAIR~ robopair uses an attacker LLM to jailbreak an LLM-controlled robot into executing harmful actions. BadRobot~ badrobot shows that adversarial prompts and objects can make embodied LLMs violate their safety constraints in the physical world. On the evaluation side, SafeAgentBench~ safeagentbench and IS-Bench~ isbench test whether embodied agents recognize and avoid hazardous household tasks in simulated environments. Beyond the household, Coscientist~ coscientist demonstrates that an LLM agent can autonomously plan and execute chemical experiments, raising dual-use concerns about agents that act in laboratories. In contrast with these work, adds unintentional users and third-party injection, robot-specific injection channels, and tasks that require the general capabilities of frontier agents. Closest to our work is RoboHarm~ roboharm , which pairs frontier models such as GPT-6-Astra with Inspect Robots~ roboharm , a harness purpose-built for robot control, and measures whether the model refuses harmful manipulation requests. differs along three axes. (i) Unit of study: we evaluate a general coding agent that drives the robot through open-ended tools with web access, a shell and a filesystem, rather than a model inside a fixed robot harness, so a harmful outcome can be assembled from individually benign API calls. (ii) Threat source: alongside user-issued requests, we instantiate the same harmful goals as third-party indirect injection through channels that exist only for coding agents. (iii) Task space: we add capability-enabled harms that a VLA or WAM policy cannot produce, and tasks whose risk only becomes visible once the scene is observed rather than from the instruction alone. The agent pairs a backbone model with an agent framework such as Codex or Claude Code, and it has access to a shell, a file system, and a robot interface that exposes camera capture, pose queries, and manipulation primitives. An episode begins with a natural language instruction and an initial environment state . At step , the agent obtains an image from the robot camera together with the textual outputs of its tool calls, which include file contents, emails, web pages, and values returned by the robot driver. The second is what information the agent needs to recognize the harm, which determines how difficult recognition is. Source of risk. We consider three threat models.
