title: Beyond Memory Limits: A Hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Map Representation for Large-Scale 3D Autonomous Exploration
comment: 16 pages, 12 figures, preprint submitted to Elsevier
summary: Autonomous UAV exploration is increasingly used for large-scale surveying and inspection in inaccessible or disaster-affected environments, where onboard memory and computational resources are often severely constrained. Most existing UAV exploration systems maintain globally queryable geometric map representations for motion planning and exploration decision-making, causing memory consumption and spatial-query costs to increase with the explored area. Robot-centric local mapping bounds dense-map memory and computation but discards global task context needed for long-horizon exploration.We present FLAVOR, a hierarchical spatio-temporal framework that confines dense metric geometry to a robot-centric local map while retaining compact global observation and task context. At the observation level, lightweight LiDAR-keyframe visibility records preserve ray-wise evidence for frontier reasoning. At the task level, unresolved frontiers beyond the local-map extent are retained as compact pending tasks associated with odometry anchors. A sparse topological graph connects these anchors through retained routes for future revisits.Upon returning to a task region, FLAVOR reconstructs the frontier and exploration viewpoint from observations, while the topological route is instantiated and validated against the current local map before execution. Dense-map capacity remains fixed as exploration expands, with exploration-dependent memory growth confined to compact observation and task context.FLAVOR achieves 31.98--41.88% shorter exploration time and a 94--99% smaller map memory footprint than the best baseline that completes all three simulated scenes. In real-world deployments, it reduces this footprint by 92.67% in the forest and 62.42% at the construction site relative to an explicit point-cloud ikd-tree while preserving long-term task continuity under constrained onboard resources.
full_text: Fig. .\@gobble > X Beyond Memory Limits: A Hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Map Representation for Large-Scale 3D Autonomous Exploration Yizhe Zhang organization= State Key Laboratory of Information Engineering in Surveying, Mapping and Remote Sensing , addressline= Wuhan University , city= Wuhan , postcode= 430079 , country= China Jianping Li organization= School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering , addressline= Nanyang Technological University , postcode= 639798 , country= Singapore Yilun Gao organization= Electronic Information School , addressline= Wuhan University , city= Wuhan , postcode= 430072 , country= China Liangliang Yin Pengfei Wan Bisheng Yang Autonomous UAV exploration is increasingly used for large-scale surveying and inspection in inaccessible or disaster-affected environments, where onboard memory and computational resources are often severely constrained. Most existing UAV exploration systems maintain globally queryable geometric map representations for motion planning and exploration decision-making, causing both memory consumption and spatial-query costs to increase with the explored area. Robot-centric local mapping can bound dense-map memory usage and geometry-intensive computations but discards the global task context needed for persistent, long-horizon exploration. To overcome this limitation, we present , a hierarchical spatio-temporal framework that confines dense metric geometry to a robot-centric local map while retaining compact global observation and task context. The framework organizes exploration context into a cascaded hierarchy spanning observation level and task level. At the observation level, lightweight LiDAR-keyframe visibility records preserve fine-grained ray-wise evidence for frontier reasoning. At the task level, when an unresolved frontier moves beyond the local-map extent, it is retained as a compact pending task associated with an odometry anchor, rather than retaining its dense local geometry. The task context also includes a sparse topological graph connecting these anchors through retained routes for future revisits. Upon returning to a selected task region, progressively recovers the required metric information: the corresponding frontier and exploration viewpoint are reconstructed from current observations, while the topological route is instantiated and validated against the current local map before execution. This hierarchical map representation allows to explore beyond the spatial extent of its dense local map. As the explored range expands, dense-map memory capacity remains fixed, and exploration-dependent memory growth is confined to compact observation and task context. The proposed framework achieves 31.98--41.88 shorter exploration time and a 94--99 smaller memory footprint of the map representation than the best baseline that completes all three simulated scenes. In real-world deployments, it reduces this footprint by 92.67 in the forest and 62.42 at the construction site relative to an explicit point-cloud ikd-tree while preserving long-term task continuity under constrained onboard memory and computation budgets. The project page can be found at LiDAR Large-scale 3D exploration Hierarchical map representation Robot-centric mapping Autonomous UAV Introduction sec:introduction Autonomous exploration on resource-constrained UAV platforms enables rapid spatial data acquisition for large-scale surveying, infrastructure inspection, and post-disaster assessment, especially in environments where prior maps are incomplete and direct human access is difficult faria2019autonomous,kerle2019uav . While human-in-the-loop operation is essential for mission-critical surveying zhang2026aware , sustained exploration across vast or hard-to-access environments requires greater onboard autonomy to reduce the need for continuous operator intervention. LiDAR sensing and odometry provide geometric measurements and motion estimates that support surveying and associated decision-making li2019nrli,zhang2026armor,li2026aeos . To construct a map autonomously, a UAV must identify unobserved regions, select informative sensing poses, and generate feasible trajectories as the mapped workspace expands bircher2016receding,zhou2021fuel,zhou2026eame . Supporting these functions with a persistent global metric map incurs growing memory and query costs. Existing methods reduce this overhead by making persistent geometry cheaper to store and query duberg2020ufomap,reijgwart2023efficient , simplifying planning through multi-resolution and topological abstractions cao2021tare,chen2022fast,zhang2024falcon , or retaining selected geometric elements huang2024efficient,geng2025epic . Many of these systems still base long-term decisions on metric geometry accumulated over the mission. Fixed-window mapping bounds this geometric workload ren2024rog , but discarding old regions also removes the evidence needed to distinguish previously observed boundaries from unfinished tasks. The gap is therefore how to preserve exploration continuity after historical geometry is discarded: the map representation must retain observation context for recognizing prior coverage and task context for recovering unfinished objectives, while confining detailed occupancy, clearance, and collision queries to the current neighborhood. To bridge this gap, we propose , a hierarchical spatio-temporal map representation for large-scale 3D exploration, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:framework . By unifying Frontier tasks, a Local map, Anchors, historical Visibility, Odometry, and topological Routing, it couples local geometry with retained mission context to support exploration planning without a persistent global point cloud. Our key insight is that historical geometry and historical exploration state support different decisions and therefore need not be retained at the same fidelity. We organize persistent information into two levels: observation context retains evidence of prior sensing, while task context preserves unfinished objectives together with the anchors and topological routes needed to revisit them. Dense metric geometry remains confined to a robot-centric local map. This separation assigns compact history to long-term exploration decisions and current geometry to viewpoint validation, collision checking, and trajectory generation. carries exploration tasks from initial observation through deferred completion in three steps. First, as the UAV observes a region, the observation context preserves visibility evidence for recognizing previously observed boundaries after map shifts. Second, when an unresolved frontier leaves the local window, the task context preserves the pending objective, its associated anchor, and a return route while the surrounding dense geometry is discarded. The task remains pending outside the local map, and its stored anchor and route guide the UAV back for further exploration. Finally, when no valid local target remains, the task context guides a return to a pending region. Current sensing validates each local route segment before execution and, upon re-observation of the task, determines what remains unfinished and supports viewpoint reconstruction. This sequence allows exploration to continue across map shifts while reserving detailed geometric reasoning for the region currently being observed. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: (1) We propose a hierarchical spatio-temporal map representation that confines dense geometry to a fixed-window local map while retaining compact observation context and task context for large-scale exploration. (2) We develop cascaded frontier updates that use LiDAR-keyframe visibility to filter repeated boundaries and retain unresolved tasks across map shifts for reconstruction upon revisits. (3) We develop anchor-associated planning that prioritizes local tasks and retrieves historical tasks through topological routes, with local route validation before execution. (4) Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate reduced map memory and computational overhead, along with improved exploration efficiency, compared with the evaluated baselines. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related_work reviews exploration-oriented map representations, frontier-based exploration and persistent task management, and hierarchical and topological planning for large-scale 3D exploration. Section~ sec:method presents the proposed map representation, its online update mechanism, and the anchor-associated exploration framework. Section~ sec:experiments reports the experimental evaluation, and Section~ sec:discussion analyzes the resulting design implications and scalability. Finally, Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper. Related Work sec:related_work Autonomous exploration couples three functions: maintaining a map, identifying what remains to be observed, and planning motion toward the selected task. In this section, we review map representations, frontier-based exploration and persistent task management, and hierarchical and topological planning. Map Representations for Exploration Dense occupancy grids expose unknown--free boundaries directly, but at a fixed resolution their storage is proportional to the voxelized volume. Octree maps reduce repeated storage in homogeneous regions. OctoMap established a probabilistic octree map representation of occupied, free, and implicitly unknown space hornung2013octomap ; UFOMap made all three states explicit and optimized map queries and updates for robotic planning duberg2020ufomap . Wavemap uses a wavelet hierarchy to adapt occupancy-map detail to the spatial structure of the observations reijgwart2023efficient . For surface reconstruction, Voxel Hashing allocates voxel blocks around observed surfaces rather than preallocating the full volume niessner2013real . Using voxel hashing for storage, Voxblox incrementally derives an ESDF from a TSDF for onboard planning oleynikova2017voxblox . TARE combines dense local data and a detailed local path with sparse global subspaces and a coarse global route; its later dual-resolution formulation makes this local--global division explicit cao2021tare,cao2023representation . M3 communicates star-convex free-space polytopes and summarized frontier information gao2022meeting . FAOMap stores obstacle and frontier data while omitting extensive free and unknown space huang2024efficient . EPIC removes the global occupancy grid by storing surface-observation quality in a spatial hash and constructing an incremental topological graph directly from point clouds geng2025epic . Its global point-cloud map nevertheless remains a metric input to planning. Recent work has also focused on local map representations for robotics. ROG-Map keeps occupancy and obstacle inflation in a robot-centric sliding grid, thereby bounding the dense map by a configured local window ren2024rog . However, without a global representation, this local map alone offers limited support for large-scale exploration. In , occupancy, clearance, and collision queries are restricted to a sliding local map. What persists outside that map is exploration history: observation evidence, unfinished tasks, odometry anchors, and routes previously used to reach them. Frontier-Based Exploration and Persistent Task Management Frontier exploration treats the boundary between known free and unknown space as a source of navigation goals yamauchi1997frontier . Receding-horizon next-best-view planning instead samples informative trajectories online bircher2016receding . Witting et al. record visited locations to bias next-best-view sampling and escape confined-space dead ends witting2018history . Dai et al. generate candidate views from frontier voxels organized in an octree and evaluate their information gain by sparse ray casting dai2020fast . FUEL incrementally updates a frontier information structure before refining global and local tours zhou2021fuel

title: ClearForm: Shared-Surface Gaussian Splatting for Transparent and Opaque Scenes
comment: 15 pages, 9 figures
summary: Transparent-interface reconstruction must recover glass surfaces even when most observed color comes from the scene behind them. We present ClearForm, a shared-planar-Gaussian method for jointly reconstructing transparent interfaces and the appearance seen through them. We identify and analyze the Geometry-Appearance Compositing Dilemma (GACD): when the same transparency-dependent alpha controls both color and geometry, revealing the background can weaken a transparent surface's contribution to geometric reconstruction. We derive its effect on plane-based depth estimation, identify a mechanism that can weaken geometric learning, and quantify the loss of interface support through controlled comparisons. To address this conflict, we develop geometry-preserving dual-opacity surface reconstruction. Shared planar Gaussians retain interface contributions in geometry compositing while modeling transmission and sparse reflection in RGB, supported by transparency-aware geometric constraints. To manage the different primitive-visibility requirements of these compositors, we introduce Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL), which retains Gaussians supported by multi-view geometry or RGB reconstruction evidence. On 3D-FRONT-T, ClearForm achieves 27.05 mm Chamfer distance (CD) and 0.928 F1, compared with 59.18 mm CD for our PGSR reproduction and the reported 34 mm CD and 0.836 F1 for GLINT. On TransLab, it achieves 1.65 mm CD, 0.963 F1, and 40.14 dB PSNR. In matched ablations, dual-opacity compositing reduces CD from 59.25 to 27.09 mm, while DEL improves PSNR by 2.06 dB. Our project page is available at https://hajeongx.github.io/clearform/.

Our project page is available at . Introduction Glass transmits light while introducing a physical boundary between materials. We call this boundary a transparent interface. Along a camera ray, the near-side interface lies before the scene surfaces visible through the glass, which we call background geometry. The appearance of these background surfaces as seen through the interface constitutes transmitted appearance. Reconstruction must therefore recover interface geometry while preserving the observed appearance. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023 renders color through front-to-back alpha compositing, where each Gaussian is weighted by its opacity and the transmittance remaining after nearer Gaussians. Surface-oriented methods improve geometry through surface alignment, planar primitives, or opacity-field extraction~ guedon2024,huang2024,yu2024gof,chen2024pgsr . Planar-based Gaussian Splatting (PGSR)~ chen2024pgsr also uses these compositing weights to blend plane normals and distances for depth estimation. When the same alpha is reduced to reveal background appearance through a transparent interface, its geometric contribution is reduced as well. We call this conflict the Geometry--Appearance Compositing Dilemma (GACD). For a single plane, its alpha weight cancels out in PGSR's depth calculation. However, when transparent interfaces and background surfaces contribute to the same pixel, transparency changes their relative weights and can shift the estimated depth. It can also weaken a geometric gradient pathway and cause small interface contributions to be skipped during rendering. We derive these effects and measure how shared alpha reduces support for the ground-truth first surface. Separate training ablations assess whether geometry-preserving compositing improves reconstruction accuracy. Guided by this analysis, we develop geometry-preserving dual-opacity surface reconstruction over shared planar Gaussians. The geometry path blends plane attributes without transparency attenuation, while the appearance path reveals background color through learned transparency and represents sparse reflection on the same surface. Transparency-aware depth--normal consistency and multi-view geometric constraints then supervise the interface without requiring it to block transmitted color in RGB. Together, these components reconstruct transparent-interface geometry, transmitted appearance, and reflection. Dual-opacity compositing also separates the visibility conditions for geometry and RGB. A transparent interface can contribute strongly to geometric rendering while allowing background color to pass through. It may therefore occlude background Gaussians in the geometry pass even though they remain useful for transmitted RGB. If their learned opacity becomes small during optimization, conventional opacity-based pruning can remove them; a geometry-only visibility test likewise misses their appearance contribution. We introduce Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL), which retains Gaussians supported by geometry-pass visibility or positive RGB-loss contribution across distinct camera views, and maintains evidence across cloning and splitting. At a fixed Gaussian state, changing only the geometry alpha rule raises ground-truth first-hit coverage from 7.08 to 14.70 . In the cumulative 3D-FRONT-T ablation, dual-opacity compositing reduces Chamfer distance (CD) from 59.25 to 27.09\,mm; DEL then raises PSNR from 32.05 to 34.11\,dB while retaining similar mesh accuracy. The complete model achieves 27.05\,mm CD and 0.928 F1 on 3D-FRONT-T, and 1.65\,mm CD and 0.963 F1 on TransLab. Our contributions are summarized as follows: Geometry--Appearance Compositing Dilemma. We analyze how transparency-dependent alpha can weaken the geometric contributions of transparent interfaces while revealing the background, including its effects when different surfaces overlap along a ray. We derive the consequences for depth rendering and geometric optimization and quantify the loss of first-surface support. Geometry-preserving dual-opacity surface reconstruction. We formulate separate geometry and appearance compositing over shared planar Gaussians so transparent interfaces can contribute to surface reconstruction without obscuring transmitted color. Transparency-aware PGSR regularization constrains interface geometry, while learned transparency and sparse reflection reproduce the observed appearance. Dual-Evidence Lifecycle. We introduce a multi-view Gaussian survival criterion that addresses the geometry--RGB visibility mismatch in dual-opacity reconstruction. By retaining primitives supported by geometry-pass visibility or positive RGB-loss contribution across distinct cameras, DEL helps preserve transparent interfaces and appearance-useful background Gaussians with different rendering roles. Related Work Surface reconstruction with neural and Gaussian representations. Neural surface methods including VolSDF, NeuS, and Neuralangelo~ yariv2021,wang2021neus,li2023neuralangelo extend radiance-field optimization~ mildenhall2020 with surface structure or geometric regularization. Gaussian methods offer efficient alternatives: SuGaR aligns Gaussians to surfaces~ guedon2024 , 2DGS uses oriented disks~ huang2024 , Gaussian Opacity Fields extracts surfaces from opacity~ yu2024gof , and PGSR estimates depth from alpha-blended plane normals and distances while enforcing single- and multi-view constraints~ chen2024pgsr . GS-2DGS adds learned geometric guidance for reflective objects~ tong2025gs2dgs . In ClearForm, PGSR's plane representation provides the surface attributes for a distinct geometry-compositing path. Reflective and refractive appearance. Ref-NeRF, NeRFReN, and NeRO address non-Lambertian appearance through directional representations, radiance decomposition, and geometry/material estimation~ verbin2022,guo2022nerfren,liu2023nero . GlassGaussian models glass reflectance~ cao2025glassgaussian ; Ref-GS and EnvGS capture view-dependent reflections~ zhang2025refgs,xie2025envgs , and GUS-IR combines forward and deferred shading~ liang2025gusir . Other methods model refractive transport: Eikonal Fields traces curved rays~ bemana2022 , NU-NeRF reconstructs nested transparent objects~ sun2024nunerf , and TransparentGS uses deferred refraction~ huang2025transparentgs . ClearForm instead uses straight-ray splatting and learned view-dependent appearance without explicitly modeling refracted light paths or estimating refractive indices. Transparent surfaces and depth extraction. TSGS~ li2025tsgs separates geometry learning from transparency-aware appearance refinement using normal and de-lighting priors and a first-surface depth rule. TSPE-GS~ xu2026tspe and UniGS~ min2026unigs represent multiple depths per ray; G-GSTR~ tian2026geometryaware and TSTR~ tian2026specular add geometric or specular constraints. ClearForm focuses on how transparency changes the interface's geometric contribution during plane-based rendering and optimization. Geometry--appearance factorization and scene decomposition. RT-Splatting~ shi2026rt factorizes geometric occupancy and optical opacity for surface-attribute aggregation in deferred reflection and volumetric transmission. GLINT~ na2026glint represents interface, transmission, and reflection using separate Gaussian components and secondary-ray transport. AlphaSurf and Car-GS also distinguish geometric from optical roles~ wu2025alphasurf,li2025cargs ; related appearance methods include TR-Gaussians, RT-GS, and TransmissiveGS~ liu2025tr,zeng2026rtgs,liang2026transmissive . ClearForm investigates the geometric consequences of sharing transparency-dependent alpha, including the depth shift caused by overlapping interface and background planes. We derive the associated gradient and rasterization effects and quantify interface support using fixed-Gaussian comparisons. Our geometry-preserving dual-opacity formulation combines transparency-independent plane compositing, transmitted appearance, and sparse reflection on shared planar Gaussians with transparency-aware PGSR constraints. Gaussian pruning. LightGaussian and PUP 3D-GS prune by significance or reconstruction sensitivity~ fan2024lightgaussian,hanson2025pup , while MaskGaussian preserves gradients for masked primitives~ liu2025maskgaussian . FastGS and birth--death structural learning use multi-view reconstruction signals~ ren2026fastgs,tran2026birthdeath . RT-Splatting~ shi2026rt prunes by geometric occupancy to preserve transparent surfaces. In dual-opacity reconstruction, a geometry-visible transparent interface can occlude background Gaussians in the geometry pass even though they contribute to transmitted RGB. Opacity-based pruning may discard such Gaussians when their learned opacity is low, while geometry-only visibility cannot capture their RGB usefulness. ClearForm's Dual-Evidence Lifecycle (DEL) instead retains primitives supported by geometry-pass visibility or positive first-order RGB-loss contribution across distinct cameras. Lineage aggregation and temporary evidence inheritance extend this criterion to clone/split children. title: RefineSplat: Reconstruction-Guided Object-Centric Gaussian Splatting for Open-Vocabulary Querying
summary: Open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding aims to segment and retrieve arbitrary objects in 3D scenes using natural language queries. Most existing methods typically follow a splat-then-segment paradigm, where 3D Gaussian Splatting is first reconstructed and then augmented with labels or language features for subsequent segmentation. However, this pipeline often suffers from view inconsistency, ambiguous object boundaries, and weak object-level correspondence, especially in complex static and dynamic scenes. Building on our prior Segment-then-Splat framework, we present RefineSplat, a reconstruction-guided extension that retains its object-centric paradigm: it first tracks objects in 2D and then reconstructs each object with a dedicated set of 3D Gaussians, preserving explicit object-Gaussian correspondence for unified open-vocabulary segmentation and retrieval. To improve robustness, we further close the loop between 2D tracking and 3D reconstruction. Since off-the-shelf video trackers can produce unreliable masks that propagate errors into object reconstruction, we introduce a reconstruction-guided feedback mechanism that refines object tracking using rendered masks and multi-view consistency. Moreover, instead of assigning each object a single language embedding, we propose a viewpoint-aware embedding assignment strategy, where each object maintains multiple view-clustered embeddings to capture view-dependent semantic cues. We also introduce Blender-OVS, a synthetic benchmark of static and dynamic sequences with exact object meshes and point clouds, enabling direct evaluation of extracted geometry. Experiments on static and dynamic benchmarks show improved rendered-view segmentation and lower object-level Chamfer distances, with competitive scene reconstruction quality.

We also introduce Blender-OVS, a synthetic benchmark of static and dynamic sequences with exact object meshes and point clouds, enabling direct evaluation of extracted geometry. Experiments on static and dynamic benchmarks show improved rendered-view segmentation and lower object-level Chamfer distances, with competitive scene reconstruction quality. Open-Vocabulary Scene Understanding, 3D Gaussian Splatting, Language Embedded Scene Representation, Language-guided Segmentation. Introduction 3D open-vocabulary querying is a key step toward language-driven interaction with 3D environments, allowing users to localize, segment, and retrieve objects without predefined category labels. Such a capability is fundamental for large-scale scene exploration, scene understanding, robotic navigation and manipulation, where free-form language serves as a natural interface between human intent and machine perception. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians has recently become a compelling representation for this problem because it supports high-fidelity reconstruction, efficient optimization, and real-time differentiable rendering. However, standard 3DGS is primarily a radiance representation: its anisotropic Gaussian primitives encode geometry and appearance, but not object identity or language-aligned semantics. To enable open-vocabulary querying, recent methods~ shi2024language,qin2024langsplat,zhou2024feature,gaussian_grouping typically augment a reconstructed 3DGS scene with semantic labels or vision-language features. We refer to this family as the splat-then-segment paradigm because these methods first reconstruct the scene with 3DGS and subsequently assign semantic or identity embeddings to individual Gaussians for object segmentation and open-vocabulary querying. Although it benefits from the reconstruction quality of 3DGS, it inherits a structural mismatch between scene-level radiance optimization and object-level language querying. First, the Gaussians are optimized to explain the entire scene rather than to form object-level entities. Without explicit constraints on object boundaries and fine-grained geometry, individual Gaussians may overlap or span multiple objects, and object boundaries are only implicitly captured through appearance. This leads to object-level geometric ambiguity. Second, language supervision is often imposed through alpha-blended feature rendering. This constrains the accumulated feature along a camera ray, but does not guarantee that each contributing Gaussian has an object-consistent semantic meaning. The resulting semantic ambiguity is especially pronounced around occlusion boundaries, thin structures, and regions where multiple objects project to nearby pixels. Consequently, a method may render a plausible 2D relevance map while lacking a clean 3D object representation that can be directly queried. We reverse this pipeline and propose the framework~ lu2026segment . Instead of first reconstructing a scene-level Gaussian field and then searching for objects inside it, it first obtains multi-view object masks, assigns object identities to Gaussians, and reconstructs the scene as a composition of object-specific Gaussian sets. Enforcing this object-level decomposition from the very beginning of reconstruction encourages Gaussians to align with object boundaries, and hence reduce geometric ambiguity. Language features are then attached to each object rather than mixed along each viewing ray, reducing both geometric and semantic ambiguity. Related studies, including COB-GS~ zhang2025cobgs , COS3D~ zhu2025cos3d , and ObjectGS~ zhu2025objectgs , also emphasize object-level structure in Gaussian representations. These methods share the goal of aligning Gaussian representations with object identities and boundaries to support more reliable instance separation and object-level scene understanding. However, for reconstruction pipelines that use initial 2D masks to define object-specific Gaussian groups, mask reliability remains a central limitation. These masks are typically produced by off-the-shelf segmentation~ kirillov2023segment and video tracking models~ ravi2025sam, cheng2023tracking . Such 2D supervision may contain inaccurate boundaries, missed regions, identity switches, and temporal or cross-view inconsistencies. Once these observations are used to initialize or supervise object-specific Gaussians, their errors can be propagated into the corresponding Gaussian groups and subsequently degrade both reconstruction and open-vocabulary querying, with no mechanism for recovery. -1 This paper presents , a reconstruction-guided extension of Segment-then-Splat that closes the loop between 2D supervision and 3D object reconstruction (Fig.~ fig:teaser (c)). Our key insight is that an intermediate object-specific reconstruction consolidates evidence across multiple views and can thus serve as a geometric consistency signal for assessing the reliability of its 2D supervision. We render reconstructed objects into the training views and compare their support with the tracked masks to reject globally unreliable tracks (track-level filtering) and select suitable observations for object-level supervision (observation-level filtering). The retained masks then provide cleaner supervision for the final object-specific Gaussian optimization, preventing tracking errors from propagating into 3D. RefineSplat further revisits how language information should be attached to object-centric Gaussians. Prior object-centric methods, including our conference version, collapse all observations of an object into a single globally averaged embedding, which suppresses view-dependent semantics ( , the face of a clock versus its back). We instead introduce a viewpoint-aware embedding assignment strategy. By grouping object observations according to viewpoint and maintaining multiple view-clustered embeddings for each object, the proposed strategy preserves view-dependent semantic cues and enables more discriminative open-vocabulary querying. Finally, we address an evaluation gap in open-vocabulary 3D segmentation. Existing benchmarks such as LERF~ kerr2023lerf , Mip-NeRF360~ barron2022mip , and HyperNeRF~ park2021hypernerf rely on 2D mask annotations and evaluate segmentation in the rendered image space. A method can score well on rendered views while its underlying 3D object geometry is incomplete or entangled with neighboring objects. We therefore introduce , a benchmark covering both static and dynamic scenes with exact 3D-level ground truth, including per-object meshes and point clouds. Together with direct 3D evaluation, Blender-OVS complements rendered-view metrics and enables a more faithful assessment of 3D open-vocabulary segmentation. This paper is an extended version of our NeurIPS 2025 work, ``Segment then Splat: Unified 3D Open-Vocabulary Segmentation via Gaussian Splatting''~ lu2026segment . Building on the explicit object-Gaussian correspondence established by the original framework, this work makes the following new contributions: Reconstruction-guided supervision refinement. We introduce RefineSplat, a reconstruction-guided extension of Segment-then-Splat that uses intermediate object-specific reconstructions to identify unreliable 2D supervision, thereby mitigating the propagation of tracking errors into 3D reconstruction. Viewpoint-aware open-vocabulary querying. We represent each object with multiple view-clustered language embeddings rather than one globally averaged descriptor, preserving view-dependent semantic cues. Blender-OVS benchmark and direct 3D evaluation. We introduce Blender-OVS, a 3D open-vocabulary segmentation benchmark with exact per-object meshes and point clouds for both static and dynamic scenes, together with an evaluation protocol that measures the geometry of queried objects directly in 3D, beyond 2D views. Experiments on static and dynamic benchmarks show improved rendered-view segmentation and lower average Chamfer distances for queried 3D objects compared with the evaluated baselines, while maintaining competitive scene reconstruction quality. Related Work Gaussian Scene Representations Neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2020nerf have driven substantial progress in novel-view synthesis by representing a scene as a continuous volumetric field and rendering it with differentiable volume integration. However, their dense ray sampling and repeated network evaluation make training and rendering costly, especially when additional semantic or language fields are optimized on top of them. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians replaces implicit volumetric sampling with explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives and fast differentiable rasterization, achieving high-fidelity reconstruction with real-time rendering. This efficiency has made 3DGS a strong substrate for 3D scene understanding beyond view synthesis. Dynamic 3DGS and 4D Gaussian representations further extend this explicit representation to time-varying scenes~ yang2023gs4d,yang2024deformable,Wu_2024_CVPR . These methods typically combine a canonical Gaussian representation with time-dependent deformation, enabling reconstruction of moving objects and changing visibility. Together, static and dynamic Gaussian representations provide the reconstruction backbone for open-vocabulary querying, but their original formulations model appearance and geometry rather than object identity or language semantics. Language-Embedded Scene Representations Open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding requires associating 3D structures with free-form language queries. title: Kimodo-Policy: Learning Kinematic Action Models for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures, 4 tables. Project page: https://kimodo-policy.github.io/
summary: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires continuous coordination of high-dimensional whole-body motion to realize task objectives. While vision-language-action models and world action models transfer semantic and visual-dynamics priors to robot control, these priors do not necessarily capture the structure of robot motion. We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that treats whole-body motion as a direct pretraining target and uses a pretrained motion generator as the primary action-generation backbone. KAMs ground learned temporal and cross-body coordination priors through task conditioning, visual observations, and execution feedback. We present Kimodo-Policy as an initial instantiation, combining a frozen Kimodo text-to-motion backbone with lightweight ControlNet-based visual conditioning. A root-body-hand hierarchy coordinates locomotion and manipulation, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction bridge motion synthesis and closed-loop control. Following large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining, the policy achieves the highest overall success among compared policies on multi-task HumanoidArena (72.14%), competitive performance on SIMPLE, and 60% mean success across eight real-world tasks, with 678M parameters (92M trainable). Ablations support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone. Together, these results provide initial evidence for motion generation as a complementary foundation for humanoid action learning.

Introduction sec:introduction 0.25em plus 0.05em minus 0.03em 10pt plus 2pt minus 2pt Humanoid loco-manipulation integrates task understanding, visual perception, and high-dimensional whole-body coordination~ psi0,openhlm . Beyond the requirements of conventional manipulation, it demands that robots continuously coordinate their root, torso, arms, and legs throughout an interaction~ leverb . For example, reaching for an object while moving requires a robot to simultaneously adjust its body position, maintain dynamic balance, and coordinate joint movements according to the object's location and contact state. Whole-body motion is therefore an integral part of accomplishing the task, rather than merely an execution stage that follows task-level decision-making. Even with accurate task understanding and perception, a robot cannot complete the task without generating temporally and spatially coordinated, executable whole-body motion. The central challenge of loco-manipulation thus extends beyond determining what the robot should do to generating the high-dimensional, continuous, and coupled whole-body motion required for task execution. Recent advances in vision--language--action models (VLAs) and world action models (WAMs) offer two representative approaches to robot action generation. VLAs typically extend the semantic understanding and visual representations acquired by pretrained vision--language models to robot action prediction~ rt2,openvla,pi0,grootn1 . WAMs draw on the visual dynamics learned by pretrained video generation models to connect future-state prediction with action generation~ dreamzero,motionwam,wholebodywam_wbc . These approaches provide important foundations for task understanding, environmental perception, and interaction planning. However, pretrained knowledge of visual semantics and dynamics does not necessarily capture the structural regularities of high-dimensional robot motion. Although these models can acquire whole-body motion capabilities through action supervision and downstream policy learning~ wholebodyvla , translating visual or semantic representations into coordinated whole-body motion still requires action representations and dependencies that reflect the structure of the robot's motion space. This motivates a complementary question: beyond semantic understanding and visual dynamics, can the structure of whole-body motion itself serve as a distinct target for generative pretraining? Motivated by this observation, we introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm that uses a pretrained motion generation model as the primary backbone for action generation (Fig.~ fig:policy_routes ). The central premise of KAMs is that, for humanoid robots whose behavior is expressed through high-dimensional whole-body motion, motion should be a direct target of foundation-model pretraining, in addition to being the final output of a policy. Whereas visual and language pretraining primarily captures visual semantics or the evolution of visual states, motion generation pretraining directly models the temporal evolution of body configurations, learning patterns of joint motion, root motion, and coordination across body parts~ mdm,kimodo . This allows the model to acquire structural priors in a motion space closely aligned with the target action-generation problem, reducing its reliance on downstream task learning to acquire these basic motion . KAMs then use the pretrained motion generator as the policy's generative backbone, conditioning it on task information, visual observations, and robot states to adapt its existing whole-body motion capabilities to specific environments and objectives. Motion generation thereby becomes a foundation for policy pretraining, rather than solely an output stage following task understanding. Transferring pretrained motion generation capabilities to robot control nevertheless requires addressing the gap between motion synthesis and closed-loop interaction. Conventional motion generation models typically produce coherent motion sequences from text or kinematic constraints~ mdm,omnicontrol,kimodo , whereas loco-manipulation requires robots to continually revise their subsequent motion based on current observations and their own states. The challenge is therefore both to acquire priors that capture whole-body coordination and to preserve these priors while making action generation responsive to task requirements and environmental changes. Within this framework, the pretrained motion generator provides reusable whole-body motion structure, perceptual conditioning grounds motion predictions in the current scene and task, and motion history together with continually updated action predictions allows the generation process to incorporate execution feedback. By combining motion structure with task conditioning and closed-loop feedback, KAMs provide a path from general-purpose motion generation to embodied interaction and control. To investigate this paradigm, we present Kimodo-Policy, an initial instantiation of KAMs for humanoid loco-manipulation (Fig.~ fig:overview ). We combine Kimodo's pretrained text-to-motion backbone~ kimodo with a lightweight ControlNet-based visual adapter~ zhang2023adding to directly examine whether strong motion priors can support visually conditioned action generation. The motion backbone remains frozen, while the adapter injects egocentric visual features to guide its predictions. A three-stage root--body--hand architecture first generates a root trajectory, then produces body joint motion conditioned on that trajectory, and finally predicts hand control signals from body features and visual context. Large-scale loco-manipulation pretraining adapts this architecture to robot interaction, while motion-history conditioning and repeated action-chunk prediction support closed-loop execution through a whole-body tracking controller~ sonic . The resulting policy contains 678 million parameters, of which 92 million are trainable. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot tasks, Kimodo-Policy achieves the highest overall success rate among the compared policies on multitask HumanoidArena~ humanoidarena , remains competitive on SIMPLE~ simple , and outperforms the evaluated baselines on real-world loco-manipulation tasks. Ablation studies support the contribution of the pretrained motion backbone, while comparisons across motion priors show that the choice of pretrained motion model affects downstream performance. These results provide initial evidence that motion generation can serve as a practical foundation for humanoid action models. Our main contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=*,topsep=0pt,itemsep=0.15em,parsep=0pt,partopsep=0pt] We introduce Kinematic Action Models (KAMs), a paradigm built on pretrained motion generators. By making whole-body motion a direct pretraining target, KAMs transfer temporal and cross-body coordination priors to downstream control, establishing a complementary foundation for humanoid policy learning. We develop Kimodo-Policy, an initial KAM instantiation with a frozen motion backbone and lightweight visual conditioning. Its root--body--hand hierarchy and motion-history conditioning support closed-loop loco-manipulation in a compact policy with 678M parameters, of which only 92M are trainable. We achieve the highest overall success among the compared methods on multitask HumanoidArena (72.14 ), competitive SIMPLE performance, and 60 mean success across eight real-world tasks, outperforming the evaluated real-world baselines. Ablations substantiate the contribution of pretrained motion priors to humanoid control. Related Work sec:related_work Whole-Body Control for Loco-Manipulation sec:related_whole_body Humanoid loco-manipulation integrates spatial grounding~ wang2026limitsvisionandlanguagenavigation,uniground and navigation planning~ wang2025dreamnavtrajectorybasedimaginativeframework,hero with whole-body coordination~ leverb,openhlm , enabling robots to approach interaction targets and manipulate objects while maintaining balance. HumanVLA~ humanvla distills a reinforcement-learned teacher into a vision--language policy. OASIS~ oasis combines simulated teleoperation with visual randomization, while FetchMan~ fetchman refines policies learned from synthetic demonstrations through reinforcement learning. Foundation policies such as GR00T N1~ grootn1 and ~ psi0 transfer pretrained visual--semantic representations to robot action experts. LeVERB~ leverb and WholeBodyVLA~ wholebodyvla further investigate learned latent interfaces and loco-manipulation-oriented controllers that connect task understanding to whole-body execution. These developments highlight the complementary roles of perceptual generalization, interaction data, and the control interface. World action models (WAMs) additionally use future visual or latent-state prediction to inform action learning. MotionWAM~ motionwam conditions whole-body action generation on intermediate video-denoising features, whereas the WBC-grounded WholeBodyWAM of wholebodywam_wbc adapts pretrained world--action priors through a unified controller interface and coordination-aware attention. More recent formulations address distinct aspects of predictive control: -0~ omega0 couples latent visual prediction with whole-body action generation, HWAM~ hwam jointly predicts reference actions and their realized body states, and Language-Forcing~ li2026languageforcing aligns predictive visual features with task-relevant language supervision. These approaches strengthen semantic grounding, predictive modeling, and execution awareness. However, pretraining on visual semantics or dynamics does not by itself provide a generative model of the coupled kinematics required for whole-body control. KAMs address this gap by making whole-body motion a direct target of generative pretraining and reusing the resulting generator as the action backbone. Perception then conditions an existing model of temporal and cross-body coordination, making coordinated movement a transferable foundation for humanoid policy learning. title: ScanDreamer: A Map-Grounded World Model for Quadrotor Navigation
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to AICAP 2027; decision pending
summary: Quadrotors inspecting buildings and tunnels must navigate unknown clutter with a forward-facing depth camera whose limited field of view constrains scene understanding and collision-avoiding navigation. Recent world-model agents learn navigation through imagined experience (e.g., AirDreamer), but remain data-intensive and often lack explicit geometric memory and awareness of what the camera can observe. We propose ScanDreamer, a map-grounded world model that constructs an online 2D scan-memory map from depth images and vehicle pose. Our world model, actor, and critic are conditioned on this map, which also defines a geodesic progress reward. Moreover, a forward-cone penalty discourages horizontal motion outside the camera's viewing direction. During imagination, ScanDreamer propagates the quadrotor pose over a frozen map and derives progress and wall-contact signals from the mapped geometry. We train ScanDreamer for 0.8 million environment steps (5.5 h on one GPU) and evaluate it in NVIDIA Isaac Sim over 1560 episodes spanning unseen layouts and parameter ranges. Across three seeds (mean $\pm$ SD), ScanDreamer achieves 96.3 $\pm$ 0.3% success with 3.6 $\pm$ 0.3% collision, compared with 59.6 $\pm$ 3.0% success and 28.8 $\pm$ 2.8% collision for AirDreamer at the same online-interaction budget. Removing the forward-cone penalty increases collisions to 9.9 $\pm$ 3.1%. These results show that combining explicit map memory, map-grounded imagination, and perception-aware motion substantially improves navigation performance and data efficiency. The source code is available at https://github.com/WANGSHUAIzzzz/ScanDreamer.

Autonomous navigation, collision avoidance, depth sensing, model-based reinforcement learning, occupancy mapping, unmanned aerial vehicles, world models Introduction sec:intro In buildings, tunnels, and caves, where sending people is slow or dangerous, small unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are used for inspection, search and rescue, and exploration~ tranzatto2022cerberus . Such missions often lack a reliable link to a human pilot and rarely come with prior maps, so the vehicle must find its own way through unknown clutter with its onboard sensors alone. Since a collision usually ends the mission, avoiding one matters as much as reaching the goal. Classical systems map, plan, and track in a chain of modules~ zhou2020ego,tordesillas2021faster . This modular structure is interpretable, but its objectives and costs typically require manual design, while errors in perception or mapping can propagate through the remaining pipeline. Learning-based methods instead optimize navigation policies through interaction in simulation. Such policies have enabled high-speed flight through clutter using depth images~ loquercio2021learning , autonomous drone racing against human champions~ kaufmann2023champion , and avoidance of moving obstacles~ xu2025navrl . World-model agents~ hafner2020dream,hafner2025dreamerv3 seek to reduce environment interaction by learning a predictive model and training the policy on rollouts imagined within it. On drones, however, they still train slowly. AirDreamer~ liu2026airdreamer uses 2.5M environment steps for depth-based navigation, while Dream to Fly~ romero2026dream reports approximately 240\,h of training to converge on pixel-based drone racing. Autonomous flight in confined environments is still limited by costly training, by obstacles forgotten once out of view, and by motion into poorly observed space. Existing world-model agents do not fully use depth images and poses to build a geometric memory or account for the direction of sensing, which leaves them with four limitations. First, a recurrent memory retains obstacle geometry poorly in large or maze-like environments~ liu2026airdreamer,romero2026dream,pasukonis2023evaluating . Second, Euclidean progress can reward flight into dead ends, while standard geodesic progress needs ground-truth geometry~ savva2019habitat,wijmans2020ddppo , which the vehicle lacks. Third, if the reward ignores the camera direction, it can encourage sideways or backward flight into poorly observed space. Fourth, imagined rollouts are purely latent: the learned heads for progress, wall contacts, and arrival see neither the imagined pose nor mapped walls, and the actor can exploit their errors~ ha2018recurrent . To address these limitations, we propose (Fig.~ fig:overview ), a map-grounded navigation agent. It builds on DreamerV3~ hafner2025dreamerv3 and adds one component for each limitation. We evaluate it in simulation on five test suites of new scenes, including layouts, parameters, and obstacle cases absent from training, against AirDreamer, NavRL~ xu2025navrl , and TD-MPC2~ hansen2024tdmpc2 . At the same training budget, succeeds far more often than AirDreamer and collides far less often, and it stays ahead when AirDreamer trains for 2.5 times as many steps. World-model agents for small UAVs can thus learn safer flight from less data by building on what the vehicle knows and sees. Because pose estimates and known sensor orientations are available on many mobile robots, these principles may also extend beyond quadrotors. Our contributions are as follows: Scan-memory map. We construct a persistent 2-D occupancy map from depth observations and poses, and condition the world model, actor, and critic on local map crops (Sec.~ sec:map ). Map-grounded imagination. In imagined rollouts, a calibrated pose moves over the frozen map, and progress, contacts with mapped walls, and goal arrival are computed analytically (Secs.~ sec:imag and~ sec:ablation ). Map- and perception-aware rewards. We compute geodesic progress from a cost-to-go field over the accumulated map (Sec.~ sec:geo ). We also introduce a forward-cone penalty that discourages horizontal motion away from the camera axis and toward poorly observed space (Secs.~ sec:cone and~ sec:ablation ). Related Work sec:related Learning-Based Navigation Learning-based methods have been studied across aviation, from traffic-level decision support to autonomous flight pham2019reinforcement,tran2020interactive, loquercio2021learning,song2023learning . Depth-based flight policies have been learned by imitating privileged experts loquercio2021learning,song2023learning and through differentiable dynamics~ zhang2025learning,lee2025depthnav . Model-free NavRL~ xu2025navrl uses PPO~ schulman2017ppo to train a policy that reads distances ray-cast against a map rather than depth images. Perception-aware methods keep a point of interest in view~ falanga2018pampc , restrict commanded velocity to the sensor's field of view~ kulkarni2024reinforcement , reward yaw alignment with a privileged reference path~ song2023learning , or align the body -axis with a smoothed velocity~ lee2025depthnav . These approaches either constrain motion or rely on privileged reference information. This motivates perception-aware guidance that favors motion toward observed space while preserving the full action space and requiring neither a reference path nor a heading target. World Models for Robot Learning and Flight Learned predictive models have been applied across flight and robot learning~ hafner2020dream,hafner2025dreamerv3, goh2021tunnel,goh2023unstable . Dreamer agents have been applied to depth-based drone navigation~ liu2026airdreamer and drone racing from pixels~ romero2026dream . Whereas these agents act using policies learned through imagination, TD-MPC2~ hansen2024tdmpc2 , a planning-based method, selects each action using model predictive path integral control in the latent space of a decoder-free world model. In concurrent work, MAD~ zhang2026mad decodes robocentric occupancy and visibility maps from its latent state, but its imagined rollouts remain latent. DreamerNav~ shanks2025dreamernav , a DreamerV3 agent for ground robots, observes a local occupancy map with an A* route planned on a known static map. Existing methods therefore either keep imagination purely latent or depend on a known map. A map constructed online offers a natural way to ground imagined rollouts, combining learned prediction with explicit geometric reasoning. Spatial Memory and Progress Rewards Spatial reasoning shapes decision-making in both human-operated and autonomous systems~ zhong2022spatial,chaplot2020learning, pasukonis2023evaluating . Active Neural SLAM chaplot2020learning constructs a top-down metric map online and guides a learned local policy using a planner over this map. MAVRL~ yu2025mavrl retains past quadrotor depth observations in a learned latent representation rather than an explicit map. R2I~ samsami2024mastering strengthens latent memory using state-space models and, after 400M environment steps, exceeds human scores on all but the largest mazes in Memory Maze pasukonis2023evaluating . Point-goal progress is commonly measured using geodesic distance over ground-truth meshes~ savva2019habitat,wijmans2020ddppo or time-of-arrival maps of the training environments lee2025depthnav . These approaches provide accurate training signals but depend on privileged knowledge of the environment. The agent's partial online map can instead serve two roles: preserving previously observed geometry and providing a measure of geodesic progress. Method sec:method Problem Formulation and Base Agent sec:problem We formulate point-goal navigation without a prior map as a partially observable Markov decision process. An episode is truncated at the step limit of its scene and terminates earlier on arrival, collision, or exit from the altitude band of 0.3 to 3.2\,m. The quadrotor arrives when its 3D distance to the goal falls below \,m and collides when its horizontal distance to the nearest obstacle falls below 0.3\,m. At each step, the agent observes a depth image from a forward-facing camera with an horizontal FOV and a range of 0.6 to 6\,m. A 15-D state vector holds the goal direction and distances, the velocity, the body rates, and the attitude. Each action is applied at 20\,Hz. Its first three components are a velocity setpoint in the yaw-aligned heading frame, scaled by \,m/s, followed by the cosine and sine of an absolute yaw command. To build its map, also reads its height above the ground and the planar pose in the take-off frame. builds on DreamerV3~ hafner2025dreamerv3 , using its recurrent state-space model (RSSM)~ hafner2019learning and actor--critic training. The actor and critic learn from -returns over imagined steps. As in AirDreamer~ liu2026airdreamer , the actor loss includes an action-smoothness term. At each step, the agent receives where replaces AirDreamer's Euclidean progress reward and penalizes motion outside the forward cone. The remaining terms follow AirDreamer: penalizes obstacle proximity, and penalizes the vertical goal offset. Arrival gives , while collision gives . Scan-Memory Map sec:map The scan-memory map (Fig.~ fig:overview ) is a persistent occupancy map in the take-off frame, built online from depth and pose, and retains obstacles outside the camera's view. Depth pixels are back-projected with the attitude, and those 0.25 to 3.4\,m above ground are taken as obstacle points. The nearest obstacle point per image column terminates a horizontal ray. Rays update a 0.15\,m grid with clamped log-odds~ hornung2013octomap , and occupied cells are never cleared during an episode. title: FlowEval: How Much Adaptation Does an Embodied Foundation Model Need at Deployment?
summary: Large-scale pretraining is reducing the amount of adaptation required to deploy embodied foundation models, but it is not guaranteed that a pretrained model already provide the level of performance required in every deployment. Practitioners therefore need to understand how well a pretrained model matches a target deployment and how much adaptation data is left to be collected. We study whether a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations can reveal whether and how much target-domain data will be required before any adaptation. We introduce FlowEval, a set of training-free metrics that use the flow-matching objective to probe an embodied foundation model with a set of demonstrations. FlowEval quantifies predictive disagreement on successful target demonstrations to assess how well a pretrained model fits a target deployment. Across four embodied foundation model families: Pi-0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T, and DreamZero, FlowEval distinguishes seen from unseen deployments across real-world and simulated manipulation. Further, by finetuning Pi-0.5 and GR00T on 17 RoboCasa365 manipulation tasks, we showed that FlowEval correlates with how success rate improves as additional adaptation data is provided. Together, these results suggest that FlowEval can serve as a lightweight, training-free diagnostic of how much model--deployment adaptation may be required.

Introduction Large-scale pretraining is enabling embodied foundation models to generalize across increasingly broad variation in tasks, environments, and robot embodiments kim2024openvla, physical_intelligence2025pi05, octo_2023, embodimentcollaboration2025openxembodimentroboticlearning . Yet broad generalization does not imply that a pretrained model will already provide the level of performance required in every downstream deployment octo_2023, kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodelsoptimizing, geminiroboticsteam2025geminirobotics15 . In practice, models may still require target-domain adaptation to acquire novel physical behaviors, transfer to another action space, or improve behaviors that are only partially captured by the pretrained prior. While broad pretraining increasingly reduces the amount of task-specific learning required, adaptation remains an important component of deploying today's embodied foundation models physical_intelligence2025pi05, fang2026molmoact2, ye2026dreamzero . As embodied models become more general-purpose, this changes the deployment problem itself. Rather than asking only how to adapt a pretrained model to a downstream setting, practitioners increasingly need to understand how much of the required behavior is already provided by pretraining and how much additional adaptation remains. Importantly, poor zero-shot performance does not reveal whether the desired behavior can be recovered with a small amount of target-domain data or requires substantially more adaptation, and a model with stronger broad capabilities need not require less adaptation for a particular deployment. This motivates two questions: 1) whether the target deployment is already seen by the model, and, ultimately, 2) how much additional data will be required to achieve the desired level of performance? We study whether the answer to these questions can be probed directly with a small set of successful target-domain demonstrations. Such trajectories provide examples of the behavior the deployed system is expected to reproduce, and can often be collected with substantially less effort than the full datasets required for finetuning. This suggests a simple hypothesis: downstream adaptation difficulty should depend on how well the pretrained model already fits the intended target behavior. Rather than first finetuning several candidate models and observing which one adapts successfully, we ask whether this model--deployment relationship can be measured before adaptation. A natural quantity to examine is the pretrained model's training loss on successful target-domain trajectories. In language modeling, held-out cross-entropy and perplexity have long been used to characterize how well a model fits a target domain and to select data that better matches that domain moorelewis2010intelligent,gururangan2020dontstoppretrainingadapt,DoReMi2023 . Flow matching is particularly well suited to assessing model--data fit because its training objective probes not only the predicted action, but the model's local direction of improvement toward the demonstrated action lipman2023flowmatchinggenerativemodeling . We therefore introduce , a set of training-free metrics derived from the flow-matching objective that measure how well a pretrained model fits successful target-domain demonstrations by computing the predictive disagreement. requires no finetuning and applies whether or not the pretrained model and target deployment share the same action representation. This is particularly important for deployment, as action representations and deployment interfaces can differ widely across model families and robot embodiments. embodimentcollaboration2025openxembodimentroboticlearning, gr00tn1_2025 We evaluate on Pi-0.5, MolmoAct2, GR00T, and DreamZero, across real-world and simulated manipulation and multiple robot embodiments. Across these settings, predicted directional disagreement correlates distinguishes seen deployment distributions from unseen deployment distributions. More importantly, by finetuning Pi-0.5 and GR00T on 17 RoboCasa365 manipulation tasks, we find that the same signal correlates with how performance scales as additional adaptation data is provided. Together, these results suggest that can serve as a training-free diagnostic of how much target-domain adaptation may be required. Related Work Adapting embodied foundation models sec:related_work_adapting Downstream finetuning is the widely adopted approach to adapt a general pretrained policy. State-of-the-art open source embodied foundation models, including but not limited to DreamZero ye2026dreamzero , MolmoAct2 fang2026molmoact2 , Pi-05 physical_intelligence2025pi05 , and GR00T gr00tn1_2025 , provide finetuning pipelines and include finetuning guidelines at release. Prior to them, OpenVLA kim2024openvla , OpenVLA-OFT kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodelsoptimizing , and Octo octo_2023 expected downstream finetuning even more. On the proprietary end, Generalist Gen1.5 generalist2026gen15 reported using few gradient step adaptation to better learn novel tasks; and Gemini Robotics deepmind2026geminirobotics2,geminiroboticsteam2025geminirobotics15 reported finetuning the model to target embodiments. Although Figure AI figure2026helix02 , Skild skild2026s1 , and Genesis AI genesis2026gene265 do not report downstream fine-tuning, notably, their pretraining datasets are directly built for their deployment settings. This is fundamentally different from the situation faced by practitioners, who lack the ability to construct a large-scale pretraining dataset specifically for their deployment. Learning In-Context is a promising yet constrained approach for a pretrained embodied foundation model to adapt to a new task. DreamZero ye2026dreamzero and Skild S1 skild2026s1 provided video as context and shows the model is able to infer tasks from the world to state information in the videos. Generalist Gen1.5 generalist2026gen15 provided one-shot state to action demonstration as context and shows emerging ability of the model generalizing to novel objects. However, all require the embodiment and action representation to align between the pretrained and deployment settings. generalist2026gen15 also reported that skills learned in-context are more brittle than finetuned models. Zero-shot execution is possible in scenarios the embodiment and action representation between pretrained and deployment settings are aligned. fang2026molmoact2,octo_2023,rewardai2026om1 showed zero-shot execution of tasks on supported embodiments. Similar to in-context learning, their prerequisites are more restrictive than most practical deployment settings. Training objectives as Evaluations sec:related_work_training_objectives The optimization objective, such as loss or negative log-likelihood (NLL), is commonly used as an evaluation metric for model performance in machine learning zhang2017understandingdeeplearningrequires,guo2017calibrationmodernneuralnetworks and especially on large language models kaplan2020scalinglawsneurallanguage, hoffmann2022trainingcomputeoptimallargelanguage . In robotics, validation loss is often used a proxy for performance to select policies ross2011reductionimitationlearningstructured, zhao2023learningfinegrainedbimanualmanipulation . As to embodied foundation models including RT-2 brohan2023rt2 , Octo octo_2023 , and OpenVLA kim2024openvla , however, multiple works li2024evaluatingrealworldrobotmanipulation,zhou2025autoevalautonomousevaluationgeneralist showed that validation loss poorly reflects actual robot performance. Interestingly, none of these work li2024evaluatingrealworldrobotmanipulation,zhou2025autoevalautonomousevaluationgeneralist tested flow-matching based models. Flow objectives as evaluations Likelihood-based flows naturally allows likelihood evaluations. A common use case is to evaluate the model on an entire held-out dataset, using the likelihood to measure how well the model fits unseen data durkan2019neuralsplineflows,Papamakarios2021normalizing . In contrast, using the likelihood of a single data point as a measure of whether that point is in- or out-of-distribution is a stronger assumption and is not generally guaranteed nalisnick2019deepgenerativemodelsknow,han2026conditionalflowmatchingreplace . However, in robotics, where the generated distribution is conditional action likelihoods , likelihood have been successfully applied as measures of action plausibility or anomaly: Wenger2025anomalously use it to detect several types of antagonistic robot behavior, while NEURIPS2023_zhang_constrainedpolicy,chae2026flowactorcriticofflinereinforcement effectively applied it inside offline-RL algorithms as an OOD score. The flow matching loss shares some common properties with likelihood-trained normalizing flows, such as evaluating how well a policy fits a held-out demonstration set. zha2026laplanguageactionpretrainingenables evaluates the validation loss of its flow-matching action expert on a held-out split and uses it to compare model scaling. Recent robot policy evaluations also compute the flow matching objective on held-out episodes as an offline action-prediction loss robocurve2026groot . park2026behavioral evaluated the relationship between flow-matching loss and success rate, and discovers that lower training loss is associated with higher validation loss and higher performance. differs from prior works in two meaningful ways. (1) We discovered that starting from pure noise provided us with cleaner evaluation signals than noisy actions (Appendix.~ appendix:why-pure-noise ) (2) Instead of using loss to select checkpoints from the same training run, we use pre-adaptation loss to probe how finetuning outcomes vary across target deployments and demonstration budgets. Methodology We begin by clarifying the deployment settings considered in this work. We distinguish the conditions that fall within and outside the scope of our metric evaluation. Demonstration: We define a demonstration as an observation-state-action trajectory demonstrating successful completion of a task. In this work, we primarily consider demonstrations collected via human teleoperation. Although approaches such as MimicGen mandlekar2023mimicgendatagenerationscalable , DemoGen xue2025demogensyntheticdemonstrationgeneration , and other forms of augmenting existing demonstrations may be interesting directions to explore, they are beyond the scope of this study (Appendix. ~ appendix:counter-case ). Deployment settings: We define a deployment setting as one or more manipulation tasks performed under a fixed environment, embodiment, and action

title: Look Ahead: Search-Driven Reasoning in Embodied AI
summary: Search allows a robotic policy to evaluate candidate futures before committing to an action. Motivated by test-time planning for vision-language action (VLA) models, we study selective search over action chunks in PushT using a frozen Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy. Beam search generates perturbed alternatives around the policy prediction and scores them through rollouts from cloned simulator states. Across 50 evaluation episodes, beam search raises task success from 0% to 18% and increases average cumulative reward from 39.44 to 103.2. We introduce One Step Ahead (OSA), a gate that simulates the nominal policy chunk and invokes full search only when its predicted coverage drop exceeds a threshold. In the reported ablations, OSA preserves or improves success while reducing runtime by approximately 3x relative to full beam search. Ablations over tree depth, branching factor, beam width, and replanning frequency show that larger search budgets do not consistently improve performance. The results support selective test-time search for action-chunking policies; evaluation on language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots remains future work.

Beam search generates perturbed alternatives around the policy prediction and scores them through rollouts from cloned simulator states.
