Ablations over tree depth, branching factor, beam width, and replanning frequency show that larger search budgets do not consistently improve performance. The results support selective test-time search for action-chunking policies; evaluation on language-conditioned VLAs and physical robots remains future work. Introduction Vision--language--action (VLA) models map visual observations and task instructions to robot actions, offering a route toward generalist control pi0,smolvla,octo . Predicting plausible actions, however, does not ensure that their consequences will complete a task. In contact-rich manipulation, a locally reasonable movement can displace an object away from its goal, and errors can accumulate over successive action chunks. Test-time search addresses this problem by evaluating candidate futures before the controller commits to a trajectory vlareasoner,vlaps . Policy-guided search combines a learned action prior with a transition model and a scoring function. The policy restricts exploration to plausible actions, the model predicts their effects, and the score identifies promising futures. This can improve action selection without updating policy parameters, but repeated policy queries and simulated transitions increase inference cost. The practical question is therefore when additional search changes the decision enough to justify that cost. We investigate this question in PushT, a simulated planar manipulation task in which an agent pushes a T-shaped object toward a target pose pusht . We augment a pretrained ACT policy act with beam search over locally perturbed action chunks. ACT is a vision-based action-chunking policy rather than a language-conditioned VLA. This isolates action selection from language grounding while retaining the proposal-and-rollout interface used in VLA planning. Full search often returns the same nominal action chunk that the policy would have executed directly. To reduce this overhead, we introduce One Step Ahead (OSA). OSA first simulates the nominal chunk and invokes beam search only if its final predicted coverage is lower than the current coverage by more than a fixed threshold. This makes search conditional on a concrete signal of predicted regression. Figure~ fig:pusht-rollout-comparison illustrates the resulting action selection. Our contributions are: A beam-search controller for PushT that proposes perturbed ACT action chunks, evaluates their consequences using simulator rollouts, and selects a chunk without retraining the policy. One Step Ahead, a coverage-based gate that selectively invokes search when the nominal policy prediction is expected to reduce task progress. An evaluation over 50 episodes per configuration, including tree-structure, replanning-frequency, and OSA ablations, with success, reward, alternative-selection, and runtime measurements. Related Work Action-chunking policies and VLAs. ACT predicts short sequences of actions from visual observations and robot state using imitation learning act . Diffusion Policy represents visuomotor behavior through action diffusion and uses receding-horizon execution pusht . Generalist policies extend these ideas to broader task specifications: Octo supports language- and goal-image-conditioned control, combines a pretrained vision--language backbone with a flow-based action model, and SmolVLA emphasizes efficient language-conditioned action generation octo,pi0,smolvla . Our method operates on the action-chunk interface and keeps the policy frozen. Its evaluation uses ACT, so transfer to language-conditioned policies is an architectural possibility rather than an established result. Search for VLA policies. VLA-Reasoner uses online Monte Carlo tree search with a learned world model and value estimates to evaluate action-conditioned futures vlareasoner . VLAPS integrates model-based search with pretrained VLA action priors and evaluates language-specified manipulation in LIBERO vlaps,libero . Its experiments assume access to an accurate simulator. These approaches establish the relevance of test-time planning for VLA control. We study a simpler local beam-search procedure in PushT, using continuous coverage feedback and a gate based on the nominal chunk's predicted effect. Our experiments focus on the cost of tree expansion and the value of selective search, rather than a direct performance comparison with these methods on different benchmarks. Method Policy and Action Representation At control step , the policy receives an observation , where is an RGB image and is the agent position. The frozen policy predicts a nominal chunk where each action is a 2D target position in the workspace. We distinguish the candidate rollout length from the execution horizon : search evaluates candidate chunks, but the controller executes only the first actions before observing the environment and replanning. This distinction allows replanning frequency to vary independently of the policy's prediction length. Simulator-Based Beam Search A search state contains the simulator configuration, including the agent coordinates, object position and orientation, and the dynamic variables needed to restore the state. At each planning point, we snapshot the current simulator state. Every hypothetical rollout starts from the appropriate restored state, and the root state is restored before any action is committed to the environment. The task provides a coverage measure describing overlap between the movable T and the target T. We use this feedback to rank candidate futures. Success is defined by at least 95 coverage; an episode ends at success or after environment steps. Unlike real-world control, this setup provides both a simulator transition model and privileged access to task coverage. At each expanded node, ACT predicts a nominal chunk. A candidate set contains this chunk and locally perturbed alternatives: where is the total number of candidate chunks, is action noise, and clipping enforces the workspace action bounds. Including the nominal chunk allows the controller to retain the policy prediction when the alternatives are worse. Each candidate is simulated from its parent state, producing a child state scored by its coverage-based rollout outcome. At each level, beam search retains the highest-scoring nodes and expands them until depth , success, or the episode limit. The selected action is the root chunk leading to the best-scoring explored outcome. The controller restores the real state and commits its first actions. Only committed transitions contribute to episode reward; hypothetical search rollouts do not. The execution horizon determines how often the controller replans. For and , full beam search can be invoked at most times per episode. Increasing lowers the number of planning calls but also delays opportunities to correct a poor action sequence. One Step Ahead We measure how often search changes the policy prediction through the alternative selection ratio (ASR): ASR is reported as a percentage. When search repeatedly selects the nominal chunk, evaluating all alternatives adds cost without changing the committed action. OSA uses a preliminary rollout to decide whether full search is needed. Let be the current coverage and the coverage at the end of the simulated nominal chunk. We define Full beam search is triggered only when Otherwise, the nominal chunk is selected directly. Here, ``one step'' refers to one candidate-chunk rollout, not a single low-level control step. The gate still incurs the cost of this rollout, but can avoid the remaining tree expansion. Algorithm~ algo:one_step_ahead describes the decision procedure. The gate detects predicted regression rather than all forms of policy failure. In particular, a nominal chunk that makes no progress can bypass search, and a small final coverage drop can hide a harmful intermediate transition. OSA is therefore a heuristic for allocating computation, with no guarantee of optimality or safe execution. Experiments Evaluation Setup We use the pretrained checkpoint with frozen parameters. Each configuration is evaluated on 50 PushT episodes with a maximum length of 300 steps. We compare direct ACT inference, full beam search, and OSA-gated beam search. The tree-structure ablation varies depth , total candidate count , and beam width . The replanning-frequency ablation varies the execution horizon , and the OSA ablation uses a coverage-drop threshold of 0.05. We report average cumulative reward, average maximum reward, task success, ASR, and runtime. For an episode of executed steps, cumulative reward is and maximum reward is . These episode metrics are averaged across the evaluation set. Cumulative reward is an accumulated score, not a coverage percentage. Success is the fraction of episodes that meet the 95 coverage criterion. Runtime values describe the reported evaluation setup; no claim of real-time physical control is made. Effect of Tree Structure Table~ tab:pusht-search-configurations shows that beam search improves substantially over the evaluated ACT baseline. The configuration with , , and achieves the highest average cumulative reward, 103.2 versus 39.44 for direct inference. Its average maximum reward rises from 0.36 to 0.81, and success improves from 0 to 18 . This comes at a runtime increase from 2 to 47 seconds, or approximately . Increasing depth alone yields little improvement. With and , depths 2, 4, and 8 produce the same reported average reward values and 18 success. Increasing the number of candidates generally increases ASR: at , , ASR rises from 37.5 with to 75.6 with . This shows that a larger candidate set more often changes the policy's action, but the corresponding gains in task success remain modest. Wider beams also do not guarantee better outcomes. At and , increasing from 4 to 8 raises runtime from 47 to 87 seconds while reducing average cumulative reward from 103.2 to 92.2 and success from 18 to 10 . The larger tree performs best at short horizons, but its advantage disappears at longer horizons. title: Brain-Aligned Latent Actions: Imposing Premotor Cortex Geometry on a Robot's Action Vocabulary
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables. Robot manipulation results (CALVIN) will be added in a later version
summary: Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We find this choice highly unstable: two independently trained runs of Moto's latent motion tokenizer assign the same robot clips to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index 0.001), and evaluating one tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74% of its tokens. We use this freedom to impose the representational geometry of macaque ventral premotor cortex (PMv), recorded while a monkey drew shapes, on the tokenizer's code assignment, with a straight-through similarity loss trained alongside its reconstruction objective on robot video. In one training run per target, on five shape categories the loss never saw, the PMv-trained tokenizer reaches a representational similarity of 0.52 with PMv, against 0.20-0.26 for released and no-prior tokenizers and 0.42 for the 95th percentile of random kinematic encoders. Kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer (-0.17 to -0.03). Two results limit the claim: a hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv better (0.65), and a label-shuffled PMv control scores 0.41. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it.
full_text: Brain-aligned latent actions. (A)~Moto's latent-action tokenizer encodes robot video into 128 discrete codes, trained as usual to reconstruct the next frame. It also encodes shapes drawn by a macaque (one typical recorded stroke per shape; dot: start), and a loss pulls the geometry of its code use toward the geometry recorded in ventral premotor cortex (PMv). Highlighted codes are illustrative. (B)~On five held-out shape categories, only the PMv-trained tokenizer exceeds a kinematic yardstick (dashed), but an untrained descriptor, the stroke's initial pen direction, scores higher (dotted; ). fig:teaser Robot policies increasingly act through a small vocabulary of discrete latent actions learned from unlabeled video, yet training leaves open which motion receives which code. We specify the downstream manipulation test, on a CALVIN pipeline that reproduces Moto's published results, before running it. Introduction sec:intro Robot foundation models increasingly learn to act from video that carries no action labels. A widely used recipe compresses the change between two frames into a few discrete latent actions: tokens from a learned vocabulary that a policy predicts on the way to motor commands~ bruce2024genie,ye2025latent,chen2025moto,bu2025learning . Because the vocabulary sits on the policy's inference path, the way it groups motions decides what the policy treats as the same action and what it treats as different. Nothing in the training objective fixes that grouping, and we find that it varies greatly between runs. Two independently trained runs of the Moto latent motion tokenizer~ chen2025moto assign the same 10 , 240 tokens, from 1 , 280 robot clips, to nearly unrelated codes (adjusted Rand index , seed A after 150k steps and seed B after 99k; ). Evaluating a single trained tokenizer in bf16 instead of fp32 reassigns 74 of its tokens ( ). The objective decides how well frames are reconstructed, not which motion receives which token. A design choice that the data leave open is an opening for a prior. In vision, imposing measured brain structure on artificial networks has repeatedly paid off. A fixed model of primary visual cortex at the front of a convolutional network improves its robustness~ dapello2020simulating ; regularizing a network toward the representational similarity of mouse V1 makes it more robust~ li2019learning ; aligning a network to macaque inferior temporal cortex improves both its agreement with human behavior and its adversarial robustness~ dapello2023aligning . These works did not wait for brain-like structure to emerge; they imposed it. On the action side, this approach has only begun to be explored~ kapitonova2026distilling , and it has not been applied to the discrete action vocabularies that robot models learn from video. The primate motor system offers a natural target: ventral premotor cortex (PMv) represents drawn shapes as reusable, categorical action symbols~ tian2026neural , the role that a latent-action vocabulary plays for a robot. We therefore ask whether premotor cortex can choose a robot's action vocabulary. We impose the representational geometry of macaque PMv, recorded while a monkey drew shapes~ tian2026neural , on the code assignment of the Moto tokenizer ( A). The tokenizer keeps its original reconstruction objective on robot video. On alternating batches it also encodes the monkey's strokes, and a straight-through similarity loss pulls the geometry of its code usage toward the PMv geometry of each recording session. The loss acts on which code each input selects, not on continuous features, because the discrete choice is all the policy sees. We built the evaluation around controls. Alignment is measured only on stroke categories that the loss never saw. Four control tokenizers are trained identically toward kinematic, language, label-shuffled PMv, and spectrum-matched random targets. We measure alignment with representational similarity analysis (RSA): the rank correlation between the tokenizer's and PMv's dissimilarity structure over the same shape categories. Every score is compared with a kinematic yardstick: the 95th percentile of 100 random nonlinear encoders of the pen's motion, scored the same way on the same held-out categories ( ). Contributions. The vocabulary is unstable. Seed and numerical precision each reassign most tokens of a latent-action tokenizer while reconstruction stays good, so the objective does not pin down the assignment of motions to codes ( ). A method to impose neural geometry on a discrete action vocabulary. A dual-stream objective aligns the geometry of the code assignment to per-session neural similarity, across two domains that share no inputs: monkey drawings and robot video ( ). Premotor geometry reaches held-out shapes; non-neural targets do not. In one training run per target, the PMv tokenizer reaches held-out RSA with PMv, above the released tokenizer ( ), the two no-prior runs ( and ), and all 100 random kinematic encoders (maximum ), while kinematic, language, and random targets do not transfer. A hand-picked kinematic descriptor, the stroke's initial direction, matches PMv's held-out geometry better still ( ), so we do not claim structure beyond kinematics; and a label-shuffled PMv control scores ( ). A validated path to manipulation. Our evaluation reproduces the published CALVIN performance of Moto's released policy, our one-GPU fine-tuning reproduces its reported low-data result (whose sampling and fine-tuning length Moto does not publish), and we fix the downstream test and its decision rules before running it ( ). The Action Vocabulary Is Unstable sec:vocab The tokenizer. We study the latent motion tokenizer of Moto~ chen2025moto , an open-source latent-action model trained on CALVIN~ mees2022calvin . It reads a pair of frames , summarizes their difference with eight query tokens, and quantizes each token to its nearest entry in a codebook of vectors of dimension 32~ vandenoord2017neural . A decoder reconstructs from and the eight codes, and the reconstruction error is the training loss. In Moto's policy the codes are the targets of video pretraining and the inputs from which actions are decoded, so the codebook acts as the policy's action vocabulary. We train the tokenizer from random initialization for 150k steps in fp32, as in Moto, on a single A100 ( ). Two seeds, two unrelated vocabularies. We trained the tokenizer twice with Moto's objective alone, from different random seeds, and encoded the same 1 , 280 CALVIN validation clips (10 , 240 tokens) with both (seed A after 150k steps, seed B after 99k; ). The two assignments are nearly unrelated ( ). Their adjusted Rand index, which ignores how codes are labeled, is (a random pairing of the same tokens gives ). After the best one-to-one relabeling of codes, they agree on 4.1 of tokens, against 3.9 for a random pairing. Both checkpoints reconstruct frames well (mean squared error for seed A and for seed B), so good reconstruction is reached by nearly unrelated assignments. Two caveats apply: the runs differ in training length and seed B changed GPU type midway ( ), and token-level disagreement does not show that the full eight-token codes carry unrelated motion information; it shows that the objective does not fix the partition. Precision rewrites the vocabulary. Limited precision is known to change the discrete outputs of language models~ yuan2025understanding ; here it rewrites the action vocabulary. Evaluating Moto's released tokenizer on identical inputs in bf16 instead of fp32 changes 74 of its token assignments; TF32 changes 21 . A randomly initialized tokenizer changes only 2 under bf16, so the fragility is a property of the trained solution, which places many inputs close to the boundary between codes. Training for 200 steps from the same initialization on the same batches in bf16 and in fp32 ends at nearly the same reconstruction loss ( and ) while assigning only 46 of tokens alike. Why it matters. The objective fixes how well frames are reconstructed but leaves open which motions share a code. That choice is not cosmetic: the policy decodes actions from the codes, and in an open-loop check, perturbing a trained policy's codes through bf16 moved its predicted arm actions by 60 of their magnitude, though bf16 also changes the decoder itself ( ). We take the freedom as an opportunity. If many vocabularies serve reconstruction equally well, a prior can choose among them, and a measured prior is one we can test. Imposing Premotor Geometry on the Vocabulary sec:method Our method has three parts: a neural target that says which drawn shapes premotor cortex treats as similar ( ); a loss that pulls the tokenizer's code assignment toward that similarity structure while it keeps learning from robot video ( ); and a test that asks whether the imposed structure reaches shapes the loss never saw, relative to matched controls ( ). Neural target: premotor geometry of drawing sec:target We use recordings from ventral premotor cortex of one macaque monkey drawing shapes~ tian2026neural : four sessions with 49, 40, 55, and 52 PMv units and 307, 241, 348, and 399 strokes. We group strokes by their shape label, keep categories with at least four strokes (19, 18, 24, and 26 per session), and summarize each stroke by the population response from 0.6\,s before to 0.2\,s after stroke onset, projected onto its first eight principal components. The target for a session is its representational dissimilarity matrix (RDM)~ kriegeskorte2008representational : for every pair of categories, the Euclidean distance between the mean response of one category in a random half of its strokes and that of the other in the complementary half, averaged over 25 splits. Unlike cross-validated distances, this estimator is still inflated by noise, more so for categories with few strokes ( ). Because the four sessions record different units, we never pool them: each session contributes its own RDM, and every score is computed per session and then averaged. The target is reliable. The split-half reliability of the RDMs (the noise ceiling) is over all categories and -- over the five held-out categories, and RDMs of different sessions correlate at over the 18 categories they share. Aligning the code assignment sec:loss Two streams, one tokenizer. The tokenizer trains on two kinds of input that share no examples, following the dual-stream design of li2019learning . On CALVIN video it minimizes Moto's reconstruction loss, unchanged. On monkey drawings it encodes renderings of each stroke: the pen trace drawn so far, shown at four points along the stroke and fed as four frame pairs in the same format as robot frames. We describe a stroke by its code usage: the fraction of its tokens assigned to each of the 128 codes. The loss acts on the assignment. title: Streaming Failure Forecasting: VLA Failure Monitors That Keep Learning After Deployment
comment: 25 pages, 13 figures, 9 tables. A short version was accepted at the Sim2Real2Field and EEAI workshops at CoRL 2026. Project page: https://sff-research.org
summary: Failure monitors for vision-language-action (VLA) policies are trained offline and then frozen. After deployment, lighting, objects and cameras drift, and the policy itself is updated or moved to new tasks. On recorded real-robot runs, after a switch of task or policy version, a frozen monitor fit on the old task ranks failures little better than chance. We present Streaming Failure Forecasting (SFF), a monitor that keeps learning from the one label every episode provides: whether it succeeded. SFF keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last linear layer after each episode, at 2.18 ms per policy call on a Jetson CPU core. Its alarm threshold moves only after successes, which in simulation kept false alarms near target except when two drifts came at once. With every setting locked before testing, SFF ranks failures better than the same monitor kept frozen on 4 of 5 simulated test suites under unannounced drift, and above resetting on detected drift on every suite. Carried with its locked learner settings to 434 recorded runs of four VLAs on real SO-101 arms, replayed across unannounced switches of task or policy version, it ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA and, in an exploratory comparison, above a full reset at the true switch. A deployed failure monitor need not stay frozen: refitting its readout from outcomes is cheap and helps after the changes we tested.

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) policies carry out manipulation tasks from a language instruction~ shukor2025smolvla,black2024pi0,pi2025pi05 , but they still fail often, so a deployed robot needs a failure monitor: a model that watches each episode through onboard signals and raises an alarm before a failing episode ends. SAFE~ gu2025safe learns such a score from the policy's internal features; other monitors measure uncertainty, action consistency or feature distances~ romer2025fiper,xu2025faildetect,agia2024sentinel,seligmann2026vlafail . All of them are trained and calibrated offline, then frozen. A deployed robot does not stand still. The light changes, objects are swapped, a camera gets bumped and gripper pads wear, and the policy itself is updated or moved to a new task as the fleet improves. Nobody tells the monitor. Each change can break the monitor's ranking, so failing episodes no longer score above successful ones: on recorded real-robot runs of four VLAs, a frozen monitor's within-task AUROC falls from on the task it was fit on to after a switch, close to chance (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Recalibrating the alarm threshold cannot repair ranking, because the order of the scores does not depend on the threshold. Yet the deployed system learns how every episode ended. We ask whether this one label is enough to keep a monitor useful, if it updates the right part. keeps the offline monitor's network fixed and refits only its last, linear layer after each episode, in closed form, pulled toward the offline layer so that it starts out ranking exactly as the offline monitor does (Fig.~ fig:method ). Its alarm threshold moves only after successful episodes, the only ones on which an alarm is false, which bounds the long-run false-alarm rate for any bounded score, even one that is still learning. An update is one solve, no episode is stored, and the monitor is never told when or how conditions changed. We designed on one LIBERO suite, chose each suite's features and two settings on its own development streams, locked them, and tested each suite once; we then carried the locked learner settings to recorded real-robot runs of four VLAs. We find: 1pt 0pt Refitting the readout improves ranking under drift. ranks failures better than the frozen monitor on of simulated test suites, including the primary test specified in advance, and above a monitor that resets on detected drift on every suite (Sec.~ sec:sim ). The locked settings carry to recorded real-robot runs. After unannounced switches of task or policy version, ranks failures better than the frozen monitor for every VLA, and above a full reset at the true switch (exploratory; Sec.~ sec:real ). In our tests, the readout was the part worth adapting. Our whole-network streaming learner barely moved its hidden weights, and resetting 's head, even at the true change, ranked lower on every suite (exploratory; Sec.~ sec:what ). It is cheap, and calibrated in simulation. \,ms per call on a Jetson CPU core, a \,MB state that never grows, and a false-alarm rate near target except under compound drift (Sec.~ sec:alarms ). Every monitor we ran, and where does not help, is reported in Secs.~ sec:what and~ sec:discussion and App.~ app:all . Related work sec:related Failure monitors for robot policies are fitted before deployment, then fixed. SAFE, Hide-and-Seek and Foresight learn a failure score from episode outcomes on VLA features or world-model latents~ gu2025safe,park2026hideandseek,zhang2026foresight . is not a new offline detector: it refits the last layer of such a monitor, and on real runs the same refit also helps SAFE's probe (App.~ app:posthoc ). FAIL-Detect, FIPER and VLA-FAIL need no failure data and score uncertainty, novelty or action-chunk consistency~ xu2025faildetect,romer2025fiper,seligmann2026vlafail . Sentinel pairs action consistency with a vision-language judge of task progress~ agia2024sentinel , and linear observers read robot state from VLA activations~ buurmeijer2026features . A linear probe on OpenVLA's activations separates the steps before a failure under visual shift in hindsight, but on clean episodes it raises many warnings~ mahato2026earlywarning . Most set their alarm by conformal prediction, which can guarantee a warning system's miss rate~ luo2023safety . Monitors facing distribution shift mostly prepare for it offline or detect it. VLA success falls sharply under the camera, lighting and object changes of perturbed versions of LIBERO~ liu2023libero , such as LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-PRO~ fei2025liberoplus,zhou2025liberopro . SAFECAST and VLA-Scope train for shift with contrast-set perturbations or a shift-type classifier~ rajaprakash2026safecast,zhu2026vlascope . FARM tests readout-only adaptation on frozen world-model states, but fits it in batch on labelled target rollouts~ pei2026farm . Levy et al.\ adapt a distilled fault detector online by recursive least squares, which recovers it from unseen mechanical wear~ levy2026onlinefd . Shift detectors flag changed inputs~ luo2022recency , yet unusual inputs need not cause failure, so Lin et al.\ predict safety violations directly from forecast trajectories and keep updating the predictor by incremental learning, with an adaptive conformal threshold~ lin2025safety . AdaptNC adapts the nonconformity score and the conformal threshold online, with a replay buffer~ tumu2026adaptnc . Test-time adaptation updates a network from unlabelled data~ wang2021tent , but over long streams it often ends below a model that never adapts~ press2023rdumb . Unlike these methods, updates a VLA policy's failure score from episode outcomes alone, episode by episode during deployment, in closed form and constant memory. Deployment outcomes already train policies and thresholds, but monitors learn from them only between rounds. Sirius, Sirius-RM and Sirius-Fleet retrain the policy and its failure predictors on human interventions between rounds~ liu2023sirius,liu2024siriusrm,liu2024siriusfleet . and Learning While Deploying improve the policy by reinforcement learning on deployment data~ pi2025recap,wang2026lwd . The value function of is itself a failure predictor retrained on deployment outcomes between rounds; our retraining baseline follows that pattern, while updates after every episode. ARMADA moves its alarm threshold after missed failures and false alarms~ armada2025 , and TimelyDAgger adapts its takeover threshold from expert feedback~ zhao2026timelydagger . ConformalDAgger and Feldman et al.\ calibrate uncertainty from intermittent expert labels or binary human flags~ conformaldagger2024,feldman2025sparse . instead updates its failure score after every deployed episode, from its outcome. builds on standard tools for online regression, calibration and streaming learning. Its online head is recursive least squares with exponential forgetting~ haykin2014adaptive , akin to Kalman-filter tracking of a linear head~ titsias2024kalman . Last-layer retraining alone undoes much of a network's reliance on spurious features~ kirichenko2023dfr , and our anchor to the offline head is an L2-SP penalty~ li2018l2sp . The threshold follows adaptive conformal inference, which keeps long-run coverage under arbitrary shift, and its later variants~ gibbs2021aci,gibbs2024dtaci,angelopoulos2024online . Two baselines use the kernel two-sample test and a Mahalanobis distance~ gretton2012mmd,lee2018mahalanobis ; -TD follows stream-x~ elsayed2024streamx . Streaming RL adapts robot policies online~ vitchutripop2026stream but can lose plasticity~ dohare2024plasticity . Related work Problem: monitoring a deployed policy as a stream sec:setup What a monitor sees and when. A frozen policy runs one episode after another while conditions change without notice. At every policy call , once per action chunk, a monitor reads the policy's internal features and the elapsed fraction of the task's step limit , and returns a risk score . It alarms once the episode's running maximum of exceeds a threshold , fixed for that episode. After the episode it receives the outcome (1 for failure), assumed correct. It is never told when or how conditions changed, keeps a state of fixed size, and every score is logged before any update that uses it. Two goals: ranking and calibration. Ranking is the chance that a failing episode reaches a higher peak score than a successful episode of the same task, over all such pairs under one condition, with ties counting half. We call it within-task AUROC; 0.5 is chance. Peaks are taken only up to the task's shortest recorded episode, as in SAFE~ gu2025safe : in simulation every failure runs to the step limit, so this is the shortest success; on real runs a failure can end early. Without this cut, elapsed time alone would flag of LIBERO-Spatial's failures at a false-alarm rate of ; with it, its within-task AUROC is . Comparing within a task stops a score from gaining by recognizing harder tasks. Calibration is the false-alarm rate on successful episodes (FAR), against a target chosen by the operator; we use . A threshold rule can change FAR but not ranking, so the two goals need two mechanisms. Streaming Failure Forecasting sec:method has three parts: fixed features from an offline monitor, an online readout that learns ranking, and a success-only threshold that keeps calibration. Fig.~ fig:method shows what happens at every policy call and after each episode; Algorithm~ alg:sff in App.~ app:settings lists it step by step. Fixed features. title: PAIR: Proprioception-Aligned Image-Ray Representations for Viewpoint-Robust Manipulation
summary: While imitation learning has made substantial progress toward generalizable robot manipulation through scaling, viewpoint robustness remains a major bottleneck. Visuomotor policies rely heavily on visual inputs, yet images provide an inherently ambiguous signal under viewpoint change: similar scenes may appear markedly different across viewpoints, while distinct states may share certain visual overlaps. A policy must therefore infer not only the task-relevant state, but also how it is visually projected under a particular camera configuration. This entanglement of viewpoint-dependent appearance and task-relevant state can make learning inefficient and limit generalization to unseen viewpoints. Recent work has begun to address this challenge through camera-ray conditioning and representation learning using geometric cues to induce invariance. However, providing camera information as additional context does not by itself ground visual representations in how the task scene is visually projected, while geometric alignment without camera context can introduce spurious correspondences by ignoring viewpoint-dependent projection. We propose PAIR, a contrastive learning framework that aligns joint image-ray representations using robot proprioception. PAIR encourages observations with similar robot states to remain close in representation space across viewpoints, providing a structured grounding signal for learning viewpoint-robust features. PAIR is a highly adaptable framework: it can be used to train Diffusion Policy (DP) or post-train vision-language-action (VLA) models. In simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks with camera variation, PAIR consistently outperforms the behavior cloning baseline without ray conditioning by 12.7% and 26.7% points, respectively, demonstrating stronger generalization to unseen viewpoints. Project website: PAIRrobot.github.io.
full_text: PAIR: Proprioception-Aligned Image-Ray Representations for Viewpoint-Robust Manipulation Sung-Wook Lee , Xuhui Kang , Dylan Losey , Yen-Ling Kuo University of Virginia \ dcs3zc,xuhui,ylkuo\ @virginia.edu Virginia Tech losey@vt.edu -15pt Resolving visual ambiguity with camera geometry. (A) Robot datasets often contain visually confounding observations, where similar robot appearances correspond to substantially different robot states. (B) Camera-ray information provides explicit camera-to-robot geometry to help disambiguate such observations. fig:teaser While imitation learning has made substantial progress toward generalizable robot manipulation through scaling, viewpoint robustness remains a major bottleneck. Project website: PAIRrobot.github.io. Introduction Robot imitation learning has made significant progress toward general-purpose manipulation by scaling training data, model capacity, and compute~ ICLR2025_88b7b2c8 . Recent visuomotor policies can learn increasingly more general manipulation behaviors directly from image observations, and can transfer across different objects, tasks, and scenes. However, robustness to viewpoint variation remains a key challenge for generalizable manipulation pang2025reviwo . This challenge stems from a fundamental property of visual observations: images do not directly encode the physical state of the world, but instead capture a viewpoint-dependent projection of that state. As the camera viewpoint changes, a fixed underlying task state can give rise to substantially different visual observations through changes in perspective and visibility. Conversely, distinct physical states may appear deceptively similar when they share similar camera-relative geometry or when the task-relevant context is only partially captured within the camera’s field of view (See ). This ambiguity is further exacerbated by typical camera-independent action spaces, in which visual observations vary with camera viewpoint while the corresponding action targets remain unchanged. Consequently, to infer which actions are appropriate for the given task, a visuomotor policy must not only capture the task-relevant information in the image, but also reason about how exactly they are visually projected. Consider a robot approaching a mug for grasping. From one view, the gripper may appear to the left of the mug, while from another view, the same physical configuration may make the gripper appear to the right of the mug. Yet this change in image-space geometry does not imply a corresponding change in what the robot should physically do. The policy must therefore determine how the observed visual relationship between the robot and the mug corresponds to their underlying spatial relationship. This implicitly demands that the policy look for additional visual cues such as the robot base to establish the robot's spatial frame or fuse the vision features with the internal robot state for viewpoint-invariant action prediction. However, such visual context is not always guaranteed to be available in full, nor reliably utilized when learning from demonstrations. In addition, existing visuomotor policies typically rely on shallow, non-principled fusion between vision and robot state, where images are processed by a vision encoder and robot-state features are incorporated later through simple fusion mechanisms~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,pi05_corl2025 . Recent studies have explored improving viewpoint invariance for visuomotor policies through camera-ray conditioning~ jiang2026knowyourcamera to use the camera state governing the visual projection as input, or use geometric signals such as proprioception to construct positive pairs for representation alignment~ lee2025class,kim2026contrastive . However, while camera-ray conditioning provides useful viewpoint context, it does not by itself ground visual representations in the projected task state. Similarly, while alignment using physically grounded signals can encourage invariance across physically similar states, this can produce conflicting supervision by ignoring viewpoint-dependent projection without camera context. In light of this, we propose PAIR, a contrastive learning framework for viewpoint-robust manipulation that jointly learns image–ray representations using Plücker embeddings with supervised proprioceptive alignment. PAIR is a highly adaptable framework: it can be used to train lightweight policy classes such as diffusion policy (DP) or fine-tune pre-trained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. Specifically, PAIR builds on the pre-trained SigLIP-family encoders and incorporates the proposed alignment objective as an auxiliary loss alongside the standard behavior cloning objective. We make the following contributions. First, we introduce PAIR, a general training framework that unlocks the benefit of proprioceptive alignment through joint image--ray representation learning. Second, we show that PAIR consistently improves the performance of both diffusion policies and VLA models when trained on the same demonstration data. Third, we conduct extensive evaluations across multiple simulated and real-world benchmarks under systematic viewpoint variations, demonstrating strong robustness to changes in camera viewpoint both quantitatively and qualitatively. Related Work Vision Representations for Robotic Manipulation A dominant paradigm in visual representation learning is vision-language alignment, which has enabled VLA models with strong semantic understanding and instruction-following capabilities. Accordingly, many VLM and VLA architectures adopt pre-trained vision encoders such as CLIP~ radford2021clip and SigLIP~ zhai2023siglip , whose representations are explicitly aligned with language semantics through large-scale image-text pre-training. While this semantic alignment provides strong high-level visual understanding, such representations often lack the fine-grained spatial and geometric awareness required for robotic manipulation~ ICLR2025_88b7b2c8 . Several methods study viewpoint robustness directly from RGB observations with data augmentation techniques including systematic data collection~ xie2026multi or novel-view synthesis~ chen2024roviaug , while other methods improve the learning signal through cross-view supervision~ seo2023multiview and contrastive learning~ lee2025class,kim2026contrastive . Recent efforts attempt to directly use camera extrinsic information to account for viewpoint changes. For example, zhang2026grounding express robot actions in the camera frame to unify action representations across heterogeneous robot datasets, while jiang2026knowyourcamera condition the policy on Plücker ray maps derived from the camera pose. Rather than using camera geometry solely as an input signal or as a reference frame for expressing actions, PAIR grounds the image-ray representation in the underlying robot proprioceptive state using contrastive learning. Rays as Positional Embeddings Recent vision models increasingly incorporate camera rays as an explicit geometric signal for vision tasks including video generation~ he2025cameractrl , novel-view synthesis~ chen2026wildrayzerselfsupervisedlargeview , and pose estimation~ zhang2024raydiffusion . Similar lines of work have also explored ray injection as positional encoding. For example, RayPE~ yin2026raype incorporates Plücker ray geometry directly into Transformer attention for video generation. In robotics, xu2025seeing builds on RayPE for modality-balanced action generation in VLAs, while RayViT~ wang2026rayvit injects patch-aligned Plücker ray features into a pre-trained DINOv3 ViT backbone as geometry-aware positional embeddings. PAIR similarly introduces Plücker rays as positional embeddings, but applies this during post-training of SigLIP/SigLIP2~ zhai2023siglip,tschannen2025siglip encoders to ground the camera-ray-aware visual representations using robot proprioception. Method In this section, we formalize the problem in Sec. sec:problem_statement , analyze the visual ambiguity that motivates our method in Sec. sec:visual_ambiguity , introduce the image-ray fusion mechanism in Sec. sec:ray_alignment_theory , and describe the training procedure in Sec. sec:supcon . Problem Statement sec:problem_statement We consider visuomotor policy learning from visual observations , robot proprioceptive state , camera rays , and a task specification (e.g., language), where we augment imitation learning with a spatially grounded visual representation learning problem. Specifically, a vision encoder maps the visual observation and optionally its associated camera geometry to a latent representation , where the ray information provides a geometry-aware positional encoding for the visual tokens. We assume that camera positions change across episodes, but remained fixed within each episode. Our goal is to learn such that is grounded in the underlying robot state . In particular, observations of the same physical robot configuration from different viewpoints should induce consistent latent representations. The resulting representation is then used by a visuomotor policy , which predicts a sequence of future robot actions over an action horizon . Visual Ambiguity of Proprioceptive Alignment sec:visual_ambiguity While proprioceptive alignment of visual representations provides a potential mechanism for inducing viewpoint invariance, aligning image representations according to proprioception alone is inherently ambiguous: proprioception specifies a state in a fixed physical frame, whereas the corresponding visual observation is largely affected by the camera–robot geometry. Let and denote the end-effector pose and the camera pose in the robot-base frame, respectively. Conversely, the same physical state can appear substantially different under varied camera poses. This leads to conflicting signals for the vision encoder: visually similar observations may be pushed apart, while visually dissimilar observations are pulled together, without specifying the camera transformations respons

title: Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH): Latency-Agnostic Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models for Humanoid Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System 2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System 1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. The action head fuses stale semantics from a frozen backbone with fresh vision from its own ResNet encoder, desynchronized training exposes it to the staleness it meets at deployment, and an adaptive temporal aggregator aligns overlapping action chunks under variable inference latency. On an asynchronous RoboTwin benchmark that charges inference latency in simulated time, DASH holds 20 Hz control rate from 0.8B to 8B backbones while the synchronous rate falls from 9.7 to 4.1 Hz, with higher success at every size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline.
full_text: Vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a vision-language backbone with an action head, but in closed-loop control the backbone sits on the control-critical path: while it computes, the robot keeps moving, so each executed action is conditioned on an increasingly stale observation. A larger backbone therefore directly blocks reactivity, especially in humanoid dexterous manipulation. We present DASH, a Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids that removes this coupling. DASH splits the policy into a slow vision-language model (System~2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System~1) that run as concurrent processes over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone, independent of backbone size. On a real humanoid with dexterous hands, DASH achieves clearly higher pick-and-place success than the synchronous pipeline. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a default recipe for generalist robot manipulation, pairing a pretrained vision-language backbone with an action head trained end-to-end on demonstrations~ rt2,openvla,pi0,gr00tn1 . Deploying them on a real humanoid (Fig.~ fig:teaser ), however, is a fundamentally time-sensitive problem. Unlike open-loop evaluation, where a policy is scored on a fixed dataset with no regard for inference cost, closed-loop control couples the model to a world that never stops moving: while the model computes the next actions, the robot is already acting and cannot pause to wait. This mismatch is intrinsic to embodied systems, and it grows with model latency. Concretely, an action chunk computed from the state at time becomes available only after the inference time , when the robot has already moved on, so executing it produces delayed, spatially misaligned actions. This error is invisible to open-loop metrics such as validation loss, but in closed loop it surfaces as slow, hesitant, discontinuous, and even shaking manipulation, precisely the regime that matters for dexterous humanoid hands. This temporal gap collides head-on with the scaling law that drives VLA progress. Larger vision-language backbones generalize better and follow instructions more reliably~ rt2 , but they are also slower, and higher latency degrades closed-loop control through exactly the staleness above. Model size thus becomes a trade-off between semantic generalization and control reactivity, a trade-off that is especially punishing for humanoid manipulation, which demands both broad world understanding and high-frequency, contact-rich dexterity. We argue that this trade-off is an artifact of synchronous execution rather than a law of nature. A real robot is already asynchronous: sensing, high-level understanding, and low-level actuation run at different natural rates. We therefore decouple the VLA into a slow semantic stream (the vision-language backbone, ``System~2'') and a fast reactive stream (a flow-matching action head, ``System~1'') that advance at independent rates and communicate through a lightweight, non-blocking interface, as in dual-system designs~ gr00tn1,helix,fisvla . Once the backbone leaves the control critical path, its latency no longer bottlenecks the action rate: the VLM can be scaled up for generalization at almost no cost to control frequency. We call this latency-agnostic scaling: backbone size no longer trades against reactivity, so model scale becomes a free design axis rather than a speed--quality compromise. Decoupling also sharpens action quality on two axes: it removes most of the inference-to-execution delay, and it raises the action-update frequency so the fast stream can exploit sensory evidence that arrives far faster than a synchronous policy can emit actions. Because the early actions of a predicted chunk are far more reliable than its autoregressively uncertain tail (Fig.~ fig:intro a), updating chunks more often keeps execution on the high-confidence portion of each prediction and curbs divergence between successive chunks (Fig.~ fig:intro b). Asynchrony is not free: at deployment the action head must fuse stale VLM semantics with fresh perception, a distribution that synchronous training never presents. We close this gap architecturally, with a fresh-vision encoder inside the action head, and in training, by exposing the policy to the desynchronized inputs it will meet at test time. We propose Decoupled Asynchronous System for Humanoids (DASH) and evaluate it on a real humanoid with dexterous hands and in a RoboTwin simulator that we modify to run the environment and policy asynchronously, closer to real deployment. As the backbone grows from B to B, the synchronous control rate falls from to \,Hz, whereas DASH holds \,Hz at every size, a -- higher control rate with higher success ( to \,pp); on the real humanoid, DASH succeeds in pick-and-place trials against for the synchronous pipeline. The policy is split into a slow VLM (System~2) and a fast flow-matching action head (System~1), run as three concurrent processes (environment, VLM server, action server) over the LCM communication protocol, so the control rate is set by the action head alone. title: Action Representation for Spatial Generalization in Robot World Models
summary: Spatial generalization in robot world models depends on whether action representations capture the physical relationships that remain valid across changing spatial configurations. Yet different coordinates can describe the same interaction, whereas similar motions can produce different outcomes when local physical conditions change. How these distinctions affect learned prediction remains insufficiently understood. This study evaluates matched action representations defined in world, object, and surface coordinate frames using a controlled robotic peeling benchmark. Global pose and contact relocation experiments reveal a cost associated with limited training data when equivalent interactions receive different spatial descriptions. Removing information about peel thickness creates an irreducible ambiguity because identical predictive inputs can correspond to different material removal outcomes. Coordinates defined relative to the surface improve consequence prediction and counterfactual action selection under accurate local observations, but learned predictors remain vulnerable to uncertainty in the coordinate frame. Joint centering of the surface and tool removes sensitivity to translation of their common origin, whereas incorrect contact geometry and actual execution deviations introduce different failure mechanisms. These results show that effective spatial generalization depends on preserving the relationships between actions and states that determine physical consequences, rather than simply minimizing coordinate variation. This perspective provides a principled basis for designing robot world models that reuse physical knowledge across spatial configurations while retaining the distinctions essential to prediction and planning.

title: Latent-WAM++: Shaping World and Action Representations for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: 16 pages, including supplementary material
summary: We introduce Latent-WAM++, a representation-centered World Action Model (WAM) for end-to-end autonomous driving. Existing WAMs are primarily trained to predict future states or final actions, leaving the intermediate world and action representations that connect prediction to planning only indirectly constrained. Latent-WAM++ matches the supervision of each representation to its role in planning. World Representation Construction combines scene-ego future prediction, SIGReg-based distribution stabilization, and frozen geometric priors to learn a temporally predictive, non-degenerate, and geometry-aware world representation without an EMA target encoder. Trajectory MeanFlow Planner directly predicts multimodal trajectory proposals while being optimized with an Improved MeanFlow velocity-space objective, enabling one-step sampling. Visual-Action Representation Alignment further aligns the resulting pre-output action features with a stop-gradient target derived from current visual semantics. Latent-WAM++ achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v2 and under zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM, reaching 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 47.0 average RC and 30.1 average HD-Score on HUGSIM. Training the planner end to end costs 190 GPU-hours for Latent-WAM++ versus 1,600 for Latent-WAM, a reduction of 88.1%.

Introduction sec:introduction Driving World Action Models (WAMs) couple world modeling with action generation to enable end-to-end driving planning~ law,world4drive,epona,dreamerad,latentwam . From a representation perspective, a WAM first encodes the observed scene and its anticipated dynamics into a world representation, transforms this representation into an action representation, and subsequently decodes it into future ego trajectories. The world representation determines what scene information is available for planning, whereas the action representation governs how that information is translated into future trajectories. Planning performance therefore depends critically on both representations and, more importantly, on how effectively they interact. This leads to a central question: How should world and action representations be jointly shaped to better support WAM-based driving planning? Early studies primarily supervise predicted future states or final actions~ law , leaving the internal representations to emerge as a by-product of these output-oriented objectives. More recent approaches, such as World4Drive and Latent-WAM, strengthen representation learning through visual foundation models and predictive latent world modeling, respectively~ world4drive,latentwam . Nevertheless, existing conditioning exposes world features to the decoder, but does not impose a representation-level alignment on its pre-output action representations. Such isolated optimization can limit representation learning efficiency and lead to suboptimal planning performance, as shown in Figure~ fig:teaser . Specifically, future latent prediction alone cannot prevent the learned feature distribution from collapsing toward a low-variance solution when the encoder and predictor are jointly optimized~ balestriero2025lejepa . Moreover, conditioning an action decoder on world representations merely makes scene information accessible; it does not explicitly align the two representation spaces or ensure that the action representation preserves the planning-relevant information encoded by the world model. These limitations are not isolated implementation details. Together, they motivate a unified representation-learning problem: learning informative, non-collapsed world representations while explicitly aligning them with action representations, so that future trajectories can fully benefit from knowledge acquired through world modeling. We address the question through a unified principle: match the supervision of each intermediate representation to its role in planning. The world representation should encode scene dynamics, maintain a non-degenerate distribution across driving scenes, and preserve geometric context. The action representation should directly parameterize the trajectories ultimately required by the planner. Their correspondence should be explicitly encouraged without forcing the two representations to share identical semantics. Guided by this principle, we introduce , which jointly shapes world and action representations through three coordinated components. World Representation Construction (WoRC) combines Scene-Ego future prediction with SIGReg~ balestriero2025lejepa , using direct distribution regularization in place of an EMA-updated target encoder, and incorporates frozen geometric priors. Trajectory MeanFlow Planner (TrajMF) directly predicts multimodal trajectory proposals and induces an Improved MeanFlow velocity-space objective from these predictions~ improvedmeanflow , yielding trajectory-predictive action features and enabling one-step generation. Visual-Action Representation Alignment (VARA) asymmetrically aligns these action features with a stop-gradient target derived from the current visual representation. Thus, WoRC constructs the world representation, TrajMF defines the action representation, and VARA explicitly regularizes the visual-action interface. establishes new state-of-the-art results with 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2~ navsimv2metrics and 47.0/30.1 average RC/HD-Score under zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM~ hugsim . As shown in Figure~ fig:teaser , under the same H20 hardware and data-loading pipeline, training our planner end to end costs GPU-hours versus for Latent-WAM, a reduction of . Our contributions are summarized as follows: We formulate joint representation shaping in WAM-based planning as the combination of role-matched representation objectives and explicit regularization of the visual-action interface. We introduce , which constructs a predictive, non-degenerate, and geometry-aware world representation, produces trajectory-predictive action features through one-step multimodal generation, and asymmetrically aligns these features with visual semantics. achieves state-of-the-art results on NAVSIM v2 and zero-shot HUGSIM while reducing the cost of training the planner end to end by compared with Latent-WAM ( versus GPU-hours). Related Work sec:related_work World Models for Autonomous Driving Research on driving world models has focused on three properties of planning-oriented representations: capturing temporal evolution, maintaining stable predictive features, and encoding scene geometry. Some approaches~ drivedreamer,epona,drivelaw model future scene evolution through video generation, but pixel-level generation incurs substantial computational cost. Latent world models~ law,world4drive,latentwam instead predict future states in representation space, providing temporal supervision without reconstructing future images. Jointly optimizing the encoder and latent predictor without an anti-collapse mechanism may produce degenerate representations~ balestriero2025lejepa . Drive-JEPA~ drivejepa and Latent-WAM~ latentwam use an EMA-updated, stop-gradient target encoder to prevent representation collapse. LeWorldModel~ leworldmodel instead applies SIGReg to stabilize latent learning without maintaining an additional target encoder. Geometry is incorporated through different forms of supervision and representation. Latent-WAM~ latentwam transfers geometric priors into visual features through geometry distillation, while occupancy-based methods~ occworld,sparseworld represent the driving scene explicitly in structured 3D space. The former shapes the learned visual features, whereas the latter provides explicit spatial context for planning. Accordingly, within our latent future-prediction framework, WoRC addresses both representation stability and geometric structure: SIGReg stabilizes latent learning without a target encoder, while occupancy context augments geometry-distilled visual features. Action Decoding for Driving Planning Driving planners mainly decode future ego motion through query-based trajectory regression, autoregressive prediction, or generative modeling. Query-based planners~ law,world4drive,latentwam directly decode action queries into future trajectories, whereas autoregressive planners~ drivinggpt sequentially predict discrete action tokens. Generative planners provide a natural mechanism for modeling multiple plausible futures. DiffusionDrive~ diffusiondrive and GoalFlow~ goalflow generate multimodal trajectories using diffusion and flow-based formulations, respectively. MeanFuser~ meanfuser further adapts MeanFlow~ meanflow with Gaussian-mixture noise for one-step multimodal trajectory generation. Our TrajMF follows this one-step generative direction and directly parameterizes clean trajectory proposals under Improved MeanFlow optimization~ improvedmeanflow . Method sec:method Overview sec:overview Figure~ fig:overview shows the three components of our method. The Trajectory MeanFlow Planner (TrajMF) retrieves a planning condition and directly predicts and aggregates multimodal trajectories in one step (Section~ sec:trajmf ). Its world-conditioned pre-output features form the action representation, which Visual-Action Representation Alignment (VARA) relates to current visual semantics (Section~ sec:vara ). title: Distilling Instructions into Weights: Closed-Form Edits Fix a Robot Policy's Misreading
comment: 23 pages, 7 figures. Project page with videos: https://ali-adeeb.com/weightsmith/ ; code and benchmark: https://github.com/adeeb10abbas/weightsmith
summary: Generalist robot policies often fail at one step of a task they can otherwise perform. We ask whether such a failure can be repaired by editing the policy's weights directly, without gradients, training data, or a change to the instruction. Told to put the cube then the banana in the bowl, a zero-shot $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy in RoboLab releases the cube before it reaches the bowl. Replaying 21 of these decisions under rewordings shows that it binds "in the bowl" to the wrong object. Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into the language model's MLP weights. On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken ($p=7\times10^{-22}$), while an update of the same size in random directions leaves success unchanged. The edit also lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13, and a variant that stores 0.16% of the parameter count keeps most of its effect. Placed in the action expert or action head instead, the same distillation helps less or not at all. Our released tool reproduced the fix end to end on new held-out seeds, from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, a missing grasp, contact physics, or the gripper threshold did not help, and of seven blind Claude Opus editors, only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring. These results suggest that weight edits work best when a known-good input already exists to distil. Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds.

Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds. 2.5pt 8pt plus 2pt minus 2pt 12pt plus 2pt minus 2pt Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map camera images and an instruction to robot actions~ pi2025pi05 . A generalist policy often fails at a single step of a task whose skills it already has, and the usual remedy is to collect demonstrations and fine-tune. Weight-space programming offers another route: a language model reads a network's weights and activations, locates the computation that goes wrong, and patches the weights directly, without gradients~ takehi2026sparks . Which failures of a robot policy can such a patch fix? Early robot results are encouraging but hard to compare. Guo and Xie report a task rising from 28/92 to 82/92 held-out episodes after changing four parameters, on checkpoints fine-tuned for each task~ guo2026robotweights,xie2026robotweights . Gupta et al.\ report gains on five of ten tasks, and a folding gain from 51 to 75 , with an update built from the difference between two trained models~ gupta2026robotweights . In our companion study, four sparse edits that GPT-6 Astra wrote for a zero-shot stacking policy all failed a preservation gate~ abbas2026wspstudy . We did not reproduce these results. Together, they leave open which failures gradient-free edits can fix in a policy that was never trained on the task. We study this question with the DROID version of ~ pi2025pi05,khazatsky2024droid on 16 RoboLab tasks~ yang2026robolab , comparing every edit with the unedited policy on identical simulator seeds. Told to ``put the cube then the banana in the bowl,'' the policy grasps the cube and lets go before reaching the bowl, yet the same weights succeed under an explicit rewording. Robot policies are known to respond differently to equivalent wordings~ fei2026liberoplus,kim2026liberopara,abbas2026samegoal ; here that sensitivity points to a repair. We introduce closed-form instruction distillation, which finds such a failure by replaying recorded decisions under rewordings and then writes the internal effect of the working wording into the weights with a multi-key closed-form update~ meng2023memit . To our knowledge, it is the first edit that distils an instruction rewording into a robot policy in closed form. On a held-out start, the edited policy keeps hold of the cube that the unedited policy drops three control steps after grasping it (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). With the instruction unchanged, the edit raises held-out success from 27/128 to 106/128, while an update of the same size in random directions does nothing. A variant that stores 0.16 of the parameter count keeps most of the effect, and the edit lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13. Where the edit is placed matters: written into the action expert or action head instead of the VLM, the same distillation helps less or not at all, and it no longer transfers. We release the procedure as a command, weightsmith distill; with decisions selected by rule rather than by hand, it raised held-out success on new seeds from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, missing competence, contact physics, and gripper commitment did not help. Seven autonomous editors working blind, one per failure kind, confirm this pattern: only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring, and a gated stacking edit removed the wrong decision it targeted without raising success. Finally, we measure the noise floor of paired closed-loop evaluation, where rerunning unchanged weights flips about a third of paired outcomes, and we release the protocol, code, and paired-episode data. Closed-Form Instruction Distillation sec:method To repair a misreading without training, we first find an instruction that works and then write its effect into the weights. We replay recorded failure decisions under rewordings until one wording removes the failure, distil that wording into the weights in closed form, and check the edit offline before confirming it in closed loop, first on practice seeds and then on held-out seeds. Every step uses only weights, recorded inputs, and activations. combines an 18-layer PaliGemma vision-language model (VLM) with an 18-layer Gemma action expert~ pi2025pi05,beyer2024paligemma . The VLM processes image tokens from two cameras together with the instruction and robot-state tokens. Its attention is bidirectional, so image tokens can attend to the instruction. The action expert attends to the VLM's keys and values and produces 15-step action chunks, including a gripper command, by flow matching~ black2024pi0 . The cube-then-banana task illustrates the diagnosis. Under the original instruction the unedited policy succeeds in 9 of 64 episodes. It goes for the cube first in 63 of 64, grasps it, lifts it a few centimetres, and lets go well short of the bowl. We call this a premature release. When the cube does reach the bowl first, the episode usually succeeds (about 7 times in 9), so the skill is present. We replayed 21 recorded premature-release decisions with images, robot state, and flow-matching noise fixed, changing only the instruction (Fig.~ fig:construction a). Renaming the cube leaves all 21 releases, whereas moving ``in the bowl'' next to the cube leaves only one to three. In one VLM attention head, the destination words also attend far more to the adjacent noun than to the first (Appendix~ app:construction ). We read this as a binding error. While holding the cube, the policy treats the banana as the object that belongs in the bowl. We call the explicit wording a known-good instruction. With unchanged weights it succeeds in 22 of 32 closed-loop episodes against 3 of 32 for the original on the same seeds (20 fixed, 1 broken). Distillation makes the network process the original instruction as it processes the known-good one. At each VLM layer we form 72 keys, the rows of . A key is the mean input to the layer's MLP down-projection under the original instruction, averaged over 6 recorded premature-release decisions. The keys sit at 40 positions shared by both prompts (the beginning-of-sequence, ``Task:'', and robot-state tokens) and at 32 image cells (16 per camera). The matching rows of hold the layer's residual increment at each position under the explicit instruction minus that under the original. With activations as row vectors, we apply the regularized minimum-norm update that maps each key to its value, so that . Eq.~ is the multi-key closed form used to rewrite stored associations in language models~ meng2022rome,meng2023memit . We compute it once per layer and aim it at a rewording. Context distillation trains a model to act as if a prompt were present~ snell2022distilling , whereas Eq.~ needs no training. The update has rank at most 72 per layer. Offline, the edit removes all 21 premature releases. It leaves unchanged all 9 recorded correct carries and all 19 phase-two decisions, in which the policy fetches the banana after placing the cube. Its actions also land closer to the explicit wording's actions than the unedited ones do (4.5 versus 8.1\,cm at the end of the chunk). On the 32 practice seeds, closed-loop success rises from 3/32 to 25/32, with 22 episodes fixed and none broken (exact McNemar ). We then froze the edit for held-out evaluation. Paired Weight-Edit Evaluation sec:eval We compare each edited policy with the unedited policy from identical simulator starts, using the OpenPI DROID joint-position checkpoint with about 3.35 billion parameters~ openpi2025,pi2025pi05 . It was trained on DROID data~ khazatsky2024droid and on none of our tasks, so every result is zero-shot. It receives two camera images and the joint and gripper state. It outputs 15-step chunks of seven joint commands and a gripper command, which is binarized at 0.5. We run 16 RoboLab tasks in Isaac Sim with 16 parallel environments per evaluation~ yang2026robolab . An episode counts as a success when RoboLab's terminal success flag is set. A 16-episode survey of the unedited policy on each task sorted its failures into levels (Appendix~ app:survey , Table~ tab:levels ). We call a failure language binding when the wrong object counts as the current target, and perception when the arm goes for a similar-looking object. Missing competence means that no working motion is produced. In a contact physics failure the decisions look right but the grasp slips, and in a gripper commitment failure open and close decisions sit near the threshold. A motor decision that stalls inside a learned skill did not occur among our tasks. Edits came from two frontier models run headless, Claude Opus in this work and GPT-6 Astra in the companion study~ abbas2026wspstudy . An editor can read and write every weight in a NumPy sandbox, capture activations on the exact inputs of any recorded decision, and roll the policy out. It may not use gradients, optimizers, fine-tuning, or black-box search. Every edit is a closed-form computation from weights and activations, and its hypothesis is written down before evaluation. The instruction text stays fixed. The operator session, also Claude Opus, built some edits under the same rules, including the distilled one. Seven autonomous editors repeat the protocol blind in Section~ sec:blind . A simulator slot fixes the random seeds and scene of one episode. Every comparison runs both policies on the same slots, and we call these paired seeds. Each pair ends in one of four outcomes. Both policies succeed, both fail, only the edited policy succeeds, or only the unedited policy succeeds. We call the last two fixed and broke. Edits are developed on practice seeds. An edit that passes practice is frozen, and the operator scores it on held-out seeds never used during editing. The two policies alternate run order between the halves of the slots. We report paired differences with 95 bootstrap intervals over the four outcome types (20,000 draws), exact McNemar tests on the fixed and broke pairs~ mcnemar1947note , and Wilson intervals for single rates~ wilson1927probable . Because paired seeds do not make episodes identical, we also rerun unedited and identically edited policies as noise controls. title: SHIN: Scalable Hierarchy for INcremental 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: 8 pages of main text (13 pages including references and supplementary material), 7 figures
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides high-quality real-time novel-view synthesis, but deployment budgets vary across devices and network conditions. Most compact methods target one operating point, so another budget requires a separate representation. SHIN is a scalable 3DGS hierarchy with a reusable Base and additive enhancement layers, so each higher-quality operating point extends rather than replaces the decoded representation. Constructing this hierarchy requires deciding which Gaussians each stage adds and how much spherical-harmonic (SH) appearance each retains, because these choices remain fixed in later prefixes. SHIN derives one shared Gaussian order from multi-scale position-scale sensitivity and divides each stage budget between adding Gaussians and retaining SH bands using calibrated gradient-based scores per byte.
