These methods are effective when the deployment budget is known in advance. In practice, however, the same scene may serve devices with different storage capacities, and the available network bandwidth may change over time. Maintaining a separate asset for every target budget duplicates storage, while moving an existing client to a higher-quality point requires transferring a replacement representation. This paper presents SHIN, a scalable 3DGS hierarchy built from one reusable asset ( (a)). A Base is transmitted once, and each higher operating point is reached by appending an enhancement layer, so previously decoded spatial and appearance records remain useful as the available budget increases shi2025lapisgs . This cumulative requirement differs from Level-of-Detail (LoD; (b)), which may expose multiple rendering states from one shared representation without requiring those states to form an additive transmission sequence cheng2026clodgs,octree,seo2025flod,Shen_2025_CVPR . The distinction is not the number of operating points, but whether moving between them preserves the data already delivered. Cumulative reuse requires the Gaussian contents of successive operating points to be nested. If each budget independently selects its own subset, a Gaussian used by the Base may disappear at a higher rate, forcing previously decoded data to be replaced. SHIN enforces this nesting with one shared Gaussian order, so that every operating point extends the same prefix rather than redefining it. Ordered-prefix representations provide this nesting along the Gaussian-count axis guo2026matryoshka . Gaussian count is only one dimension of 3DGS storage. Each Gaussian also carries view-dependent spherical-harmonic (SH) coefficients, and retaining additional bands increases the size of its record. Under a limited stage budget, richer SH appearance for existing Gaussians leaves fewer bytes for additional spatial support, whereas lower retained degrees allow more Gaussians to be added but restrict their appearance. A shared order guarantees nested Gaussian contents, but it does not determine how much SH representation is stored with each Gaussian. The hierarchy must therefore decide both which Gaussians are added at each stage and how much SH representation each retains. These choices affect all later operating points: spending early bytes on higher-order SH can delay additional spatial support, whereas retaining too little SH can limit later view-dependent refinement. Because transmitted records are reused by all subsequent prefixes, the stages cannot be optimized independently. This coupled decision is a persistent allocation problem. Neither the Base nor the largest operating point can be designed in isolation. Optimizing only the Base may spend early bytes on choices that later stages cannot revise, while optimizing the largest point first can leave shorter prefixes poorly balanced. A useful cumulative hierarchy must therefore maintain strong reconstruction throughout the sequence, not only at its final size. This makes the interaction between stage budgets and persistent Gaussian records central to the construction, rather than a post-hoc truncation of one endpoint model. The shared order must remain useful across the full prefix range: early prefixes should establish broad scene structure, whereas later prefixes should add Gaussians that resolve finer residuals. This motivates measuring structural sensitivity across multiple image scales before constructing the order. SHIN converts a 3DGS model into a reusable Base and additive enhancement layers. title: Thermo-VLA: A Thermal-Aware Vision-Language-Action Model with Gated Residual Modulation for Robotic Manipulation
summary: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have begun incorporating thermal sensing, but existing approaches typically treat thermal images as ordinary visual inputs, providing limited support for temperature-aware relational reasoning in manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder, which decomposes thermal images into cold and hot attribute representations and injects them into the RGB token through language-conditioned residual modulation, enabling temperature-driven target selection and continuous manipulation. We further construct six real-world robotic tasks on a dual-arm Unitree G1 platform, spanning basic grounding to relational reasoning. Experiments show that Thermo-VLA achieves an average success rate of 0.86 across four thermal-dependent tasks, outperforming a pi_0.5 baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations by 18 percentage points. Under unseen-object and scene variations, Thermo-VLA maintains an average success rate of 0.78, achieving the best generalisation performance among the compared methods. Beyond thermal sensing, we transfer the same residual modulation mechanism to colour attributes and observe consistent improvements in both simulation and real-robot experiments, indicating its potential to generalise beyond thermal attributes. Project Website Introduction Instruction-driven robotic manipulation aims to generate continuous actions that are consistent with task goals based on language instructions and environmental observations. In recent years, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models pi0,pi0.5,pi0.7,gr00t,rt2,openvla have substantially advanced language-driven robotic manipulation through heterogeneous pretraining and downstream fine-tuning. However, existing VLAs still rely predominantly on RGB observations for perception. When language instructions involve invisible physical attributes such as temperature, RGB-based policies are not natively equipped to perceive and model such attributes, limiting both target selection and subsequent action generation. Recent VLA studies musevla,thermoact,safenightvla have begun incorporating physical modalities such as thermal sensing to support manipulation beyond RGB-only perception. Nevertheless, existing thermal research anythermal,cmx,thermovl,irgpt remains largely focused on perceptual and understanding tasks, including image fusion, detection and segmentation, grounding, and visual question answering. Thermal manipulation in robotics also remains limited in several aspects. First, existing studies have primarily demonstrated thermal-aware manipulation in relatively straightforward settings like recognising and grasping thermally salient targets, whereas more complex thermal-dependent capabilities, such as relative temperature comparison, conditional selection, and exclusion-based reasoning, remain less explored~ thermoact . Second, even when temperature-related targets can be accurately identified, improper integration of thermal information can introduce instability, leading to manipulation failures. Finally, existing systems musevla,thermoact are predominantly evaluated on fixed-viewpoint, single-arm platforms, leaving their effectiveness in bimanual egocentric manipulation insufficiently studied. To address these limitations, we propose Thermo-VLA, an end-to-end thermal-aware VLA framework that integrates RGB, thermal, and language information for temperature-driven manipulation. At its core, Thermo-VLA introduces a dedicated ThermoRes Encoder to incorporate instruction-relevant thermal information while preserving the original RGB representation. Specifically, the ThermoRes Encoder consists of Dual-Branch Attribute Decomposition and Gated Residual Injection. The former decomposes thermal observations into complementary temperature-attribute features, while the latter adaptively injects thermal residuals into RGB tokens under language guidance. As illustrated in the centre of Fig. head , the resulting multimodal tokens then condition the action generation module, enabling temperature-driven target selection, grasping, and continuous manipulation. We systematically evaluate Thermo-VLA on a Unitree G1 bimanual humanoid robot across six real-world manipulation tasks of varying difficulty, covering basic RGB spatial and appearance grounding, thermal perception, thermal grounding, relative temperature ranking, and thermal reasoning. Thermo-VLA outperforms ThermoAct thermoact and the baseline that directly incorporates RGB-thermal observations, achieving the best overall performance among the compared methods on the proposed benchmark. As illustrated in the example in Fig. head , Thermo-VLA activates the correct right arm and closely follows the ground-truth trajectory, whereas ThermoAct uses the wrong arm and shows little movement in the required right arm. Thermo-VLA also maintains more stable performance under unseen objects, attribute recombination, illumination changes, and scene variations. Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of the ThermoRes Encoder in injecting task-relevant temperature information into visual representations through text-guided residual modulation. Further representation analysis suggests that these residuals provide compact complementary corrections to the RGB representation. Our main contributions are summarised as follows: We introduce a real-world benchmark for thermal-aware robotic manipulation, comprising four temperature-related tasks and two RGB-based tasks for evaluating representative VLA methods under RGB and thermal settings. We propose Thermo-VLA with a ThermoRes Encoder that combines temperature-attribute decomposition and text-conditioned residual injection for temperature-driven manipulation. Thermo-VLA achieves the best overall performance on the proposed benchmark and demonstrates strong generalisation to unseen objects and scene variations. Related Work Generalist Robotic Manipulation Methods Early end-to-end imitation learning methods act, diffusionpolicy, vqbet demonstrated the ability to directly generate continuous actions from visual observations for simple manipulation tasks like grasping and placing. Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models subsequently introduced large-scale vision-language priors into robotic control. RT-2 rt2 represents actions as text tokens, allowing vision-language knowledge to directly contribute to action prediction, while OpenVLA openvla enables efficient adaptation of pretrained vision-language representations to downstream robotic manipulation tasks. The series pi0,pi0.5,pi0.7 and GR00T series gr00t further improve cross-task, cross-embodiment, and long-horizon manipulation through large-scale heterogeneous robot data and generative action modelling. More recently, world-model-based approaches robodreamer,gr1,gr2,lingbotva,dreamzero enhance temporal decision-making and closed-loop control by predicting future environment states. Nevertheless, they remain predominantly RGB-based. Multisensory Vision-Language-Action Models Recent studies have begun to extend VLA models beyond RGB-centric perception toward richer sensing of the physical world. DepthVLA depthvla introduces explicit depth representations to enhance spatial reasoning, while ForceVLA forcevla and TA-VLA tavla augment VLA models with force/torque feedback. Tactile-VLA tactilevla , VTLA vtla , and TacVLA tacvla leverage tactile sensing for adaptive physical interaction, while Audio-VLA audiovla and E-VLA evla further extend VLA perception with acoustic and event-based signals, respectively. Beyond individual physical modalities, recent approaches have explored unified multisensory VLA frameworks. Safe-Night VLA safenightvla combines thermal and depth information to support temperature-conditioned manipulation and safety-aware control. OmniVLA omnivla and MuseVLA musevla integrate multiple physical modalities, including thermal, acoustic, and mmWave sensing; the former emphasises unified sensor representations, while the latter dynamically selects required modalities according to the instruction. Thermal Perception, Understanding, and Action Recent studies have investigated effective thermal representations and cross-modal fusion cmx,raccm,freqfusion . AnyThermal anythermal learns a general-purpose thermal backbone through distillation from visual foundation models and transfers it to downstream vision tasks such as segmentation and depth estimation. IRGPT irgpt and Thermo-VL thermovl further align thermal representations with the language space, supporting infrared image recognition, captioning, and grounding, as well as text-guided RGB-thermal visual question answering and cross-spectral reasoning. More recent work has further incorporated thermal information into robotic manipulation. ThermoAct thermoact adopts a hierarchical architecture with a Gemini 2.0 Flash gemini planner and a executor. However, within the executor, thermal images are converted to pseudocolour and processed by the generic visual encoder, leaving their temperature-specific information insufficiently integrated into action-relevant representations. title: DPGS-SLAM: Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Dynamic Visual Sensing
summary: This paper presents DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM) for dense mapping in environments containing dynamic objects. Dynamic observations can contaminate camera tracking and scene reconstruction in visual SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping). Although 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) enables efficient dense mapping, existing 3DGS-SLAM systems may exhibit instability when dynamic objects violate their underlying static-scene assumption. Excluding dynamic observations can reduce their influence on tracking and mapping, but may leave occluded static backgrounds missing or weakly constrained. Our proposed DPGS-SLAM is a monocular RGB SLAM framework that supports provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds through asynchronous diffusion-based background completion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Dynamic regions are identified through optical-flow-based motion discovery and temporally consistent mask propagation by SAM2 (segment anything model 2). For selected keyframes, a fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance in occluded regions, while Metric3D v2 predicts metric depth from the completed images to initialize provisional Gaussian primitives. Provenance labels distinguish generated primitives from observation-supported primitives, excluding generated content from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are removed, and observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. Experimental results demonstrated competitive camera tracking, with average ATE RMSE values of 1.2 cm on TUM RGB-D and 2.7 cm on BONN RGB-D. On StaDy4D, DPGS-SLAM improved average PSNR by 4.60 dB over WildGS-SLAM using only monocular RGB input.

Introduction sec:introduction his paper proposes DPGS-SLAM (Diffusion-Prior and Provenance-Aware Monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM), a monocular RGB SLAM (simultaneous localization and mapping) framework for dynamic visual sensing, designed to address insufficient real observation support for static-background reconstruction through asynchronous static-background completion via diffusion-based inpainting~ diffusion,latentDiffusion and provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Here, inpainting refers to the general technique of synthesizing image content within masked regions, whereas background completion refers to the specific task of generating plausible static-background content in regions occluded by dynamic objects. A real observation of a static-background surface is defined as an RGB measurement acquired when that surface is directly visible to the camera. Insufficient real observation support occurs when such measurements are absent or too sparsely distributed across the available views to reliably constrain the reconstruction of the corresponding surface. Achieving reliable SLAM in dynamic environments remains a long-standing challenge in the computer vision community. Many traditional SLAM systems, such as ORB-SLAM (2015)~ orbslam and DSO (2017)~ dso , are built upon the assumption of a rigid scene and therefore tend to suffer from tracking drift or reconstruction instability when independently moving objects are present. Recently, NeRF (neural radiance fields) (2020)~ nerf -based volumetric representations have been explored as a dense-mapping paradigm for SLAM, due to their strong photometric modeling capability and high-quality novel-view synthesis. However, NeRF-SLAM methods typically incur high computational costs and limited rendering efficiency, and often rely on additional depth sensors or predefined dynamic priors, such as DN-SLAM (2023)~ dnslam and RoDyn-SLAM (2024)~ rodyn , to handle dynamic regions. These constraints restrict their applicability in purely monocular RGB settings and limit their robustness in complex dynamic scenes. More recently, 3DGS (3D Gaussian splatting) (2023)~ 3dgs has emerged as an efficient and expressive scene representation for dense scene modeling. By modeling scenes as a collection of learnable 3D Gaussian primitives and enabling fast, differentiable rasterization, 3DGS has been widely adopted in recent SLAM systems, such as SplaTAM (2024)~ splatam and MonoGS (2024)~ monogs , achieving high-fidelity mapping in static environments at substantially lower computational costs. Nevertheless, existing 3DGS-SLAM approaches typically assume a static scene, leading to temporally inconsistent updates of Gaussian primitives in dynamic regions, which accumulate over time and contaminate the reconstructed map. This behavior results in tracking instability, persistent noise in long-term mapping, and ghosting artifacts, thereby limiting the applicability of 3DGS-SLAM in real-world dynamic scenarios. In dynamic SLAM systems such as MaskFusion~ maskfusion , DG-SLAM~ dgslam , and RoDyn-SLAM~ rodyn , detected dynamic regions are excluded or downweighted during tracking and mapping. While this strategy reduces the influence of moving objects from directly contaminating camera-pose estimation and map optimization, it does not supply static-background observations for the masked regions. Consequently, backgrounds that remain insufficiently observed, whether under persistent or intermittent occlusion, may be missing or only sparsely represented in the reconstructed map. When only sparse or inconsistent static observations are available, their reconstructed appearance and geometry may also be weakly constrained, resulting in local blur, ghosting, or unstable Gaussian structures. Therefore, suppression alone removes unreliable dynamic observations but does not provide the missing background information needed for reconstruction. To address this limitation, our DPGS-SLAM introduces asynchronous diffusion-based background completion together with provenance-aware Gaussian mapping. Here, provenance-aware denotes the explicit labeling of Gaussian primitives as observation-supported or diffusion-generated, with each label determining whether a primitive participates in optimization and how it is updated. For selected keyframes, a diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background content for regions masked as dynamic, providing an appearance prior where direct observations are unavailable. The completion process runs asynchronously, without blocking camera tracking or observed-map optimization. Metric3D v2 (2024)~ metric3d predicts metric depth for the completed regions, allowing the generated content to be lifted into 3D and represented by provisional Gaussian primitives. These generated Gaussian primitives remain fixed and are excluded from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. When the corresponding background becomes visible in subsequent keyframes, a depth-aware projective rule removes eligible generated Gaussian primitives, while observation-supported Gaussian primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. In this way, DPGS-SLAM provides provisional representations of insufficiently observed static backgrounds while keeping generated Gaussian primitives separate from camera tracking and observation-supported map optimization. Our main contributions are as follows: We design a motion-aware dynamic-region identification pipeline for motion mask generation that integrates periodic optical-flow-based motion discovery with SAM2 (segment anything model 2) (2025)~ sam2 for mask refinement and temporal propagation, supporting dynamic-object discovery and spatiotemporally consistent motion masks. We introduce an asynchronous diffusion-based background completion strategy for static-background regions with insufficient observation support. A fine-tuned diffusion inpainting model generates plausible background appearance for selected keyframes, while Metric3D v2 (2024)~ metric3d predicts depth to initialize provisional Gaussian primitives without blocking camera tracking or observed-map optimization. We propose a provenance-aware Gaussian mapping strategy that explicitly distinguishes observation-supported primitives from diffusion-generated primitives. Generated primitives are excluded from camera-pose estimation and observed-map optimization. As previously occluded backgrounds become visible, eligible generated primitives are selectively removed using a depth-aware projective rule, while observation-supported primitives are independently initialized from real RGB observations and predicted depth. We evaluated DPGS-SLAM on TUM RGB-D~ tum , BONN RGB-D~ refusion , and StaDy4D~ stady4d using monocular RGB input. Our DPGS-SLAM achieved average ATE (absolute trajectory error) RMSE (root mean squared error) values of 1.2\,cm and 2.7\,cm on TUM RGB-D and BONN RGB-D, respectively, demonstrating competitive camera tracking. On the three evaluated StaDy4D sequences, it improved average PSNR (peak signal-to-noise ratio) by 4.60\,dB over WildGS-SLAM (2025)~ wildgs , while quantitative ablation studies and qualitative comparisons further support the effectiveness of background completion and observation-based replacement. Section~ sec:met presents our proposed method, DPGS-SLAM. Section~ sec:exp presents the experimental setup, comparative results, ablation studies, and limitations. Section~ sec:con concludes this paper. Their ability to generate plausible content in unobserved regions has motivated their application to 3D reconstruction. summary: Large-scale representation learning has produced public foundation models that provide strong general-purpose visual features. However, their pretraining objectives are not designed for robot representation learning, so the resulting embeddings tend to emphasize global semantics rather than the temporally sensitive representations required for robot control. Training robot models from scratch is also undesirable due to the limited scale and high collection cost of robotics data, as well as the substantial computational burden of pre-training. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models to robot control. SPARK is built on two principles: temporal abstraction, which encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model to retain useful pretrained semantics. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models to robot control. SPARK is built on two principles: temporal abstraction, which encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure, and knowledge preservation, which aligns patch-level representations with those of the original foundation model to retain useful pretrained semantics. These objectives yield compact visual state representations that remain semantically meaningful while preserving useful prior knowledge. Experiments across multiple robotics benchmarks show that SPARK consistently improves success rates and generalization over vanilla foundation models, and further demonstrate that these gains transfer to real-world robot manipulation. Introduction Robot representation learning~ nair2022r3m, ma2022vip, radosavovic2023mvp, cortexbench, parisi22, data4robotics has primarily centered on capturing dynamics in spatiotemporal observations, producing representations effective for imitation learning and robot control. In parallel, general-purpose visual representation learning has increasingly emphasized visual-language alignment for broad transfer. From this perspective, conventional robot models remain limited, being largely optimized for narrow control distributions rather than language-grounded semantics. Learning robot representations directly from paired video-language data offers a direct route to unifying embodied dynamics with language-level semantics. However, collecting robot vision-action data at scale~ cortexbench,ego4d,data4robotics is expensive and typically limited to laboratory settings, making it difficult to cover diverse scenes, objects, and interactions. Therefore, prior work has turned to large-scale video data without robot actions to capture physical dynamics that may benefit downstream robot learning. While such approaches improve scalability and provide temporal supervision, they still lack the broad semantic coverage and vision-language alignment available in foundation models trained on web-scale corpora. This motivates a different strategy that adapts already well-aligned foundation models~ clip, siglip, siglip2, theia, oquab2023dinov2 to the requirements of robot control. In this paper, we propose SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge), a post-training method that adapts foundation models and general-purpose vision models to robot control. The central goal of SPARK is to make pretrained representations more suitable for control without sacrificing the general visual knowledge acquired during large-scale pretraining. To this end, SPARK is built on two key principles: temporal abstraction and knowledge preservation. Temporal abstraction encourages the encoder to produce compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes by leveraging the prior knowledge acquired during large-scale pretraining. However, naively enforcing such compact abstraction can degrade useful prior knowledge inherited from large-scale pretraining. Thus, we adopt a retention objective that aligns the patch-wise representations of the adapted encoder with those of the original foundation model. We empirically demonstrate that SPARK yields consistent improvements across multiple robotics benchmarks~ dmc,metaworld,franka_kitchen, liu2023libero . Models adapted with SPARK yield higher success rates and better generalization than their vanilla models on average on robot manipulation tasks, highlighting that cost-efficient post-training can substantially facilitate the generalizability of the foundation model on robot control. Moreover, experiments on real-world robot tasks show that these gains extend beyond simulation. Consequently, SPARK presents a promising recipe for mitigating the mismatch between foundation models and the visual representations required for embodied intelligence. Related Work Pretrained Vision and Foundation Models. Large-scale vision and vision-language models, including the CLIP and SigLIP families~ clip, siglip, siglip2 as well as self-supervised models such as DINO, DINOv2, MAE, SimCLR, and MoCo variants~ dino, oquab2023dinov2, mae, simclr, moco, mocov2, mocov3 , provide strong general-purpose visual features and have become standard backbones for many vision tasks. However, their objectives target recognition and language alignment rather than the temporally fine-grained structure crucial for control, motivating post-training recipes that adapt these models to robotic perception without pre-training from scratch. Visual Representations in Robotics. Pretrained vision backbones are widely used to encode observations for downstream manipulation, navigation, and policy learning~ data4robotics, rlbench , and even frozen generic features can yield strong representations for imitation learning and control~ parisi22 . To further improve transfer, robotics-oriented pretraining has exploited egocentric viewpoints and temporal structure through time-contrastive learning with language supervision~ nair2022r3m , value-implicit pretraining~ ma2022vip , MAE-style reconstruction on egocentric corpora~ radosavovic2023mvp, cortexbench , language-guided semantic supervision~ karamcheti2023voltron, zeng2024mpi , and distillation of diverse foundation models into a single backbone~ theia . However, these recipes typically demand substantial computational cost and paired language annotations, limiting their accessibility relative to web-scale foundation models. Post-training and Adaptation. Post-training reduces the cost of adapting pretrained encoders to new domains or tasks. Parameter-efficient methods introduce small learnable components such as prompts and adapters~ zhou2022coop, zhou2022cocoop, gao2021clip or apply low-rank updates~ hu2022lora , while in robotics prior work has used masked-autoencoding~ mae reconstruction to enhance pretrained encoders for control~ cortexbench , STP~ stp learns content and motion features through spatiotemporal pixel prediction, and Lossless Adaptation~ sharma2023lossless inserts parameter-efficient adapters to preserve the original representation. Our approach follows this spirit but targets the representation more directly. SPARK introduces a temporal abstraction loss that trains a single class token as a compact state, together with a knowledge preservation loss that aligns token-level features with those of the original foundation model. Method Overview The goal of SPARK (Simple Post-training for Adapting pRetrained Knowledge) is to adapt pretrained foundation models to robot control without sacrificing the broad visual knowledge acquired during large-scale pretraining. To this end, SPARK is built on two complementary principles: temporal abstraction and knowledge preservation. Temporal abstraction encourages the encoder to derive compact features that preserve information essential for understanding temporal changes and action-relevant scene structure. Knowledge preservation regularizes this adaptation so that the learned representation remains aligned with the semantically meaningful features of the original foundation model. Together, these principles enable pretrained representations to become more suitable for robot control without requiring training from scratch. To realize temporal abstraction, SPARK trains the encoder so that a compact feature extracted from a reference observation can support the prediction of a temporally offset target scene. Specifically, the encoder processes a reference scene and produces patch tokens together with a class token, where the class token serves as a compact feature. A decoder then reconstructs token representations of the target scene from this compact feature, conditioned on only a small subset of visible target patches as hints. Because accurate prediction requires information that explains how the scene changes over time, this objective encourages the compact feature to preserve temporal and action-relevant structure rather than only static global semantics. However, adapting the encoder solely through this abstraction objective can distort useful pretrained knowledge. To mitigate this issue, SPARK introduces a retention objective that aligns the patch-wise representations of the adapted encoder with those of the frozen original foundation model on the same input. This regularization preserves semantically meaningful local features while allowing the compact feature to specialize toward dynamic understanding for control. title: PLS-GS: Probabilistic Lidar Scaffolds for Compact, Surface-Aligned Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. Main paper and supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS
summary: While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is typically optimized from images only, many robotics and mapping applications provide both camera and high-definition LiDAR data, combining rich visual appearance with accurate geometric structure. We introduce PLS-GS, a probabilistic LiDAR scaffold for Gaussian Splatting that exploits this complementary sensing setting to construct a compact 3DGS representation aligned to the measured surface. PLS-GS fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model jointly over position and color, yielding a continuous and adaptive scaffold that eliminates the need for discrete scene partitioning such as voxel grids or octrees. The fitted mixture then guides the renderable 3DGS Gaussians: each rendering Gaussian is associated with a GMM component and constrained in the local surface frame induced by that component's covariance. A Mahalanobis support loss bounds the deviation of the rendering Gaussians from the corresponding LiDAR-derived surface. Across five large outdoor scenes, PLS-GS places primitives markedly closer to the LiDAR measurements than both image- and LiDAR-initialized baselines, while employing substantially fewer primitives, yielding a considerably more compact model and faster rendering. At matched capacity, PLS-GS places primitives closer to the LiDAR measurements, with comparable rendering quality. Code is available at https://github.com/k-harikumar/PLS-GS.

At matched capacity, PLS-GS places primitives closer to the LiDAR measurements, with comparable rendering quality. Code is available at . Introduction sec:introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl2023gaussian has rapidly become a leading representation for photorealistic novel-view synthesis, achieving high visual quality and real-time rendering with anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized through differentiable rasterisation. While most 3DGS pipelines are driven by image supervision alone, many robotics and mapping platforms provide both cameras and high-definition LiDAR, where images supply rich appearance and LiDAR supplies accurate geometry. This complementarity creates an opportunity to construct 3DGS representations that retain high rendering quality while being more compact and more faithful to the scene geometry. We study 3DGS in exactly this setting. Image-only 3DGS optimizes primitives to reproduce training views, which is effective for photometric quality but constrains geometry only indirectly: the learned primitives may be redundant and depart from the underlying surfaces~ gauuscene , and storage grows with scene scale~ PapantonakisReduced3dgs . Where measured geometry is available, it offers a direct way to ground the representation in the scene's true structure. Two lines of work each capture part of what is needed. Scaffold-based methods~ scaffoldgs, ren2024octree improve compactness by decoding neural Gaussians from structured supports such as voxel grids or octrees, but these supports are discrete and seeded from image-derived structure rather than measured geometry. Separately, LiDAR-grounded methods~ gssdf,ligs improve alignment to measured geometry, but their primitives remain free to drift under photometric optimization, retaining the unstructured densification and per-primitive storage of vanilla 3DGS. Neither yields a scaffold that is both compact and grounded in measured geometry. We propose PLS-GS, a probabilistic LiDAR scaffold for Gaussian Splatting that is continuous, adaptive to local scene structure, and grounded in measured geometry. PLS-GS fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model jointly over the position and color of the input point cloud, so that its components separate surfaces that are spatially adjacent but photometrically distinct. Unlike a discrete grid cell, each component carries a full covariance, representing not merely occupancy but the orientation and extent of the surface occupying it. Each component's covariance defines a local surface frame in which the neural Gaussians decoded from that anchor are expressed, and a Mahalanobis support loss bounds their deviation from it. PLS-GS is a scaffolded Gaussian Splatting method that builds its supporting structure from measured LiDAR geometry instead of image-derived points. PLS-GS aligns its Gaussian primitives with the LiDAR measurements, resulting in a compact model that renders faster than baselines initialized from either images or LiDAR, with only a modest tradeoff in rendering PSNR. Concretely, our experiments validate the following claims: Our probabilistic scaffold achieves substantially higher surface-alignment precision than initialization from measured LiDAR geometry alone. Seeding the Scaffold-GS baseline directly from the LiDAR improves its alignment only marginally over image-derived points, whereas PLS-GS improves it by (Sec.~ sec:main_comparison ). Decoding primitives in the scaffold's local surface frame substantially improves alignment to the measured geometry. At identical anchor counts and identical anchor positions, PLS-GS improves every geometric metric on every scene, at comparable rendering quality (Sec.~ sec:matched ). Constrained probabilistic growth densifies under-reconstructed regions while keeping the representation compact. PLS-GS grows its anchor count by during training against Scaffold-GS's , yielding a model smaller that renders faster (Sec.~ sec:main_comparison ). Related Works sec:related_works Gaussian Mixture Models for 3D Representation. Gaussian Mixture Models have a long history in point cloud modelling. Eckart et al.~ eckarthgmm, Eckart_2018_ECCV introduced hierarchical GMMs for multi-resolution representation, showing that recursive Expectation-Maximisation yields surface-aligned components whose covariance eigenvectors encode local surface geometry, a compact, continuous, and adaptive description of geometry in contrast to the discrete voxel grids and octrees commonly used to structure 3D data and reporting higher fidelity at smaller model size than NDT-based alternatives. To the best of our knowledge PLS-GS is the first method to repurpose this hierarchical GMM from a geometric representation into a rendering scaffold: its components serve as anchors, and their eigenvector frames define the surface-aligned frames in which neural Gaussians are decoded. Structured and Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting. 3DGS~ kerbl2023gaussian enables real-time photorealistic rendering through differentiable rasterisation of anisotropic Gaussian primitives, but produces large, redundant primitive sets. Scaffold-GS~ scaffoldgs reduces this redundancy by decoding neural Gaussians from anchor points through shared MLPs, and Octree-GS~ ren2024octree extends this with a level-of-detail octree. Anchoring primitives to such discrete structures inherits the limitations of discretisation: quantisation at cell boundaries, and a dependence on partitioning to scale. VastGaussian~ vastgaussian , CityGaussian~ citygaussian and Hierarchical-GS~ hierarchicalgs likewise address scale by partitioning the scene into independently trained blocks. In all of these the supporting structure is seeded and grown from photometric optimization rather than from scene geometry, so the decoded primitives are not constrained to physical surfaces and image quality need not reflect geometric accuracy~ gauuscene . Geometrically Accurate Gaussian Splatting. A separate line of work targets geometric accuracy through supervision during training. 2DGS~ 2dgs and SuGaR~ sugar constrain primitives towards the underlying surface, and CityGaussianV2~ citygaussianv2 attains strong accuracy on GauU-Scene V2 benchmark~ gauuscene with 2D Gaussian surfels and depth regression, at the cost of multi-GPU training, scene partitioning and mesh extraction. Closer to our setting, several methods supervise from measured LiDAR geometry. LI-GS~ ligs voxelises the cloud, fits a plane per voxel by RANSAC and estimates a mixture over in-plane position and intensity, so its components are planar by construction and inherit the discretisation of the underlying grid. ARSGaussian~ Yao_2026 prunes primitives that drift beyond a distance threshold from the nearest measured point, GS-SDF~ gssdf regularises against a neural signed distance field, and Gaussian-LIC~ gaussianlic and GS-LIVO~ gslivo embed LiDAR within real-time SLAM. In each method, every Gaussian carries its own position, covariance, opacity and spherical-harmonic coefficients, so each primitive costs tens of floats to store. Preliminaries sec:prelim 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3DGS~ kerbl2023gaussian represents a scene as anisotropic Gaussian primitives, each with a centre , an opacity , view-dependent color, and a covariance factored into a rotation and diagonal scaling to preserve positive-definiteness during optimization: Pixel colors are obtained by projecting the primitives to the image plane and compositing them front-to-back, where is the depth-sorted set of primitives covering and is weighted by the projected 2D Gaussian at . All parameters are optimized against a photometric loss combining and structural-similarity terms: Scaffold-GS. Scaffold-GS~ scaffoldgs replaces the unstructured primitive set with a two-tier hierarchy of anchors and neural Gaussians. Each anchor at position carries a learnable feature , a scaling vector , and offset vectors , where the first three components of govern the offset extent and the remaining three the scale of the spawned Gaussians. Anchors are initialised by voxelising a sparse Structure-from-Motion point cloud at resolution , with duplicate centres removed. For each anchor within the view frustum, neural Gaussians are spawned at their opacity, color, scale, and rotation decoded from and the viewing parameters by shared MLPs and rasterised through Equations~ -- . During training, Scaffold-GS densifies the anchor set at voxel centres where the averaged photometric gradient exceeds a threshold, so that the supporting structure, both its initial placement and its growth, is determined by a discrete voxel grid. Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Models. A Gaussian mixture models a point set as a weighted sum of Gaussian densities, fitted by Expectation-Maximisation. Where points are sampled from a surface, a component's covariance is anisotropic: its two largest eigenvalues span the local tangent plane and the smallest aligns with the surface normal, so each component encodes the position, extent and orientation of the surface it covers. Eckart et al.~ eckarthgmm, Eckart_2018_ECCV fit such a mixture recursively, refining each component over the points assigned to it, so that a leaf at level carries the product of its ancestors' weights, and resolution follows local data density rather than a fixed cell size. For more details about HGMM construction, please see the supplementary material. PLS-GS sec:method Given a colored point cloud, PLS-GS fits a Hierarchical Gaussian Mixture Model (HGMM) jointly over the spatial and color dimensions of the points, recursively refining a coarse mixture into progressively finer levels and taking the leaf components as anchors whose positions and orientations follow the local geometry of the scene. Unlike scaffold-based methods, which decode neural Gaussians from anchors on a discrete grid oriented in an arbitrary world frame, we decode each within the surface frame of its component and constrain it through a Mahalanobis support loss, so that both placement and rendering are governed by the measured geometry. A growth stage then adds anchors in regions of high photometric residual. Probabilistic Scaffold Construction sec:scaffold Let the input

title: Motion Belief Action: From a Visual Scene Map to Physical Decisions
summary: A robot that works among people must judge what it cannot see: whether an object is still where it was last seen, and whether a pull on a door or drawer is worth its risk. Maps that track object change hold nothing about force, maps of physical properties answer a risk question at a fixed risk level, and vision-language-action models keep no explicit estimate of hidden physics. We propose Motion Belief Action (MBA), a decision layer on the scene map. From how often people move an object and how much force it needs, how much load it holds and whether it is blocked, MBA chooses under a force limit to look again, nudge, open, brace or decline, with its risk set by the task's costs. On real activity in 9 kitchens, it predicts whether an object is still in place better than FreMEn and Perpetua, and decides when to look again at lower cost than these and the persistence filter, because about a quarter of placements end in a pick-up within 30 s. On real pulls of doors and drawers in 17 locations, made by a person with a force-sensing gripper, the map's force estimates decide better than a part-type average. Setting the risk from the costs also beats a published risk rule at its fixed level. In simulation, with the force limit at the training parts' median force, MBA raises SmolVLA's and Octo's scores by declining pulls; most declined door pulls would fail, but on drawers more would have opened, and a part-type average gets about half of this gain. In both, a published risk rule set to the risk these costs imply is MBA's rule for a single pull and decides as well in the main settings. A link between opening and holding force, a probing nudge and an action prior for camera tracking do not help in the main settings, and over the real-pull sweep the nudge costs a little.

Introduction sec:intro A robot that works among people must act on what it cannot see. People move things: a mug put down a moment ago may be picked up again within a minute. Doors and drawers hide their physics. Before pulling a drawer, the robot does not know how hard it will resist. Before leaning on an open door, it does not know whether the door will hold. A pull with too much force can damage the part, so the robot works under a force limit. For each, it can look again, act or decline, and for a door or drawer first test it; the right choice depends on what a mistake costs in the task. The evidence is in the robot's scene map, which records what people move and what the robot felt when it touched a part. Maps that track change estimate whether an object is still in place. The persistence filter~ rosen2016persistence estimates how likely a mapped object is to still be there, and FreMEn~ krajnik2017fremen models objects that come and go periodically. Perpetua~ saavedra2025perpetua mixes several such filters with different lifetimes but predicts from the most likely one, and builds them into scene graphs~ saavedra2026predictive ; PreSIST~ adkins2026presist sets an object's prior from a vision-language model; HiPer~ canh2026hiper pools per-object rates, and an earlier model adds a second component~ toris2017temporal . Open-vocabulary maps label every object~ gu2024conceptgraphs , VLMM~ ghosh2026vlmm records which objects people move, and semantic exploration revisits places whose objects may have moved~ bogenberger2026glasses , and active perception re-inspects changed objects~ qian2026active . These maps tell the robot where to look, but they hold nothing about force, so they cannot tell the arm how to act. Methods that learn by touching estimate a part's physics~ ewen2024feel . The joint of a door or drawer, its type and axis, is estimated from the robot's own motion~ sturm2011probabilistic,martinmartin2014online,hausman2015active . PhysVLMM~ ghosh2026physvlmm keeps an estimate of each part's forces in the scene map, shares it between parts that look alike, and tells whether an action will succeed. Phys2Real~ wang2026phys2real and Law-to-Action~ mabrok2026l2a combine vision-language priors with estimates made by touch. Test actions reveal whether an object moves or a drawer is locked~ yuan2026wontknow,liu2026aquamend , TANav~ li2026tanav nudges an obstacle and decides from costs whether to push it, a force-capped pull is refused when it would move the furniture~ zhou2026trading , and MessyMem~ banwasi2026messymem remembers what the robot learned by doing. Law-to-Action comes closest: it chooses to look again or test by expected value under hand-set costs and refuses at a fixed threshold~ mabrok2026l2a . In our method, every choice, to look again, test, act or decline, follows from the task's costs, as in the classical reject rule~ chow1970optimum , with no other threshold set by hand. Vision-language-action models~ kim2024openvla,octo2024,shukor2025smolvla,black2025pi0 map an image and an instruction directly to motion, and active visual reasoning~ zhou2025physvlmavr lets a model move to see what is hidden, and calibrated abstention refuses actions likely to be unsafe~ singh2026bokbo,zhang2026rcdh . They hold no explicit estimate of a part's force, so they cannot judge whether a test is worth its cost, or decline a pull from the part's own estimated force. Tracking the camera while the robot acts is a smaller problem: methods for moving scenes remove pixels of classes that usually move~ bescos2018dynaslam,murartal2017orbslam2 or track rigid objects~ long2021rigidfusion , but a drawer the robot pulls moves with the wrist camera, so its pixels stay still. We present Motion Belief Action ( ), a decision layer on the scene map ( ). For each object, keeps a belief, a probability distribution, over how often people move it, the force needed to open it, the load it holds when the robot leans on it (a brace), and whether it is blocked. The force estimates start from PhysVLMM's~ ghosh2026physvlmm . adds the rest: a still-in-place model, the blocked state, updates from whether a touch moved or held the part, the planner and the camera tracker. Under the force limit, the planner chooses whether to look again, test the force with a light push (a nudge), open, brace or decline. It weighs each choice by its expected outcome under the task's costs, so the risk it takes follows the task. PhysVLMM's risk query instead takes the risk level as an input; for a single pull, with that level set from the same costs, the two choose alike. We test each part on its own data. Our contributions are: ( ). A decision layer in which every choice follows from the task's costs. On real pulls, the map's force estimates decide better than a part-type average ( ); in simulation it raises the scores of two vision-language-action policies, mostly by declining pulls ( ). Still-in-place prediction ( ). One quick pick-up shared by all objects, since people often pick an object up again soon after putting it down, and a slow rate per object, estimated together for objects with the same name. On real kitchen activity, its decisions to look again cost less than those of three published methods ( ). Evaluation ( ). Real pulls, real kitchen activity and simulation, against published methods run from their authors' code where released. It also reports what does not help: the link between opening force and held load, the nudge, and the tracker's prior on where the held part appears. Methodology sec:method Problem formulation sec:formulation Scene map. runs on a Vision-Language-Motion Map (VLMM)~ ghosh2026vlmm , which gives each object its name and records whether and when people move it. Each map element has a position , an open-vocabulary label , a category and a motion class . PhysVLMM~ ghosh2026physvlmm adds to each door and drawer its joint (its geometry : joint type , axis ), its group of look-alike parts, and a first estimate of its forces from the measured look-alikes. adds the belief defined below to every element that the map classes as movable and to every door and drawer ( ), and leaves the other fields unchanged. Hidden state. Object has the hidden state : , where [s ] is the object's own rate of being picked up (the slow rate of ); , where is the force needed to move it in the opening direction and the largest constant load in the closing direction that it holds still (its support); and indicates a blocked part that cannot reach the target opening. title: LHNav: Long-Horizon Humanoid Navigation via Multirate Coordination and Physics-Grounded Action Data
summary: We study humanoid navigation across multiple destinations under long-horizon language instructions. This task is challenging because robots must maintain progress across successive goals while continuously producing natural, stable whole-body motion through confined spaces. However, task decomposition in existing methods does not by itself ensure progress throughout execution, while waypoint-based navigation does not guarantee natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. Our key idea is to organize navigation into three complementary roles operating at different time scales: a Brain for task reasoning, a Cerebellum for local motion generation, and a Brainstem for whole-body execution. We realize this idea in LHNav, an asynchronous system that uses progress and arrival feedback to coordinate navigation goals, VLA motion-token prediction, and whole-body control. To train the Cerebellum for natural, route-faithful motion, we develop a physics-grounded data engine that improves physical tracking of motion references along collision-aware routes and pairs the resulting demonstrations with rendered visual observations. Together, these designs allow task planning to proceed alongside continuous movement and extend single-goal navigation to successive destinations with natural, route-faithful whole-body motion. In simulation, our navigation VLA outperforms OmniNav and DualVLN in single-goal success and motion smoothness, with fewer collisions and falls. Using a VLA trained only on single-goal demonstrations, LHNav achieves a 75.56% success rate on long-horizon navigation tasks. Deployment on the Unitree G1 further demonstrates single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon task execution in real-world environments, including layouts with repositioned objects. Project website: https://robbyant-research.github.io/LHNav/.

Introduction sec:introduction Humanoid robots assisting people in everyday environments need to follow long-horizon language instructions that involve multiple destinations and task dependencies~ ahn2022saycan,zhou2026holoagent0 . For example, preparing a meal may require visiting the refrigerator, chopping board, stove, and dining table in an appropriate order. In this work, we focus on the navigation required by such instructions, where a humanoid must infer navigation goals and maintain progress across destinations without step-by-step guidance. This setting requires both task-level coordination across successive goals and natural, stable whole-body motion along long routes through confined spaces. Long-horizon humanoid navigation is challenging because task progress must remain consistent with continuous execution across multiple destinations. Existing methods couple navigation decisions to reasoning~ cai2025clcotnav,gao2025octonav,zuo2026fantasyvln , while asynchronous and hierarchical approaches allow task planning and action to proceed at different time scales~ wei2025dualvln,huang2026ticvla,su2026sagenav,zhou2026holoagent0 . However, separating these processes does not itself ensure coherent task progression: goal transitions must reflect actual execution progress while navigation continues. A second challenge is reconciling route constraints with natural, stable whole-body motion, particularly in confined spaces. Waypoints, trajectories, and velocity commands describe intended movement but leave its whole-body realization to downstream controllers~ krantz2021waypoint,huang2026ticvla,zhou2026holoagent0 , so a collision-free route does not directly guarantee collision-free physical execution. Recent methods introduce richer body-level actions and multi-stage behaviors~ ding2025humanoidvla,wang2026vlk,rayyan2026fetchman,kim2026legs , yet maintaining natural motion while limiting position and heading errors over long, confined routes remains challenging. We present , combining asynchronous navigation with a physics-grounded data engine for long-horizon humanoid navigation. Inspired by the human brain, it comprises three layers: a Brain that maintains task context and dispatches goals, a Cerebellum that predicts motion tokens with auxiliary waypoint-based geometric supervision, and a Brainstem that executes whole-body motion through a frozen SONIC decoder~ luo2025sonic . Progress and arrival feedback coordinate successive goals, allowing a single-goal policy to execute navigation while task planning proceeds asynchronously. Our data engine uses ARDY~ zhao2026ardy to generate natural motion references along collision-aware routes and trains the SONIC encoder with additional reference-root and velocity information for accurate tracking through the frozen decoder. Rendering closed-loop rollouts in reconfigurable Gaussian--mesh scenes~ kerbl20233dgs pairs visual observations with synchronized motion-token targets for VLA training. Together, asynchronous coordination and physically executed supervision support natural, route-faithful whole-body navigation across multiple goals. Joint training on these simulated navigation demonstrations and real teleoperated manipulation data further enables navigation followed by tabletop pushing on Unitree G1. Our contributions are threefold: An asynchronous multirate system integrating task reasoning, motion-token prediction, and whole-body execution, using progress-aware transitions that extend a single-goal policy to long-horizon humanoid navigation. A scalable, physics-grounded data engine that improves global motion-reference tracking through a privileged encoder and frozen SONIC decoder, generating execution-aligned navigation demonstrations in Gaussian--mesh scenes. Experimental validation demonstrating higher navigation success in unseen simulation scenes, smoother motion, fewer collisions, and faster long-horizon completion, alongside real-world single-goal navigation and zero-shot long-horizon navigation. Related Work sec:related From navigation commands to whole-body motion. Navigation policies typically output motion primitives~ krantz2020vlnce , metric commands~ zhang2024navid,cheng2024navila , or local waypoints and trajectories~ krantz2021waypoint,sridhar2023nomad,cai2025navdp . While natural for wheeled robots, these interfaces rely on downstream controllers for actuation and, on humanoids, whole-body coordination. Richer interfaces expose body targets: LEGS combines wrist poses with base commands~ kim2026legs , FetchMan uses base height and upper-body joint targets~ rayyan2026fetchman , and VLK predicts root-and-joint trajectories with contacts~ wang2026vlk . Others encode motion as pose tokens~ ding2025humanoidvla , learned latents~ xue2025leverb , or FSQ tokens~ luo2025sonic . SONIC decodes such tokens with proprioceptive feedback and supports direct VLA prediction. We adopt this interface for navigation, motivating supervision aligned with executed humanoid motion. Physics-grounded navigation supervision. Navigation data draw on instruction--route datasets~ anderson2018vln , simulators~ savva2019habitat , Gaussian scene representations~ kerbl20233dgs,interiorgs2025 , and geometric experts that synthesize routes~ cai2025navdp,abotn02026 . These provide visual context and geometric routes, but humanoid supervision must also specify how the body executes them. VLK synthesizes whole-body kinematics in reconstructed scenes~ wang2026vlk , while LEGS and FetchMan collect control commands from physical rollouts~ kim2026legs,rayyan2026fetchman . Tracking reveals failures and route deviations missed by kinematic references; LEGS therefore retains only successful episodes~ kim2026legs . Our data engine targets global route fidelity and pairs rendered executed states with the post-FSQ tokens consumed during rollout, matching the deployment action interface. Reasoning and execution for long-horizon tasks. Long-horizon navigation couples semantic planning with local execution. summarizes representative strategies. FantasyVLN uses reasoning supervision only during training~ zuo2026fantasyvln , whereas NavGPT and CL-CoTNav reason online before acting~ zhou2023navgpt,cai2025clcotnav . OctoNav and AwareVLN reduce overhead by adapting reasoning frequency or switching between reasoning and action modes~ gao2025octonav,guo2026awarevln . OmniNav connects planning and execution through subgoals~ xue2025omninav , while DualVLN enables asynchronous action prediction from cached goals and current observations~ wei2025dualvln ; TIC-VLA further models latency and egomotion~ huang2026ticvla . Task coordination also requires execution feedback: SAGE-Nav updates semantic waypoints upon completion or deadlock~ su2026sagenav , while Uni-LaViRA, Being-0, and HoloAgent-0 organize multistage execution through subgoal or skill interfaces~ ding2026unilavira,yuan2025being0,zhou2026holoagent0 . We use asynchronous execution, with short instructions and target images linking task planning to single-goal navigation. Arrival verification and progress feedback guide advancement and recovery; motion tokens drive high-rate proprioceptive whole-body control. Method sec:method We consider a G1 humanoid robot operating in a scene with a catalog of reference images depicting candidate destinations. Given a long-horizon language instruction, selects the required destinations from this catalog and navigates the robot to them in sequence. As shown in , the Brain decomposes the instruction into navigation subtasks ( ), the Cerebellum predicts local motion tokens, and the Brainstem decodes them into whole-body actions ( ). All three layers execute asynchronously. Brain: Agent with Tools sec:method:architecture The Brain coordinates long-horizon navigation through a planning agent with task-management and arrival-verification tools, tracking progress, revising the remaining plan, and deciding when to advance. The planning agent receives the full instruction and target catalog, together with task-decomposition and tool-use guidance and recent observations, decisions, and execution feedback. It can be implemented with GPT-6 or Qwen3.8-27B. The task management tool (Tool~1 in ) maintains an explicit plan of completed, active, and pending navigation subtasks. The agent uses this tool to create the plan and revise pending subtasks during execution using new observations, task updates, and execution feedback. Revisions can remove goals that are no longer needed, while preserving completed visits and the active goal. The arrival verification tool provides goal-completion feedback through an independent Qwen VLM, which checks arrival at up to 1~Hz using the active subtask, target reference image, and temporal observations. Diagnostic analyses and subtask-specific arrival judgments are written to a shared buffer for the planning agent to access. At a navigation stop, the runtime harness blocks new VLA requests and discards outstanding predictions. It records completion after verified arrival, motion-plan exhaustion, and odometry-confirmed root stability, then dispatches the next subtask from the updated plan following the external stage-completion event. At each stage, the Brain supplies the Cerebellum VLA with a simple textual instruction specifying the active navigation goal, such as ``go to the table.'' title: Embodied First Exam
comment: Preprint version
summary: Early successes on agentic robotics point to a potential paradigm shift toward using coding agents to control robots. Existing robotics benchmarks are built around visuomotor policy learning, leaving it open whether coding agents can reliably control diverse robots under physical-world constraints. We therefore introduce the Embodied First Exam, a unified, comprehensive, and agent-native evaluation framework where coding agents can choose their own control approach: direct control, code to control, or train a policy to control. We hope it serves as a first exam for coding agents before they enter the physical world, with 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots, including 9 new suites that go beyond pick-and-place to spatial puzzles, dexterous manipulation, multi-robot interaction, dynamic whole-body control, and sim-to-sim engineering. Each task can be run in up to three evaluation settings. The Standard Setting mimics the real world: the agent receives only sensor observations and, by default, cannot reset the environment. Its Realtime variant keeps the environment running while the agent reasons. The Privileged Setting gives the agent access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution for training purposes. Success rates in this setting serve as an approximate upper bound. On the 456 core tasks, the strongest of eight agents, GPT-6 Astra in Codex, achieves a success rate of 34% in the Standard Setting, leaving much room for improvement. To see where agents fail, we label the stage at which failed attempts go wrong and compare failures across agents, settings, and stage categories.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Robots acquire new skills either by manual programming or by learning from data, as in recent vision-language-action models~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black20240,intelligence2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00t,team2025gemini and world action models~ ye2026world,wang2026world,shen2026world . Coding agents powered by large language models suggest a third way. They already complete challenging software engineering tasks in the digital world~ jimenez2023swebench,merrill2026terminalbench,miserendino2025swelancer,kwa2025measuring . What makes these agents promising for robotic engineering is their capabilities to turn instructions into executable code and revise their plans through automated experimentation~ liang2022code,singh2023progprompt,vemprala2023chatgpt . Recent early success in agentic robots suggests such a potential paradigm shift, where agents directly control robots~ hu2026via,zhang2026unexpected,zhou2026gpt6,sensenova2026astra , write robot programs~ jia2026agent,fu2026capx,merler2026coding,xie2026pusht,tan2026forca,hu2026simex , or train policies~ xiao2026enpire,li2026harbor . This motivates a systematic assessment of the capability boundary of coding agents: What robotic tasks can general-purpose coding agents solve, under what physical-world constraints, and where do they fail? Existing benchmarks do not yet fully address this question. The capability boundary cannot be established from a focused set of robotics tasks ~ james2020rlbench,yu2020metaworld,liu2023libero,li2024behavior1k,nasiriany2024robocasa,chen2026robodojo , nor from automated programming tasks without imposing physical-world constraints~ jimenez2023swebench,merrill2026terminalbench,zhou2023webarena,xie2024osworld,chan2024mlebench,ouyang2025kernelbench . This requires defining which robotic capabilities to evaluate, measuring how physical-world constraints affect success, and supporting different models and harnesses through task interfaces. To answer this question, we introduce the ( ) , a unified evaluation framework that connects coding agents to simulated robots ( ), following three principles. First, include diverse tasks that go beyond pick-and-place. Spatial puzzles test reasoning about spatial constraints, while sim-to-sim engineering tests how agents revise controllers from execution feedback under unfamiliar dynamics. Dynamic tasks test responses to a changing world. Multi-robot interaction and whole-body control test coordination. therefore contains 1,156 tasks in 35 suites on 47 robots. It combines 26 suites adapted from existing robotics benchmarks with 9 new suites covering these capabilities and safety. Second, measure how success depends on physical-world constraints. Its tasks should follow the constraints of a real robot as closely as possible. Success with full simulator state and resets does not establish what an agent can achieve through partial observations, with no resets, or while the dynamic world keeps running. We therefore define up to three evaluation settings per task. Setting follows real-robot conditions: the agent observes the environment only through the robot's sensors and cannot reset it by default. The simulation waits while the agent reasons, and its variant keeps the environment running while the agent makes decisions. Setting provides an approximate upper bound and can be used to generate training data, where the agent has access to the full simulator state and unlimited resets, allowing it to search for an oracle solution by trial and error. We call each <task--setting> pair a test. Tests of the same task share the initial scene and success rule, allowing us to compare success as state access, reset limits, and timing change. Third, provide unified infrastructure for different models, harnesses, and control approaches. With a single command, runs different combinations of models and harnesses across diverse robotics tasks. Given a natural-language task instruction, the agent chooses its control approach ( ). In Direct control, it directly outputs actions after receiving observations~ hu2026via,zhang2026unexpected,zhou2026gpt6 . In Code to control, it outputs a planner, controller, or other program that generates the robot's actions~ liang2022code . In Train a policy, it trains a policy in simulation and uses it to control the robot~ ma2024eureka,li2026harbor . The framework enforces the access permitted by each evaluation setting, and a verifier outside the agent's control grades every attempt~ zhu2025establishing,zhong2025impossiblebench . We evaluate eight coding agents on a core set of 456 hard tasks. The strongest agent, GPT-6 Astra~ openai2026gpt6astra in Codex, solves 77 of the tests but only 30 of the tests of the same 391 tasks. Apart from the three strongest agents, GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, the best result comes from Kimi 3.1 Pro, which solves 9 of the tests of the same 391 tasks (34 tests, ) and 7 of the tests ( ). The Setting is harder still: 63 of its tests remain unsolved by any agent, compared with 50 of the tests of the same 54 tasks. To identify where failures occur within a task, we divide each task into stages. Each stage corresponds to a change in the world required to complete the task. For example, the task of putting a tomato into a closed fridge has three stages: the fridge is open, the tomato is inside, and the fridge is closed again. For each failed attempt of the eight agents on 427 tasks, a separate coding agent labels the stage at which the failure occurred. Our main findings are as follows. The Embodied First Exam: A Unified Evaluation Framework for Coding Agents in Robotics sec:benchmark In this section, we describe how we evaluate coding agents on robotics tasks ( ), the resource constraints of each task ( ), and the tasks of the exam ( ). Framework and Evaluation Protocol sec:test sec:settings sec:honest Existing robotics benchmarks focus on visuomotor policy learning with a relatively fixed input-output interface, whereas we evaluate coding agents that can choose their own control approach. Our design principle is therefore to give the agent broad freedom over how it acts and to constrain only the result: we fix where it starts, what resources it gets, and how success is checked. To achieve this, we package every robotics task in the format of Harbor~ harbor2026 , the evaluation framework of Terminal-Bench~ merrill2026terminalbench , which runs the task in containers, as shown in . The agent has its own workspace, where it can install packages, write and run programs, and train models. Each task starts from a fixed initial state; a verifier outside the agent's container reports whether the agent's answer meets the task's success rule. =-1 On top of this framework, we define a unified evaluation protocol with up to three settings per task ( ). We design as an approximate upper bound on performance, with full access to the simulator for trial and error, while and make the evaluation as close to a real robot as possible. The bound holds over a set of tasks, not for every single task, because an agent can solve a task in that it fails in ( ). For a given task, all settings share the same initial scene, success rule, and time limit, so their results are paired. They differ in what the agent observes, whether it can reset, whether the world waits, and where the simulator and the verifier run, never in the control approach the agent may choose. We ablate the first two differences in . Privileged. In , the agent runs in the same container as the simulator, so it can read the full simulation state and reset without limit. The agent must submit a low-level robot trajectory (or a controller program for some tasks). The verifier replays the trajectory (or runs the controller) in a separate container to determine task success. Standard. In , we run the simulator as a service in a separate container. Through predefined APIs, the agent has limited access to the simulator: it can query proprioceptive state (e.g., joint positions, velocities, and torques), and sensor data (e.g., calibrated RGB-D images), and send action chunks to control the robot. The simulation is paused between API requests, so the agent faces no real-time pressure. Resets are disallowed unless the task provides an explicit reset budget. The verifier grades task progress online as the agent controls the robot, and in most suites the interface reports a success to the agent and ends the episode. Realtime. is the same as , except that the simulation does not pause between agent actions but keeps running in real time; for computationally expensive tasks, it runs at a fixed fraction of real time (e.g., 0.5 ). Due to compute constraints, we currently evaluate only on dynamic tasks. details each setting. Resource Constraints for Coding Agents sec:limits As shown in , we set resource constraints for each task: a time limit and a token budget for the agent, a reset budget and, in some tasks, a step limit for the robot (RoboDojo's own limit in , or a cap on the episode length that the instruction states), and caps on CPU, memory, GPU memory, and disk. The token budget is high enough that no attempt reaches it. The time limit is the same in every setting of a task, and when it runs out we stop the agent and grade the result it has at that point. Resets are unlimited in . In and , there are no resets unless the task grants a budget, which nine suites do, with 3 to 50 resets. We set the compute caps per task from its measured needs and monitor usage throughout the run ( ). We observe that coding agents may choose different control approaches under different resource constraints and in different settings ( ). For example, if we provide a GPU, agents can train a policy to control the robot ( ). Task Suites sec:tasks The exam contains 1,156 tasks in 35 suites. A suite is a set of related tasks on one simulator. Each task states a goal, usually in natural language, such as untying a knot or turning the page of a book with a dexterous hand, and the agent must control the robot to reach that goal. We built 9 suites with 411 tasks for the exam and adapted the other 26 suites with 745 tasks from existing robotics benchmarks. Together, the tasks use 47 robots of nine types ( in , which lists the simulator, the robots and the number of tasks of every suite). New suites. We built nine new suites because the adapted suites contain few tasks for several embodiments and capabilities. Most of their original benchmarks focus on visuomotor policy learning ( ), and 618 of their 745 tasks use single-arm, bimanual or mobile manipulators. title: Graph-Based RL for Sequential Rendezvous Planning with Multiple Patrolling USVs
summary: In patrol missions involving multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs), a designated command USV can support fleet management by sequentially rendezvousing with each patrolling USV. These operations require motion-feasible route planning and priority-aware rendezvous sequencing, with the objective of minimizing mission completion time and total tardiness relative to priority-dependent due dates. We propose a framework combining grid-based path planning, surrogate travel-time prediction, and graph-based reinforcement learning. The path planner accounts for ocean currents and approximates turn-rate constraints through multi-stage maneuvers, with path feasibility empirically validated through trajectory-tracking simulations. For rendezvous sequencing, a Feasible Transition Graph (FTG) represents candidate rendezvous events and temporally feasible transitions, enabling a graph neural network to exploit spatiotemporal rendezvous relationships for policy learning. A surrogate predicts travel times from compact current and motion features to avoid repeated path searches during FTG construction and policy training. Evaluation using grid-based path planning shows statistically significant average objective reductions of 10.5%, 3.5%, and 1.5% compared with greedy, MLP-RL, and 2-step lookahead greedy, respectively. The policy achieves these improvements while requiring approximately 1/35 of the latter's computation time. It maintains its advantage over MLP-RL under unseen priority-tier settings, with larger gains as fleet size increases.

title: A Game-Theoretic MPC Planner for Cooperative and Adversarial Drone Coordination
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, submitted to European Control Conference (ECC27)
summary: We present and evaluate a game-theoretic model predictive control planner for cooperative goal reaching and adversarial pursuit-evasion with drones. The planner combines 3D prediction, individual objectives, optional shared separation constraints and trajectory-tracking interfaces. A comparison of cooperative game solvers assesses their ability to find feasible trajectories that resolve conflicts. A computational study quantifies how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time and numerical acceptance. Move blocking holds control inputs constant over groups of prediction steps, reducing the number of independent control variables and lowering computation time. Timing measurements identify the practical limits of real-time planning in the tested configurations. PyBullet simulations demonstrate cooperative goal reaching and pursuit-evasion. A laboratory flight complements the simulations by validating the trajectory-tracking interfaces on physical drones. The planner can serve as a basis for further evaluation and controller development.
