Multi-agent systems, game-theoretic control, model predictive control, generalized Nash equilibrium, aerial robotics, drones Introduction sec:intro Coordinating multiple drones requires planning trajectories that account for both vehicle dynamics and the motion of other drones. Cooperative inspection and environmental monitoring motivate such planning in shared airspace chung2018survey,du2025survey . In cooperative goal reaching, each drone seeks its assigned position while maintaining separation from the others nascimento2023safe . In adversarial pursuit--evasion, the drones have opposing objectives: pursuers seek to approach evaders, while evaders seek to avoid them hoogendoorn2026conflict . Model predictive control (MPC) provides a way to plan motion using a dynamics model and state and input constraints mayne2000constrained,nguyen2021mpcsurvey . It optimizes future control inputs over a finite horizon and repeats the optimization after executing the first part of the plan. In this work, MPC serves as a trajectory-planning layer that supplies predicted positions and velocities to a tracking controller. Each drone's preferred motion depends on how the other drones move. This interaction can be modeled as a game in which each drone chooses a control sequence to minimize its own cost fridovichkeil2020ilqgames . In game-theoretic MPC, this game is solved over the prediction horizon at each planning update liu2024stability . A Nash equilibrium (NE) is a set of plans in which each drone's plan is optimal given the plans of the others rosen1965existence . If minimum separation is enforced through shared constraints, each drone's feasible plans also depend on the other drones' trajectories. This leads to a generalized Nash equilibrium (GNE) problem facchinei2007generalized . Implementing this game-theoretic MPC planner requires assessing both the computed plans and the time needed to obtain them. The interaction costs and separation constraints can make the game nonconvex. A numerical solver may then return a candidate that satisfies necessary optimality conditions without being an equilibrium bemporad2025nashopt . We also assess whether the computed plans resolve conflicts. Computational cost depends on the number of drones, prediction horizon and control parameterization. We therefore investigate how to implement the planner, how to evaluate its solutions and whether their computation fits the available planning period. We address these questions by implementing and evaluating a game-theoretic MPC planner for cooperative and adversarial drone coordination. Our contributions are: A reusable game-theoretic MPC planner for 3D drone coordination, accompanied by executable cooperative and adversarial scenarios. A numerical comparison of joint equilibrium searches and exact-potential minimization, assessing numerical acceptance, unilateral improvements and conflict resolution. Flight simulations evaluate closed-loop behavior. A computational study quantifying how number of drones, prediction horizon and move blocking affect computation time, constraint satisfaction and numerical acceptance. A five-drone laboratory flight additionally tests the tracking interfaces. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related reviews game-theoretic drone planning and numerical game solvers. Section~ sec:problem presents the drone models and game formulation. Section~ sec:mpc describes objective function design, numerical game solution and receding-horizon implementation. Section~ sec:experiments evaluates numerical solution reliability and computation. Section~ sec:flight presents flight simulations and laboratory tracking integration. Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper and outlines future work. Related Work sec:related Game-theoretic drone planning already covers both cooperation and conflict. In competitive drone racing, Wang et al. wang2020seibr use shared collision constraints and sensitivity-enhanced iterative best response, including flight experiments. For cooperative coordination, Shi et al. shi2022potential use generalized potential games and sequential drone responses, while do Nascimento et al. nascimento2023safe combine GNE-MPC with control barrier functions for distributed drone control. Hoogendoorn et al. hoogendoorn2026conflict describe 3D conflict resolution and pursuit--evasion within a receding-horizon Nash framework using soft proximity penalties. These studies establish the planning approach. They also motivate distinguishing hard shared constraints from interactions represented only in the costs. Numerical methods address different parts of this planning problem. iLQGames fridovichkeil2020ilqgames uses iterative linear-quadratic approximations for nonlinear multiplayer games. ALGAMES lecleach2022algames handles constrained dynamic games through an augmented-Lagrangian method and a common shared-constraint multiplier formulation. NashOpt bemporad2025nashopt provides joint optimality-condition solvers for standard and variational GNE formulations. Hall and Bemporad hall2025multiparametric derive explicit equilibrium maps for quadratic games with linear constraints, while Liu and Kolmanovsky liu2024stability study Newton methods for computing and tracking equilibria in MPC. We complement the cooperative coordination studies of Shi et al. and do Nascimento et al.~ shi2022potential,nascimento2023safe by comparing standard and variational GNE candidates with exact-potential minimization under matched cooperative costs. We relate numerical acceptance and feasible unilateral cost improvements to conflict resolution, following the response checks recommended for NashOpt~ bemporad2025nashopt . Our cooperative game includes hard shared separation constraints, whereas Hoogendoorn et al.~ hoogendoorn2026conflict represent proximity through soft costs. Flight simulations and matched computational measurements assess task completion and computation time. title: VLA-MOPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Task VLA Policy Consolidation
summary: Physical intelligence requires embodied agents to ground language in observations and execute actions while retaining useful skills. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies offer a shared interface, but task-specific post-training often produces separate specialists. Consolidation is difficult: mixed-task reinforcement learning provides sparse trajectory-level credit, while offline distillation may miss student-visited observations and endpoint distillation does not supervise intermediate action-generation states. We introduce VLA Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (VLA-MOPD), a protocol for consolidating flow-matching VLA specialists. After acquiring task or suite experts, a shared student collects robot rollouts and queries the instruction-routed frozen teacher at each visited observation and intermediate ordinary differential equation (ODE) state. Detached per-flow-step transition targets supervise valid action chunks through a masked local matching loss; an optional reference-policy term supports retention on other tasks. Starting from one trajectory per LIBERO task, VLA-MOPD raises mean success-once from 75.4% to 98.9%, compared with 98.15% for endpoint action distillation. It improves mean RoboTwin 2.0 success from 73.0% to 89.3%; on a Piper robot, two consolidation rounds improve average success from 70.0% to 90.0%. In a near-matched Spatial-adaptation study, reference matching limits the Object suite decrease to 3.0 points, versus 13.2 without the reference term.
full_text: Code and model links: 0.9 Introduction sec:intro Physical intelligence requires agents to connect language and perception to actions whose consequences change future observations. Embodied agents must therefore ground instructions in the current physical state and execute actions with feedback. PaLM-E incorporates visual and robot-state inputs into a language model for embodied reasoning, while SayCan grounds high-level plans in the feasibility of pretrained robot skills~ palme,saycan . VLA models provide a direct interface from observations and instructions to robot actions. RT-1 and RT-2 established large-scale language-conditioned control, while Open X-Embodiment broadened the available training data across institutions and embodiments rt1,rt2,openx . Octo and OpenVLA provide reusable generalist initializations~ octo,openvla . Diffusion- and flow-based policies generate continuous action chunks through an iterative trajectory diffusionpolicy,pi0,pi05 . Yet task-specific post-training often leaves improvements distributed across separate specialist checkpoints. We study how to consolidate these specialists into one flow-matching VLA. A flow-matching VLA encounters two coupled trajectories: the outer robot trajectory, whose states are observations reached after executing action chunks, and the inner flow trajectory, whose ODE states transform noise into each action chunk. Fixed specialist demonstrations may miss observations reached by the changing student. Because closed-loop errors alter future states, the relevant training distribution is the student's own occupancy. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) naturally visits this distribution, but the multi-task Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) baseline, which we refer to as MixRL~ simplevla,pirl , assigns one binary success value to an entire rollout. This gives limited credit information for individual action chunks, especially before successful rollouts become common, and shared updates can encounter cross-task gradient interference~ pcgrad . Distillation provides direct teacher targets on student states. Classical interactive imitation learning such as Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) queries an expert for an action at each learner-induced observation~ dagger . In our setting, matching the teacher's final action at these observations gives the endpoint action distillation baseline. We instead draw on DiffusionOPD and Flow-OPD, which study local transition or vector-field matching in continuous generative models~ diffusionopd,flowopd , to provide denser supervision: the routed teacher supplies a detached per-flow-step transition target at every inner flow state. VLA-MOPD first acquires and freezes task or suite specialists, then lets a student collect robot rollouts and routes each instruction to its teacher. The student matches these targets across valid action chunks, including failed rollouts, while an optional reference term applies the same rule to a frozen copy of the initial policy on retained tasks. We evaluate VLA-MOPD on four LIBERO suites and three RoboTwin 2.0 tasks libero,robotwin2 , as well as three tasks on a Piper robot. Starting from one demonstration per LIBERO task, mean success-once rises from to , compared with for endpoint action distillation. The RoboTwin mean rises from to ; on the Piper robot, two consolidation rounds raise average success from to . In a near-matched Spatial-adaptation comparison, reference matching limits the Object suite decrease to points, versus without the reference term. Our contributions are (i) a two-stage recipe that decouples specialist acquisition from multi-task VLA consolidation; (ii) a local ODE transition matching objective evaluated at student-induced outer observations and inner flow states; and (iii) evidence of capability consolidation across simulated benchmarks and real-robot tasks, together with an analysis of retention. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models Scaling robot data and model capacity has produced policies that transfer across tasks, embodiments, and language instructions. RT-1 and RT-2 study large-scale real-robot and vision--language policy training, while Open X-Embodiment standardizes multi-institution robot data for cross-embodiment learning rt1,rt2,openx . Octo and OpenVLA provide open generalist initializations; OpenVLA-OFT shows that action representation, chunking, and decoding choices affect downstream adaptation octo,openvla,openvla_oft . Diffusion Policy and the family instead generate continuous action sequences through diffusion or flow matching diffusionpolicy,pi0,pi05 . Recent VLA designs explore partial reasoning--action decoupling, instruction tuning, hybrid diffusion--autoregressive generation, fast--slow control, latent spatio-temporal reasoning, multi-frame modeling, execution-status monitoring, adaptive test-time compute, and motion-aware planning fang2025dualvla,instructvla,chen2025fast,liu2025hybridvla,liu2026last,li2025cronusvla,sentinelvla,vlaattc,dsdynvla . These works provide the policy and adaptation substrate for our study. Interactive and Reinforcement Learning for VLA Post-Training Interactive imitation learning addresses distribution shift by querying an expert on learner-induced observations. DAgger is the canonical example dagger ; our setting retains this outer on-policy idea and adds targets at intermediate states of a continuous action generator. Recent embodied learning methods use environment interaction as additional supervision, including agentic reward verification for broader rollout exploration rewardasagent ; in VLA post-training, SimpleVLA-RL applies GRPO to an autoregressive action-token VLA, while introduces Flow-Noise and Flow-SDE variants for Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) or GRPO on flow-based and policies simplevla,pirl . VLA-OPD queries a frozen teacher for action-token distributions on student-visited states and optimizes a reverse Kullback--Leibler (KL) objective vlaopd . Residual controllers and lightweight actor--critic heads offer other adaptation routes residual_policy,residual_rl,rltoken,pld . Most of these methods emphasize task-specific adaptation or direct improvement from interaction. Our setting first acquires task- or suite-level specialists and then integrates them into one shared student, emphasizing consolidation across complementary capabilities. On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Teacher Consolidation Building on multi-teacher knowledge distillation you2017multiple , on-policy distillation (OPD) separates specialist acquisition from integration by training domain specialists and distilling them into one student on the student's own rollouts. Language-model work uses dense token-level supervision for OPD opd,mopd,mimo_report,deepseekv4 , while process-reward policy optimization provides intermediate reasoning-level credit for multi-step reasoning prpo . VLA-OPD applies this idea to an autoregressive action-token policy and matches token distributions at visited observations. Our student instead matches continuous flow-action transitions: the flow-matching action expert exposes intermediate ODE states and step means that provide the local targets used for consolidation. MergeVLA instead preserves task-specific components through sparse task masks and composable action experts, whereas our focus is teacher-guided on-policy consolidation of a shared flow-matching policy mergevla . For continuous generative models, DiffusionOPD derives a closed-form per-step KL objective for diffusion transitions. Flow-OPD adapts the same idea to flow matching: it routes student samples to the relevant specialist and uses vector-field discrepancies as dense feedback for policy-gradient updates diffusionopd,flowopd . We transfer this transition-matching recipe to flow-matching VLA action experts: the outer robot rollout supplies visited observations, the inner flow trajectory supplies intermediate states, and the task-routed teacher supplies a target at each state. title: Be My Eye: Learning to See Beyond a Robot's Own Perspective
summary: Robots operating in the real world are inherently subject to partial observability, particularly in multi-robot collaboration, where individual observations may be insufficient for effective task execution. A key challenge is leveraging complementary observations from partner robots to support collaborative decision-making. We argue that information sharing should go beyond passively transmitting raw observations or generic visual features. Instead, robots should selectively encode task-relevant information according to task objectives and execution progress. To this end, we propose a task-oriented active context sharing framework that transforms robot observations into compact representations, preserving critical information under constrained communication budgets. The framework adopts a two-stage training paradigm. In the first stage, onboard observations and task instructions are jointly encoded into compact context representations. Task-oriented future prediction and soft task-progress correspondence learning guide this collaboration-agnostic compression, preserving information about task objectives and execution progress. In the second stage, the learned representations are integrated into a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy, enabling bidirectional context exchange. Each robot combines complementary partner information with local observations to guide action generation. Action supervision jointly refines the context representations and policy, aligning information sharing with collaborative decision-making. Controlled experiments demonstrate substantial performance gains under constrained communication budgets, while three real-world experiments validate the framework in complex dual-robot tasks. These results highlight a shift from passive visual transmission toward active, task-oriented context sharing that directly supports collaborative decision-making.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro --- , Shared Intentionality Partial observability is a fundamental constraint on perception in the physical world. For robots, limited fields of view, sensor placement, spatial constraints, and environmental occlusions restrict access to the information needed to execute complex tasks. In multi-robot settings, this limitation also creates an opportunity: robots can exploit complementary observations of their shared environment. Consider two robots collaboratively transporting a large cabinet through a narrow passage. The cabinet may obscure critical regions, leaving obstacles or clearance visible to one robot but hidden from the other. These observations can directly affect whether its partner should slow down, adjust its posture, or change direction. Similar dependencies arise in warehousing, assembly, and everyday collaborative manipulation, where information distributed across robots jointly informs task execution. We argue that the potential of multi-robot systems lies not only in their collective physical capabilities but also in the complementary perspectives afforded by distributed sensing. Translating this perceptual complementarity into coordinated action requires each robot to integrate the observations of its partners into its own decision-making, a fundamental challenge and opportunity in tightly coupled multi-robot collaboration. A common approach to multi-robot coordination relies on centralized planning, in which a high-level planner decomposes global objectives into subtasks or commands that individual robots execute using local observations. Although effective for task allocation and high-level coordination, systems that communicate primarily through task descriptions or discrete instructions provide limited support for sharing fine-grained perceptual information. Object states, spatial relationships, and execution progress observed by one robot may therefore remain unavailable to another robot's action policy. This limitation is particularly pronounced in dynamic, partially observable environments, where effective collaboration requires continuous adaptation to environmental changes and partners' actions. Without access to complementary perceptual information, coordination is often restricted to parallel task execution or sequential handoffs, rather than tightly coupled behaviors grounded in shared situational awareness. Conditioning a robot's policy on its partners' visual observations provides a natural mechanism for coupling perception and action across robots. However, transmitting raw images or generic dense visual features incurs substantial communication and computational costs and introduces redundant or task-irrelevant information. Moreover, the value of an observation depends on task objectives, robot roles, and execution progress: visual details essential to one decision may be irrelevant to another. Generic visual compression may preserve appearance or semantic content without retaining the information most useful for collaborative action. The central challenge is therefore to selectively encode local observations into compact representations that preserve their relevance to collaborative decision-making. We refer to this process as active context sharing. Here, active denotes task-conditioned information compression, rather than selection of communication timing or recipients; these decisions may still be managed by a centralized planner. Active context sharing aims to preserve task-relevant perceptual content together with relationships among task objectives, observed states, and execution progress, providing partners with informative context under a limited representation budget. In this work, we propose a two-stage active context sharing framework for multi-robot collaboration. In Stage~1, we introduce a task-oriented context compression module that uses learnable queries to aggregate frozen multi-camera visual features into compact latent tokens conditioned on task instructions. We train this module with two complementary objectives to preserve task-relevant visual information and capture the structure of task execution: (i) task-oriented future prediction encourages the latent tokens to encode information predictive of future visual states, emphasizing task-relevant regions and state transitions; and (ii) soft task-progress correspondence learning structures the latent space according to task identity and execution progress, promoting inter-task discriminability and intra-task temporal continuity. In Stage~2, we perform joint context optimization and collaborative policy learning. Context tokens produced by the Stage~1 encoder are projected into the hidden space of a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy and integrated into its multi-modal prefix, conditioning action generation alongside local visual observations, task instructions, and proprioceptive states. This interface supports variable numbers of shared tokens without modifying the action-generation architecture. Joint optimization of the context encoder and collaborative policy allows the receiving robot's action supervision to refine the sending robot's representations for collaborative decision-making. Symmetric encoding and policy interfaces enable bidirectional sharing, allowing each robot to incorporate complementary context from its partners. We systematically evaluate our framework across diverse real-world dual-robot manipulation tasks involving visual occlusion, spatial separation, state-dependent interactions, and role coordination, all of which require robots to leverage complementary observations for successful execution. We compare our approach against communication-free policies and alternative information-sharing strategies under varying communication budgets, while conducting ablation studies to assess the contribution of key design choices. Our main contributions are as follows: Active context sharing framework for multi-robot collaboration. We propose a two-stage training framework that encodes each robot's local observations into compact, task-conditioned latent representations, which are integrated into partner robots' action policies and jointly optimized through downstream action supervision. This approach complements high-level coordination with shared perceptual context, enabling information from complementary observations to directly inform collaborative action generation. Progress-aware, task-conditioned observation compression. We introduce a query-based compression module supporting joint and per-camera visual encoding. Task-oriented future prediction and soft task-progress correspondence learning jointly encourage the retention of predictive visual information, inter-task discriminability, and intra-task temporal continuity under a fixed representation budget. Joint context optimization for collaborative policy learning. We integrate compressed context into pretrained VLA policies through a flexible conditioning interface supporting variable token budgets and bidirectional context sharing. Action supervision from the receiving robot jointly optimizes the context encoder and policy, aligning shared representations with the requirements of collaborative decision-making. Real-world evaluation and representation analysis. We systematically evaluate our framework on dual-robot manipulation tasks through comparisons against no-sharing and alternative information-sharing baselines, communication-budgets, and component-wise ablation studies. title: AutoVLA-D: Learn a Trajectory-Geometric Condition from Reasoning for Autonomous Driving VLA
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026
summary: Autoregressive VLA planning usually predicts continuous trajectories as the final output, but driving instructions often describe actions rather than ego states, which weakens direct conditioning on the final continuous trajectory. We address this gap with TrajCond, which introduces a discrete trajectory-geometric condition for VLA planning. Specifically, we represent TrajCond as a 1D-Brohan differential action trajectory and learn it with a two-stage training framework before final continuous trajectory prediction. With the simultaneous autoregressive generation of discrete and numeric trajectories, we name our method AutoVLA-D (Double). Experiments on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP show that discrete trajectories are weaker as direct outputs but more effective as TrajCond, consistently improving final continuous trajectory prediction across closed-loop and open-loop driving benchmarks. Code is available at https://github.com/ShivaTeam/AutoVLA-D.

Introduction sec:introduction Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action (VLA) planning has become a practical Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM)-native paradigm for autonomous driving. Given camera observations and driving instructions, a VLA planner follows the next-token interface of modern MLLMs: it conditions on visual-language inputs, produces intermediate driving reasoning, and then decodes the future ego trajectory~ rowe2025poutine . Recent methods have demonstrated strong closed-loop planning capability with this input--reasoning--trajectory generation process~ zhou2025autovla,chen2026devil,luo2025adathinkdrive,luo2026elfvla,li2025drivevlaw0 . Despite this progress, existing VLA planners can also be distinguished by the trajectory form used for the final ego plan. One line of work models the future ego states, including the relative -axis position, -axis position, and heading in the current ego frame, over the next few seconds as numeric text waypoint tokens~ luo2025adathinkdrive,luo2026elfvla,chen2026devil , which we call continuous trajectory in this paper; while another line, i.e., discrete trajectory, represents the step-wise ego motion, or state transition, as discrete action tokens~ wu2024smart,li2025drivevlaw0,zhou2025autovla . These two trajectory forms have complementary strengths and limitations. Action tokens introduce reconstruction error when discretizing continuous trajectories, and our experiments over multiple discretization strategies, e.g., K-Means, K-Disks~ zhou2025autovla,wu2024smart,philiontrajeglish , and Brohan-style discretization~ zitkovich2023rt , show that directly regressing discrete trajectories is consistently weaker than directly regressing continuous trajectories. However, driving instructions often describe actions such as yielding, keeping, or turning, and such local motion changes are naturally aligned with discrete trajectory tokens because each action token describes a local state transition. This creates a formulation gap when instructions are mapped directly to the final continuous trajectory. To address this, we propose AutoVLA-D (Double), a two-stage VLA planner that uses a discrete trajectory as a Trajectory-geometric Condition (TrajCond) before regressing the final continuous trajectory. This approach features three core innovations: Discrete trajectory as trajectory-geometric condition. TrajCond first predicts a discrete trajectory and then uses its geometric-semantic as a condition for final continuous prediction. This keeps the final output in the stronger continuous space while using the discrete condition to transmit action-oriented information. Action tokens with 1D-Brohan discretization. We construct TrajCond from differential ego motions and discretize the , , and yaw differentials with separate Brohan-style codebooks. Compared with shared-codebook clustering tokenizers, such as K-Means and K-Disks~ zhou2025autovla,wu2024smart,philiontrajeglish , this design gives the strongest tested TrajCond result and the lowest tested reconstruction error. Two-stage alignment training. After constructing Brohan TrajCond by discretizing the ground-truth trajectory, the newly constructed action vocabulary has no VLA-task-related initialization. Stage 1 therefore warms up TrajCond's semantics by aligning observations and instructions with the action-token sequence that encodes TrajCond. Stage 2 uses the decoded TrajCond and the available reasoning context to regress the final continuous trajectory. This separates condition learning from final trajectory prediction. We evaluate AutoVLA-D on NAVSIM navtest, nuScenes, and NeuroNCAP. AutoVLA-D achieves state-of-the-art results across these settings, including 92.0 PDMS and 86.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM navtest. Beyond benchmark comparisons, our experiments are organized to verify how and why trajectory forms matter for driving VLAs. In TrajCond Ablation and Progressive Analysis, we examine the staged performance gains of AutoVLA-D and validate the contribution of its training and reasoning components. In TrajCond Form Analysis, we compare continuous trajectories with different action-token forms, showing that discrete trajectories are weaker as final autoregressive outputs but become more effective when used as TrajCond for final continuous prediction. In TrajCond Semantic Analysis, we qualitatively and quantitatively verify whether TrajCond absorbs action-oriented planning semantics in addition to providing geometric guidance. Together, these experiments suggest that in autoregressive VLAs, discrete trajectories used as TrajCond can encode instruction semantics while preserving trajectory geometry, thereby reducing the formulation gap between instructions and continuous trajectories and improving VLA planning performance. Related Work sec:related Driving VLA. Autonomous driving planning first developed through end-to-end systems that map sensor observations to future trajectories, including ST-P3~ hu2022st , VAD~ jiang2023vad , UniAD~ hu2023planning , DiffusionDrive~ liao2025diffusiondrive , SparseDrive~ sun2025sparsedrive , and BridgeAD~ zhang2025bridging . With the emergence of vision-language models (VLMs), recent VLA methods exploit visual-semantic knowledge for driving understanding, reasoning, and planning. They follow two patterns: planner-style methods, including ReCogDrive~ li2025recogdrive , ImagiDrive-S~ li2025imagidrive , DriveVLA-W0~ li2025drivevlaw0 , and FLARE~ xie2026flare , use the VLM as a feature extractor or semantic reasoner with an external planner or action head; autoregressive methods, including EMMA~ hwang2024emma , OpenEMMA~ xing2025openemma , OpenDriveVLA~ zhou2025opendrivevla , Impromptu VLA~ chi2025impromptu , AutoVLA~ zhou2025autovla , AdaThinkDrive~ luo2025adathinkdrive , Curious-VLA~ chen2026devil , and ELF-VLA~ luo2026elfvla , predict waypoint or action-token sequences through the next-token interface. Unlike autoregressive VLAs that directly decode the final trajectory after reasoning, AutoVLA-D inserts a learned trajectory-geometric condition before final continuous trajectory generation. Form in Autoregressive VLA. Autoregressive VLA planners represent the future ego trajectory over three degrees of freedom: -axis position, -axis position, and heading. Existing trajectory forms can be grouped into two types. Continuous-trajectory methods, including Impromptu VLA~ chi2025impromptu , AdaThinkDrive~ luo2025adathinkdrive , Curious-VLA~ chen2026devil , and ELF-VLA~ luo2026elfvla , serialize each future ego state as numeric text waypoint tokens; among them, Curious-VLA~ chen2026devil further improves performance with step-wise trajectory normalization. Discrete-trajectory methods instead serialize each local ego-state transition as an action token and recover the future trajectory by temporal integration. AutoVLA-D differs by using discrete trajectories as trajectory-geometric conditions rather than final outputs, and adopts a 1D-Brohan form where each action token represents a 1-DoF local motion. title: PCTac: Mechanochromic Photonic-Crystal Tactile Sensor for Dexterous Manipulation
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures
summary: Modern visuotactile sensors primarily sense contact by imaging the deformation of a compliant interface. Using techniques such as photometric stereo, they can recover detailed contact geometry, often represented as surface normals or depth. However, force-related information typically still needs to be inferred indirectly through calibration, geometric reconstruction, or learned mappings. Mechanochromic photonic-crystal (PC) materials offer an alternative physical encoding mechanism: contact loading changes their periodic microstructure and spectral response, directly transforming local stress into a spatially resolved structural-color field. Despite this potential, PC materials have rarely been explored as visuotactile sensors for closed-loop robot learning. We present PCTac, an open-source mechanochromic PC fingertip that uses a dense hue field as its tactile observation. Loading characterization demonstrates a repeatable relationship between the applied normal load and the observed hue response. We further integrate this representation directly into a Diffusion Policy and evaluate it on three real-robot manipulation tasks. Across 90 physical rollouts, PCTac Hue achieves 68 successes (75.6\%), compared with 60 (66.7\%) for PCTac RGB, 57 (63.3\%) for Wedge RGB, and 29 (32.2\%) for vision-only. PCTac Hue also achieves the highest observed success rate on each evaluated task, including Perturbed Test-Tube Insertion, where it achieves 16/30 successes versus 13/30 for tactile RGB baselines and 1/30 for vision-only. These results demonstrate the potential of mechanochromic structural color as a compact, load-sensitive tactile representation for robot learning and closed-loop manipulation. Project page: https://bey0ndt1me.github.io/PCTac-page/.

Using techniques such as photometric stereo, they can recover detailed contact geometry, often represented as surface normals or depth. However, force-related information typically still needs to be inferred indirectly through calibration, geometric reconstruction, or learned mappings. Despite this potential, PC materials have rarely been explored as visuotactile sensors for closed-loop robot learning. We present PCTac, an open-source mechanochromic PC fingertip that uses a dense hue field as its tactile observation. Loading characterization demonstrates a repeatable relationship between the applied normal load and the observed hue response. We further integrate this representation directly into a Diffusion Policy and evaluate it on three real-robot manipulation tasks. Across 90 physical rollouts, PCTac Hue achieves 68 successes (75.6 ), compared with 60 (66.7 ) for PCTac RGB, 57 (63.3 ) for Wedge RGB, and 29 (32.2 ) for vision-only. PCTac Hue also achieves the highest observed success rate on each evaluated task, including Perturbed Test-Tube Insertion, where it achieves 16/30 successes versus 13/30 for tactile RGB baselines and 1/30 for vision-only. These results demonstrate the potential of mechanochromic structural color as a compact, load-sensitive tactile representation for robot learning and closed-loop manipulation. Project page: https://bey0ndt1me.github.io/PCTac-page/. Introduction Visuotactile sensors have emerged as a powerful sensing modality for dexterous manipulation, offering exceptionally high spatial resolution and rich multimodal contact information~ Yuan2017GelSight, Wang2021Wedge, Taylor2022GelSlim, Lambeta2020DIGIT, Padmanabha2020OmniTact, Gomes2020GelTip, li2024minitac . By imaging deformation over a compliant interface, they provide dense observations of contact geometry, local motion, and material interaction, enabling applications such as grasping, slip detection, and dexterous manipulation~ Wang2021Wedge,Yuan2015Slip,Dong2019IncipientSlip,James2021Stabilization . Their ability to capture spatially resolved contact patterns makes them particularly attractive for learning-based robot control, where tactile observations can complement vision when contact geometry and interaction dynamics are difficult to observe externally~ Calandra2018Feeling,Lee2019VisionTouch . However, visuotactile images primarily capture local surface deformation, and extracting force-related information often requires additional calibration, geometric reconstruction, or learned mappings~ Yuan2017GelSight,Taylor2022GelSlim,Sferrazza2019Optical,Ma2019DenseForce . Moreover, their reliance on illumination and imaging optics imposes packaging constraints, making it challenging to reduce fingertip size without compromising sensing performance~ Wang2021Wedge,Taylor2022GelSlim,Donlon2018GelSlim . To bridge the gap, mechanochromic PCs offer a novel means of encoding such contact information: changes in their periodic microstructure produce corresponding changes in reflected structural color~ Gao2025Instant,Sasso2026Mechanochromic . Such material-level responses could simplify the optical system by reducing the need for engineered illumination to visualize contact-induced deformation. Although mechanochromic materials have been investigated for deformation and force sensing~ Sasso2026Mechanochromic,Chen2026CLCE , their use as tactile sensors for robotic manipulation and robot learning remains largely unexplored. In particular, whether mechanochromic structural-color changes can provide sufficiently informative and robust observations for closed-loop robotic manipulation remains an open question. Our key insight is to treat the structural color of a mechanochromic interface as a direct robot observation rather than as an intermediate representation for reconstructing contact mechanics. Based on this idea, we develop PCTac, a mechanochromic visuotactile fingertip equipped with an embedded OV5647 camera and paired with a reference-relative hue representation. We first characterize the repeatability of its color--force response under controlled optical conditions. We then evaluate its utility in real-world tasks with Diffusion Policies~ Chi2023DiffusionPolicy , comparing task performance across visual and tactile representations. Our experiments show that PCTac provides a repeatable relationship between recorded normal load and hue response. It can be incorporated directly into real-robot policies without explicit geometric or force reconstruction. Across three contact-rich tasks and 90 physical rollouts, PCTac Hue achieves 68/90 successes (75.6 ), compared with 60/90 (66.7 ) for PCTac RGB, 57/90 (63.3 ) for Wedge RGB, and 29/90 (32.2 ) for vision-only. This corresponds to observed gains of 8.9, 12.2, and 43.3 percentage points over these respective baselines. Task-wise, PCTac Hue achieves 24/30 successes in Whiteboard Wiping, 28/30 in Test-Tube Insertion, and 16/30 in Perturbed Test-Tube Insertion, giving the highest observed success rate among the evaluated configurations in all three tasks. Together, these results support the feasibility of using mechanochromic structural color as a direct tactile observation for closed-loop robot manipulation under the evaluated conditions. The paper makes three main contributions. PCTac fingertip. We introduce PCTac, an open-source mechanochromic visuotactile fingertip that produces stress-related color signals under contact, without requiring geometric reconstruction. Signal processing and learning integration. We develop a signal-processing pipeline for extracting observations from PCTac's color response and integrating them into robot learning systems. Validation in contact-rich manipulation. We evaluate PCTac in contact-rich robotic tasks and examine the utility and limitations of mechanochromic observations for learning-based manipulation. Related Work Visuotactile Sensors Visuotactile sensors estimate contact information by imaging the deformation of a compliant interface~ Johnson2009Retrographic . GelSight-style systems recover dense contact geometry from surface appearance, enabling high-resolution measurements of contact shape and deformation~ Yuan2017GelSight,Wang2021Wedge,Taylor2022GelSlim , whereas marker-based designs track surface displacement induced by deformation~ WardCherrier2018TacTip and have been widely used for slip detection and contact-state estimation~ Yuan2015Slip,Dong2019IncipientSlip,James2018TacTipSlip,James2021Stabilization . These approaches therefore provide complementary trade-offs: image-based systems offer rich spatial observations but may require marker tracking, normal estimation, or depth reconstruction to extract task-relevant quantities, while marker-based systems provide more direct deformation measurements but with sparse spatial sampling. In particular, contact force is generally not directly observable from these visual representations and must be recovered through calibration~ Yuan2017GelSight,Taylor2022GelSlim . Recent robot-learning methods have demonstrated that tactile images or learned tactile representations can instead be directly incorporated into policies for contact-rich manipulation~ Chen2023VTT,Yu2025MimicTouch,Xue2025RDP , avoiding the need to explicitly expose such intermediate quantities to the policy. Nevertheless, the underlying observation remains primarily an image of surface appearance or deformation, leaving the downstream model to understand the physical contact state. This motivates exploring sensing representations that encode mechanical state more directly while retaining the spatial richness of image-based tactile sensing. Mechanochromic Structural Color Structural color is widespread in nature and arises from the interaction of light with periodic or nanoscale structures. For example, the iridescent colors of butterfly wings and beetle exoskeletons originate from hierarchical photonic architectures~ Kinoshita2002Morpho,Parker2003Weevil , while structural colors in bird feathers and other organisms can change with viewing or structural conditions~ Osorio2002Plumage,Prum1998Feather . Inspired by these natural photonic systems, artificial photonic structures have been developed whose optical appearance changes under mechanical deformation, enabling mechanical states to be encoded directly as visible color~ Fudouzi2006PhotonicRubber,Sandt2018Optomechanical,Gao2025Instant . Recent studies have further explored mechanochromic photonic structures for tactile sensing, demonstrating that contact-induced deformation can be directly encoded in spatially varying structural color~ Sasso2026Mechanochromic,Chen2026CLCE,miller2022scalable,li2024minitac . Table~ tab:sensor_mechanisms compares the key characteristics of mechanochromic structural-color tactile sensors with those of conventional tactile sensing approaches. Despite these advances, existing studies have primarily focused on material fabrication and optical characterization. A systematic evaluation of structural color as a tactile observation for manipulation remains lacking, particularly regarding its utility for robot learning and control. Moreover, existing studies have not established an open and reproducible evaluation framework that connects sensing, tactile representation, robot learning, and manipulation performance. PCTac addresses this gap by treating the mechanochromic color field as the primary tactile observation and systematically evaluating it across sensor characterization, robot-learning deployment, and closed-loop manipulation. Method This section describes the sensing principle of the PC interface (Sec.~ sec:pc_principle ), the mechanical and optical design of PCTac (Sec.~ sec:sensor_design ), the tactile representation (Sec.~ sec:tactile_processing ), and its integration into the robot-learning system (Sec.~ sec:robot_system ). The overall system pipeline is shown in Fig.~ fig:system_pipeline . Sensing Principle of the PC Interface sec:pc_principle A PC contains a periodic optical structure that selectively reflects part of the incident white light. The reflected wavelength depends on the spacing of this structure. For an idealized first-order reflection, the peak wavelength can be approximated by the Bragg--Snell relation Sasso2026Mechanochromic,Chen2026CLCE : where is the effective spacing between periodic lattice planes, is the effective refractive index, and is the incident angle in air. Under approximately normal incidence, this relation reduces to . When an object contacts PCTac, it locally deforms the PC film and the supporting elastomer. This deformation changes the periodic structure and therefore the reflected wavelength, producing a visible color change. Different contact locations and deformation states produce different spatial color patterns. The observed colors also depend on the material, illumination, and viewing geometry~ Gao2025Instant,Sasso2026Mechanochromic . PCTac records these color patterns with an RGB camera rather than measuring the reflection spectrum directly. We compare each tactile image with an unloaded reference image to emphasize contact-induced color changes in hue representation. The resulting color field is provided directly to the robot policy as a tactile observation. Thus, PCTac does not require explicit force estimation or surface-geometry reconstruction. title: VLA Adaptation with Real and Simulated Data: A Case Study on Robotic Chess
comment: CoRL 2026 Workshop "Pretrain to Adapt: What Makes a Pretrained Policy Adaptable?". 8 pages main text, 15 pages total, 15 figures, 4 tables
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are trained as general-purpose foundation models for robot learning, and require fine-tuning for each downstream task and robot. This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. In this task, an SO-101 arm moves a chess king between two squares that are given only by their names, such as e4 and a5. We fine-tune $π_{0.5}$ with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations.

This raises practical questions such as how much data and training updates are needed, how checkpoints should be selected, and whether simulation can be leveraged to alleviate the cost of real data collection. We study these questions on a task that requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. We fine-tune with various dataset sizes and update budgets, using teleoperated demonstrations as well as simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert that imitates the variability of human demonstrations. In simulation, the success rate scales with both data and updates. Importantly, we find that a short learning-rate cool-down adds up to 31 points and is necessary for comparing checkpoints, and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations and evaluate ten policies in 25 trials each. Partial results indicate that pretraining on the simulated demonstrations helps substantially, most clearly when real data is scarce. We also present a negative result, in which training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning, corrections from an automatic coach, or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over plain behavior cloning in our setting. We release the simulator, the expert and the real demonstrations. Introduction sec:intro A common way to teach a robot a new manipulation task is to fine-tune a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model~ pi0,pi05,smolvla on human-collected demonstrations of that task. This raises practical questions, such as how many demonstrations to collect, how long to train, which checkpoint to deploy, and whether pretraining in simulation is worthwhile. Each of these choices carries a substantial cost in data, compute or robot time. A central challenge is that closed-loop task success, the quantity of interest, is expensive to measure. On a real robot, each trial takes minutes and requires a person to reset the scene. It is therefore tempting to rely on offline proxies such as validation loss or action error, or on a few dozen trials per setting. Our study complements the fine-tuning experiments reported with the VLA models themselves~ pi0,pi05,smolvla and data-scaling studies of imitation learning~ lin2024datascaling with a detailed look at a single task, where a simulator lets us evaluate every model on many trials. In this paper, we study the task of moving a chess king on a board with a low-cost robot arm. Given an instruction such as ``Move the king from e4 to a5,'' the policy must locate the named squares on the board it sees and then grasp, carry and place the king (Fig.~ fig:stages ). The task therefore requires both precise manipulation and spatial understanding of the scene. We fine-tune ~ pi05 on teleoperated demonstrations and on simulated demonstrations from a randomized scripted expert. The simulator provides demonstrations in any quantity and lets us evaluate every model on the same 1,000 graded trials. On the real arm, we fine-tune on up to 256 teleoperated demonstrations, starting either from the base model or from a policy pretrained on the simulated demonstrations. We also test whether the policy improves when it is trained on its own rollouts. Beyond king moves, we also built a system on the same arm that plays full games with all pieces, but only as a demonstration, without evaluation or ablations. In summary, our contributions are: In a simulated version of the task, we present quantitative experiments indicating that the success rate scales with both data and updates, that checkpoints must be compared after a learning-rate cool-down or stochastic weight averaging (SWA)~ swa , and that validation loss and action error are unreliable for model selection (Section~ sec:bc ). On the real arm, partial results indicate that pretraining on simulated demonstrations helps when real data is scarce (Section~ sec:real ). As a negative result, training on the policy's own rollouts with filtered behavior cloning, RECAP-style advantage conditioning~ pistar06 , corrections from an automatic coach or residual reinforcement learning did not yield a measurable improvement over behavior cloning in our setting (Section~ sec:experience ). We release the simulator with its randomized scripted expert and the teleoperated demonstrations, and contribute the recordings of the real evaluation trials to the Oopsie Data collection of real-robot policy rollouts (Section~ sec:sim , Appendix~ app:data ). Setup sec:setup sec:task The task is to pick up the king from one square of an otherwise empty chess board, place it on another square and return to the ready pose (Fig.~ fig:stages ). The source and target squares are given only in the instruction. We study the task on a real robot arm and in its simulated counterpart. Real Arm sec:robot The real setup consists of a low-cost 3D-printed arm with five joints and a gripper, the SO-101~ so101,lerobot , a second arm of the same type as the leader for teleoperation, and two cameras (Appendix~ app:hardware ). One camera is mounted on the wrist and looks along the gripper. The other is fixed above the board on a 3D-printed overhead mount (Fig.~ fig:policy ). Both have wide-angle fisheye lenses, and the policy sees their images rectified to the simulator's pinhole model. The board is wooden with 31\,mm squares. The king is a wooden piece, 64\,mm tall on a 20\,mm base. The task is difficult for this arm for four reasons. First, the policy has to find each square from its name alone. Second, the arm's posture varies considerably across the board, from steeply folded near the base to almost fully extended at the far ranks. Third, the gripper has one fixed finger and one moving jaw, and a grasp that is a few millimeters off the king's axis topples the piece. Fourth, the printed links flex under load by up to 2\,cm, so the arm cannot be positioned precisely without visual feedback. Simulator and Scripted Expert sec:sim The simulator is a MuJoCo~ mujoco twin of the real setup. It reproduces the arm's kinematics and servo dynamics, the measured pose of the board, the scanned king, and the poses and fields of view of the two cameras. A motion planner would execute every move identically, which neither resembles teleoperation nor gives enough variation for imitation learning. Our scripted expert therefore imitates the variability of a human operator. It reaches for a target with a perception error, observes the remaining error after a latency and corrects, and repeats this until the error is below a tolerance. Each episode samples its own tempo, errors, tolerances and grasp parameters, so paths and speeds differ between episodes (Fig.~ fig:paths ). Grasp errors arise from the same mechanism, and the expert detects a missed grasp, reopens and retries. It succeeds in 93 of its episodes. The paths of the human operator on the real arm show a similar spread, although the operator's carries are straighter. The fine-tuned policies vary less than both the expert and the operator, in simulation and on the real arm. Policy sec:policy We start from the model, which combines a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert that attends to it. The model was not pretrained on the SO-101 arm. The policy receives the two camera views, the six joint positions, the instruction and the current stage. It outputs chunks of 50 joint targets at 15\,Hz and executes 10 of them before planning again (Fig.~ fig:policy ). We fine-tune the action expert and the language model, 2.7 of the model's 4.1 billion parameters, and keep the vision encoder frozen. The language model also learns to predict the current stage as one token (Fig.~ fig:stages ), and the action expert attends to that token (Appendix~ app:stage ). At test time the policy re-scores the current and the next stage once per action chunk and advances when the next one wins twice in a row. Experiments sec:experiments Our experiments address three questions, namely how behavior cloning scales with data and training (Section~ sec:bc ), whether the policy can improve from its own rollouts (Section~ sec:experience ), and how much simulation pretraining helps on the real arm (Section~ sec:real ). Appendix~ app:tables lists all simulation results. Behavior Cloning in Simulation sec:bc This section studies behavior cloning on the simulated demonstrations, where every model can be evaluated on many trials. Data. The simulated demonstration set holds about 11.4k expert episodes with the piece offset by up to 8\,mm inside its square, of which 93 are successes. Training sets are nested subsets of the successes with , 316, 1,000, 3.2k and 10k episodes, and 30 further successes are held out for validation. Training. Every run uses a constant learning rate of after 500 warm-up steps and a global batch of 32 frames. The update budgets form a geometric ladder of eight steps from 1,000 to 165k (one epoch of the largest set), extended to 237k for the two largest sets. For each dataset size, one constant-rate trunk keeps a checkpoint at 90 of every update budget, and a branch from each checkpoint cools the rate to zero over the remaining updates~ minicpm,hagele2024scaling . Each configuration is trained once. Evaluation. Each model runs 1,000 closed-loop trials on a fixed schedule of moves, with the piece offset by up to 8\,mm as in the data, and with real-time chunking~ rtc at deployment settings. A trial succeeds if the king ends standing with its center inside the target square and the arm is back at rest. Strict success also requires the king's whole base to be inside the square. We report success rates with Wilson 95 intervals, which are about points at 30--60 . Success increases with data and with updates. sec:scaling Below about 4k updates no model succeeds, independent of the dataset size (Fig.~ fig:scaling ). Above that, success increases along both axes. With 10k demonstrations it is still increasing at the largest budgets, from 60 at 165k updates to 64 at 237k. At small update budgets, additional data has little effect (10 and 11 with 1,000 and 10k demonstrations at 9k updates). In our grid, a smaller dataset performs as well as a larger one until its first epoch is complete, and performs worse afterwards. Training for many epochs still helps, and in no case does it lower success beyond the evaluation noise. title: Sliding into Balance: Benefits of a Sliding Payload for Load Distribution and Disturbance Rejection in Dual-UAV Transportation
comment: 6 pages, 6 figures
summary: This paper analyzes the cooperative transportation of a payload suspended from two drones in which, instead of being attached to two independent ropes, the payload is allowed to slide along a single rope connecting both UAVs. First, a planar nondimensional dynamical model of the sliding motion with viscous friction is presented. Then, considering stationary drones, this configuration is compared with a fixed payload with the same total rope length, both at equilibrium and under disturbances. The analytical results show that the sliding payload equalizes the tension in both rope segments for any relative position of the drones, so that no rope loses tension at equilibrium; it doubles the region reachable by the payload and, except for low friction combined with a large drone separation, it enlarges the set of admissible disturbances. Finally, a dynamic simulation also shows that under realistic gusty wind profiles, the average tension imbalance between the drones is reduced with respect to the fixed-payload solution.

First, a planar nondimensional dynamical model of the sliding motion with viscous friction is presented. Then, considering stationary drones, this configuration is compared with a fixed payload with the same total rope length, both at equilibrium and under disturbances. The analytical results show that the sliding payload equalizes the tension in both rope segments for any relative position of the drones, so that no rope loses tension at equilibrium; it doubles the region reachable by the payload and, except for low friction combined with a large drone separation, it enlarges the set of admissible disturbances. Finally, a dynamic simulation also shows that under realistic gusty wind profiles, the average tension imbalance between the drones is reduced with respect to the fixed-payload solution. Introduction In recent years, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have attracted growing interest for transporting payloads in logistics or emergency response, often to hard-to-reach locations~ Villa2019JIRS, Estevez2024Drones . Suspending the payload by cables is a mechanically simple and agile solution, although it poses significant planning and control challenges~ Li2023RAL . However, the capacity of a single vehicle is limited by its thrust, which has motivated the use of teams of drones that share the weight of the payload~ Fink2011IJRR . In this regard, the literature on cooperative transportation is extensive. Early contributions addressed the static equilibrium and the inverse kinematics of the system formed by the drones, the cables, and the payload~ Fink2011IJRR, Jiang2013TRO , while later works have developed dynamical models and geometric controllers~ Sreenath2013RSS, Lee2018TCST , studied the role of internal forces in the stability of the equilibrium~ Tognon2018RAL , or interpreted the whole system as a reconfigurable cable-driven parallel robot~ Masone2016IROS . Distributed model predictive control~ Wehbeh2020IROS , control barrier functions for obstacle avoidance~ Hegde2022LCSS , and agile maneuvers~ Sun2025SciRob have also been proposed. In all of them, the payload is attached to each vehicle at a fixed point, either by cables or by rigid links. Thus, the load sharing is determined by the formation geometry: one drone may bear most of the weight, or a cable may lose tension~ Jiang2013TRO, Tognon2018RAL . An alternative is not to attach the payload to the rope. Some works have exploited the interaction between cables held by drones and the object~ DAntonio2021RAL, DAntonio2026TRO : a cable suspended between two quadrotors can wrap around an object to manipulate it, or be interlaced with it to lift and transport it. However, they focus on grasping and maneuvering, and do not analyze how free sliding of the payload affects the load sharing and the response to disturbances, nor the role of friction at the contact. In this paper we analyze, as a proof of concept, the effects of letting the payload slide along a single rope connecting both drones versus attaching it to two ropes with the same total length (Fig.~ fig:render_drones ). A preprint published during the writing of this manuscript~ DAntonio2026ARXIV has already introduced this concept. However, our work explicitly considers friction and, additionally, presents results that clearly demonstrate the benefits of this solution. To isolate the analysis from the controller, the drones are considered fixed points and the study is restricted to a vertical plane. The main contributions~are: Model: a nondimensional Euler--Lagrange model of the sliding motion with viscous friction, whose conclusions are independent of the system scale. Static analysis: the sliding payload equalizes the tensions for any drone position, so that each bears half the weight and no rope loses tension. Hence, the formation can be chosen freely without overloading either drone. Besides, the region reachable by the payload is doubled. Disturbance analysis: the admissible disturbances are characterized, and friction is shown to set a trade-off between tension balance and payload displacement, which guides the design of the contact point. Overall, sliding provides a simple way, with no additional actuators, to decouple load sharing from formation geometry. title: Learning Heterogeneous Tactile Representation for General Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Tactile sensing is an indispensable modality for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, a capability that hints at the ultimate frontiers of embodied intelligence. However, commercially available tactile sensors are still at a relatively early stage of development, with each type of sensor offering irreplaceable strengths alongside its own drawbacks. A key challenge is thus to free tactile understanding from sensor-specific physics, so that embodied models can effectively leverage heterogeneous tactile data. To this end, we develop LingBot-Touch, a tactile foundation model characterized by the following properties. (i) Our model yields a unified representation across different tactile sensors (i.e., piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors), and is easily extensible to new sensor types. (ii) The resulting tactile tokens are plug-and-play: they can be seamlessly integrated into policy models across paradigms, from diffusion policy to vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ and LingBot-VLA, consistently enhancing manipulation dexterity. (iii) Extensive experiments, spanning simulation and real-robot deployments across multiple hardware platforms, demonstrate that our tactile representation substantially benefits complex manipulation tasks while maintaining strong computational efficiency. We believe the findings in this work demonstrate the potential of leveraging cross-sensor data to scale tactile learning, and offer encouraging insights for the design of future hardware and embodied models.

Introduction sec:intro Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is among the most remarkable abilities of humans, and giving robots the same ability is a central goal of physical intelligence. Much of that ability rests on touch: with fingertip sensation blocked, people struggle with tasks as simple as striking a match or buttoning a shirt, even with vision intact~ johansson2009coding . Robots, by contrast, still manipulate objects almost entirely by sight~ chi2023diffusionpolicy,pmlr-v305-black25a, wu2026foundation , and sight cannot tell them how hard they are pressing, whether a grasp is slipping, or what is happening under an occluding finger. Why not touch? Not for lack of sensors. Piezoresistive, magnetic, and visuotactile sensors are all commercially available (Fig.~ fig1 , top), but touch remains an early-stage modality that lacks the three ingredients that let vision and language scale. There is no common input format: each sensor type defines its own channels, layout, resolution, and sampling rate~ zhao2025t3,bi2026htt , so a reading from one sensor means nothing to a model trained on another. There is no large curated corpus, because data from one sensor cannot be pooled with data from the next and every hour requires a sensorized hand touching the world. And there is no established recipe: evidence that touch helps robot learning~ higuera2025sparsh,zhao2025t3 is scattered across sensor-specific studies and individual tasks, with no shared representation to compare them on. The three gaps share a root: tactile data are tied to the physics of the sensor that produced them. Contact itself is not. A fingertip pressing on an edge is the same event whether a magnetometer, a resistive grid, or a camera behind a gel records it, so a representation of contact can be shared once sensor-specific physics is removed from the input. In this paper, we present , a tactile foundation model that learns such a representation from the three dominant sensing principles, piezoresistive, magnetic, and optical, with one encoder, and extends to new sensors without retraining. Three design decisions make this possible. We map every sensor's taxels into a canonical fingertip space, so that a model sees positions on a finger rather than indices in a sensor-specific array (Sec.~ sec:method:tjepa ). We train with a joint-embedding predictive architecture~ assran2023ijepa,vjepa that predicts representations of masked taxels in latent space, which suits signals that are sparse and carry no labels (Sec.~ sec:method:tjepa ). And we assemble a 5 , 000-hour corpus from human tactile gloves and teleoperated robot hands, the first at a scale where representation learning for touch becomes possible (Sec.~ sec:method:corpus ). Trained once on this corpus, behaves the way a foundation model should (Fig.~ fig1 , bottom). Its frozen features recover contact force, location, extent, and short-term dynamics from fingertip signals and retrieve the matching video frame from touch alone, on an optical hand seen in pretraining and on a magnetic hand whose sensor model was not; on the latter it outperforms FTP-1~ ftp1 fitted with a sensor-specific adapter on all five probing tasks (Secs.~ sec:ContactPhysics , sec:exp:scalingtransfer ). Its tokens plug into existing policies without changing them: on 26 real-world dual-arm tasks, adding the frozen 5.46M-parameter encoder raises the success rate of Diffusion Policy~ chi2023diffusionpolicy , ~ pmlr-v305-black25a , ~ wu2026foundation , and T-Rex~ niu2026trextactilereactivedexterousmanipulation by 14 to 26 percentage points, while feeding the same policies raw tactile signals yields at most about half that gain~(Sec.~ sec:exp:robot ). In simulation, reinforcement learning on features succeeds on 69 of attempts across twelve dexterous tasks, against 46 with features from a task-specific CNN and 21 without touch, and with far lower variance across seeds (Sec.~ sec:exp:robot:sim ). The representation also scales: the Small model improves monotonically from 1K to 5K hours of pretraining on every probing task and both hands (Sec.~ sec:exp:scalingtransfer ), data from one sensor improves the representation of another (Sec.~ sec:Multi-Source ), and latent prediction outperforms signal reconstruction by a wide margin, with a VAE objective even degrading as data grow (Sec.~ sec:exp:vae ). Our contributions are as follows. [leftmargin=*] A tactile corpus at scale. 5 , 000 hours of recordings, 464K episodes, and 1.33 billion frames across piezoresistive, magnetic, and optical sensing, collected from human tactile gloves and teleoperated robot hands over 24 task categories. A tactile foundation model. combines a canonical fingertip space, modality-specific tokenizers, and a shared Haptic Transformer, trained with , a latent-prediction objective adapted to sparse, unlabeled tactile signals through a mask warm-up and layout augmentation. One encoder serves all three sensing principles and transfers to an unseen sensor model without retraining. Evidence across the stack. Frozen-encoder probing of contact physics on two hands, 26 real-world manipulation tasks with four policy families, and twelve reinforcement-learning tasks in simulation, together with scaling, multi-source, and objective analyses that explain where the gains come from. An open release. The inference code, a small set of sample tactile recordings, and checkpoints for the Tiny and Small variants pretrained on approximately 5 , 000 hours of tactile data will be released. These resources will help researchers integrate the tactile encoder into downstream robot learning systems. Related Work sec:related Tactile Sensing sec:related:sensing Tactile sensors capture contact geometry, forces, and interaction dynamics through diverse transduction mechanisms. Magnetic sensors, such as ReSkin~ bhirangi2022reskin and AnySkin~ bhirangi2025anyskin , sense contact through deformation-induced changes in magnetic fields; PaXini's commercial systems also employ Hall-effect sensing~ paxiniPXCapIII . Optical tactile sensors, including GelSight~ yuan2017gelsight , DIGIT~ lambeta2020digit , and the fingertip sensors integrated into Sharpa Wave~ sharpa2025wave , use internal imaging to capture contact-induced deformation. Resistive and capacitive sensors encode contact through changes in electrical resistance or capacitance, exemplified by the piezoresistive Scalable Tactile Glove (STAG)~ sundaram2019stag and the conformable capacitive electronic skin DexSkin~ wistreich2025dexskin . These technologies observe shared properties of physical contact through different measurement mechanisms, producing signals that vary in channel semantics, spatial resolution, sampling rate, and sensing layout. Similar interactions can therefore yield substantially different observations across sensors. addresses this heterogeneity through a common interface that accommodates diverse measurements while preserving contact geometry and temporal structure, enabling unified spatiotemporal contact representations across sensing modalities. Tactile Representation Learning Self-supervised representation learning has driven recent advances in large language and multimodal models, contributing to the emergence and development of world models, vision-language-action (VLA) models, and world-action models. Relevant approaches can be broadly grouped into joint-embedding architectures, such as DINO~ caron2021dino , CLIP~ radford2021clip , SigLIP~ zhai2023siglip , and VideoCLIP~ xu2021videoclip ; generative architectures, such as MAE~ he2022mae and VideoMAE~ tong2022videomae ; and joint-embedding predictive architectures, including I-JEPA~ assran2023ijepa , V-JEPA~ vjepa , V-JEPA 2~ vjepa2 , LeJEPA~ balestriero2025lejepa , and V-JEPA 2.1~ vjepa21 . Tactile representation learning adapts these approaches to tactile observations. Sparsh~ higuera2025sparsh investigates reconstruction, self-distillation, and joint-embedding prediction for optical tactile sensing. T3~ zhao2025t3 combines sensor-specific encoders with a shared Transformer backbone to enable transfer across optical tactile sensors and tasks. UniTouch~ yang2024unitouch connects tactile representations to pretrained multimodal embeddings, while AnyTouch~ feng2025anytouch combines masked modeling, multimodal alignment, and cross-sensor matching to learn static and dynamic tactile features. AnyTouch 2~ feng2026anytouch2 further emphasizes force perception and temporal dynamics across optical tactile sensors. Sparsh-skin~ sharma2025sparshskin learns contextual representations from magnetic tactile histories and sensor geometry, whereas Sparsh-X~ higuera2025sparshx integrates image, audio, motion, and pressure signals from Digit 360~ lambeta2024digit360 . HTT~ bi2026htt addresses heterogeneous optical and array-based sensors through modality-specific reconstruction and representation alignment between paired sensors. FTP-1~ ftp1 maps heterogeneous observations into morphology-aware tokens for foundation-policy pretraining and supports adaptation to new hardware through sensor-specific encoders. To address the high sparsity, low signal-to-noise ratios, and multi-source heterogeneity of tactile observations, we introduce , a tactile foundation model that combines a multi-branch tokenizer with a shared Haptic Transformer to learn unified, reusable representations of contact physics across sensors and heterogeneous layouts. sec:method learns actionable tactile representations for dexterous manipulation policies from data. Two challenges stand in the way. First, tactile data are scarce. Unlike vision and language, no tactile corpus exists today at the scale that representation learning requires. We address this directly by collecting 5 , 000 hours of tactile recordings ( ). Because this effort spans human tactile gloves and robot hands with different sensors, the resulting data are heterogeneous in transduction principle, taxel layout, resolution, and sampling rate, which we handle through a canonical geometric interface and modality-specific tokenizers that feed a shared Haptic Transformer ( ). Second, these recordings come with at most coarse task-level descriptions, and nothing that labels the contact physics inside a clip, such as the forces exerted, where and how widely contact occurs, or when it begins and ends. title: ForeAct: Geometry-Guided Action Learning from World Representations
summary: Robotic manipulation requires representations that capture both scene geometry and its evolution during interaction. Existing approaches have largely treated these two aspects separately. World action models capture such dynamics by coupling action prediction with future video generation, but their reliance on iterative diffusion or rectified-flow inference leads to high computational cost, while their representations lack explicit spatial structure. Explicitly modeling scene geometry typically requires auxiliary modules that increase both parameter count and computational cost. Conversely, geometry-centric policies primarily recover observed spatial structure and often lack explicit supervision for anticipating future geometric changes during interaction. To address these limitations, we introduce ForeAct, which repurposes a pretrained video world model as a single-pass representation backbone for low-latency control. ForeAct directly processes the clean latent of the current observation in one forward pass, eliminating future-frame synthesis and iterative denoising while retaining the backbone's pretrained spatiotemporal priors. Rather than introducing a separate geometry backbone, ForeAct uses learnable tokens supervised by next-frame relative depth to shape the shared video representation through bidirectional self-attention. This compact interface turns the spatial knowledge already encoded in the backbone into a future-aware representation for action generation, with little parameter overhead. The lightweight geometry readout is used only during training and removed at deployment, enabling low-latency, geometry-aware control without depth input or an external geometry backbone. Without additional large-scale pretraining, ForeAct achieves 96.6% average success on LIBERO, 63.5% on SimplerEnv-Bridge, and a 74.4% success rate across 90 real-world rollouts.

Latency is evaluated following the corresponding inference settings on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU with batch size 1, covering observation encoding through action-chunk generation. Inference Efficiency.
