It approaches the accuracy of larger world action models with fewer parameters and lower latency, while substantially outperforming the faster conventional VLA baseline. At a comparable success rate, its latency is roughly one-third that of Cosmos Policy, and it is also faster than Fast-WAM while using a considerably smaller model. This efficiency comes from extracting predictive representations and decoding actions with a single world-model backbone pass, without iterative future-frame denoising, making ForeAct suitable for closed-loop manipulation. Ablation Study We ablate ForeAct on LIBERO to evaluate single-pass world representations and token-mediated future-geometry supervision. Table~ tab:libero_ablation examines component contributions, while Fig.~ fig:ablation_sensitivity analyzes geometry-token capacity and supervision horizon. Components and Design. Table~ tab:libero_ablation shows that the clean action-only baseline outperforms Diffusion WAM ( vs.\ ), supporting a single video-backbone pass for action prediction without iterative video denoising. Adding geometry tokens without future-depth supervision yields a modest gain to , whereas incorporating future-depth supervision raises success to . This result indicates that the improvement extends beyond additional token capacity. The supervision pathway is also important. Directly imposing depth supervision on the visual features yields only , supporting a dedicated geometry-token interface. Restricting attention to one-way visual-to-geometry information flow reduces success to , supporting bidirectional interaction through which depth-supervised geometry tokens can shape the visual features before action decoding. Together, these results demonstrate the complementary benefits of clean world representations and token-mediated geometric supervision. Geometry Tokens and Supervision Horizon. Fig.~ fig:ablation_sensitivity (a) shows that increasing the geometry-token count from one to eight improves success from to , whereas expanding it to 32 and 64 lowers performance to and , respectively. This suggests that a compact token set provides sufficient capacity for effective geometric supervision, while additional tokens provide no further gain. Fig.~ fig:ablation_sensitivity (b) shows that next-frame depth supervision outperforms current-frame depth supervision ( vs.\ ), supporting the value of anticipating spatial changes beyond encoding observed geometry. Extending the supervision horizon to and reduces success to and , suggesting that immediate-future geometry provides a more effective learning signal under the single-observation formulation. These findings support the default choice of eight geometry tokens with next-frame depth supervision.

title: SurgTAP-3D: A Large-Scale Cross-Surgery Video Dataset with Contact-Aware 3D Motion Tracking
comment: Accepted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO)
summary: Understanding 3D scene dynamics in minimally invasive surgery (MIS) is a fundamental step toward physically intelligent and autonomous surgical systems. However, existing public datasets offer limited scalability and diversity in real-world clinical scenarios. Moreover, annotations typically focus on either tissue or instruments alone, overlooking tool-tissue interactions. This gap limits applications such as augmented reality guidance and autonomous surgery driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models or world models, which demand large-scale, high-quality 3D supervision. In this work, we construct SurgTAP-3D, a large-scale in-vivo pseudo-3D surgical motion tracking dataset and benchmark, comprising 520K frames, 4,549 action clips, and 1.4M 2D/3D point trajectories from diverse robotic and manual procedures under unified action categories. To make annotation scalable, we design a unified framework for surgical 3D point tracking that converts uncalibrated monocular surgical videos into structured 4D annotations through contact-region prompting, active-tool segmentation, dynamic bundle adjustment, and global 4D refinement. This pipeline adapts foundation priors to surgical videos and produces temporally consistent trajectories, pseudo-scale geometry, camera poses, and instrument masks. The dataset captures realistic challenges inherent to surgical environments, including occlusions, smoke, bleeding, and rapid instrument motion. We establish a comprehensive benchmark on SurgPose, SurgT, and STIR, covering both instrument and tissue tracking. We demonstrate instrument displacement estimation, deformable surface reconstruction, and foundation-model fine-tuning. Extensive experiments and analysis demonstrate the effectiveness of our dataset and annotation framework for 3D surgical point tracking, reconstruction, and surgical action understanding. full_text: SurgTAP-3D In this work, we aim to achieve 3D contact-aware motion tracking, to recover high-fidelity 4D trajectories and 3D geometry from uncalibrated monocular surgical videos. Building upon this, we construct a large-scale dataset of contact-aware surgical clips collected from diverse publicly available surgical videos. Each clip is automatically annotated with rich motion, geometric, and semantic information through our proposed pipeline. Formally, given a dataset containing video clips, each clip is associated with an action label , a manually annotated contact region , and an active-tool prompt used to initialize grid-sampled query points for tracking. For each clip consisting of frames, the goal of the annotation framework is to generate comprehensive geometric, motion, and semantic annotations, including the intrinsic camera matrix , camera poses , depth maps , active-tool segmentations , 2D point trajectories , corresponding 3D trajectories , and per-point visibility estimates . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig: pipeline , the pipeline for SurgTAP-3D is composed of three main stages: input data preprocessing, canonical labelling, and contact-aware automatic annotation. In Sec.~ sec: data_source , we describe the data sources used in SurgTAP-3D, which include diverse in-vivo surgical videos covering both manual and robotic procedures, organized under a unified set of action categories. Sec.~ sec: data_preprocess presents the data preprocessing process, including frame extraction, quality filtering, and sequence organization. Sec.~ sec: pipeline details the annotation pipeline, which generates spatial and temporal labels through 3D reconstruction, iterative motion refinement, and active instrument segmentation. Finally, we provide dataset statistics and analysis in Sec.~ sec: data_stat . Dataset Source sec: data_source In-vivo Diverse Surgery Types Manual and Robotic Surgeries The dynamics and operational paradigms of robotic and manual surgeries differ substantially. Robotic surgeries~ xu2025surgripe often exhibit smooth, stable, and kinematically constrained tool motions with a fixed camera view, while manual procedures feature freehand endoscope movement and more dynamic tool trajectories, introducing frequent camera motion, rapid zoom changes, and viewpoint shifts. These differences are crucial for downstream policy learning, scene reconstruction, and motion prediction tasks. Unlike prior datasets that isolate robotic or manual modalities, SurgTAP-3D explicitly distinguishes and includes both, enabling cross-domain learning and generalization analysis. Specifically, we categorize collected videos according to their surgical modality to facilitate modality-specific training and benchmark tasks. Unified Action Categories Previous datasets~ nwoye2025cholectrack20 are often restricted to a single type of surgery, resulting in inconsistent or incompatible action labels across various datasets. Following these design principles, as presented in Tab.~ tab: release_dataset , SurgTAP-3D aggregates multiple high-quality datasets under a unified framework: 1) Robotic surgery: GraSP~ ayobi2025pixel , SAR-RARP50~ psychogyios2023sar , 2) Manual Surgery: SLAM~ ye2025comprehensive , SurgicalActions160~ schoeffmann2018video , AutoLaparo~ wang2022autolaparo , the proctocolectomy and rectal-resection subsets of HeiCo~ maier2021heidelberg , CholecT50~ nwoye2022data , and MultiBypass140~ lavanchy2024challenges . In total, we collect 4549 clips, 519,642 frames, and 1,376,987 trajectories. Dataset Preprocessing sec: data_preprocess First, we extract frames from the videos at their original frame rates. Based on the unified action categories, we select sequences that contain visually clear and well-defined actions. Since our motion tracking begins from prompts given in the first frame of each clip, we ensure that this initial frame clearly exposes the active instrument under the camera. To guarantee the overall quality and reliability of the dataset, we apply a multi-stage filtering process prior to annotation. We use a luminance-based filtering method to detect and remove frames with excessive brightness variation or strong overexposure. Next, we perform motion blur detection using gradient-based sharpness metrics, such as the Laplacian variance, to identify and exclude frames where tool or camera motion causes significant blurring. Finally, after filtering out noisy frames, we retain clips ranging from 5–30 seconds in duration, corresponding to 20–300 frames. Contact-aware Data Annotation Pipeline sec: pipeline Contact-aware Labeling and Segmentation To efficiently annotate such regions, we design a simple yet effective one-frame labeling process. The annotator first draws a bounding box enclosing the contact region, including both the instrument tip and its immediate interaction area. Then, the annotator selects 3–5 positive points on the active instrument and 3–5 negative points on the background. These point prompts are provided to SAM2~ ravi2024sam to generate a precise segmentation mask of the active instrument for subsequent video tracking, generating active instrument masks for each frame as . 2D Tracking Given query points collected from the contact region, we utilize TAPNext~ zholus2025tapnext to obtain the 2D point tracking , visibility predictions , confidence score . TAPNext~ zholus2025tapnext offers an online tracker to perform point tracking via a masked decoding manner. Unlike previous methods, which focus on correspondence matching and introduce complex inductive biases like cost volumes and iterative inference, TAPNext uses TRecViT as the backbone, which consists of ViT layers and state-space model layers for spatial and temporal processing, respectively. Traditional methods like ORB-SLAM, COLMAP will fail in such a highly dynamic scene, resulting in inaccurate camera poses and incomplete 3D geometry. It is proposed as a feed-forward 3D foundation model, with an uncertainty-aware dual-memory mechanism to enable long-term dynamic 3D reconstruction. To adapt to diverse surgery scenes, Endo3R designs a self-supervised training scheme for training across datasets even without ground truth. As a feed-forward method, Endo3R may still accumulate temporal drift over long clips. To mitigate long-term drift, we additionally employ a dynamic bundle adjustment inspired by~ li2025megasam, teed2021droid . To improve the robustness of 3D point tracking on surgical instruments, we leverage the inherent consistency of the instrument and design a surface constraint loss to optimize the 3D instrument points lying directly to the 3D surface of the instrument. This constraint encourages the optimized 3D keypoints to lie directly on the instrument surface, correcting drift that commonly arises in 2D tracking due to occlusion, specular highlights, or motion blur. For each frame, we first reconstruct the instrument surface pointcloud by backprojecting depth within the segmentation mask . We then enforce geometric consistency by minimizing the Chamfer-style distance between the predicted 3D keypoints and the instrument surface. ARAP Loss. To regularize the 3D trajectories of the instrument keypoints and ensure physically plausible motion, we introduce an As-Rigid-As-Possible (ARAP) constraint. Unlike classical ARAP, which assumes global rigidity, surgical instruments contain rigid shaft and non-rigid articulating joints (e.g., wrist, grasper). title: From Game Generation to Game Playing: Fully Automated Ability Training for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, Script2Play, by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that Script2Play follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision.
full_text: Training vision-language-action (VLA) models to follow gameplay instructions across diverse games is limited by the cost of collecting demonstrations. We introduce a framework that automatically generates game environments and expert demonstrations. An LLM-powered agent uses game-building tools to construct executable environments and tasks targeting specified skills. Programmatic experts then use privileged simulator state to generate aligned instructions, rendered observations, and keyboard and mouse actions. We train our game policy, , by post-training a 4B vision-language model with behavior cloning on 150.3 hours of synthetic Minecraft and Roblox gameplay, without human gameplay demonstrations or reinforcement learning. Evaluation on multiple public game benchmarks demonstrates that follows gameplay instructions effectively and generalizes across game engines, highlighting the effectiveness of targeted synthetic supervision. Introduction sec:intro Developing generalist agents that ground free-form language instructions in visual observations and execute low-level actions in interactive environments is a central step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence~ sima2024scaling,simateam2025sima2,wang2025gametars,tan2025lumine . Video games offer a rich testbed for studying these capabilities: a single agent must map an instruction and rendered frames into human-compatible actions, such as key presses and mouse movements, across worlds with varying visuals, physics, and interaction logic~ sima2024scaling,guo2026gamewam,zhang2026scaling . However, training vision-language-action (VLA) models that generalize across games faces a persistent supervision bottleneck. Existing approaches largely rely on human gameplay demonstrations~ baker2022vpt,sima2024scaling,li2025jarvisvla,wang2025gametars,yue2025pixels2play,yue2026openp2p or online reinforcement learning (RL)~ kempka2016vizdoom,ouyang2026player1 . Collecting human demonstrations with aligned instructions and actions is costly across diverse tasks and titles. Public gameplay recordings and internet video corpora~ guss2019minerl,baker2022vpt,fan2022minedojo,yue2025pixels2play,choi2026d2e,magne2026nitrogen,yue2026openp2p,markov2026gaming500 may lack explicit task boundaries and verifiable completion signals, or require retrospective captioning. RL requires interactive access, reward shaping, and extensive rollouts for each game. Hand-built training suites~ cobbe2020procgen,ouyang2026player1 also require substantial engineering effort whenever a new gameplay skill or mechanic is introduced. Our core insight is that both skill-targeted game creation and expert demonstration generation can be framed as coding-agent tasks~ aggarwal2026gymanythingrobotics,aggarwal2026gymanythingrt . Because game engines represent scenes, mechanics, and task logic as code, an LLM-powered agent can invoke game-building tools from a natural-language skill specification (such as navigation, dynamic obstacle avoidance, moving-target aiming, combat, or object interaction) to construct playable environments paired with programmatic task verifiers. Crucially, unlike commercial games that expose only rendered pixels, a generated environment exposes its full privileged ground-truth state, including character poses, target locations, enemy trajectories, and collision geometry. The coding agent can therefore also write programmatic expert controllers (using pathfinding, analytic target tracking, or finite-state machines) that read this privileged state to solve each task while issuing actions strictly through standard keyboard and mouse inputs. Automated playability and verification checks retain only successful rollouts, turning privileged simulator state into a purely synthetic, data-efficient stream of aligned instructions, frames, and actions. Every trajectory targets a specified skill, with exact instruction boundaries and verified completion, avoiding the idle traversal and label noise of raw human gameplay. We obtain by post-training Qwen3.5-4B on 150.3 hours of synthetic gameplay: 26.9 hours from Minecraft and 123.4 hours from Roblox, with zero human gameplay demonstrations. The same unified checkpoint is evaluated on all three benchmarks~ wang2025openha,lin2026omnigamearena,kempka2016vizdoom . outperforms policies trained on thousands of hours of human play on OpenHA and OmniGameArena~ wang2025gametars,magne2026nitrogen,yue2026openp2p,zhang2026scaling . A separate comparison holds the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone fixed and uses only our Minecraft subset to compare programmatic supervision with human-play and RL-based training pipelines. These results show that our framework can train game agents with strong instruction-following abilities and cross-engine generalization using a modest amount of scripted demonstration data. Our contributions are three-fold: We design an automated, skill-conditioned game generation framework in which a tool-using coding agent constructs executable game environments, diverse instruction-following tasks, and state-based verifiers directly from natural-language specifications. We introduce a purely synthetic, data-efficient programmatic expert supervision pipeline that leverages privileged simulator state to synthesize verified, human-compatible keyboard-and-mouse demonstrations for post-training pixel-to-action VLA models without human gameplay data. Using only 150.3\,h of scripted teacher data, outperforms policies trained on thousands of hours of human gameplay on public game benchmarks. Related Work sec:related Visual Game-Playing Agents Visual game agents learn low-level control directly from rendered frames and human-native input interfaces. In Minecraft, early policies learn behavioral priors from video~ baker2022vpt,lifshitz2023steve1,cai2025rocket1 , while recent approaches post-train VLMs for keyboard-and-mouse actions~ wang2024omnijarvis,li2025jarvisvla or combine high-level planners with frame-level controllers~ wang2025openha,tang2026histeve,wang2026taskframe . Across broader virtual worlds, generalist agents scale screen-to-action learning through unified keyboard, mouse, or gamepad interfaces~ sima2024scaling,simateam2025sima2,tan2024cradle,qin2025uitars,wang2025gametars,tan2025lumine , large-scale behavior cloning~ yue2025pixels2play,magne2026nitrogen,yue2026openp2p , joint world-action modeling~ guo2026gamewam , and multi-world continued pretraining~ zhang2026scaling . Our work differs in the source of post-training supervision: we use programmatic experts in automatically generated game environments rather than newly collected human gameplay or target-game RL. RL in Generated Environments Procedural generation~ cobbe2020procgen,chevalier2019babyai and generative world models~ bruce2024genie diversify training experience, whereas LLM-driven pipelines can further synthesize executable tasks and environments in code for embodied agents~ zala2024envgen,wang2024gensim,wang2024robogen , tool use~ wang2026awm , and game engines~ chi2026gamedevbench,luo2026gamecraft,zhou2026unitybench . Gym-Anything-RT~ aggarwal2026gymanythingrt uses coding agents to construct real-time minigames for evaluation, while Gym-Anything for Robotics~ aggarwal2026gymanythingrobotics builds audited robotics simulations and uses privileged code policies to train VLAs. Our pipeline targets transferable game-playing skills: it generates games from skill specifications, audits them to reject trivial and instruction-agnostic tasks, and records scripted teachers acting in real time at the student's control rate. These demonstrations train visual policies by behavior cloning without VLM annotation. Game Datasets and Benchmarks Large-scale datasets for training game and computer-use agents include Minecraft recordings and knowledge corpora~ guss2019minerl,baker2022vpt,fan2022minedojo , multi-game and desktop action trajectories such as Pixels2Play (Open-P2P)~ yue2025pixels2play,yue2026openp2p , D2E~ choi2026d2e , Gaming-500-Hours~ markov2026gaming500 , and NitroGen~ magne2026nitrogen , as well as synthetic capture platforms such as Isekai3D SDG~ karp2026isekai3d . For evaluation, public benchmarks span first-person combat in ViZDoom~ kempka2016vizdoom , open-world Minecraft tasks in MineStudio~ cai2024minestudio , MCU~ zheng2025mcu , and OpenHA~ wang2025openha , classic console and DOS titles in VideoGameBench~ zhang2025videogamebench , verifiable browser games in GameWorld~ ouyang2026gameworld , and real-time UE5 games in OmniGameArena~ lin2026omnigamearena . Rather than relying on human recordings or retrospective video labeling, our pipeline synthesizes aligned instruction, frame, and action trajectories with programmatic verifiers, and evaluates transfer across these public benchmarks. Method sec:method gives an overview. A coding agent turns a natural-language specification of a gameplay skill into a playable game. For each episode, the game samples a scene---its layout, assets, and dynamics---and assigns an instruction with a task verifier. A scripted teacher attempts the task, and successful episodes become training demonstrations. We first define the student, teacher, and behavior-cloning objective ( ), then describe game generation and verification ( ). Instruction-Following Training sec:method:problem sec:method:training Student and teacher. Let index control decisions, spaced 200\,ms apart; is the engine state, the rendered observation, the instruction, and a keyboard-and-mouse action chunk. The student policy, , is denoted by and observes : the instruction, current frame, and previous frame--action pairs. It never observes engine state. All reported benchmark policies use , so each decision depends on the instruction and current frame alone. The teacher is a program written by the coding agent for each game. It reads character poses and velocities, target coordinates, enemy and projectile states, and collision geometry. Depending on the task, it uses pathfinding, motion prediction for aiming, finite-state control, or timing rules to select actions. The teacher executes these actions through the same keyboard-and-mouse interface and at the same control rate as the student. It never teleports objects or bypasses game physics. Teacher rollouts. A task consists of an initial scene , an instruction , and a verifier . The verifier uses engine state to check task completion within a time budget and to detect prohibited events, such as reaching the wrong target or falling. A teacher rollout with control decisions is and the training corpus retains only successful rollouts: . Videos are recorded at 20\,fps and aligned with 200\,ms action windows. Instructions come from the task specification, action labels from the teacher, and success labels from the verifier; no human gameplay demonstration or retrospective VLM annotation is needed. Behavior cloning. Starting from a pretrained open-weight VLM, we train on the teacher's action labels. The unweighted gameplay loss is where indexes a retained rollout and a control decision within it. For , training uses the teacher's action history; this history is empty in the reported setting. All of our benchmark policies in use behavior cloning on synthetic gameplay. To emphasize changes in control, we increase the token-loss weight for action windows whose held-key set differs from the preceding window: by a factor of 5 for Roblox and 3 for Minecraft. We also include generic visual question answering, optical character recognition, and text examples in 15 of each batch to help retain general capabilities. These auxiliary examples contain no gameplay. At inference, the model runs in closed loop on each benchmark's native engine, mapping frames and instructions directly to keyboard and mouse actions. Following Lumine~ tan2025lumine , the model generates each action chunk autoregressively as plain text: . title: Compass 1: Towards Open-World and Persistent Embodied Navigation from Monocular RGB Videos
comment: Technical Report. Project Page: https://www.archon.tech/research/compass1
summary: Embodied navigation requires agents to achieve persistent spatial awareness and long-horizon execution stability in open-world environments. However, existing navigation architectures struggle to sustain both capabilities, remaining effective only over a handful of recent frames. We present Compass 1, the first embodied navigation foundation model to unify language understanding and video generation while enabling memory backtracking through nearly 2mins of visual history. Without altering the underlying architecture, we introduce History Representation, which integrates sparse visual keyframes with an explicit History Representation Map to preserve long-term spatiotemporal context. To effectively leverage this history, we further introduce History Utilization, a structured VQA supervision protocol comprising three categories: task-stage grounding, exploration consistency, and spatiotemporal target retrieval, enabling map-grounded reasoning and stable persistent long-horizon navigation. To fuel this system, we establish a complete annotation pipeline for monocular RGB videos and open-source a massive dataset featuring over 500 hours of high-quality real-world interactions and over 2,000 hours of annotated web videos. Trained mainly on the distribution of 1m height camera, Compass 1 generalizes seamlessly across diverse embodiments and scenarios, ranging from indoor environments to pedestrian-dense streets, spanning wheeled robot at 0.35m, quadruped dog at 0.5m, humanoid at 0.85m, and aerial drone at 1.5m. Compass 1achieves a dominant overall success rate of 79.4% across open-world evaluations, compared to 17.8% for the strongest baseline. It demonstrates exceptional zero-shot execution exceeding 90% on foundational tasks, a 250% boost in exploration, and an unparalleled leap from 0% to 58% in challenging persistent history backtracking.
full_text: Introduction Embodied navigation in unstructured, open-world environments requires physical agents to dynamically perceive visual signals, reason over high-level task instructions, and generate precise motor controls. Historically, the field has been dominated by the traditional training-free paradigm~ wu2024voronav, rgpt2024, instructnav2025 . These systems rely heavily on specialized hardware, such as LiDAR sensors~ sayplan2023, l3mvn2023 for dense point-cloud acquisition and depth cameras~ vlfm2024, gu2024conceptgraphs for spatial geometry, to reconstruct explicit topological maps onto which off-the-shelf Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are plugged in for decision-making. Despite their modularity, these systems suffer from severe error accumulation and spatial degradation when confronting complex dynamic scenes, exposing a fragile generalization ceiling. More recently, emerging agentic navigation paradigms have attempted to execute decision-making via harness~ zhang2026qwen or pre-defined skill primitives~ zhang2026supernav . Yet, their practical deployment remains significantly bottlenecked by high inference latency, leaving them at a preliminary stage for physical deployment. In stark contrast, large-scale training-based navigation paradigm~ zhang2024uni, zhang2026sparse offers a far more effective alternative -- by unifying perception, reasoning, and execution within a monolithic and streamlined learning formulation. Notwithstanding the impressive metrics achieved by recent large-scale training-based navigation approaches~ awarevln2026, navida2026, wang2026lightnav, huang2026wnm on simulated benchmarks~ vlnce2020 , a pronounced disconnect emerges in physical deployment: prior arts overfit to simulation excessively and fail to generalize to real-world environments. For instruction-following navigation tasks (IFN)~ vlnce2020 , these methods frequently exhibit erratic behaviors, such as premature stopping, reversed turning, drifting off the intended direction specified by language instructions, and failing to stop accurately even when the target is directly in sight. For beyond-the-view navigation tasks (BVN)~ zhang2026sparse , these models are prone to left-right turning deadlocks driven by intention inconsistency between consecutive inference steps. Worse still, existing long-horizon formulations typically either naively feed the entire uncompressed visual history into the backbone~ huang2026wnm or apply heuristic, non-uniform compression~ wang2026lightnav . We observe that both strategies yield merely spurious context usage, failing to preserve granular spatiotemporal topology and rendering true history backtracking navigation (HBN) completely unachievable. These pervasive failure modes underscore the fundamental challenges in building a truly persistent, robust embodied navigation system in the real-world. To resolve these deficiencies, we introduce , a navigation foundation model that addresses open-world and persistent embodied navigation without architectural modifications. For long-horizon history representation, we replace full visual streams with sparsely sampled visual keyframes as input and render their associated actions into a History Representation Map (HRM), which is processed natively by the backbone as an image input. We further design three visual-question-answering (VQA) categories encompassing task-stage grounding, exploration consistency, and spatiotemporal target retrieval, thereby fully unleashing the history utilization capabilities. To better incorporate spatial information and alleviate the short-horizon supervision problem inherent to language backbones~ zhang2026sparse , we naturally house these mechanisms within a unified understanding and generation backbone. Beyond algorithmic innovations, a primary bottleneck to achieving robust open-world navigation stems from the scarcity of high-quality training data. While scaling monocular RGB videos offers a promising avenue to bridge this gap~ zhang2026sparse , raw video clips inherently lack metric action trajectories, language instructions, and the specialized VQA annotations, making the whole labeling process prohibitively expensive. To overcome this bottleneck, we establish a semi-automated annotation pipeline designed for minimal human overhead. Human annotators are tasked solely with verifying language accuracy at stage boundaries and inspecting visualized action trajectories to filter out severe noise, significantly reducing human labor and annotation cost. Leveraging this pipeline, we curate a massive navigation corpus comprising over 500 hours of high-quality real-world data and 2,000 hours of annotated web-scale video data, providing an unprecedented multi-modal foundation to fuel open-world embodied navigation. We structure our real-world evaluation benchmark around essential navigation capabilities across highly diverse physical scenarios. Across these evaluations, achieves exceptional zero-shot execution exceeding on foundational tasks, including initial-sight target navigation, basic two-stage navigation, and basic history backtracking. In exploration tasks covering target-driven navigation and demand-driven navigation, achieves an average success rate of , delivering a performance improvement over the strongest baseline. Most notably, across challenging long straight-line navigation, multi-stage navigation, and persistent history backtracking, demonstrates an unparalleled performance leap, boosting the average success rate from to . Crucially, despite being trained primarily on a single camera height distribution at 1.0 meter (1m), exhibits exceptional zero-shot transferability across varied embodiments, smoothly adapting to distinct camera heights, ranging from wheeled robots at 0.35m and quadrupeds at 0.5m to humanoids at 0.85m and aerial drones at 1.5m. Research Questions The pivotal gist in this work boils down to -- How could a model excel at executing open-world and persistent navigation while generalizing across diverse scenarios and embodiments? This breaks into three concrete questions: How can we efficiently represent navigation history such that the policy can pinpoint previously observed targets, track current task stages, and discern how to navigate back over long horizons? How can we utilize this history representation to support diverse navigation tasks and learn a generalizable policy from limited high-quality data? How can we establish an effective annotation pipeline for raw video corpora to significantly reduce human labor and resource overhead? Contributions The main contributions are: Keyframe-Level Unified Backbone History Representation Map: To our knowledge, we present the first keyframe-level foundation model built on a unified backbone for embodied navigation. By condensing keyframes and actions into a compact HRM, our method grants the agent persistent spatiotemporal reasoning and nearly two-minute memory backtracking capabilities with zero architectural modification. Structured VQA Supervision Protocol: We design three structured VQA categories to fully utilize the history reasoning capability and effectively resolve physical execution failure modes including premature stopping, reversed turning, direction drifting, left-right turning deadlocks, and spurious history utilization. Cost-Effective Data Annotation Pipeline: We establish a semi-automated annotation pipeline requiring human oversight solely at stage boundaries and trajectory noise filtering, enabling the release of a massive navigation corpus featuring over 500 hours of real-world interactions and over 2,000 hours of annotated web videos. Thorough Physical Evaluation Zero-Shot Cross-Embodiment Generalization: Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that drastically outperforms strong baselines across all physical navigation tasks. Remarkably, despite being trained mainly on a fixed camera height distribution, it generalizes zero-shot across diverse embodiments, and substantial camera height variations. Methodology The design of is guided by two fundamental pillars: history representation and history utilization ( ), alongside the synergistic orchestration of multimodal understanding and generation ( ). The whole architecture and HRM are shown in~ . History Representation sec:history_repr Given the intrinsic scarcity of high-quality, real-world navigation data, a primary design philosophy of is to preserve the pre-trained foundation backbone without introducing any architectural modifications. To achieve this, our history representation is built upon two core aspects: keyframe-level sparsification and history representation map construction. Keyframe-Level Sparsification: Existing methods face inherent trade-offs in long-horizon history modeling. Naively appending all visual inputs severely degrades attention quality with heavy computational overhead~ zhang2024navid . Uniformly sampling visual frames at a fixed frequency to fit a limited context window leads to severe information loss~ cheng2025navila , whereas employing specialized pooling mechanisms inevitably introduces extra network modules~ zhang2024uni, wang2026lightnav . To circumvent these limitations, we summarize visual context through action-guided keyframe selection. This strategy effectively isolates critical spatial observations without adding structural overhead. Details of keyframe selection are deferred to . Crucially, deploying a policy trained on keyframe sequences proves essential during inference for mitigating the impact of control uncertainty across diverse embodiments. Particularly for embodiment like humanoids, micro-actions often fail to overcome physical execution limits to produce actual physical movement, rendering continuous visual inputs non-uniform and inducing severe out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts relative to continuous training video frames, which inevitably degrades policy performance. We find that simply triggering keyframe selection at inference time based on fixed distance and angle thresholds effectively addresses this issue and yields impressive navigation performance. History Representation Map Construction: For tasks requiring true history utilization, such as HBN, the policy must not only pinpoint previously observed targets but also discern how to physically navigate back to them. Over such extended horizons, language-based summaries fail to adequately capture subtle scene information and historical action trajectories~ torne2026memmultiscaleembodiedmemory . Inspired by explicit map construction in training-free paradigms~ wu2024voronav, instructnav2025 and trajectory visualization during data annotation, we format past action trajectories into a 2D visual canvas, termed the History Representation Map (HRM). Specifically, keyframes are projected onto the HRM canvas and labeled with their corresponding frame indices. To resolve spatial clutter in densely visited regions, spatially proximal keyframe indices are dynamically aggregated (e.g., denoted as ``2--5'' to indicate multiple keyframes within the localized neighborhood). Furthermore, since video streams possess an intrinsic temporal directionality, directional arrows are rendered along the trajectory to encode past headings. The current step is explicitly highlighted with a red letter C accompanied by a red arrow specifying its heading. By directly feeding the generated HRM alongside keyframes into the backbone as native image inputs, achieves long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning with zero architectural modification. Under this design, while the visual sequence fed into the backbone remains compact and keyframe-sparse, the HRM provides dense, explicit topological grounding over the entire navigation trajectory. History Utilization sec:history_util To maximize the efficacy of historical contexts without architectural modifications, the optimal strategy is to intrinsically embed spatiotemporal reasoning capabilities into the foundation backbon

title: Map2SLAM: From Streaming Map Prediction to Real-Time SLAM
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures. Project page: https://robbyant-research.github.io/Map2SLAM/
summary: Streaming 3D foundation models (3DFMs) estimate camera poses and dense geometry online, but they fall short of SLAM: their predictions are fixed once emitted, so loop closures cannot correct accumulated drift. With such models already providing strong geometric capability, a central question for SLAM becomes how to schedule their inference and how to keep its results as revisable state. We present Map2SLAM, which keeps LingBot-Map frozen, trains only a lightweight retrieval head, and builds SLAM on the model's inference interface, turning its predictions into observations of an external persistent SLAM state. The front-end tracks every incoming frame with the model's causal streaming inference and decides which frames are written to the persistent state as keyframes. The back-end asynchronously decides when and which past frames to re-observe, re-running the model's joint inference over them with fresh context; verified loop observations correct the trajectory online, and segment observations refine dense geometry after the sequence. All invocations share a single frame encoder pass per image, whose cached features also drive loop retrieval, so frequent re-invocation incurs no additional encoding cost. Map2SLAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by over 40% compared with the best uncalibrated baselines, while maintaining real-time tracking at over 28 FPS at a resolution of $518\times154$ on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Please visit our project page at https://robbyant-research.github.io/Map2SLAM/.
full_text: 1 fig:teaser Streaming 3D foundation models (3DFMs) estimate camera poses and dense geometry online, but they fall short of SLAM: their predictions are fixed once emitted, so loop closures cannot correct accumulated drift. With such models already providing strong geometric capability, a central question for SLAM becomes how to schedule their inference and how to keep its results as revisable state. We present Map2SLAM, which keeps LingBot-Map frozen, trains only a lightweight retrieval head, and builds SLAM on the model's inference interface, turning its predictions into observations of an external persistent SLAM state. The front-end tracks every incoming frame with the model's causal streaming inference and decides which frames are written to the persistent state as keyframes. The back-end asynchronously decides when and which past frames to re-observe, re-running the model's joint inference over them with fresh context; verified loop observations correct the trajectory online, and segment observations refine dense geometry after the sequence. All invocations share a single frame encoder pass per image, whose cached features also drive loop retrieval, so frequent re-invocation incurs no additional encoding cost. Map2SLAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by over 40 compared with the best uncalibrated baselines, while maintaining real-time tracking at over 28 FPS at a resolution of \(518 154\) on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Please visit our project page at https://robbyant-research.github.io/Map2SLAM/ . Introduction sec:introduction Feed-forward 3D foundation models (3DFMs) infer camera poses and dense scene geometry directly from unposed images~ wang2024dust3r,wang2025vggt . Streaming 3DFMs extend this capability to online video, producing a geometric prediction for each incoming frame~ zhuo2026streaming,chen2026geometric . However, these predictions are fixed once emitted: drift accumulates over long sequences, and even when the camera revisits a known place, earlier estimates cannot be corrected (Figure~ fig:teaser , left). Current streaming 3DFMs therefore cannot yet replace SLAM. Prior work has combined 3DFMs with SLAM in several ways: aligning chunk-wise predictions~ deng2026vggt-long,lee2026swiftvggt , using a 3DFM as the front-end of a classical SLAM pipeline~ murai2025mast3r, maggio2025vggt-slam,maggio2026vggt-slam2 , or attaching loop closure to a streaming model~ cheng2026horizonstream,han2026revisiting . These methods invoke the model in a fixed pattern, over predefined chunks, frame pairs, or a single causal pass, rather than scheduling its inference. Given the strong geometric capability of current models, we argue that the key to building SLAM lies in how to schedule model inference and how to keep its results as revisable state. Just as LLM agents rely on a harness to schedule a fixed model, a 3DFM needs a similar mechanism to decide which frames enter its context, when to re-observe history, and which state each prediction updates. Following this principle, we build Map2SLAM upon LingBot-Map~ chen2026geometric with a framework that schedules its inference and turns its predictions into persistent SLAM state, yielding accurate real-time SLAM. The prefix-causal structure of LingBot-Map supports two inference modes: Bidirectional Prefix jointly reasons over multiple frames, and Causal Continuation infers frame by frame autoregressively over long videos. Map2SLAM assigns the two modes to the two ends of the system: the front-end processes the live stream with Causal Continuation, and the back-end re-observes history with Bidirectional Prefix. The front-end decides which frames enter the context and are written to the state. To avoid the trajectory jitter caused by an ever-growing context, it tracks within bounded windows and treats each Causal Continuation step as a Keyframe Probe: based on the projective motion induced by the predicted geometry, an accepted frame is committed as a keyframe without repeated inference, and a rejected frame has its KV update rolled back. Windowed tracking still accumulates drift over long sequences. The back-end revises the state asynchronously, deciding when and which past frames to re-observe. Whereas LingBot-Map uses Bidirectional Prefix only for initialization, the back-end re-invokes it with fresh context. Loop Retrieval proposes revisit candidates from cached features. Because appearance matches do not guarantee geometric consistency, Pairwise Geometry verifies each candidate with a two-view prefix, and verified constraints enter Incremental Pose Graph Optimization (iPGO), which corrects the trajectory online. The back-end also re-observes sequential and loop segments with multi-view prefixes, whose results feed Dense Geometric Refinement after the sequence ends. All invocations share a single Frame Encoder pass per image: both the downstream Geometry Reasoner and the retrieval head reuse its cached features, so frequent re-invocation incurs no additional encoding cost. We evaluate Map2SLAM on KITTI~ geiger2012we , VBR~ brizi2024vbr , and Oxford Spires~ tao2026oxford . Map2SLAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, reducing mean ATE by more than 40 relative to the best-performing uncalibrated baselines, while running in real time at over 28 FPS with an input resolution of \(518 154\) on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Our contributions are threefold: We propose a design principle for building SLAM on streaming 3DFMs: given their strong geometric capability, the key lies in scheduling model inference and managing the state formed by its results. We present Map2SLAM, which realizes this principle on a frozen LingBot-Map: a causal front-end writes the state through commit-or-rollback Keyframe Probes, and an asynchronous back-end revises it by re-invoking Bidirectional Prefix with fresh context, with all invocations sharing one Frame Encoder pass per image. Map2SLAM achieves the lowest mean ATE among uncalibrated methods on KITTI, VBR, and Oxford Spires, 42.7--48.3 below the second-best results, while tracking at over 28 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 5090D GPU. Related Work sec:related Long-Sequence Visual SLAM Visual SLAM has evolved from feature-based systems~ klein2007parallel,mur2015orb , through direct methods~ engel2014lsd,engel2018direct , to learned geometric frontends~ teed2021droid,teed2023deep . Long-sequence SLAM, however, requires more than estimating motion as frames arrive. It must retain past estimates in its state so that a loop can introduce long-range constraints and revise the trajectory~ mur2015orb,campos2021orb,engel2014lsd,gao2018ldso,lipson2024deep . 3D Foundation Models Recent 3D foundation models (3DFMs) infer camera and scene geometry in a feed-forward pass over image collections~ wang2024dust3r,zhang2025flare,wang2025vggt,wang2026vggt,fang2026dens3r,gao2026more . Streaming 3DFMs extend this inference to video frames as they arrive~ zhuo2026streaming,chen2026geometric,cheng2026horizonstream,han2026revisiting , enabling geometric prediction over increasingly long sequences. In particular, first processes an initial set of frames jointly to establish scene context, and then incrementally incorporates subsequent frames in an autoregressive manner. Long-Sequence 3D Reconstruction Recent work extends 3DFMs to long sequences by composing local predictions into globally consistent reconstructions~ deng2026vggt-long,lee2026swiftvggt,zhang2026vggtalign,ding2026laser,zhang2026talo,xiong2026vggt . Related efforts increasingly integrate 3DFM predictions with incremental estimation, loop closure, and global optimization~ murai2025mast3r,maggio2025vggt-slam,maggio2026vggt-slam2,mandal2026vggt,jeon2026aim,lee2026unisim,fang2026slamformer . Together, these developments are carrying long-sequence reconstruction beyond a purely offline setting and progressively closer to the system-level concerns of SLAM. Method sec:method Map2SLAM turns streaming geometric predictions into observations that update persistent trajectory and dense-geometry states. It builds on LingBot-Map~ chen2026geometric , which first processes an initial frame set jointly with bidirectional attention for coordinate grounding and then handles later frames causally, one at a time, for online inference. We call these executions Bidirectional Prefix and Causal Continuation; together, they form a prefix-causal architecture~ dong2019unified . Map2SLAM uses Causal Continuation for live tracking and runs Bidirectional Prefix again on selected historical frames to produce fresh geometric observations for optimization. System Overview In our Map2SLAM system, Front-end tracking and Back-end re-observation run asynchronously on separate GPUs. The Frame Encoder processes each image once: the Front-end consumes its geometric features immediately, while Back-end queries reuse cached outputs from the same pass. Within each tracking window, the Front-end maintains one active Geometry Reasoner context; each Back-end geometric query starts from a fresh context. Figure~ fig:pipeline summarizes this architecture. Front-end Tracking Extending LingBot-Map's streaming context over long sequences leads to trajectory jitter. We therefore track in bounded windows and reinitialize the active Geometry Reasoner context at each boundary. This bounds the context and stabilizes local tracking, but introduces drift between windows. To initialize the first window, we process its first \(N_p\) frames as a Bidirectional Prefix, establishing the initial tracking context. For each subsequent frame, one Causal Continuation step tentatively extends the active context to form a Keyframe Probe, yielding the pose, depth, and intrinsics used to measure projective motion. Let \(k(i)\) denote the latest keyframe before frame \(I_i\). We measure the projective motion induced by the probe as where \( \) denotes a pixel coordinate in keyframe \(k(i)\); \(T_i\), \(K_i\), and \(D_i\) are the predicted camera pose, intrinsics, and depth, respectively; \( \) and \( ^ -1 \) denote perspective projection and back-projection; \( _ k(i) \) contains valid pixels of keyframe \(k(i)\); and \(T_ i k(i) =T_i^ -1 T_ k(i) \). If \(m_i> \), the front-end accepts the candidate frame as a keyframe and commits its KV cache update; otherwise, it rejects the frame and rolls back the update. When the context reaches its budget \(N_b\), accepting a frame triggers context reinitialization rather than a commit. The front-end clears the KV cache and forms the successor Bidirectional Prefix from the accepted frame and the last \(N_p-1\) keyframes. This prefix has its own similarity gauge, which we align to the existing trajectory using the replayed keyframes: their depth ratios determine the scale \(s_w\), while their poses determine the rotation \(R_w\) and translation \(t_w\). Each local prediction \(( R_i, t_i, D_i)\) in the successor context is then mapped as This alignment preserves cross-window continuity for subsequent causal outputs. For each accepted keyframe, the Front-end records its pose relative to the preceding accepted keyframe as a sequential observation. For each non-keyframe, it retains the causal pose relative to the latest keyframe for final trajectory recovery. Online Trajectory Correction combines the sequential observations with verified loop constraints to correct accumulated long-range drift. Back-end Optimization The Back-end comprises two paths with the same three stages: selection, geometric re-observation, and optimization. Online Trajectory Correction updates the trajectory while tracking continues; Dense Geometric Refinement jointly refines keyframe poses and depths after the sequence. title: SWAM: Scaling World Action Models with Cross-Modal Alignment
summary: World action models jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language. Existing studies focus primarily on architectures and training mechanisms, typically treating language-video alignment acquired through video pretraining as an established foundation. However, introducing action learning may impair this alignment. Principled guidance on data and supervision design for maintaining language-video alignment during action learning remains limited. To investigate this, we curate a pool of approximately 47,000 hours of general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. Building on this, we systematically study how language-video supervision, language-video-action supervision, and the joint use of these two forms affect WAM performance. In particular, we examine how language annotation quality affects pretrained language-video capabilities, and how action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations extends these capabilities to language-video-action modeling. To better scale the model, we further conduct detailed studies on joint training recipe and model architecture. Under a fixed training budget, mixing egocentric videos and UMI demonstrations improves control generalization. Model architecture affects how effectively these experiences are used, while scaling pretraining under the selected configuration brings further gains. The resulting recipe, post-trained on RoboTwin Clean demonstrations only, achieves success rates of 88.10% and 61.56% under Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) conditions, respectively. Our model achieves 40.00% SR across three real-world tasks, compared with 23.33% for the strongest baseline, indicating better generalization under unseen conditions. We release the curated data, training code, and model weights.
full_text: =10000 =10000 =2em Introduction Pretrained video models learn associations between language descriptions, visual content, and visual dynamics, acquiring visual and dynamics priors across scenes, objects, and interactions wu2025hunyuanvideo,wan2025wan,DBLP:conf/iclr/YangTZ00XYHZFYZ25,seedance2026seedance . These experiences provide a foundation for robots to understand manipulation goals and predict environmental changes wu2024unleashing,DBLP:conf/icml/HuGWCWZSL025 . World action models (WAMs) jointly predict video and actions conditioned on language, connecting visual changes to robot actions and providing a route from video pretraining to robot control ye2026world,li2026causal . This paper studies how to better use these priors to extend language-conditioned video modeling into generalizable action capabilities. When we introduce action prediction, the language--video capabilities acquired in video pretraining should be preserved. This requires further alignment between language, video, and action. It bridges the gap between language-described targets, visual observation, and executed actions. Existing work on WAMs largely focused on model architectures and training mechanisms yu2026openwam,sun2026ego4wam . Methods on video pretraining often treat the language--video alignment as an established foundation ye2026world,li2026causal . However, introducing action learning raises a basic question: how to preserve established language--video prior and further solve language--video--action misalignment? The roles of different experiences and forms of supervision in this process, particularly for control generalization, remain unclear yu2026openwam,sun2026ego4wam,yeom2026makes,jiang2026rethinking . To study these questions, we first construct a multisource data pool with approximately 47,000 hours, comprising approximately 11,000 hours of general videos, 11,000 hours of egocentric videos, 15,000 hours of in-house UMI demonstrations, and 10,000 hours of robot demonstrations, as shown in Figure~ . These sources provide different forms of cross-modal supervision. General and egocentric videos primarily provide language--video supervision, covering general visual dynamics and human interactions, respectively. UMI demonstrations record video and action trajectories of humans manipulating objects with handheld grippers, while robot demonstrations provide observations, states, and actions during robot task execution. Both include language descriptions corresponding to the manipulation process, supporting language--video--action learning in addition to language--video supervision. UMI demonstrations provide scalable human manipulation experience, whereas robot demonstrations provide direct but more limited robot control experience DBLP:conf/rss/ChiXPCB0TS24,zhaxizhuoma2025fastumi,fang2026robopocket . The sources differ in scene and task coverage and in the completeness of language and action supervision. Multisource pretraining therefore requires combining these experiences appropriately: language--video supervision preserves video pretraining capabilities, while human and robot action supervision establishes video--action correspondences wei2026xpace,miao2026internw0,guo2026video . Building on the constructed multisource experience, we conduct systematic studies at three levels: language--video alignment, language--video--action alignment, and joint learning. Specifically, at the language--video level, we examine how to preserve the visual prior in pretrained video generation with the design of language supervision. At the language--video--action level, we investigate how to utilize action supervision from UMI and robot demonstrations to help action prediction and robot control. In joint training, we study the data recipe and model architecture for better cross-modality modeling. The data recipe determines the coverage of the visual and interaction experience in tasks, scenes, and the proportions of different experiences. The model architecture answers how to conduct cross-modal supervision through modality interactions and language conditioning pathways, as shown in Figure~ . We further examine the benefits of scaling training with the resulting data and supervision recipe. Our study shows that preserving language--video capabilities and extending language--video--action capabilities jointly support control generalization in WAMs. Detailed manipulation descriptions and environmental cues improve language--video supervision, which maintains language--video alignment and thereby improves control generalization. And UMI demonstrations improve robot control in simulation and real scenes, proving the value of human manipulation experience with action supervision for robot learning. In joint learning, the benefits of multisource experience depend both on data and model supervision recipe. Experiments show that increasing training investment under the selected data and model recipe further improves control generalization. These findings provide empirical guidance for data collection and organization, supervision design, and joint training in WAMs. The pretraining recipe derived from these findings achieves success rates of 88.10 and 61.56 under the RoboTwin Easy (Clean-to-Clean) and Hard (Clean-to-Random) settings, respectively. Ours achieves 40.00 SR under the Hard setting across three real-world tasks, exceeding OpenWAM's 23.33 . This result indicates better generalization to unseen objects and backgrounds. 2em Related Work Action Models. World action models aim to connect visual observations with executable robot actions ye2026world . Early work treated video as a transferable visual plan or dynamic representation. UniPi first generates a language-conditioned visual plan and then recovers actions with an inverse-dynamics module DBLP:conf/nips/DuY0DN0SA23 . VPP conditions a policy on predictive representations from a video model DBLP:conf/icml/HuGWCWZSL025 . Motus, DreamZero, and LingBot-VA place visual dynamics and action prediction within unified or interactive architectures, exploring discrete tokens, latent actions, joint flow matching, and causal video--action modeling bi2026motus,ye2026world,li2026causal . Fast-WAM and InternW0- further distinguish future supervision during training from action generation at inference, showing that the prediction target and the deployment interface can be separated yuan2026fast,miao2026internw0 . VPP2 and LingBot-VA adapt video pretraining to robot manipulation by studying how manipulation data organization, temporal and video representation modeling, and action-branch adaptation can preserve video prediction capabilities while supporting action learning guo2026video,li2026causal . We build on this foundation and focus on how language--video capabilities from video pretraining can transfer to language--video--action learning and action control. Data for Robot Learning. Robot learning increasingly draws on cross-embodiment trajectories, general videos, egocentric videos, and human manipulation demonstrations rather than a single source of robot data. Open X-Embodiment, Octo, and OpenVLA aggregate and filter multi-robot data to study shared representations, observation adaptation, and action-space alignment, showing that cross-embodiment learning requires source normalization and interface alignment collaboration2023open,DBLP:conf/rss/GhoshWPBMDHK0LT24,kim2024openvla . General and egocentric videos expand coverage of scenes, objects, and interaction dynamics, but usually lack action labels directly corresponding to robot execution grauman2022ego4d,punamiya2026egoverse . EgoMimic and EgoScale study how such human experience can be transferred through view and embodiment alignment, including settings with limited robot data kareer2025egomimic,zheng2026egoscale . UMI complements these sources by using portable interfaces to record manipulation trajectories in an end-effector-like interaction format, thereby providing action supervision associated with the manipulation process DBLP:conf/rss/ChiXPCB0TS24,zhaxizhuoma2025fastumi,fang2026robopocket . EgoWAM, Ego4WAM, and Motus further demonstrate the complementary roles of video, action trajectories, semantic descriptions, and world-prediction targets li2026egowam,sun2026ego4wam,bi2026motus . The central issue in multisource learning is therefore not simply adding sources, but understanding differences in scene coverage, interaction dynamics, embodiment interfaces, and available supervision. We curate approximately 47,000 hours of multisource data. We use this pool to systematically examine how experience combinations and supervision design affect WAM pretraining. Method This section presents the world action model and its multimodal supervision. We first present the problem formulation, model architecture, and training objectives, then describe multisource experience curation and supervision construction. Pretraining uses four types of experience: general videos, egocentric videos, UMI demonstrations, and robot demonstrations. These sources differ in scene and task distributions, data quality, manipulation diversity, and available action supervision. General and egocentric videos provide language--video supervision, while UMI and robot demonstrations additionally provide state and action signals where available and valid. In Table~ tab:pretraining-inventory and Figure~ fig:pretraining-composition , we summarize the composition, scale, and video-duration distribution of the pretraining pool after data curation and cleaning. World Action Modeling Problem Formulation We consider language-conditioned robot manipulation. Given the visual observations acquired so far, a language instruction, and its current proprioceptive state, the robot predicts actions over a future interval. Let be a prediction start point sampled from a trajectory, a fixed prediction horizon, the visual history including the current observation, the language condition, and the current state. The control task requires learning an action policy conditioned on visual history, the language instruction, and the current state: where denotes the action sequence over the target interval, and denotes the model parameters. Control learning primarily supervised by observation--action pairs must jointly address scene understanding, interaction dynamics, and action generation. We adopt a world action model (WAM) based on a pretrained video model, using the associations between language descriptions and visual dynamics learned during video pretraining and learning correspondences between manipulation processes and executed actions through action supervision. The model jointly predicts video changes and actions over the same interval. The video sequence describes observable scene evolution during manipulation, while the action sequence describes the corresponding manipulation behavior. The two sequences span the same physical time interval but may use different sampling rates. We denote the joint predictive distribution of video and actions by : The final equality follows from our modeling choice that the video branch is not conditioned on the proprioceptive state. The first term learns language-conditioned video prediction, corresponding to language--video learning. The second term predicts actions from language, video information, and the current state. Together, the two terms constitute joint language--video--action learning. Starting from a pretrained video model, we train a unified WAM end to end with a joint prediction objective. The action branch uses visual dynamics and language conditioning information supplied by the video branch. Training retains the video prediction objective while introducing action supervision, aiming to continue using existing language--video modeling capabilities and to learn correspondences between manipulation processes in video and executed actions.
