title: World In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot Manipulation
comment: Project Page: https://ArcheOne-AI.github.io/RoboScript
summary: Trained action policies write manipulation skill into network weights, tying what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. In-context learning (ICL) avoids this coupling but has not matched trained policies, because a demonstration recorded in another scene carries no feedback from the world the robot currently faces. We observe that what an agent learns in context is semantic, recording task steps and object roles rather than visual appearance, so experience gathered in one world transfers to another. Based on this insight, we propose World In-Context Learning (WICL), a paradigm in which a frozen model starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world such as a simulator, and writes the feedback into its context rather than its weights. We build RoboScript, a modular infrastructure that implements WICL for agentic manipulation. From a single demonstration, RoboScript learns each task through rehearsal in simulation, freezes the learned knowledge as a Task Memory, and deploys the frozen memory on new scenes with data isolation that ensures every deployment input is available on a real robot. On all 50 tasks of RoboTwin 2.0, RoboScript reaches 83.4% mean success across clean and randomized settings with one demonstration per task and no gradient updates, exceeding the strongest trained action policy by over 20 points. The method generalizes across visual distributions, improves through reflection, scales with the foundation model, and transfers to a physical dual-arm robot through cross-embodiment memory adaptation. With a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. All code is available at https://github.com/ArcheOne-AI/RoboScript
full_text: Introduction In-context learning (ICL) is a defining capability of foundation models. A model with frozen weights adapts to a new task from what its context shows, without any gradient update brown2020language,dong2023icl . Robot manipulation has long followed a different path. The dominant approach trains an action policy, either a vision-language-action (VLA) model black2024pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,liu2024rdt,kim2024openvla,zitkovich2023rt2 or a world action model (WAM) ye2026dreamzero,chen2026flowwam , and writes manipulation skill into network weights. This approach has made clear progress, but it ties what is learned to the distribution it is learned from. FastWAM yuan2026fastwam , a widely adopted WAM trained on clean demonstrations of RoboTwin~2.0, reaches 77.8 mean success on clean scenes but drops to 1.9 under domain randomization chen2025robotwin . Every new task or distribution requires new data and new training. ICL has recently emerged as a promising alternative that avoids this coupling. Recent models can perform a new manipulation task from a single demonstration given in their context, without any weight update generalist2026gen15,skild2026s1,zhou2026zerowam . This progress raises the question we study. Can a robot learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights? The in-context route avoids this coupling, but it has not matched trained policies, because its context carries no feedback from the world. A demonstration is recorded in another scene and cannot tell the robot what will happen on the table in front of it. A frontier model (e.g.\ GPT-6 Astra) did not improve when given a demonstration from a different layout in its prompt, although some of its traces show it correcting its actions after observing their outcomes zhang2026unexpected . Code as Policies and its successors can control a robot through APIs, but without world feedback their errors accumulate liang2023codeaspolicies,huang2023voxposer,singh2023progprompt,yu2023languagerewards . Coding agents show what is missing. They learn a new repository by running code in a terminal and reading what comes back yang2024sweagent,wang2024openhands . The feedback loop they rely on has no counterpart in robot manipulation. Our key observation is that what an agent learns in context is semantic. It records object roles, task steps, and what went wrong, not the visual appearance of the world. Experience gathered in one world therefore carries over to another, as long as the two worlds agree on the semantics of the task. A cheap world that is faithful to the task, such as a simulator, a learned world model, or a latent model of the scene, is enough to learn in. Rehearsal in such a world is also safe, unlike acting directly on real hardware, where unsafe actions have damaged equipment zhang2026unexpected . We formalize this insight as World In-Context Learning (WICL), a learning paradigm that extends in-context learning with feedback from a world, as illustrated in a. A WICL learner keeps its weights frozen, starts from a demonstration, rehearses the task in a world, and distills the feedback into its context. The resulting knowledge is semantic and transfers from the rehearsal world to the deployment world without retraining. After rehearsal, the context is frozen and evaluated on instances that were never rehearsed, so the result measures generalization, not memorization. The context is readable text, which allows the agent to review its own evaluations and rewrite what it has learned, enabling recursive self-improvement (RSI) without gradient updates. The world makes every round of improvement safe. Coding agents have shown that this loop already succeeds in software engineering, where the terminal serves as the world yang2024sweagent,wang2024openhands . Now that foundation models have reached this capability, a simulator can serve the same role for a robot. We build , a modular infrastructure for agent-centric robot manipulation. b illustrates the analogy and c reports the main results. In this paper, we implement WICL on with a lifecycle that the agent carries out entirely without gradient updates. The foundation model first builds skills for a new environment on shared entry points. It then learns each task from a single demonstration and from rehearsal on training scenes, and freezes what it learns as a Task Memory. At deployment, it acts with the frozen memory on new scenes, anticipating how the task should unfold and recovering from failures. After evaluation, a reflection agent reviews the records and writes guidance for the next round, realizing RSI over several iterations. Data isolation is enforced by construction. Every acting agent, whether in rehearsal or in deployment, observes only camera images with depth and proprioception, the same inputs available on a real robot. Privileged simulator information serves only as supervision during learning, and a memory linter rejects coordinates, ground-truth terms, and seed identifiers. This strict separation ensures that what is learned in simulation is directly deployable on a physical robot. As shown in , the method, environment, embodiment, and foundation model are modular like Lego blocks. Each runs as an independent service and can be replaced, making a reusable platform for agentic manipulation. We conduct extensive experiments and present the main results on all 50 tasks of RoboTwin~2.0, leading to five findings. 1) One demonstration with rehearsal is sufficient. With one clean demonstration per task, reaches 83.4 mean success across the clean and randomized settings without gradient updates, whereas the strongest trained action policy, trained with 50 demonstrations, reaches 61.7 . 2) What is learned in context generalizes across distributions. Rehearsing only on clean scenes, maintains comparable success under domain randomization, whereas trained action policies retain at most 65.1 of their clean success. 3) Reflection improves the frozen memory. Each round of reflection rescues more episodes than it breaks on difficult tasks. 4) The framework improves with the foundation model. Without any change to code, prompts, or protocol, GPT-6.1-Sol reaches 83.6/83.2 on clean/randomized scenes, GPT-5.6-Luna reaches 79.8/76.0 , and even DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, a lightweight model, reaches 77.8/78.4 , surpassing the strongest trained action policy. 5) Task Memories transfer across embodiments. With a lightweight adapter that rewrites an existing memory for a new robot, deploys on a physical dual-arm robot without retraining or re-rehearsing. These findings jointly show that with a world in the loop, a robot can learn a manipulation task in its context as well as it learns one in its weights. Our contributions are as follows. [leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=2pt] We formulate WICL, a learning paradigm that extends in-context learning with feedback from a world. WICL decouples task skill from network weights and opens a path toward recursive self-improvement without retraining. We explain why the resulting knowledge transfers across worlds. We build a modular infrastructure for agent-centric manipulation with strict data isolation that ensures deployability on real hardware. We implement WICL on with a lifecycle covering skill building, task learning, deployment, and recursive self-improvement, all without gradient updates. We conduct extensive experiments with one demonstration per task and report results on RoboTwin~2.0, across distributions, over multiple rounds of self-improvement, with three foundation models, and on a physical dual-arm robot via cross-embodiment memory transfer, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Related Work sec:related The dominant approach to robot manipulation trains an action policy and stores skill in network weights. Vision-language-action (VLA) models learn visuomotor skills end to end from demonstrations, typically after pretraining on large cross-embodiment datasets zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025gr00t,liu2024rdt,xie2026turbovla,openxembodiment2024,khazatsky2024droid,bu2025agibot , with the VLA paradigm also advancing autonomous driving fu2025orion,fu2025minddrive,zhou2026qwendrive10initialstepvisionlanguage and benefiting from efficient 3D representations liang2024pointmamba,liang2024pointgst . World action models (WAMs) generate future observations or latent plans and derive actions from them du2023unipi,cheang2024gr2,ye2026dreamzero,kim2026cosmospolicy,wu2026vega , and driving world models jointly predict future scenes and 3D structure zhou2025hermes,zhou2026hermespp,liang2026UniFuture . Reinforcement learning optimizes a policy from simulator feedback andrychowicz2020inhand,zhao2020sim2real,li2026simplevlarl or from real-robot trials kalashnikov2018qtopt,luo2024serl,luo2025hilserl . All three families have advanced rapidly, yet they share a structural limitation. Because skill resides in weights, trained policies degrade under distribution shift chen2025robotwin,zhang2025vlaarena,gao2026ebench,zhou2025liberopro,fang2026towards , and each new task or domain requires additional data and gradient updates. WICL offers an alternative route. It keeps the weights frozen and stores what it learns in context, so a new task requires rehearsal rather than retraining. In robotics, in-context learning has mainly taken the form of imitation. One-shot and few-shot methods interpret a demonstration given at test time duan2017oneshot,finn2017oneshotvisual,james2018tecnets,vosylius2025instant,oh2025rip,fu2025icrt , while other methods pass keypoints or keyframes to a frozen model dipalo2024kat,yin2025roboprompt,palma2026bicicle or retrieve demonstrations for a trained policy sridhar2025ricl,xu2026stellavla . Recent work has shown that in-context manipulation from a single demonstration is increasingly effective generalist2026gen15,skild2026s1,zhou2026zerowam . A parallel line uses frozen models as agents. Training-free systems compose APIs, value maps, or keypoints liang2023codeaspolicies,huang2023voxposer,huang2024rekep,liu2024moka,fu2026capx , while hierarchical systems place a language model above a trained policy ahn2022saycan,huang2022innermonologue,driess2023palme,shi2025hirobot,chen2026volo,liang2026cook . Embodied harnesses add tools, verification, and memory zhang2026harnessvla,liu2026guava,huang2026roboharness,gu2026harnesswam,wang2026thea . These methods place demonstrations, instructions, or tool descriptions in the context, but none distills experience from a world into a reusable memory. Among these, HarnessVLA learns from interaction but depends on a trained policy for contact zhang2026harnessvla , and FAEA reasons iteratively within an episode but reads privileged simulator state tsui2026faea . In contrast, removes the trained policy from the loop and enforces data isolation by construction. WICL adds the missing feedback. Where ICL gives the context a demonstration, WICL also gives it outcomes from a world, and the acting agent perceives the scene through cameras only. Language model agents can improve from interaction while their weights stay frozen. Reflexion stores reflections on failed trials, Voyager grows a library of code skills, and ExpeL extracts insights from past trajectories shinn2023reflexion,wang2023voyager,zhao2024expel . Later work rewrites the context itself wang2025awm,zhang2025ace,agrawal2026gepa . Coding agents solve real software tasks through the same loop yang2024sweagent,wang2024openhands , though they learn within a single episode and do not distill experience across episodes. These methods work in text and code. WICL brings the same principle to physical manipulation, where the learned knowledge is semantic and transfers across worlds. title: Reaching Is Not Finding: Map-Anchored Visual Prompting for the Last Mile of Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
summary: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) asks a drone to find an object described in natural language. The description usually locates the object relative to named landmarks, such as streets and buildings. We observe that current navigators often bring the drone close to the target and then stop at the wrong place: they reach the target without finding it. This gap is shared by navigators of very different designs, from imitation learners to a fine-tuned 7B vision-language model. A simple test reveals the cause. When we replace the target object in the instruction with another one next to the same landmarks, no navigator goes to it, and most stop where they did before. Navigators learn to reach the landmarks, not to identify the described object. We therefore propose MAP-VP, a plug-and-play module for the last step. After any navigator stops, MAP-VP draws the landmarks named in the instruction onto the drone's current view, using the landmark outlines that the benchmark provides on a map. A fine-tuned 4B vision-language model then locates the target relative to these landmarks. The training data are generated automatically from the benchmark annotations. Neither drawing the landmarks nor fine-tuning helps much alone, but together they are highly effective. Without retraining any navigator, MAP-VP significantly improves all six navigators we test on CityNav. It roughly doubles the success rate of the two strongest trained navigators, raising HETT from 25.9% to 54.6% and FlightGPT from 24.2% to 48.9%, whereas CityNav's official detector-based last step adds less than two points to HETT.

(b) At the same stop, CityNav's official goal-selection step, which detects the target phrase with GroundingDINO, picks a look-alike. (c) , applied at the same stop, draws the map landmark onto the view and finds the target. Introduction sec:intro Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) asks a drone to find an object described in natural language, such as ``the white car parked on Staffordshire Street in front of Donegal''~ liu2023aerialvln,lee2025citynav . CityNav~ lee2025citynav is a large-scale benchmark for this task built on real city scans. An episode counts as a success only if the drone stops within 20\,m of the described object. The task is hard because a city block contains many similar objects, and the description singles out one of them mainly through its relation to named landmarks. Navigators of many designs have been proposed for CityNav, including imitation learners~ anderson2018vln,krantz2020beyond , map-based goal predictors~ lee2024citynav , two-stage transformers trained with reinforcement learning~ ding2026hett,htnav2026 , and fine-tuned vision-language models (VLMs)~ cai2025flightgpt . Yet in unseen environments their success rates remain far below that of human operators~ lee2025citynav . We begin with the example in , whose instruction asks for ``a dark red vehicle parked along Grafton Street across from a dark blue car''. HETT~ ding2026hett , a state-of-the-art two-stage navigator, comes within 8\,m of this car but does not stop there. It finally stops 23\,m away, outside the 20\,m success radius, so the episode counts as a failure ( a). Yet the car is still visible in the drone's final top-down view, which covers about 100\,m 100\,m. Detecting the phrase ``dark red vehicle'' does not help either: the view contains many cars, and CityNav's official goal-selection step, which detects this phrase with GroundingDINO, picks a red car in a nearby parking lot ( b). The navigator reached the target but did not find it. This case is typical rather than rare. In two thirds of HETT's failures on the test set, the drone stops outside the 20\,m success radius while the target is still in its final view. The same holds for more than half of the failures of FlightGPT~ cai2025flightgpt , a fine-tuned 7B VLM. To see whether this is a weakness of one particular navigator, we study six navigators of very different designs ( ). Five of them are trained navigators with publicly released code and weights, covering the main design families on CityNav: end-to-end imitation learning, map-based goal prediction, a two-stage transformer with reinforcement learning, and a fine-tuned VLM. The sixth is a training-free rule that flies straight to the landmarks named in the instruction. Weak navigators often fail simply because they never get close to the target. We therefore look only at the failures in which the target is still in the final view. For these failures, all six navigators behave alike: a recognizer applied at the last step recovers 50--60 of the failures of every navigator. The last step is therefore a common bottleneck, independent of how the drone got there. We call this shared bottleneck the reaching-is-not-finding gap. Why do navigators fail at the very last step? We first report two observations and then discuss what they imply. First, navigators learn to go to the landmarks: a training-free rule that flies to them outperforms every trained navigator we test. Second, the last step ignores what the target is. When we replace the target phrase in the instruction, for example ``building'' with ``parking lot'', HETT moves by only 4\,m although the new object lies about 40\,m away, and no other navigator reaches it either. Together, these observations suggest that two things are missing at the last step. The first is the right supervision. Navigators are trained to imitate human trajectories, to regress goal coordinates, or to collect distance-based rewards; all of these signals reward getting close, but none rewards picking out the described instance. The second is a spatial anchor. The instruction locates the target relative to landmarks (``on Staffordshire Street, in front of Donegal''), yet at the last step nothing links these phrases to the pixels of the current view. Detecting the target phrase alone does not fill this gap: CityNav's official goal-selection step with GroundingDINO~ liu2024groundingdino improves HETT by less than two points. Recent works have also noticed that the final decision is weak~ tong2026visa,xu2026sbfnav,wang2026raco . Their fixes, however, add only a few points and are built into a specific navigator. In this paper, we close the last mile with map-anchored visual prompting. Our module, , runs once after any navigator stops and draws the outlines and names of the landmarks mentioned in the instruction onto the drone's current top-down view. CityNav already provides these landmarks as OpenStreetMap polygons, so the prompt adds no new information. A 4B VLM~ qwen3vl2025 then reads the image and the instruction and outputs a box around the target, and the drone flies to its center. If the model reports that the target is not visible, the drone climbs and looks once more. In the example of c, drawing Grafton Street is enough for the model to pick the right car. We fine-tune the VLM with LoRA~ hu2022lora on examples generated automatically from the training split, using the annotated object contours as boxes, so no human labeling is needed. In terms of visual prompting~ wu2024vpsurvey , our marks are references rather than answers: they show named landmarks from a map, and the model has to infer where the target lies relative to them. Our analysis ( ) shows why such a simple module helps. The visual anchors and the recognition supervision are each of little use alone, but strong together. Without fine-tuning, the VLM treats any marked region as the answer, as reported for other open multimodal models~ cai2024vipllava,yan2024somllava . After fine-tuning, the VLM uses the marks as references and locates the target relative to the drawn landmarks, so drawing the landmarks at wrong positions misleads the model. Without retraining any navigator, improves all six navigators we study. The gain is largest for the two strongest trained navigators, whose success rates roughly double: HETT rises from 25.9 to 54.6 , and FlightGPT from 24.2 to 48.9 . In summary, our contributions are: We identify the reaching-is-not-finding gap in aerial VLN, show that the gap is shared by six navigators of different designs, and trace the gap to the navigators' reliance on landmarks rather than on the target description. We propose , a plug-and-play module that combines map-anchored visual prompts with automatically generated recognition supervision. We show large gains on all six navigators and explain the gains through controlled analyses of the anchors, the supervision, and the model's attention. Related Work sec:related Aerial vision-language navigation. AerialVLN~ liu2023aerialvln and CityNav~ lee2025citynav introduced language-guided drone navigation in large outdoor scenes. CityNav builds on the object descriptions of CityRefer~ miyanishi2023cityrefer and provides the OpenStreetMap polygons of the landmarks mentioned in each description. Trained navigators on CityNav include the map-based goal predictor (MGP) of CityNav, the history-enhanced two-stage transformer HETT~ ding2026hett , and the hybrid imitation and reinforcement learner HTNav~ htnav2026 . FlightGPT~ cai2025flightgpt fine-tunes Qwen2.5-VL on a semantic map in which the landmarks are painted as masks. Zero-shot agents build on large multimodal models, GeoNav~ xu2026geonav , CLOSER-VLN~ li2026closer , and ViSA~ tong2026visa , while SBFNav~ xu2026sbfnav keeps several goal hypotheses in a spatial belief field. Several of these works point to the final decision as a weakness. ViSA attributes failures of earlier agents to missing confirmation and verifies numbered detection candidates in three stages. SBFNav reports a large gap between its best candidate and the one its selector picks, and RACO~ wang2026raco corrects unreliable coarse goals of a reproduced HETT. On TravelUAV, See-and-Reach~ xue2026seereach studies the approach phase once the target is in view. Our work differs in three ways. We measure the gap across six navigators, we identify its cause by perturbing the instruction, and we close it with a module that does not depend on the navigator. We also note that the illustrations of ViSA overlay landmark outlines on the image. Its method, however, is built around numbered detection candidates and neither describes nor ablates this overlay. In , the map-anchored landmarks are the only prompt, and we isolate their effect. Verification and stopping in embodied navigation. Deciding where to stop is a known weakness of navigation agents. ConsistNav~ wang2026consistnav adds a training-free execution layer to object-goal navigation that suppresses stops without verification, and CLOSER-VLN verifies each action with a fine-tuned VLM. instead acts once, after the navigator has finished. It treats the last step as referring-expression comprehension in drone imagery~ sun2025refdrone , as picking out the described instance among many similar ones. Visual prompting for multimodal models. The term visual prompting covers two different ideas: learning prompt tokens~ jia2022vpt , or drawing marks on the image for the model to read~ wu2024vpsurvey . We follow the second. Marks such as red circles~ shtedritski2023redcircle , Set-of-Mark labels~ yang2023som , and coordinate grids~ lei2024scaffold work well without training on strong proprietary models. Open multimodal models, in contrast, need instruction tuning before they can read arbitrary marks~ cai2024vipllava,yan2024somllava,lin2025drawunderstand . In embodied tasks, marks usually enumerate candidate actions or targets~ nasiriany2024pivot,sathyamoorthy2024convoi , and in remote sensing, EarthMarker~ zhang2024earthmarker marks the region being asked about. In all of these works, the marked region is either the object of the question or a candidate answer. VTPrompt~ jiang2024vtprompt ,

title: FastGRT: Accelerating Training of 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing
summary: Ray Tracing enables rendering capabilities that are difficult to achieve with rasterization-based approaches such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). However, the training cost of Gaussian-based ray tracing (GRT) is much higher than that of 3DGS. In this paper, we study how ray tracing using Gaussians executes on GPUs and show that a considerable fraction of the training cost arises from how the computation is organized. We develop FastGRT, which decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses work done in the forward pass for the backward pass. FastGRT further incorporates optimizations such as fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to tackle other major bottlenecks in the training pipeline. We implement FastGRT in Vulkan. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first Vulkan-based GRT implementation that supports both training and rendering. Compared to 3DGRT, FastGRT improves training time by 1.9$\times$ to 4.97$\times$, while preserving the original rendering formulation. Our code is open source.
full_text: Ray Tracing enables rendering capabilities that are difficult to achieve with rasterization-based approaches such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). However, the training cost of Gaussian-based ray tracing (GRT) is much higher than that of 3DGS. In this paper, we study how ray tracing using Gaussians executes on GPUs and show that a considerable fraction of the training cost arises from how the computation is organized. We develop , which decouples ray traversal from blending and reuses work done in the forward pass for the backward pass. further incorporates optimizations such as fast gradient accumulation and a hybrid BVH update strategy to tackle other major bottlenecks in the training pipeline. We implement in Vulkan. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first Vulkan-based GRT implementation that supports both training and rendering. Compared to 3DGRT, improves training time by , while preserving the original rendering formulation. Our code is open sourced . Introduction Novel view synthesis (NVS) reconstructs and learns a 3D scene from a collection of observed images from certain viewpoints and render photorealistic images from previously unseen viewpoints. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233dgs (3DGS) have made this NVS highly efficient both in terms of speed and quality. 3DGS is a rasterization-based algorithm. Its efficiency comes from projecting each 3D Gaussian into screen space using geometric transformations, which maps extremely well to modern GPUs. Applications like autonomous cars require wide-angle cameras (e.g., fisheye cameras), whose lenses are prone to damage, which leads to distortion. Real cameras are often not ideal pinhole cameras; for such complex camera models, the projected 2D Gaussian no longer represents the underlying 3D Gaussian with minimal approximation, and this becomes a source of reconstruction error for complex models. Additionally, consider a camera that may observe an object only through its reflection in a mirror. Here, light from the object to the camera does not follow a straight path; instead, it is reflected by the mirror. This type of secondary light effect is difficult to represent with direct projections used by splatting. Ray tracing solves the problem from the opposite direction (Figure~ fig:raytracing ): instead of projecting every scene element onto the image plane, it launches a ray for each pixel and queries which scene elements intersect that ray. Arbitrary camera models can therefore be expressed simply by changing the ray origin and direction, while additional rays can be spawned at interactions to model reflection, refraction, and shadowing. 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing (3DGRT)~ moenneloccoz20243dgrt brings this formulation to Gaussian scenes, replacing Gaussian projections with direct evaluation of Gaussians along rays. This flexibility comes at the cost of rendering and training speed. Modern ray-tracing systems organize geometry using spatial acceleration structures like BVH (Bounding Volume Hierarchy) for efficiently finding ray--Gaussian hits. Dedicated hardware like NVIDIA RT cores, AMD ray-tracing accelerators, and Intel ray-tracing units helps accelerate BVH traversal. Despite the acceleration, computing intersection remains a major cost. Existing Gaussian ray tracing systems such as 3DGRT retrace the Gaussian hits during its backward pass, even though the forward pass has already traced each camera ray and discovered the Gaussians contributing to its pixel. However, reusing the forward-pass hits instead of re-tracing is not straightforward: the number of hits per ray is unknown in advance and varies widely across pixels and training iterations, and recording them inside the tracing kernel adds memory traffic that can slow the forward pass enough to cancel the savings. Moreover, many adjacent rays compute gradients of the same Gaussian, requiring large numbers of global atomic accumulation operations, resulting in large synchronization overhead. BVH maintenance can also be costly. A BVH represents the spatial layout of the Gaussians, but this layout continuously changes to better fit the 3D scene. Exising systems update BVH structure at each training iteration. So for large scenes containing millions of Gaussians, this maintenance becomes a considerable fraction of training time. These costs stem from how training is organized around ray traversal rather than from traversal itself, so they can be reduced without changing what 3DGRT computes. Instead of retracing rays, our forward pass keeps the hits it already discovers, and splits tracing into short rounds so that recording them does not slow it down. Instead of accumulating every gradient directly to global memory, neighboring rays that update the same Gaussian first combine their contributions on-chip. And instead of rebuilding the BVH from scratch every iteration, we refit it in place whenever the set of Gaussians is unchanged. Each of these changes preserves the Gaussians blended for every pixel, so our system follows the rendering formulation of 3DGRT exactly while training substantially faster. To study these mechanisms, we implement our method in Vulkan~ vulkan14spec . In contrast to prior OptiX-based implementations~ 10.1145/1778765.1778803 , Vulkan is cross-vendor and exposes lower-level control over hardware. In summary, we make the following contributions: [leftmargin=*] We eliminate retracing in the backward pass. With adaptive multi-round traversal, the forward pass records every hit in a coalesced per-pixel archive without capping the number of rounds per ray, so the backward pass replays these hits instead of traversing the BVH again. We reduce the two other major training costs. A fast gradient accumulator combines the gradients of rays that update the same Gaussian in on-chip memory before issuing global atomics, speeding up the backward pass by up to 10 at full resolution. A hybrid BVH update strategy refits the BVH in most iterations and rebuilds it only when the Gaussian population changes or periodically thereafter. We implement these techniques in , the first open-source Vulkan implementation of 3DGRT that supports both training and rendering. Across Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks and Temples, Deep Blending, and Zip-NeRF, trains 1.9--4.97 faster than 3DGRT while matching its rendering quality and performance. Background and Motivation sec:background This section gives an overview of the standard 3D Gaussian ray tracing (3DGRT) algorithm~ moenneloccoz20243dgrt and its training pipeline, discusses its bottlenecks, and explains the optimization challenges. 3D Gaussian Scene Primitive 3D Gaussian rendering algorithms represent a scene with a large collection of anisotropic semi-transparent Gaussian primitives (aka ellipsoids)~ kerbl20233dgs distributed in the 3D world space. Each Gaussian is parameterized by a mean position , covariance , opacity , and view-dependent color represented by spherical harmonics (SH). In practice, each Gaussian is truncated to a finite ellipsoidal extent. The covariance is parameterized as , where and determine the ellipsoid's rotation and scale. SH represents view-dependent color using 48 coefficients per Gaussian. Differentiable Gaussian Ray Tracing In this paper, we use the term Gaussian Ray Tracing (GRT) to broadly refer to approaches that optimize a Gaussian scene representation through a differentiable ray-traced renderer~ condor2025dontsplat,moenneloccoz20243dgrt,blanc2025raygauss,byrski2025raysplatsraytracingbased,poirierginter2026gray,xu2026stochastic,vit20263dgaussianacceleratedray . During training, each iteration goes through three sequential phases: forward pass, backward pass, and BVH update. In the forward pass, a ray is cast from each pixel into the scene, and the contributions of the Gaussians it intersects are blended to produce the pixel color. Testing every ray against millions of Gaussians would be prohibitively expensive, so ray tracers organize the scene in a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH): a tree of nested bounding boxes, where a ray descends only into the boxes it intersects and thereby skips most of the scene. Because rendering is differentiable, the loss against the ground-truth image is back-propagated in the backward pass to obtain gradients for each Gaussian's position, covariance, opacity, and color, which the optimizer uses to update the Gaussians. These updates move and resize Gaussians, and periodically add or remove them, so the bounding boxes stored in the BVH no longer match the scene. The BVH must therefore be updated before the next iteration can trace rays correctly. 3DGRT Pipeline and Ray Tracing Algorithm sec:3dgrt We build on 3DGRT~ moenneloccoz20243dgrt , a representative and widely used GRT method with an open-source implementation~ 3dgrutrepo . It follows a pipeline similar to that of 3DGS where, instead of splatting, it uses ray tracing for rendering the scene. BVH traversal, accelerated by the GPU's ray-tracing hardware, passes each hit (aka intersecting Gaussian) to the any-hit shader in no guaranteed order. The shader therefore maintains the nearest hits in sorted front-to-back order within the ray payload. A hit is accepted only if blending actually uses it: its contribution along the ray must exceed a minimum threshold, and the ray must not have terminated yet. After each batch, the accepted hits are blended in front-to-back order to update the pixel color. If further contribution is still required (the ray transmittance has not reached the minimum threshold), traversal restarts with the ray’s search interval starting just beyond the last hit. 3DGRT runs this entire loop of traversal, sorting, and blending inside a single ray-generation kernel, which exits only once its ray has gathered and blended all contributions. We refer to such a kernel as a megakernel, following the ray-tracing literature~ 10.1145/2492045.2492060 . Unlike the operator-fusing megakernels of ML systems, the term here only denotes that the entire per-ray loop runs in one kernel. The resulting pixel colors form the rendered image, which is then compared with the ground-truth image to compute the loss. 3DGRT stores the farthest accepted hit distance for each pixel during the forward pass. This hit distance is used to bound the retracing during the backward pass to recover the same contributing Gaussians and compute gradients for their parameters. These gradients are summed together in global memory using atomic operations, and used to update Gaussian parameters. Since these updates can modify Gaussian's location, size and shape, 3DGRT rebuilds the BVH at the end of every training iteration. Like 3DGS, 3DGRT also periodically densify, prune and reset the opacity of Gaussians at scheduled intervals during training. Where is the Bottleneck in 3DGRT Training? sec:bottleneck Figure~ fig:breakdown shows the training-time breakdown for Bonsai and Bicycle from Mip-NeRF 360~ barron2022mipnerf360unboundedantialiased . In particular, Figure~ fig:breakdown shows that for full resolution, the backward pass dominates the training time across all iterations, making it the biggest target for optimization. Even for lower (e.g., 1/2) resolution, it stays the bottleneck for some indoor scenes like Bonsai; however, for outdoor scenes such as Bicycle, at 1/4 resolution, the BVH update takes over to become the bottleneck after a few iterations. In all the workloads, the backward pass contributes considerable time and thus is a major target for our optimization. This shift in bottleneck can be explained by an increase in the Gaussian population, which we will discuss further in Opportunity 3 of sec:2.5 . Effectively, with lower resolution, BVH time increases because of an increase in the Gaussian population (refer to Table~ tab:gp ), and at the same time, the backward-pass cost decreases because fewer rays are processed, and the larger spacing between neighboring rays reduces overlap in their Gaussian contrib

title: Correctness Metric Matters: NWD-Based Calibration Loss for Tiny Person Detection in UAV Infrared Imagery
summary: Detection calibration aligns predicted confidence with empirical correctness. Existing calibration losses inherit their correctness definition from box regression, specifically IoU against a hard threshold. We show that this target is geometrically ill-posed for tiny objects in UAV infrared imagery, where persons occupy less than 0.1\% of the image. The same pixel error is penalized more heavily as the target shrinks, so binary prediction calibration (BPC) actively suppresses confidences that should be high. On HIT-UAV, BPC with an IoU target degrades image-level localization-aware ECE (LaECE) from 0.0689 to 0.0761, 0.0649 to 0.0733, and 0.0653 to 0.0682 across Low, Mid, and High signal-to-clutter ratio (SCR) groups. We replace the IoU target with a continuous, scale-invariant normalized Wasserstein distance (NWD). The NWD target reduces LaECE\(_{\mathrm{NWD}}\) relative to BPC+IoU on all three groups (\(p<10^{-7}\)) with mAP neutral (0.9356 vs.\ 0.9347), and an independent center-offset anchor confirms that the gain is a genuine geometric correction. The improvement holds across a broad plateau of calibration weights. The NWD formulation requires no inference-time mapping layer. If a validation-fitted isotonic map is applied on top of it, calibration is lowered further, and the two corrections act on different components of the same error. The metric-level remedy has a measurable boundary. Target-background thermal pairing in the training distribution and detection-level aggregation under per-image detection-count heterogeneity lie outside it. Both are quantified independently of the NWD target.

Introduction Infrared person detection from unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) operates under a narrow set of conditions. The target is extremely small, with a mean area ratio of 0.09 . The local signal-to-clutter ratio (SCR) is low, with medians between 1.2 and 2.6. The background carries strong thermal structure from pavement, vehicles, and vegetation. Under such conditions a detector's confidence is not merely a ranking score. Downstream decisions in search-and-rescue triage or surveillance alerting depend on whether a confidence of 0.8 corresponds to a correct detection eight times out of ten. Calibration of object detectors has been studied mostly on general-purpose benchmarks where targets occupy a substantial fraction of the image. The dominant training-time remedy is the binary prediction calibration (BPC) loss and its variants, which penalize the gap between predicted confidence and a binary correctness label. That label is defined by intersection over union (IoU) against a fixed threshold, typically 0.5. The definition is inherited from the regression objective and is rarely questioned. For tiny targets it does not hold. On the HIT-UAV hit benchmark we measure that among detections with IoU below 0.5 and no competing ground truth, 83.8 are judged correct by normalized Wasserstein distance (NWD). Their median center offset is 4.5 pixels against a ground-truth diagonal of 22 pixels. These detections sit visually on the target. IoU penalizes them because a two-pixel shift on a box produces a large relative overlap change. A calibration loss that labels them incorrect pushes their confidence down, and the resulting model is under-confident precisely where confidence should be high. Our prior work~ thermosc established that the pairing cost survives post-hoc temperature scaling on vehicle-mounted benchmarks. We investigate whether this cost persists in the air-to-ground regime, where targets are an order of magnitude smaller and thermal backgrounds are more prominent. To address this, we focus on the correctness metric itself. We identify target scale as the geometric root cause of the IoU limitation. The pathology propagates most visibly in low SCR backgrounds, where the absolute calibration error is highest, and NWD recovers the most there. We trace the calibration cost to two sources beyond the metric. The main contributions are as follows. We diagnose a structural flaw in the correctness target of BPC: the IoU link function lacks a size-independent floor, such that a fixed pixel displacement collapses IoU toward zero for tiny targets. On HIT-UAV, BPC with an IoU target raises LaECE above the uncalibrated model in every SCR group. This pathology manifests as the highest absolute error in the low-SCR group, the largest IoU-induced increment in the mid-SCR group, and the largest NWD recovery in the low-SCR group. We redefine the calibration target as a continuous NWD score. Relative to BPC+IoU, the NWD target lowers LaECE across all SCR groups with mAP neutral on HIT-UAV. Physical localization is restored under an independent center-offset anchor. We identify and quantify two orthogonal calibration error sources that lie outside the metric itself. Preserving target-background thermal pairing in the training distribution raises LaECE by 0.023 in the low-SCR group without degrading mAP, and a data-side diagnostic intervention (block remap) confirms that this cost persists across the 50- and 300-epoch budgets. Detection-level aggregation bias under per-image detection-count heterogeneity decomposes into between-group and within-group components. Neither source is addressed by the NWD remedy. The NWD target and post-hoc isotonic calibration are complementary. The calibration error decomposes into a geometric component that NWD reduces and a residual component that post-hoc calibration addresses, and combining the two further lowers the error. Related Work Person Detection in UAV Infrared Imagery Aerial person detection differs fundamentally from street-level scenarios since targets occupy only a few tens of pixels or fewer, falling into the tiny-object regime. A comprehensive survey on small object detection identifies the extreme scarcity of pixel-level information as the primary bottleneck, leading to insufficient feature representation and degraded detection accuracy~ apd_survey . Thermal infrared (TIR) imaging is the modality of choice under low illumination, and single-stage detectors dominate practical UAV deployments. Benchmarks such as HIT-UAV provide annotated TIR imagery across flight altitudes of 60--130\,m and view angles of -- . Recent detectors on this benchmark improve tiny-target recall through feature aggregation and scale-aware assignment~ ipedet,uniscale . These works target detection accuracy. The reliability of their confidence is not evaluated. Post-hoc calibration, such as temperature scaling, is an alternative paradigm that rescales predictions after training. We avoid this route inasmuch as our prior attribution study~ thermosc demonstrated that the calibration cost originates during training and cannot be corrected by post-hoc rescaling. The present work therefore intervenes in the training objective and evaluates calibration at the image level (Section~ sec:aggregation ). Calibration of Object Detectors Training-time calibration methods incorporate a calibration term into the detection objective. BPC defines the target as a binary indicator of IoU exceeding a threshold~ bpc . Cal-DETR introduces a calibrated detection transformer~ caldetr . The evaluation of these methods has recently been revisited.Kuzucu et al. identify structural drawbacks in the prevailing combination of D-ECE and AP, including mismatched detection sets, threshold sensitivity, and neglected false negatives. They further demonstrate that under a principled evaluation protocol, post-hoc isotonic regression outperforms Cal-DETR by more than 7 D-ECE on COCO~ eccv . This implies that train-time calibration remains meaningful only if it targets a property that post-hoc rescaling cannot recover. We target the correctness label itself; post-hoc calibration merely rescales fixed predictions, whereas a mis-specified label corrupts the training signal before any rescaling can act. Unlike vehicle-mounted scenarios where IoU remains stable, the UAV regime pushes targets into the extreme tiny-object range, creating a distinct geometric pathology where the IoU link function itself fundamentally fails. We address this root cause by formulating a scale-invariant NWD target, and further expose an aggregation bias in detection-level aggregation that distorts such degradation. Normalized Wasserstein Distance for Tiny Objects NWD models bounding boxes as two-dimensional Gaussians and measures their 2-Wasserstein distance, yielding a smooth similarity that does not collapse under small pixel shifts~ nwd . On HIT-UAV, the IoU series has been diagnosed as too sensitive to targets occupying small pixels, and NWD has been substituted for IoU in label assignment, NMS, and regression loss~ nwd_hit_uav , and utilized to stabilize bounding-box regression for infrared small targets~ eflnet . These substitutions target localization tasks, namely positive anchor assignment, NMS filtering, and regression gradient scaling. Meanwhile, using NWD as a soft assignment signal uniformly across heterogeneous target sizes can loosen supervision for larger objects and erode their localization~ coswa . Instance-level recalibration of the training signal has also been explored for small objects~ semdiff , with the calibration applied to the localization branch. Our NWD integration shifts the focus from the localization pipeline to the calibration target. Furthermore, we identify background complexity as the macroscopic manifestation that amplifies the effect of target scale (Section~ sec:nwd ). Method Problem Formulation sec:link Let be the confidence of detection and its correctness target. A train-time calibration loss takes the form with being the set of all predictions and for unmatched ones. The total objective is where is the detector's standard training loss, evaluated on the assigned anchors, and is the calibration weight. In our experiments with YOLOv8-s, comprises the classification, box regression, and distribution focal loss terms. The correctness target is a link function \(L(b_i, _i)\) on the pair of boxes. IoU, its thresholded indicator, and NWD are all instantiations of \(L\)~ dece,eccv,bpc . BPC as originally formulated in~ bpc uses a hard binary IoU indicator as the correctness target. Our formulation differs in two critical respects: (i) the target is a continuous NWD score, and (ii) NWD replaces only the correctness target in the calibration loss, leaving the assigner intact. The latter distinction is essential. Table~ tab:matching demonstrates that extending NWD into the assigner degrades detection and IoU-consistent calibration. The YOLOv8 assigner relies on a soft top-k alignment metric, not a hard IoU threshold. This allows predictions with low complete IoU (CIoU) but high classification scores to be retained as matched positives, providing the exact entry point where NWD replaces the target regardless of their CIoU value. Predictions falling outside the top-k remain unmatched with \(y_i = 0\). On the diagnostic split, 83.8 of matched positives with \( <0.5\) receive a higher NWD target, directly correcting their suppressed confidence. Fig.~ fig:link-a illustrates this shared matching and divergent target assignment. For the calibration loss (1) to remain informative on tiny targets, \(L\) must provide a size-independent floor under a fixed pixel displacement and must remain continuous across box parameters. A discontinuous \(L\) would otherwise produce a training target that jumps between discrete values. title: UltraVoxelGS: Voxel-First Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for 3D Ultrasound Reconstruction
summary: We present UltraVoxelGS, a 3D ultrasound reconstruction method that achieves both fast reconstruction and physically faithful rendering for the first time, bringing live spatial feedback during 2D ultrasound scanning within reach. This is made possible by a feed-forward design that predicts a complete Gaussian scene representation from posed ultrasound images directly, entirely bypassing the per-scene optimization bottleneck that has confined prior methods to offline use. Realising such feed-forward prediction in this setting is non-trivial: unlike natural images, ultrasound slices share at most one-dimensional intersections and exhibit view-dependent appearance due to acoustic propagation and attenuation, violating the dense overlap and photometric consistency assumed by existing feed-forward Gaussian methods. Hence, to achieve fast reconstruction, we introduce a feed-forward voxel-to-Gaussian pass that decouples representation size from input count by lifting all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support and predicting Gaussian parameters directly. For faithful rendering, we propose ultrasound-aware appearance rendering strategy factorize reflection from cumulative attenuation during training and exploit appearance continuity among spatially adjacent slices for efficient Render-time Appearance Adaptation. On both real-world and simulated datasets, UltraVoxelGS achieves best PSNR/SSIM compared with per-scene optimization baselines while reducing inference from 10-20 minutes to approximately 10 seconds (over 35 times faster) and scales to sequences exceeding 1,000 frames. Code is available at https://github.com/YuebyYue/UltraVoxelGS-camera-ready.
full_text: We present UltraVoxelGS, a 3D ultrasound reconstruction method that achieves both and physically for the first time, bringing live spatial feedback during 2D ultrasound scanning within reach. This is made possible by a feed-forward design that predicts a complete Gaussian scene representation from posed ultrasound images directly, entirely bypassing the per-scene optimization bottleneck that has confined prior methods to offline use. Hence, to achieve fast reconstruction, we introduce a that decouples representation size from input count by lifting all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support and predicting Gaussian parameters directly. For faithful rendering, we propose strategy factorize reflection from cumulative attenuation during training and exploit appearance continuity among spatially adjacent slices for efficient Render-time Appearance Adaptation. On both real-world and simulated datasets, UltraVoxelGS achieves best PSNR/SSIM compared with per-scene optimization baselines while reducing inference from 10-20 minutes to approximately 10 seconds—over 35× faster—and scales to sequences exceeding 1,000 frames. Code is available at https://github.com/YuebyYue/UltraVoxelGS-camera-ready. Introduction Despite being the most widely used diagnostic imaging modality~ fenster2001three,benacerraf2002three , ultrasound remains fundamentally limited by its 2D acquisition: sonographers scan a sequence of slices and must mentally reconstruct the underlying 3D anatomy to determine which regions remain unseen. Incomplete coverage is therefore common, especially among less experienced sonographers, and often goes unnoticed during scanning. These limitations motivate the need for real-time automatic 3D reconstruction from 2D ultrasound sequences adriaans2024trackerless,shi2026real,guo2020sensorless : during acquisition, a live 3D view can provide immediate spatial feedback to guide operators toward uncovered regions. After acquisition, a compact 3D representation also facilitates subsequent diagnosis and efficient archival. Realising this vision (Fig.~ fig:runtime_workflow_pareto ) requires both —consolidating posed 2D slices into a compact 3D representation in seconds, not minutes—and —synthesizing novel ultrasound views that respect the directional, cumulative-attenuation physics of acoustic imaging. No existing approach satisfies both requirements. Classical interpolation-based methods~ solberg2007freehand,chen2014reconstruction are computationally cheap but treat ultrasound frames as generic intensity images, ignoring the directional propagation and cumulative attenuation of acoustic waves; they reproduce plausible intensities along scanned trajectories yet produce artifacts at novel viewpoints. Neural-field methods~ yeung2021implicitvol,eid2025rapidvol,wysocki2024ultra,grutman2025implicit achieve higher fidelity by learning a continuous scene representation, yet they rely on iterative per-scene optimization coupled with expensive volume rendering, making real-time reconstruction impractical. More recently, Gaussian splatting (GS) kerbl20233d has emerged as a compelling alternative: its explicit primitives support efficient rasterization-based rendering, and recent adaptations~ eid2025ultragauss show that the formulation can accommodate ultrasound imaging assumptions. However, these 3D GS methods still reconstruct each scene through iterative optimization, meaning that they enable fast rendering but not fast reconstruction. The missing piece is not simply a faster renderer, but a feed-forward pathway from input slice sequences to a high-fidelity Gaussian representation. Feed-forward Gaussian prediction has been extensively explored in natural imaging~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,jiang2025anysplat,ye2024no,xu2025depthsplat , but those methods assume dense view overlap and photometric consistency across viewpoints (Fig.~ fig:paradigm_shift (a)). Freehand ultrasound violates both assumptions: each frame captures only a thin 2D slice of the anatomy, so any two frames share at most a one-dimensional intersection (highlighted in Fig.~ fig:paradigm_shift (c)), providing far too little overlap for dense cross-view matching; and acoustic anisotropy makes the appearance of the same tissue view-dependent, undermining photometric consistency even along that shared line. The central challenge is therefore clear: each ultrasound slice carries only a thin cross-section of the anatomy, so the information from any single frame or even a small group of frames is far too sparse to support reliable Gaussian prediction. Existing multi-view feed-forward methods partially address this by jointly processing several frames (Fig.~ fig:paradigm_shift (b)), but their computational cost scales with the number of input views, making them impractical for the thousands of slices typical in freehand ultrasound. A scalable solution must therefore decouple representation size from input count (shown in Fig.~ fig:paradigm_shift (d)): first consolidate all posed slices into a fixed-size voxel support, then predict Gaussian parameters from this unified spatial context. We instantiate this idea in UltraVoxelGS, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework that, for the first time, enables both real-time reconstruction and physically faithful rendering for 3D ultrasound. Unlike prior feed-forward GS methods that generate pixel-aligned Gaussians from individual views and aggregate them afterward, we use probe poses to lift 2D ultrasound slices into 3D space and interpolate them into a unified voxel support, consolidating sparse observations into a coherent voxel support. We then predict Gaussian parameters directly from this shared voxel support, turning reconstruction into , entirely avoiding long per-scene optimization. For rendering, a separate challenge arises from the physics of ultrasound image formation: ultrasound pixel intensity couples local reflection/scattering with cumulative attenuation, making appearance strongly direction-dependent, yet this coupling also means that slices acquired under nearby probe poses can share similar local appearance. We exploit both aspects through the proposed strategy, which decouples reflection/scattering from attenuation during training and leverages the local appearance similarity among neighboring slices for lightweight Render-time Appearance Adaptation. We demonstrate for the first time that feed-forward Gaussian splatting can match the reconstruction quality of per-scene optimization methods in ultrasound while reducing inference time from 10-20 minutes to 10 seconds, bringing 3D ultrasound reconstruction within reach of real-time clinical use. In summary, our contributions are fourfold: [leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, parsep=0pt] We propose UltraVoxelGS , the first feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework for 3D ultrasound, enabling both real-time reconstruction and physically faithful rendering. We design a feed-forward voxel-to-Gaussian pass that lifts posed slices into a unified voxel support and predicts Gaussian parameters directly, achieving real-time 3D reconstruction. We introduce ultrasound-aware appearance rendering that decouples reflection/scattering from attenuation and exploits local appearance continuity for lightweight Render-time Appearance Adaptation, providing high-fidelity rendering at sub-second latency for operator inspection. We validate on two datasets spanning diverse anatomies, matching per-scene optimization baselines in quality with over speedup and scaling to sequences exceeding frames. Related Works 3D Ultrasound Reconstruction Traditional methods depend on interpolation to aggregate images, such as kernel-based interpolation~ chen2014reconstruction to create an isotropic 3D volume. ImplicitVol~ yeung2021implicitvol,chen2024neural,song2025implicitcell and RapidVol~ eid2025rapidvol extend this interpolation from discrete representation to continuous representation. However, all of these construct an isotropic volume, violating the anisotropic property of ultrasound. The emergence of NeRF-based methods, such as Ultra-NeRF~ wysocki2024ultra,dagli2024nerf , formulate ultrasound parameters as continuous parameter field, then rendering images according to ultrasound imaging, following anisotropic property. These methods achieve high-quality synthesis, but suffer from low rendering speed coupled with dense neural field querying. As an alternative, GS methods model the scene as a set of Gaussian primitives, achieving fast rendering by rasterization. Recent methods focus on ultrasound imaging assumptions, assuming the imaging plane as a slice of the scene~ eid2025ultragauss, guo2026visually,krahenmann2025slices,kong2026gaussianpile or adopting a variable frustum projection~ yang2025ultrags . These methods render high-quality images efficiently in specific settings, but still belong to per-scene optimization. Feed-Forward 3D Reconstruction Feed-forward methods~ charatan2024pixelsplat have emerged in natural imaging. These methods predict Gaussians in a single feed-forward pass. Most existing works focus on a pixel-aligned mechanism, directly predicting per-pixel Gaussian primitives and then aggregating them. More recent extensions improve scalability through structured aggregation or voxel-aligned prediction~ jiang2025anysplat,wang2025volsplat . Similar feed-forward ideas have also been explored in projection-based medical imaging such as sparse-view CT~ liu2025x . These methods rely on stronger cross-view correspondence but each observation in ultrasound is only a thin probe-aligned slice, cross-view overlap is extremely limited, and appearance is strongly view-dependent due to acoustic anisotropy. Therefore, existing feed-forward pipelines cannot be directly applied to freehand ultrasound. Methodology Problem Reformulation Before presenting UltraVoxelGS, we formalize the mismatch between optical feed-forward GS paradigm and freehand ultrasound reconstruction. We first review the pixel-aligned feed-forward GS formulation used in natural imaging, then characterize ultrasound frames as sparse posed slice observations. This motivates a voxel-first reformulation that consolidates all slices into a coherent 3D support before predicting Gaussian primitives. Pixel-aligned mechanism. This formulation implicitly assumes that different views provide sufficiently overlapping supports and approximately view-consistent appearance, so that primitives predicted in view-specific supports can be matched, fused, and regularized. title: QCC-WM: Linking Macro-State Dynamics and Visual Generation via Quotient Causal Construction
comment: Published in Medical Image Analysis
summary:
A key challenge in action-conditioned world modeling is to construct macro-states from high-dimensional observations that support recursive prediction under actions, while keeping their predicted evolution consistent with visual changes in generated observations. We propose QCC-WM, a visual world model based on Quotient-based Causal Construction. QCC-WM uses action responses to guide macro-variable construction for recursive action-conditioned prediction. A shared reference quotient measurement constrains the consistency between predicted states and observed changes, allowing macro-level predictions to provide structured constraints for future visual generation.
  Using translational and rotational actions and their predicted responses, the model aggregates local visual features into macro-nodes with spatial correspondence through causal abstraction, and recursively predicts node content and motion under a shared reference measurement. Macro-level predictions guide future observation generation, while predicted motion transports historical appearance information. Node-level errors between generated observations and macro-level targets are then mapped back to the corresponding spatial regions for correction, improving consistency between visual generation and macro-level predictions.
  On the US-VLA dataset, QCC-WM achieves an ROI-MSE of 0.01861 for four-step prediction. Compared with the best baseline at each prediction horizon, it reduces LPIPS by 48.59%, 41.68%, and 30.23% for four-step prediction and eight- and sixteen-step recursive extrapolation, respectively. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses show that motion-guided reference transport mainly improves pixel reconstruction, while node-level error feedback further improves perceptual quality and consistency between generated observations and macro-level predictions.

Action-conditioned world models; quotient-based causal construction; macro-state prediction; motion-guided reference transport; spatial error correction; ultrasound video prediction Introduction sec:introduction Causal representation learning (CRL) aims to identify high-level variables related to the underlying generative mechanisms from high-dimensional observations, providing representations for analyzing action outcomes, intervention effects, and distribution shifts~ scholkopf2021towards . For world models, this goal further requires learned states to evolve recursively under actions while maintaining their correspondence with observable changes. However, a fundamental challenge in high-dimensional visual settings is that macro-level causal variables suitable for recursive prediction are generally not given and must be constructed from fine-grained observations. Local features can describe visual appearance and changes, but they do not necessarily form macro-states with consistent measurement definitions and predictable transition rules. Building action-conditioned world models therefore requires addressing both how macro-variables are formed and how they represent state evolution under successive actions. Research on macro-variable construction and causal abstraction offers theoretical insights into this problem. Chalupka et al. studied how macro-level cause and effect variables can be constructed from the causal behavior of micro-level measurements~ chalupka2016multi . Hoel et al. showed that, for specific systems and under the effective information measure, suitable macro-level descriptions can exhibit greater causal effectiveness than micro-level descriptions~ hoel2013quantifying . Rubenstein et al. further emphasized that causal models at different levels should yield consistent predictions under explicitly defined intervention mappings~ rubenstein2017causal . These studies suggest that micro-to-macro mappings should be designed around the mechanisms and dynamics they preserve. For world models, we therefore consider a dynamics-oriented abstraction principle: macro-variable construction should be aligned with future prediction so that abstract state changes correspond to evolution at the observation level. Existing visual world models have explored various state representations and prediction methods. DINO-WM learns action-conditioned dynamics in pretrained spatial features~ zhou2025dinowm , while IRASim incorporates action trajectories into a diffusion model to generate future observations~ zhu2025irasim . For structured modeling, SlotFormer learns recursive dynamics over object-level representations~ wu2023slotformer , and Slot-JEPA organizes prediction through semantic slots and spatial masks~ wen2026slotjepa . Motion-I2V uses predicted motion to transport reference features, connecting motion modeling with visual generation~ shi2024motioni2v . These studies provide important foundations for state prediction, structured representations, and spatially organized generation. Recursive macro-state prediction nevertheless raises several questions: whether nodes have comparable measurement definitions across time steps, whether predicted state changes are constrained by observed evolution, and whether macro-level predictions retain the correspondence needed to map them back to observation space. These questions directly affect the preservation of state meaning and the accumulation of prediction errors during recursive prediction. To address these issues, we introduce QCC (Quotient-based Causal Construction) and develop the action-conditioned world model QCC-WM. It then reads back the generated observations through the same quotient measurement, computes node-level errors relative to the macro-level targets, and maps these errors back to local latent space through the node--space correspondence. The reference quotient mapping thus connects node construction, macro-state prediction, and spatial correction, linking macro-level dynamics with future observation generation. A macro-level dynamics learning method under a fixed reference quotient measurement. We fix the reference quotient mapping and content alignment within each prediction window to provide consistent measurement definitions for macro-states across time steps. Supervision on states and their temporal increments constrains recursive content and motion prediction, encouraging consistency between macro-level predictions and observed evolution under the same reference measurement. A generation correction interface combining motion transport with readback under the same quotient measurement. We use predicted motion to transport historical appearance information, then map node-level errors obtained through readback to the generation latent space through spatial correspondence, improving consistency between future observations and macro-level predictions. title: When Does Sliced Inference Pay Off? Resolution, Tiling and Dense Fusion for Small Object Detection
summary: Sliced inference such as SAHI is the standard remedy for small objects in high-resolution imagery, but its gains are usually measured against low-resolution baselines. We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare seven dense detectors from four families on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. First, much of the benefit attributed to slicing is a resolution effect: on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms tiling with box fusion (merging decoded boxes) for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6 mAP50 at 2048 px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0 mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/scahi.

We revisit sliced inference with scale as the explicit variable and ask when tiling actually pays off. We compare seven dense detectors from four families on VisDrone and DOTA, under pre-specified hypotheses, calibration-only tuning and a single evaluation on held-out test data. Two findings emerge. Second, tiles carry complementary information that box fusion wastes. We introduce SCAHI (Slicing with Coverage-Aware Hyper Inference), which accumulates the dense outputs of all passes with weights that give every image position the same total coverage, and reads objects off a peak grid fine enough to keep crowded neighbours apart. On identical passes, SCAHI outperforms box fusion for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. On DOTA, whose images far exceed the resolution a single pass can be trained at, tiles with SCAHI beat the best single pass for every detector, by 4.3 to 5.6\,mAP50 at 2048\,px, and replacing only SAHI's merge step by SCAHI adds 2.3 to 4.0\,mAP50. An ablation attributes the gain to the border weighting and the resolution of the peak grid. Introduction Tiling a large image into overlapping slices and running the detector on each slice is routine for small objects in drone and satellite imagery~ akyon2022sahi . The reported gains are large, but they are usually measured against a full-image baseline at a low input resolution. This mixes two effects. A tile shows a part of the image at a larger scale, which helps small objects, but the same effect can be obtained by feeding the whole image at a higher resolution. On VisDrone~ zhu2022visdrone , a typical image has a long side of about 1360\,px, and a 640\,px tile at native scale shows objects at almost the same size as a full image resized to 1280\,px. We therefore treat scale as the explicit variable and compare every sliced configuration with a single pass trained and run at a matched or higher resolution. All comparisons use one evaluation code path per dataset, a calibration split for every tunable choice, hypotheses fixed before the corresponding results existed, and a single evaluation on held-out test data. We use two datasets that represent two regimes. On VisDrone, images are moderately large, and a single pass at the native resolution can be trained. On DOTA~ xia2018dota , images are several thousand pixels wide and densely populated, and training a single pass beyond 2048\,px exceeds the memory of our GPU. The answer to the title question depends on this regime. Our study makes two main contributions: An insight: resolution beats tiling with box fusion as long as the resolution can be trained. In our experiments on VisDrone, a single pass trained at a higher resolution outperforms sliced inference with box fusion for every detector that could be trained at that resolution, and at equal compute a higher resolution helps more than a larger model. A method: SCAHI. Tiles nevertheless carry complementary information, but box fusion wastes it. SCAHI, a dense fusion of detector outputs with coverage-aware weights and a peak grid that keeps crowded neighbours apart, outperforms box fusion on identical passes for every YOLO detector on both datasets and matches it for FCOS. With it, tiles beat the strongest single pass on VisDrone and, by a wide margin, on DOTA. A component ablation, a decomposition of the gain and scale analyses explain where the gains come from. Related work Sliced inference. SAHI~ akyon2022sahi,akyon2021sahisoftware popularised slicing-aided inference and fine-tuning. Follow-ups make slicing cheaper or adaptive: ASAHI~ moretti2026asahi fixes the number of slices, DAHI~ suarezramirez2026dahi and GOIS~ muzammul2025gois select dense regions, ROI-Gated SAHI~ riyadh2026roigatedsahi selectively applies sliced inference to regions identified by a lightweight object proposer, skipping background regions when foreground coverage is low, and ESOD~ liu2025esod slices at feature level. Earlier, ClusDet~ yang2019clusdet and DMNet~ li2020dmnet chose crops from cluster or density maps. These works compare against full-image baselines at a fixed, usually low, input size; matched-resolution baselines are rarely reported. Scale normalisation. SNIP~ singh2018snip and SNIPER~ singh2018sniper train only on objects within a valid size range per pyramid scale; AutoFocus~ najibi2019autofocus restricts high-resolution processing to likely regions. Merging detections. Multi-pass inference needs a merge step: NMS, Soft-NMS~ bodla2017softnms , SAHI's greedy non-maximum merging~ akyon2022sahi , or Weighted Boxes Fusion~ solovyev2021wbf . All operate on decoded boxes. Voting-based detectors such as HoughNet~ samet2020houghnet accumulate evidence for objects within a single pass; SCAHI instead merges the outputs of overlapping passes with coverage-aware weights. Weighted aggregation of overlapping windows is standard in semantic segmentation, for example Gaussian-weighted sliding windows in nnU-Net~ isensee2021nnunet . There, the aggregated map is the output. In detection, individual objects must afterwards be separated from the aggregated evidence, and, as we show, this step decides whether multi-pass inference pays off. Detectors and data. YOLOv10~ wang2024yolov10 trains a one-to-many and an NMS-free one-to-one head and uses only the latter at inference. YOLOv11~ ultralyticssoftware and YOLOv12~ tian2025yolov12 Ultralytics names these models YOLO11 and YOLO12. use a single dense head with NMS. All three predict box distributions per position as in generalised focal loss~ li2020gfl . DOTA~ xia2018dota, ding2022dota is the standard benchmark for object detection in large aerial images. Study design Datasets and metrics. On VisDrone2019-DET~ zhu2022visdrone we use the standard 10 classes and the toolkit AP@[.5:.95] with ignore regions treated as in the official toolkit, whose evaluation we ported and validated against the original. On DOTA v1.5~ ding2022dota we use horizontal boxes, all 16 classes and the official mAP50 of the DOTA devkit, again through a validated port, without a cap on detections per image. The devkit ignores objects marked difficult, which include all objects below 8\,px; a pre-specified secondary evaluation counts them as normal objects. To bound memory, the DOTA pipeline keeps at most 200 , 000 detections per image (for box fusion, per pass); on VisDrone, every method is capped at 500 detections per image, as in the toolkit. We call an object crowded if another object of the same class overlaps it with IoU , and isolated otherwise; the recall of both groups is measured at IoU 0.5. Splits. On VisDrone, a calibration split of 594 images from 30 whole video sequences is held out of the training set; we report on val and evaluated test-dev once. On DOTA, a calibration split of 141 training images is held out, and the official val split (458 images) serves as the held-out test set; its test labels are not public. All model selection and tuning use the calibration splits. Hypotheses. Before the respective results existed, we fixed three questions for both datasets, the success threshold (AP or mAP50 points) and the selection rules: (Q1) does a single pass at higher resolution beat tiling with box fusion; (Q2) does SCAHI beat box fusion on identical passes; (Q3) do tiles with SCAHI beat the strongest single pass.
